**"Do you really speak justice — you 'gods'? Do you judge the children of Adam with fairness?"**

*You gods.* Sarcastic. The judges thought of themselves as divine — above the law, untouchable. David calls them what they think they are and then asks the question they can't answer.

**"No — in your heart you work out wrongdoing. Your hands weigh out violence in the land."**

*Weigh out.* Like a merchant on a scale. They're measuring out injustice — calculating exactly how much they can get away with. Not passion. *Business.*

**"The wicked are estranged from the womb. From birth they've gone astray — speaking lies. Their venom is like the venom of a snake. Like a deaf cobra that stops its ear — that won't hear the voice of the charmer, however skilled."**

*A deaf cobra.* You can't reason with it. You can't charm it. The most skilled snake-handler in the world can't get through — because it's *chosen* not to hear. That's the corrupt judge. Not ignorant. *Deaf on purpose.*

Now — the imprecations. Here they come:

**"God — break their teeth in their mouth. Tear out the fangs of the young lions, Lord."**

*Break their teeth.* Why teeth? Because that's what a predator uses. A lion with no teeth can still roar — it just can't *kill*. David's not asking for them to be erased. He's asking for them to be *disarmed*. Take away the thing they hurt people with.

That's what every prayer against injustice is actually asking: *stop the hand. Break the teeth. Make them unable.*

**"Let them melt away like water that runs off. When he aims his arrows — let them be blunted. Like a snail that dissolves as it moves. Like a stillborn child that never saw the sun."**

Five images of *disappearing*. Water running off. Blunted arrows. A snail melting into its own trail. A stillborn. Not conquered — *gone*. As if they'd never been.

**"Before your pots feel the heat of the thorns — green or burning — He'll sweep them away."**

Thorns burn fast and hot — you use them for kindling. Before the pot even gets warm, the fire's out. The wicked judge's whole reign — over before the water boils.

Now — here's the verse people can't handle:

**"The one who does right will rejoice when he sees the vengeance. He'll wash his feet in the blood of the wicked."**

Okay. Stop. Sit with that.

*Wash his feet in the blood.* That's an ancient war image — walking through a battlefield where the enemy's fallen. It's not literal for David and it's not literal for you. It means: *the victory will be total and you'll walk through it.*

But here's why it's in the Bible: because if you've been on the wrong end of a corrupt judge — if the system that was supposed to protect you *sold* you — there's a rage in you that's *righteous*. It's not sin. It's what a human being is supposed to feel when justice is perverted. And God gave you a psalm to *pour it into* so you don't pour it into a person.

That's what the imprecatory psalms are *for*. They're not commands. They're *containers*. You bring the rage here — the full, ugly, break-their-teeth rage — and you hand it to God. And you *don't* go break anyone's teeth yourself.

Psalm 37 said *don't get heated*. Psalm 58 says *when you are heated — bring it here*. Both are true. One is the goal. The other is the release valve.

And then — the last verse. The reason the whole thing was written:

**"And people will say: 'Surely there is a reward for the one who does right. Surely there is a God who judges on the earth.'"**

*Surely there is a God who judges on the earth.* That's the payoff. Not *I got my revenge*. *There is a God — and He judges — HERE.* Not just in the afterlife. *On the earth.* The corrupt judge who thought he was a god finds out there's a real one — and the people who'd started to wonder if justice was a fairy tale find out it isn't.

So — when the system sells you: say the whole psalm. Break their teeth. Melt them like snails. Let it out — *to God*. Then walk away with your own hands clean, because the One who judges on the earth has got it.
psalms.notes: *Note on translation: v. 1 —* elem *= "O gods" or "in silence"; the vocative "gods" (ironic, of judges) fits the parallel with Ps 82:1. v. 2 —* t'falesun *= you weigh out. v. 4–5 —* peten cheresh *= deaf cobra. v. 6 —* haros shineimo *= break their teeth. v. 10 — the blood-washing image is battlefield hyperbole, not a directive (cf. Ps 68:23; Isa 63:1–6). v. 11 —* ach yesh-Elohim shoftim ba'aretz *= "surely there is a God who judges in the earth." Imprecatory psalms are prayers, not commands — the rage is directed* to *God, not enacted. No* yirah*.*

psalms.title: PSALM 59 — The Dogs Come Back at Night
psalms.body:
Saul's men are outside David's house. Right now. Waiting for dawn so they can kill him. His wife's going to lower him out a window to escape. This is what he prayed while they waited.

**"Rescue me from my enemies, my God. Set me high above the ones rising against me. Rescue me from the workers of harm. Save me from men of blood."**

Four verbs. *Rescue. Set high. Rescue. Save.* He's not being elegant. He's *repeating* — because that's what you do when men with swords are outside.

**"Look — they lie in wait for my life. Strong men gather against me — not for my rebellion, not for my missing-the-mark, Lord. For no fault of mine they run and get ready."**

*For no fault of mine.* Like Psalm 44 — innocent. He hasn't done anything. Saul's just decided he has to die.

"Wake up! Come meet me! Look! You — Lord of Armies, God of Israel — wake up to punish all the nations. Show no favor to any deceitful evildoer."

*Wake up.* Psalm 44 said it. David says it. It's *allowed*.

Now — the dogs. This is the image the psalm's built on:

**"They come back at evening. They howl like dogs. They prowl around the city."**

*They come back at evening.* Every night. The same threat, returning at the same hour. Not one attack — a *pattern*. If you've had a fear that shows up every night at the same time — the 3 a.m. dread, the evening panic — you know exactly what David means. *The dogs come back.*

"Look — they spew from their mouths. Swords are in their lips. 'Who hears?' they say."

*Who hears?* They think nobody's listening. They think the dark covers them.

**"But You, Lord — You laugh at them. You mock all the nations."**

Third time we've heard God laugh — Psalm 2, Psalm 37, now here. The men with swords outside think they're terrifying. God finds them *funny*.

**"My strength — I will watch for You. Because God is my stronghold."**

*I will watch for You.* The dogs are watching *him*. He's watching for *God*. Everyone's watching — but the direction of the watching decides everything.

**"My God of loyal-love will come to meet me. God will let me look on my enemies."**

*Come to meet me.* Not "I'll find Him." *He'll come out.* Like Psalm 21 — God coming out to where you are.

"Kill them? No — my God, don't kill them — or my people will forget. Make them wander by Your power. Bring them down, Master, our shield."

Interesting. David *doesn't* want them dead — yet. He wants them *wandering*. Alive, as a lesson. *If they just die, everyone forgets. Let them stumble around so people remember what happened to the ones who hunted the innocent.*

"For the missing-the-mark of their mouth, the words of their lips — let them be caught in their pride. For the curses and lies they tell — finish them in Your anger. Finish them — until they're gone. Let people know to the ends of the earth that God rules in Jacob."

And the dogs again — second time:

**"They come back at evening. They howl like dogs. They prowl around the city. They wander looking for food. If they're not satisfied — they growl."**

Same refrain. The threat's still there. Still nightly.

But — the last two verses:

**"But I — I will sing of Your strength. In the morning I'll shout for joy in Your loyal-love. Because You've been my stronghold — my refuge in the day of my trouble."**

*In the morning.* The dogs come at *evening*. David sings in the *morning*. They own the night. He owns the dawn. And morning always comes after evening — that's the order that never changes.

**"My strength — to You I'll sing. Because God is my stronghold — my God of loyal-love."**

*My God of loyal-love.* The last words. Not "my God of vengeance." Not "my God of power." *Loyal-love.* The men outside are men of *blood*. The One inside with him is the God of *chesed*.

So — when the dogs come back at evening, same time every night: know they're watching, and watch for Him instead. Know He's laughing. And know the morning is yours. They get the dark. You get the song.
psalms.notes: *Note on translation: v. 1 —* t'sag'veni *= set me high/inaccessible. v. 3 —* lo-fish'i v'lo-chatati *= "not [for] my transgression and not [for] my sin." v. 6, 14 —* yashuvu la'erev *= "they return at evening" — refrain;* yehemu cha-chalev *= they howl like a dog. v. 7 —* mi shomea *= "who hears?" v. 8 —* tischak-lamo *= You laugh at them (cf. Ps 2:4, 37:13). v. 11 —* al-tahargem pen-yishk'chu ami *= "do not kill them, lest my people forget." v. 16 —* la-boker *= in the morning — contrast with evening (v. 6, 14). No* yirah*.*

psalms.title: PSALM 60 — Through God We Will Do Valiantly
psalms.body:
David's winning up north and getting hit at home. The army's in one place; the disaster's in another. He can't be everywhere. That's this psalm.

**"God — You've rejected us. You've broken through our defenses. You've been angry. Restore us!"**

He starts with the accusation *and* the request in the same breath. *You did this. Fix it.* No transition. Because when you've been trusting God and you get hit, that *is* the prayer — *You — and also — please.*

**"You've shaken the land. You've split it open. Heal its cracks — because it's tottering."**

*Split it open.* An earthquake image for a national disaster. The ground itself giving way. *Heal its cracks* — not "rebuild." *Heal.* Like a wound. The land's a body and it's been cut.

**"You've shown Your people hard things. You've made us drink wine that makes us stagger."**

*Wine that makes us stagger.* The cup of judgment — Psalm 75, Jeremiah 25. God poured something, and it wasn't the river of His delights (Psalm 36). It was the cup that makes you lose your footing.

David's not pretending it was someone else's hand. *You've shown us. You've made us drink.* He puts it on God — because putting it on God is the only way to ask God to change it.

**"You've given a banner to the ones who stand in awe of You — to rally to, away from the bow."**

Here's the first shift. *A banner.* A rallying point. Something you can see across a chaotic battlefield and run toward. Even in the defeat — there's a flag. And who gets it? *The ones in awe of You.* The wonder-keepers get the flagpole.

"Save with Your right hand — and answer us."

And then — God speaks. Directly. And what He says is a *land survey*:

**"God has spoken in His holiness: 'I will exult. I will divide Shechem. I will measure out the Valley of Succoth. Gilead is Mine. Manasseh is Mine. Ephraim is the helmet of My head. Judah is My scepter. Moab is My washbasin. On Edom I'll throw My sandal. Over Philistia I'll shout in triumph.'"**

Read what God's doing. He's *walking the property*. Shechem, Succoth, Gilead, Manasseh — *Mine, Mine, Mine*. Ephraim's His *helmet*. Judah's His *scepter*. The tribes aren't just territory — they're *His gear*. He wears them.

And the enemies? Moab is the *washbasin* — the bowl you rinse your feet in. Edom gets the *sandal* — you throw your shoe on what you own. Philistia gets the *shout* — the victory cry.

*I will exult.* God's not worried. He's *celebrating*. The land David sees as split open — God sees as *His*, surveyed and assigned, down to which tribe is His hat.

That's the turn. Not "God will fix it." *God already owns it — and He's happy about it.*

Now — David's response, and it's honest:

**"Who will bring me to the fortified city? Who will lead me to Edom?"**

*Who?* He still has to *go*. God's declared ownership — but the fortified city's still standing and Edom's still hostile. Faith doesn't skip the march.

**"Haven't You rejected us, God? Don't You go out with our armies anymore?"**

Still asking. He heard the survey — and he's *still* asking. Because a promise and a present reality can both be true, and you don't have to pretend the reality away to hold the promise.

"Give us help against the enemy — because human help is worthless."

*Worthless.* The Hebrew is *shav* — empty, vain, a breath. Every ally, every alliance — *vapor*. Same word for the horse in Psalm 33. Only one help that isn't hollow.

And the last verse — the reason this psalm gets sung again as 108:

**"Through God we will do valiantly. He will tread down our enemies."**

*Through God we will do valiantly.* *We* will. Not "God will do it while we watch." *We* fight — *through* Him. Both. The march is ours. The strength is His. The valor comes from the union.

Twelve verses. *You broke us — restore us. You made us stagger — but You gave us a flag. You walked the property and said Mine — but I still have to march. Human help is vapor — through You we'll do valiantly.*

When you're winning somewhere and getting hit somewhere else: say *You did this — and please*. Look for the banner. Remember Who owns the ground. And march.
psalms.notes: *Note on translation: v. 1 —* z'nachtanu *= You have rejected/cast us off. v. 2 —* r'fah sh'vareha *= heal its fractures/breaks. v. 3 —* yayin tar'elah *= wine of staggering/reeling. v. 4 —* nes *= a banner/standard;* li-re'echa *=* yirah *= for those who stand in awe of You. v. 6–8 — divine speech; the tribes and nations as God's possessions and equipment. v. 8 —* sir rachtzi *= my washbasin;* ashlich na'ali *= I will throw My sandal — claiming ownership. v. 11 —* shav *= vain, empty, worthless. v. 12 —* na'aseh-chayil *= we will do valiantly / act with strength.*

psalms.title: PSALM 61 — From the End of the Earth
psalms.body:
**"Hear my cry, God. Listen to my prayer."**

Two verbs. No preamble. He's too far away for a long introduction.

**"From the end of the earth I call to You — when my heart is faint."**

*From the end of the earth.* He's not in Jerusalem. He's not in the temple. He's somewhere so far it feels like the edge of the map — and he's calling anyway. Distance doesn't disqualify the prayer. God's range is the whole planet.

*When my heart is faint.* The Hebrew is *ataf* — to be wrapped up, overwhelmed, to lose strength. The heart *folding*. He's not praying from a position of strength. He's praying from the fold.

**"Lead me to the rock that's higher than I am."**

*Higher than I am.* He can't climb it himself. That's the point. If he could get there on his own, he wouldn't need to be *led*. He's asking to be taken to a place that's *above his reach*. That's the only kind of rock worth standing on — one you couldn't have gotten to alone.

**"Because You've been a refuge for me — a strong tower against the enemy."**

*Have been.* Track record. He's not guessing.

**"Let me live in Your tent forever. Let me take refuge under the cover of Your wings."**

*Forever.* From the end of the earth — he's asking to *live in the tent*. Not visit. *Move in.* He's as far from the sanctuary as he's ever been and he's asking for a permanent room.

"Because You, God — You've heard my vows. You've given me the inheritance of the ones who stand in awe of Your name."

*The inheritance of the ones in awe.* Psalm 37 said *the humble inherit the land*. Here's the same inheritance — and the qualifier is *awe*. The wonder-keepers get the estate.

**"Add days to the days of the king. Let his years be for generation after generation. Let him sit enthroned before God forever. Appoint loyal-love and truth to guard him."**

*Appoint loyal-love and truth to guard him.* Like bodyguards. Not soldiers — *chesed* and *emet*. God's character, assigned to stand at the door. That's a better security detail than any army.

And the king's line stretches — *generation after generation, forever* — because David's not just praying for himself. He's praying for the throne that leads to the Messiah. He doesn't know that fully. He asks anyway, and gets more than he knew to ask for.

**"Then I'll sing to Your name forever — paying my vows day after day."**

*Day after day.* Not one big payment. A daily rhythm. The prayer from the end of the earth ends with a *schedule* — every day, sing, pay the vow, repeat.

Eight verses. Here's what they give you: *You can be at the end of the earth. Your heart can be folded in half. And you can still say — lead me to the rock higher than me. Let me live in the tent. Put loyal-love on guard duty. And I'll show up every day.*

Distance isn't the problem. Silence is. Call from wherever you are.
psalms.notes: *Note on translation: v. 2 —* miktzeh ha'aretz *= from the end/edge of the earth;* ba'atof libi *= when my heart faints/is enfeebled. v. 2 —* b'tzur-yarum mimeni *= "to a rock [that] is higher than I." v. 4 —* olamim *= forever, ages. v. 5 —* yir'ei sh'mecha *=* yirah *= those who stand in awe of Your name. v. 7 —* chesed ve'emet man *= "appoint loyal-love and truth" — as guardians. v. 8 —* yom yom *= day [by] day.*

psalms.title: PSALM 62 — Only
psalms.body:
There's a word in this psalm that shows up six times, and English usually hides it. *Ach.* It means *only*. *Alone*. *Surely*. *Nothing but.* David uses it like a hammer.

**"Only in God is my soul quiet. From Him comes my rescue."**

*Only.* Not *mostly*. Not *primarily*. *Only.* There's exactly one place the soul gets quiet, and he's naming it.

*Quiet.* The Hebrew is *dumiyah* — stillness, silence, rest. Not the absence of noise — the *presence* of calm. The soul stops running.

**"Only He is my rock and my rescue — my fortress. I will not be greatly shaken."**

*Only.* Second time. Rock. Rescue. Fortress. And then — *not greatly shaken*. Notice he says *greatly*. He might get shaken a little. He's honest. But not *greatly*. Not knocked off.

Now the enemies:

"How long will you attack a man? Will all of you murder him — like a leaning wall, a fence about to fall? **They only plan to topple him from his height.** They delight in lies. With their mouth they bless — but inside, they curse."

*Only.* Third time — but now it's the enemies' *only*. Their whole plan is one thing: *topple him*. That's it. That's all they've got. David's *only* is God. Their *only* is destruction. Two singular focuses. One of them holds.

*A leaning wall.* That's how they see him — already tipping, one push from down. They're wrong about the wall. They don't know what it's leaning *on*.

And then — David repeats verse 1, almost word for word, but he *changes one thing*:

**"Only in God be quiet, my soul — because my hope is from Him."**

Verse 1: *my soul IS quiet.* Verse 5: *BE quiet, my soul.* He went from statement to command. Because between verse 1 and verse 5, the enemies showed up, and the soul that *was* quiet started making noise. So he tells it: *quiet down. Again.*

That's how it works. You don't get quiet once. You get quiet, then the wall-pushers come, then you *tell yourself* to get quiet again. It's a practice, not a possession.

**"Only He is my rock and my rescue — my fortress. I will not be shaken."**

*Only.* Fifth time. And look — verse 2 said *not GREATLY shaken*. Verse 6 says *not shaken*. He dropped the qualifier. Between the first time and the second, he got *more* sure. The repetition tightened the grip.

**"On God rests my rescue and my glory. The rock of my strength — my refuge — is in God."**

Now — the sermon. David turns to the crowd:

**"Trust in Him at all times, you people. Pour out your heart before Him. God is a refuge for us."**

*Pour out your heart.* Like emptying a pitcher. Everything in it — out. On the ground in front of Him. Not the edited version. The whole thing.

*At all times.* Not just crisis. *All.*

**"Only a breath are the children of Adam. A lie — the sons of man. On the scales they go up — together they're lighter than a breath."**

*Only.* Sixth time. Now it's humanity — *only* breath. The Psalm 39 word, *hevel*. Vapor. Put every human on one side of the scale and they *rise* — because they weigh less than the air.

That's not despair. That's *perspective*. The people threatening you — vapor. The people you're afraid of disappointing — vapor. The crowd whose approval you want — *lighter than breath*. Only one weight on the scale that means anything.

**"Don't trust in extortion. Don't set empty hopes on robbery. If wealth increases — don't set your heart on it."**

*If wealth increases.* Not *if you steal it* — *if it comes*. Even honest money. *Don't set your heart on it.* Let it sit in your hand. Not in your chest.

And then the ending — God speaks *twice*, and David hears *two things*:

**"God has spoken once. Twice I have heard this: that strength belongs to God — and to You, Master, belongs loyal-love. Because You repay a man according to his work."**

*Strength — and loyal-love.* Both. Power that could crush you, joined to a love that won't. That's the *only* thing worth leaning the wall on.

Twelve verses. Six *onlys*. *Only in God is my soul quiet. Only He is my rock. They only want to topple me. Only in God — be quiet, soul. Only He is my rock. Only breath — all of them.* Everything else is vapor. One thing isn't.

Find your *only*. Then tell your soul to be quiet — as many times as it takes.
psalms.notes: *Note on translation: v. 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 9 —* ach *= only, alone, surely — six occurrences, the structural key. v. 1 —* dumiyah *= silence, stillness, quiet waiting. v. 2 —* lo-emot rabbah *= "I shall not be greatly moved"; v. 6 —* lo emot *= "I shall not be moved" — the qualifier drops. v. 5 —* domi *= "be still" (imperative) vs. v. 1* dumiyah *(noun). v. 8 —* shifchu l'fanav l'vavchem *= pour out before Him your heart. v. 9 —* hevel *= breath, vapor (x2). No* yirah*.*

psalms.title: PSALM 63 — Better Than Life
psalms.body:
He's in the desert. Actual desert — the Judean wilderness, where nothing grows and the ground cracks. And instead of praying *for* water, he prays *like* thirst.

**"God — You are my God. I seek You at dawn. My soul thirsts for You. My flesh longs for You — in a dry and weary land without water."**

*I seek You at dawn.* First thing. Before anything else. The Hebrew is *shachar* — the dawn itself, and the verb means to seek *early*, eagerly. He wakes up hunting.

*My flesh longs for You.* Not just the soul — the *body*. His skin wants God. That's what real thirst does — it's not an idea. It's a physical ache. He's saying his need for God is as physical as his need for water in a desert.

**"So I've seen You in the sanctuary — looking at Your strength and Your glory."**

He *remembers*. He's in the wilderness, but he's been in the temple. He knows what it looks like when God shows up. That memory is what he's drinking.

And then — the verse that's the center of everything:

**"Because Your loyal-love is better than life — my lips will praise You."**

*Better than life.* Not "better than my problems." Not "better than wealth." *Better than being alive.* If he had to choose between breathing and being loved by God — he'd pick the love. Because the love is what makes the breathing worth anything.

That's the most extreme thing a human can say about God, and David says it in a desert.

**"So I'll bless You as long as I live. In Your name I'll lift my hands."**

*Lift my hands.* Body language. Open. Reaching. Empty.

**"My soul is satisfied as with rich food. With joyful lips my mouth praises You."**

*Rich food.* The Hebrew is *chelev v'deshen* — fat and marrow. The best cuts. He's in a *desert* — starving — and he says his soul is *full of fat and marrow*. Because he found the thing that feeds deeper than food.

**"When I remember You on my bed — through the night watches I meditate on You."**

*On my bed. Night watches.* Can't sleep. Lying there in the dark. And instead of spiraling — he *meditates*. Turns God over in his mind. The insomnia becomes a prayer session.

If you're up at 3 a.m. — here's what to do with it.

**"Because You've been my help — in the shadow of Your wings I sing for joy."**

Wings again. Psalm 17, 36, 57, 61. He keeps going back under the feathers.

**"My soul clings to You. Your right hand holds me up."**

*Clings.* The Hebrew is *davak* — the word for how a husband and wife become one flesh in Genesis 2. *Glued.* Stuck fast. Won't let go.

*Your right hand holds me up.* And here's the thing — he's clinging, *and* God's holding. Both. It's not that David's grip is what saves him. It's that David's grip meets God's grip. Two hands. One holds tight; one holds *up*.

Now the enemies — briefly:

"The ones seeking to destroy my life will go down to the depths of the earth. They'll be given to the sword. They'll be food for jackals."

**"But the king will rejoice in God. Everyone who swears by Him will celebrate. The mouth of liars will be shut."**

*The mouth of liars — shut.* Silence for the ones who spoke against him. Song for the one who thirsted.

Eleven verses. Here's the shape: *I'm in the desert. I'm thirsty for You the way my body's thirsty for water. Your love is better than being alive. My soul is full of fat and marrow. I can't sleep so I think about You. I'm clinging; You're holding. The liars go quiet.*

Better than life. Say it in your desert. Then see what it does to the thirst.
psalms.notes: *Note on translation: v. 1 —* ashachareka *= I seek You at dawn / eagerly. v. 1 —* kamah l'cha v'sari *= my flesh longs/faints for You — physical yearning. v. 3 —* ki-tov chasd'cha me-chayim *= "for Your loyal-love is better than life." v. 5 —* chelev va-deshen *= fat and fatness — the choicest food. v. 8 —* davkah nafshi acharecha *= my soul clings after You —* davak*, Gen 2:24;* tamchah *= holds/supports. No* yirah*.*

psalms.title: PSALM 64 — The Secret Arrows
psalms.body:
**"Hear my voice, God, in my complaint. Guard my life from the dread of the enemy."**

*The dread of the enemy.* Not just the enemy — the *dread*. The fear itself is the thing he wants guarding from. Because sometimes the fear of the attack does more damage than the attack.

**"Hide me from the secret plots of the wicked — from the mob of workers of harm."**

*Secret plots.* The Hebrew is *sod* — the same word Psalm 25 used for God's *intimate counsel*, the secret He shares with those in awe. Here it's the enemies' *sod* — their private conspiracy, their back room. Two secret councils. One is a Father telling His kids the plan. The other is a gang deciding who to hurt.

**"They've sharpened their tongue like a sword. They've aimed their arrow — a bitter word — to shoot from hiding at the blameless. Suddenly they shoot — and don't fear."**

*A bitter word — as an arrow.* Words as projectiles. Fired from cover. You never see the archer. You just feel the hit — the rumor, the review, the anonymous complaint, the thing said in a room you weren't in.

*From hiding.* That's the tell. Honest opponents face you. These ones need the bushes.

*And don't fear.* No awe. No sense that anyone's watching. They think the hiding place is *complete* — that if the target can't see them, nobody can.

**"They strengthen themselves in an evil plan. They talk about laying snares in secret. They say: 'Who will see them?'"**

*Who will see?* Same question as Psalm 59 — *who hears?* It's the working assumption of every hidden attack: *nobody's watching.*

**"They search out wrongdoing. They've finished a careful search. The inside of man — the heart — is deep."**

*The heart is deep.* Even David admits it. What's inside a person goes down further than anyone can see. The schemers think that depth is their protection — nobody can find the bottom of what they're planning.

But — verse 7:

**"But God will shoot them with an arrow. Suddenly — they're wounded."**

*Suddenly.* Same word they used. They shot *suddenly* from hiding. God shoots *suddenly* from heaven. The one who thought he was the archer finds out he's the target — and the shot comes from the one direction he wasn't covering.

**"He'll make them stumble — their own tongue against them. Everyone who sees them will shake their heads."**

*Their own tongue against them.* The weapon turns around. The bitter word they fired comes back with their name on it. The rumor gets traced. The anonymous thing gets un-anonymized. And the people who watched — *shake their heads*. Not at the victim. At the archer.

**"Then all people will be in awe. They'll declare the work of God. They'll understand what He's done."**

*In awe.* Here's the *yirah* — and look where it lands. Not on the wicked. On *everyone who watched*. When the hidden archer gets hit by the arrow nobody saw coming — the whole crowd goes quiet and says *God did that.* The wonder spreads.

**"The one who does right will rejoice in the Lord and take refuge in Him. All the upright in heart will glory."**

*Take refuge.* The blameless man was *hiding* too — from the arrows. But he was hiding in the *right place*. Two hiders. One in the bushes, one under the wings. Only one of them stays hidden.

Ten verses. Here's the shape: *They sharpen the tongue. They aim the word. They shoot from hiding and say who'll see. But the heart is deep — and God sees the bottom. He shoots back. Their own tongue turns on them. Everyone watching stands in awe. And the one who took refuge in the right place — glories.*

When the arrows come from somewhere you can't see: don't go looking for the archer. Get under the wings. God's got the return shot.
psalms.notes: *Note on translation: v. 1 —* mi-pachad oyev *= from the dread of the enemy —* pachad*, human terror. v. 2 —* sod m're'im *= the secret council of evildoers — same word as Ps 25:14 (God's* sod*). v. 4 —* pit'om yoruhu v'lo yira'u *= "suddenly they shoot him and do not fear" — no reverence. v. 5 —* mi yir'eh-lamo *= "who will see them?" v. 7 —* pit'om *= suddenly — deliberate echo of v. 4. v. 9 —* va-yir'u kol-adam *=* yirah *= "and all people will stand in awe" — reverent astonishment at divine justice.*

psalms.title: PSALM 65 — You Crown the Year
psalms.body:
After eight psalms of enemies, arrows, betrayals, and deserts — this one's a *harvest*. Rain on the fields. Grain in the valleys. The book breathes out.

**"Silence is praise to You, God, in Zion. To You the vow is paid."**

*Silence is praise.* The Hebrew is *dumiyah* — the Psalm 62 word. Sometimes the highest thing you can say to God is *nothing*. Standing in the temple, full, quiet. The silence itself is the offering.

**"You who hear prayer — to You all flesh will come."**

*All flesh.* Everyone. Not the qualified. The ones who need to eat.

**"When wrongdoing overwhelmed us — our rebellions — You covered them."**

*Covered them.* Psalm 32. He does the covering when you stop.

**"Happy is the one You choose and bring near — to live in Your courts. We'll be satisfied with the goodness of Your house — Your holy temple."**

*You choose and bring near.* God does the choosing. God does the bringing. You're not the one who got yourself into the courtyard.

Now — God's power, and it goes from mountains to oceans to *everyone*:

**"By awesome deeds in right-standing You answer us — God of our rescue — the confidence of all the ends of the earth and the farthest seas."**

*The confidence of all the ends of the earth.* Not just Israel's God. The One that people on the far side of the ocean — who've never heard His name — are *leaning on* without knowing it. Every sunrise they count on. Every rain they need. *His.*

"You set the mountains in place by Your strength — girded with power. You still the roaring of the seas — the roaring of their waves — **and the tumult of the peoples.**"

*The tumult of the peoples.* He puts it right next to the roaring seas. Nations in an uproar — same category as waves. He *stills* both. Same verb.

**"The ones who live at the ends of the earth stand in awe of Your signs. You make the going out of the morning and the evening shout for joy."**

*The morning and the evening shout for joy.* Dawn and dusk — *singing*. Twice a day the sky does a thing that makes people at the ends of the earth gasp. He set that up. On purpose. It's His signature, twice daily, for everyone.

Now — the rain. And this is where the psalm goes soft and green:

**"You visit the earth and water it. You enrich it greatly. The river of God is full of water. You provide their grain — because that's how You've prepared it."**

*You visit the earth.* Like a landlord checking on the property — but a good one. Bringing water. Making sure everyone has grain.

**"You drench its furrows. You level its ridges. You soften it with showers. You bless its growth."**

Four verbs about *dirt*. Drench, level, soften, bless. God with His hands in the soil. This isn't the God of Psalm 29 shattering cedars. This is God who *gardens*.

And then — the line:

**"You crown the year with Your goodness. Your wagon tracks overflow with fatness."**

*You crown the year.* Like a king gets crowned. The year — this year, whatever it's been — gets a *crown* put on it. Not because it earned one. Because that's what He does at the end of the season.

*Your wagon tracks overflow.* Picture God driving a cart across the land — and it's so loaded that it's *spilling*. Fatness pouring out the sides, into the ruts, onto the ground. He's not carefully rationing. He's *dripping*.

**"The pastures of the wilderness overflow. The hills wrap themselves in joy."**

*The wilderness.* Psalm 63's desert — where David thirsted — *overflows*. The dry land gets its turn.

*The hills wrap themselves in joy.* Like putting on a coat. The landscape gets dressed in gladness.

**"The meadows clothe themselves with flocks. The valleys cover themselves with grain. They shout for joy — yes, they sing!"**

*They sing.* The fields. The valleys. The whole earth breaking into a chorus because it's *full*. Psalm 19 said the heavens declare. Psalm 65 says the *ground* sings.

Thirteen verses. Here's the shape: *Silence is praise. You hear. You cover. You bring near. You still the seas and the nations. The morning and evening shout. You visit the earth and get Your hands dirty. You crown the year. Your wagon spills. The desert overflows. The hills put on joy. The valleys sing.*

After the arrows and the caves — go outside. Look at something green. He crowned the year. His wagon's leaking. The hills are wearing joy.

Be quiet. That's praise too.
psalms.notes: *Note on translation: v. 1 —* l'cha dumiyah t'hillah *= "to You silence [is] praise" — some read "praise awaits You"; the stillness reading is primary. v. 5 —* nora'ot *= awesome deeds — from* yirah*. v. 8 —* va-yir'u *=* yirah *= stand in awe (at Your signs). v. 9 —* pakadta *= You visit/attend to. v. 11 —* itarta sh'nat tuvatecha *= "You crown the year of Your goodness";* ma'galecha yir'afun dashen *= Your tracks/ruts drip fatness. v. 12 —* gil tachgornah *= gird themselves with joy. v. 13 —* yitro'a'u af-yashiru *= they shout, yes they sing.*

psalms.title: PSALM 66 — Come and Hear What He Did for Me
psalms.body:
This psalm zooms in. It starts with the planet and ends with one guy saying *let me tell you what happened to me.*

**"Shout for joy to God, all the earth! Sing the glory of His name! Make His praise glorious!"**

*All the earth.* Widest possible lens. Every continent.

**"Say to God: 'How awesome are Your deeds! Through the greatness of Your power Your enemies cringe before You. All the earth bows to You. They sing to You. They sing to Your name.'"**

*Awesome.* There's *nora* — the *yirah* word. Awe-inspiring. Jaw-dropping. Not "terrible." The whole earth isn't cowering — it's *singing*.

Now — the invitation, and it comes twice in this psalm with a different object each time:

**"Come and see the works of God. His deeds toward the children of Adam are awesome."**

*Come and see.* First invitation. *Look at what He did.*

"He turned the sea into dry land. They crossed the river on foot. There — we rejoiced in Him."

*There — we rejoiced.* The Exodus. The Jordan. He's saying *we* — as if he was there. Because in the memory of Israel, everybody was there. Every generation crossed on dry ground. Your story includes the rescues you didn't personally witness.

**"He rules by His might forever. His eyes watch the nations. Don't let the rebels exalt themselves."**

Now — the hard part. And it's honest:

**"Bless our God, you peoples. Let the sound of His praise be heard. Because You've tested us, God. You refined us like silver.**
**You brought us into the net. You laid a heavy load on our backs. You let men ride over our heads. We went through fire and through water —**
**and You brought us out into abundance."**

Read the sequence. *Tested. Refined. Net. Heavy load. Men riding over our heads. Fire. Water.* That's not one bad thing — it's *seven*. And every one has *You* in front of it. *You* brought us into the net. *You* laid the load.

He's not blaming God to complain. He's crediting God for the *whole* arc — because if God's in the net, God's also in the exit. *And You brought us out into abundance.* The Hebrew is *r'vayah* — overflow, saturation. Psalm 23's *cup runs over*.

Through fire and water — to overflow. That's the route. There isn't a shortcut around the fire.

**"I'll come into Your house with burnt offerings. I'll pay You my vows — the ones my lips spoke and my mouth promised when I was in trouble."**

*When I was in trouble.* You know the prayer. *God, if You get me out of this, I'll —*. He's here to pay it. The bargain from the foxhole gets honored in the temple.

And now — the zoom. From all the earth, to the people, to *one man*:

**"Come and hear — all you who stand in awe of God — and I'll tell you what He did for my soul."**

*Come and hear.* Second invitation. First was *come and see* the works of God. Now it's *come and hear* what He did *for me*.

*For my soul.* Not for the nation. Not for history. *Mine.* He's got a personal story and he wants an audience.

**"I cried to Him with my mouth. Praise was on my tongue."**

*Cried — and praised.* Both, at once. Same mouth. The plea and the thanks in the same breath — because he'd already decided how it would end.

**"If I'd held wrongdoing in my heart — the Master wouldn't have listened."**

He checked. Psalm 26 again — *test me*. He did the inventory before he prayed.

**"But God HAS listened. He paid attention to the voice of my prayer."**

*Has.* Done. Past tense. He's not hoping. He's *reporting*.

**"Blessed be God — who has not turned away my prayer, or His loyal-love from me."**

*Not turned away my prayer or His loyal-love.* Two things He didn't remove. The prayer got through. The love stayed put.

Twenty verses. Here's the shape: *All the earth — shout. Come see what He did in history. He put us through fire and water and brought us to overflow. I made a promise in the foxhole and I'm here to pay it. Now — come here, close — let me tell you what He did for ME.*

Your testimony isn't a footnote to the big story. It's the *zoom*. The place where all the earth's praise gets a face. Tell it. *Come and hear.*
psalms.notes: *Note on translation: v. 3 —* mah-nora *=* yirah *= how awesome (KJV "terrible"). v. 5 —* nora alilah *= awesome in deed. v. 10 —* tz'raftanu *= You refined us. v. 12 —* la-r'vayah *= to abundance/saturation/overflow. v. 16 —* kol-yir'ei Elohim *=* yirah *= all who stand in awe of God. v. 19 —* ach shama Elohim *= "surely God has heard" — perfect tense. v. 20 —* lo-hesir *= has not removed/turned away.*

psalms.title: PSALM 67 — Let Your Face Shine on Us — So That
psalms.body:
Short one. But it's got the biggest *so that* in the Psalms.

**"May God be gracious to us and bless us. May He make His face shine on us."**

That's the priestly blessing — Numbers 6. *The Lord bless you and keep you. The Lord make His face shine on you.* Every Israelite knew it. Every kid had it said over them.

But watch what the psalmist does with it. He adds two words:

**"— so that Your way may be known on the earth. Your rescue among all the nations."**

*So that.* The blessing isn't the endpoint. It's the *means*. *Bless us — so that they'll see.* The face shining on Israel is a *floodlight* — pointed at them so the rest of the world can see what God looks like.

That changes everything about how you ask for blessing. Not *bless me because I want it*. *Bless me — so that the people watching my life see You.*

**"Let the peoples thank You, God. Let ALL the peoples thank You."**

*All.* Every nation. The Korahites, the Asaphites, David — they keep saying it. Book Two of the Psalms is *relentless* about the nations. This wasn't supposed to be a private club.

**"Let the nations be glad and shout for joy — because You judge the peoples fairly. You guide the nations on the earth."**

*Judge fairly. Guide the nations.* Not "conquer." Not "punish." *Judge fairly* — so the ones who've never had a fair judge finally get one. *Guide* — the shepherd word. God shepherding *Egypt*. God shepherding *Babylon*. That's the vision.

**"Let the peoples thank You, God. Let ALL the peoples thank You."**

Refrain. Second time. Because he means it.

**"The earth has given its harvest. God — our God — blesses us."**

*The earth has given its harvest.* Psalm 65 again — the grain's in. The wagon spilled. And here's the connection: the *physical* blessing — food on the table — is *evidence*. When the nations see a people who are *fed*, who are *blessed*, whose God's face is *shining* on them — that's the sermon. Not the words. The *harvest*.

**"God blesses us — so that all the ends of the earth may stand in awe of Him."**

And there it is again. *So that.* The second one. Bookends. *Bless us so that Your way is known. Bless us so that the ends of the earth stand in awe.*

*Stand in awe.* *Yirah*. Not "fear Him." Not "cower before Him." *Be amazed by Him.* The whole point of God blessing His people is so the *far edges of the map* look up and go *wow*.

Seven verses. Two *so thats*. Here's the shape: *Shine on us — SO THAT they see. Let ALL the peoples thank You. You judge fairly. You shepherd nations. The harvest came in. Bless us — SO THAT the ends of the earth stand amazed.*

Here's what to do with it: next time you ask God for something — the raise, the healing, the house — add the two words. *So that.* Finish the sentence. *Bless me so that ____.* If you can't finish it — you might be asking for a floodlight to point at yourself.

He shines on you so *they* can see Him. That's the deal. It's a good one.
psalms.notes: *Note on translation: v. 1 — echoes Numbers 6:24–26 (the Aaronic blessing). v. 2 —* lada'at ba'aretz darkecha *= "that Your way may be known in the earth" — purpose clause. v. 4 —* tanchem *= You guide/lead (shepherding verb). v. 3, 5 — refrain:* yoducha amim Elohim, yoducha amim kulam*. v. 7 —* v'yir'u oto kol-afsei-aretz *=* yirah *= "and all the ends of the earth will stand in awe of Him" — second purpose clause, bookend with v. 2.*

psalms.title: PSALM 68 — Father of the Fatherless
psalms.body:
This is a *march*. God moving out — through the wilderness, through battle, up the mountain, into the sanctuary. Thirty-five verses of motion. Don't try to hold it all. Catch the moments.

**"Let God rise up! Let His enemies scatter! Let the ones who hate Him flee from His face!"**

These are Moses' words — Numbers 10:35, what he said every time the Ark moved out: *Rise up, Lord! Let Your enemies scatter!* The psalm opens with the marching orders.

"Like smoke is driven away — drive them away. Like wax melts before fire — let the wicked perish before God. **But let the ones who do right be glad. Let them exult before God. Let them rejoice with gladness.**"

Smoke and wax for the enemies. *Glad, exult, rejoice* — three words — for the righteous. The parade's got two kinds of people watching, and they're having very different days.

**"Sing to God! Sing praises to His name! Lift up a song to the One who rides through the deserts — the Lord is His name — and exult before Him!"**

*Rides through the deserts.* Not enthroned in a palace. *Riding.* Through the dry places. Where His people are.

And then — the verse. The one that defines the whole march:

**"Father of the fatherless. Defender of widows. God — in His holy dwelling."**

*Father of the fatherless.* Stop. This is God who rides through deserts and scatters enemies like smoke — and the *first title* He takes in this psalm is *Father to the kid with no dad.* Not King. Not Warrior. *Father of orphans.*

If your father wasn't there — if he left, or died, or was there and shouldn't have been — this is your verse. The One with the whole army behind Him stops and says *I'm yours.* Psalm 27 said *even if my father and mother abandon me, He'll gather me in.* Psalm 68 says who does the gathering.

*Defender of widows.* The woman with no man to stand for her in court — He stands.

**"God sets the lonely in families. He brings out prisoners into prosperity. But the rebellious live in a parched land."**

*Sets the lonely in families.* The Hebrew is *yechidim* — the solitary ones, the *onlys*. Psalm 25's word — *I am alone*. God takes the *only* and puts him at a *table*. Gives him a home he didn't have. That's what He does with the parade — He picks up the ones standing alone on the sidewalk and puts them in the march.

Now — the history, fast:

"God — when You went out before Your people, when You marched through the wilderness — the earth shook. The heavens poured — before God, the One of Sinai. Before God, the God of Israel."

Sinai. The mountain smoking. The ground shaking.

**"You sent abundant rain, God. When Your inheritance was weary — You restored it. Your people settled in it. In Your goodness, God, You provided for the poor."**

*When Your inheritance was weary.* Tired people. Worn-out land. And He *rained*. That's the answer to weariness in this psalm — not a lecture. *Rain.*

Then a battle — kings scattering, women dividing the spoil, "the wings of a dove covered with silver" — the war's over so fast the plunder's already being sorted.

**"The mountain of God is a mighty mountain. Why do you look with envy, you many-peaked mountains? This is the mountain God desired for His dwelling. Yes — the Lord will live there forever."**

The other mountains are *jealous*. Bashan, Hermon — bigger, higher. And God picked *Zion* — a modest hill. Because He doesn't choose by size. He chooses by *desire*. *This is the one I want.*

**"The chariots of God are tens of thousands — thousands upon thousands. The Master is among them. Sinai is in the sanctuary."**

*Sinai is in the sanctuary.* The mountain moved. What happened at Sinai — the fire, the voice, the presence — it's *in Jerusalem now*. The whole terrifying power of the wilderness mountain — living in a building in the city.

**"You ascended on high. You led captives in Your train. You received gifts from among men — even from the rebellious — so that You, Lord God, might dwell there."**

Paul quotes this in Ephesians 4:8 — about Christ ascending and giving gifts. *Even from the rebellious.* The ones who fought Him end up in the parade — not as prisoners. As *gift-bearers*.

**"Blessed be the Master — day by day He carries our load. God is our rescue."**

*Day by day He carries our load.* The Hebrew is *ya'amas lanu* — He loads Himself up for us. Like a pack animal. Every day, He picks up the weight. God with tens of thousands of chariots — *carrying your bags*.

**"Our God is a God of rescues. To the Lord — the Master — belong the exits from death."**

*The exits from death.* The Hebrew is *totza'ot* — the ways out. Death has *exits* — and He holds the keys to every one.

Then a flash of the imprecatory — enemies' heads shattered, blood, dogs — the war psalm hasn't forgotten it's a war psalm.

**"They've seen Your procession, God — the procession of my God, my King, into the sanctuary. Singers in front. Musicians behind. Between them — young women playing tambourines."**

*Here's* the parade. Singers first. Then the girls with tambourines. Then the band. It's *loud*. It's *joyful*. It's a *party moving up a hill*.

"Bless God in the great assembly! Bless the Lord, you descendants of Israel! There's little Benjamin — leading them. The princes of Judah in their crowd. The princes of Zebulun. The princes of Naphtali."

*Little Benjamin — leading.* The smallest tribe, up front. Because in God's parade, the small ones lead.

**"Summon Your power, God. Show Your strength, God — as You've done for us before."**

Now — the nations:

"From Your temple above Jerusalem — kings bring You gifts. Rebuke the beast in the reeds — the herd of bulls among the calves of the peoples. Let them come humbled, bringing silver. Scatter the nations that delight in war. **Envoys will come from Egypt. Cush will hurry to stretch out its hands to God."**

*Egypt.* The old enemy. The oppressor. *Bringing gifts.* *Cush* — Ethiopia, the far south — *hurrying* to reach out. The parade doesn't end at Zion's gate. It picks up *the whole world* on the way.

**"Sing to God, kingdoms of the earth! Sing praise to the Master! To the One who rides in the ancient heavens — listen — He sends out His voice, a mighty voice."**

**"Ascribe power to God! Over Israel is His majesty. His power is in the skies. You are awesome, God, from Your sanctuary. The God of Israel gives power and strength to His people.**
**Blessed be God!"**

*Awesome.* The last *yirah* in the psalm. Not "terrible." *Awesome.* The one you look at from the sidewalk as the parade goes by, tambourines and chariots and little Benjamin up front, and you can't say anything but *wow*.

Thirty-five verses. Here's what to carry: *He rides through the deserts. He's Father to the fatherless. He puts the lonely at a table. He rains on the weary. He carries your load day by day. He holds the exits from death. And the parade picks up Egypt on the way home.*

You're not on the sidewalk. Get in the march.
psalms.notes: *Note on translation: v. 1 — echoes Numbers 10:35. v. 4 —* rochev ba'aravot *= "rider through the deserts/steppes" (some read "clouds"). v. 5 —* avi y'tomim *= father of orphans;* dayan almanot *= judge/defender of widows. v. 6 —* yechidim *= the solitary/lonely ones. v. 18 — Ephesians 4:8 quotes this. v. 19 —* ya'amas-lanu *= "He loads [Himself] for us" / bears our burden. v. 20 —* totza'ot la-mavet *= "exits/escapes from death." v. 27 —* Binyamin tza'ir *= little/young Benjamin. v. 35 —* nora Elohim *=* yirah *= "awesome [is] God" — KJV "terrible."*

psalms.title: PSALM 69 — The Waters Have Come Up to My Neck
psalms.body:
Psalm 68 was the parade. Psalm 69 is the man drowning while the parade goes by.

**"Save me, God — because the waters have come up to my neck."**

*To my neck.* One more inch. He's not describing a hard time. He's describing the last breath before the water covers the mouth.

**"I'm sinking in deep mud — there's nowhere to stand. I've come into deep water. The flood sweeps over me."**

Psalm 40's mud — but this time he's not out of it yet. *Nowhere to stand.* The feet reach down and find nothing.

**"I'm worn out from calling. My throat is dry. My eyes fail — from waiting for my God."**

*My throat is dry* — from *praying*. He's prayed himself hoarse. *Eyes fail from waiting.* You can wear your eyes out looking for someone who isn't showing up.

**"The ones who hate me for no reason outnumber the hairs on my head. My enemies are mighty — the ones destroying me with lies. What I didn't steal — I have to return."**

*Hate me for no reason.* John 15:25 — Jesus quotes this. *They hated Me without cause.* And *what I didn't steal, I have to return* — paying for a crime you didn't commit. That's the whole crucifixion in one line.

**"God — You know my foolishness. My guilt isn't hidden from You."**

He's not perfect. He says so. Which makes the *hated without cause* land harder — he has real faults, and they're still attacking him for the *fake* ones.

**"Don't let the ones who wait for You be ashamed because of me, Master — Lord of Armies. Don't let the ones who seek You be disgraced because of me, God of Israel."**

Look at this. He's drowning — and he's worried about *other people's faith*. *If I go down, will they stop believing?* The man at his lowest is thinking about the ones watching.

**"Because for Your sake I've carried reproach. Shame covers my face. I've become a stranger to my brothers — a foreigner to my mother's sons."**

*A stranger to my mother's sons.* His own family doesn't claim him. John 7:5 — *even His brothers did not believe in Him.*

And then — the verse:

**"Because zeal for Your house has eaten me up. The insults aimed at You have fallen on me."**

*Zeal for Your house has eaten me up.* John 2:17 — when Jesus flipped the tables in the temple, the disciples remembered *this line*. The passion for God's house *consumed* Him. It's not a hobby. It *eats* you.

*The insults aimed at You have fallen on me.* He's standing where God stands, so what's thrown at God hits him. That's what it costs to represent Someone people hate.

"When I wept and fasted — it became a reproach against me. When I wore sackcloth — I became a proverb to them. The ones sitting at the gate talk about me. I'm the song of the drunks."

*The song of the drunks.* He's a *joke* in the bar. They've got a tune about him.

**"But I — my prayer is to You, Lord. In the time of Your favor, God — in the abundance of Your loyal-love — answer me with Your faithful rescue."**

*But I.* Psalm 55's two words. They do their thing. *I* pray.

"Deliver me from the mud — don't let me sink. Rescue me from the ones who hate me — from the deep waters. Don't let the flood sweep over me. Don't let the deep swallow me. Don't let the pit close its mouth over me."

*Don't let the pit close its mouth.* The grave is a *mouth*. And it's *closing*.

**"Answer me, Lord — because Your loyal-love is good. In the abundance of Your compassion — turn to me. Don't hide Your face from Your servant. I'm in trouble — hurry, answer me."**

"Come near my soul. Redeem it. Ransom me because of my enemies. **You know my reproach — my shame and my disgrace. All my enemies are in front of You.**"

**"Reproach has broken my heart. I'm sick. I looked for sympathy — there was none. For comforters — I found none."**

*Broken my heart.* Not the enemies' swords. *The reproach.* The words did it.

*I looked for comforters — none.* Nobody came. Not one.

And then — the verse everyone knows without knowing where it's from:

**"They gave me poison for food. For my thirst — they gave me vinegar to drink."**

Matthew 27:34, 48. John 19:29. On the cross — *they offered Him wine mixed with gall. They lifted a sponge full of vinegar to His mouth.* A thousand years before, David wrote down what it would taste like.

Now — the imprecatory section. And it's long, and it's brutal:

"Let their table be a trap before them. Let their feasts become a snare. Let their eyes go dark so they can't see. Make their loins shake continually. Pour out Your anger on them. Let Your burning wrath overtake them. Let their camp be desolate. Let no one live in their tents. **Because they persecuted the one You struck — and talk about the pain of the one You wounded.**"

*They persecuted the one You struck.* He was already down — from God's hand — and they *piled on*. Kicked the man God was disciplining. That's the crime: not opposing him, but *enjoying* his suffering.

"Add guilt to their guilt. Don't let them come into Your right-standing. Let them be blotted from the book of life. Don't let them be written with the ones who do right."

Peter quotes verse 25 in Acts 1:20 — about *Judas*. *Let his camp be desolate.* The imprecations landed on someone.

**"But I — I'm afflicted and in pain. Let Your rescue, God, set me high."**

*But I.* Second time.

**"I will praise the name of God with a song. I'll magnify Him with thanksgiving. And that will please the Lord more than an ox — more than a bull with horns and hooves."**

Psalm 50, Psalm 51 — the song beats the bull.

**"The humble will see — and be glad. You who seek God — let your heart live!"**

*Let your heart live.* An imperative. *Heart — LIVE.* Said by the man with water at his neck, to the ones watching him.

**"Because the Lord hears the needy. He doesn't despise His captive people."**

*Doesn't despise.* Psalm 51 — the broken heart He won't despise. Psalm 22 — the affliction of the afflicted He didn't despise. It's the same promise every time: *He doesn't look away from the ones at the bottom.*

**"Let heaven and earth praise Him — the seas and everything moving in them. Because God will save Zion. He'll rebuild the cities of Judah. They'll settle there and possess it. The seed of His servants will inherit it. The ones who love His name will live there."**

Thirty-six verses. From *water at my neck* to *heaven and earth praise Him.* From *no comforters* to *let your heart live.* From *vinegar* to *the cities rebuilt.*

Here's the shape, and it's the shape of the cross: *He's drowning. Hated without cause. Zeal ate Him. His family disowned Him. They gave Him vinegar. Nobody came. And He said: heart — live. He doesn't despise the ones at the bottom.*

If the water's at your neck — this is your psalm. Say *but I*. Say *let your heart live*. He doesn't despise you. He rebuilds cities.
psalms.notes: *Note on translation: v. 4 —* son'ai chinnam *= those hating me without cause — John 15:25. v. 9 —* kin'at beit'cha achalatni *= "zeal for Your house has consumed me" — John 2:17;* cherpot chorfecha *= the reproaches of those reproaching You — Romans 15:3. v. 21 —* rosh *= poison/gall;* chometz *= vinegar/sour wine — Matt 27:34, 48; John 19:29. v. 25 — Acts 1:20 (of Judas). v. 28 —* sefer chayim *= book of life. v. 32 —* vi-chi l'vavchem *= "and let your heart live." No* yirah*.*

psalms.title: PSALM 70 — Hurry
psalms.body:
Psalm 40 was seventeen verses — the mud, the rock, the new song, the trouble coming back. Psalm 70 is its last five verses, cut loose and set on their own. No testimony first. No build-up. Just the emergency.

That's the point. Sometimes you don't have seventeen verses in you. You have five. Here they are.

**"God — to rescue me! Lord — to help me — hurry!"**

The Hebrew has no verb in the first line. Literally: *God — to rescue me.* Not even "come." Just the direction and the need. It's what comes out when there's no time for grammar.

*Hurry.* The word is *chushah* — quick, fast, *now*. The whole psalm is built on it.

**"Let the ones seeking my life be ashamed and disgraced. Let the ones wanting my harm be turned back and humiliated. Let the ones saying 'Ha! Ha!' turn back because of their shame."**

*Ha! Ha!* The mockers. The ones who saw you go down and laughed. David's got the exact sound of it — *he'ach* — a snort. He wants the snort turned around.

**"Let all who seek You rejoice and be glad in You. Let those who love Your rescue say continually: 'God is great!'"**

Two groups. The *ha-ha* crowd and the *God is great* crowd. Same event — someone in trouble. One laughs. One turns to God. David's asking for the second group to win — and to keep saying it. *Continually.*

And the last verse — the one worth memorizing:

**"But I am poor and needy. God — hurry to me. You are my help and my deliverer. Lord — don't delay."**

*Poor and needy.* No pretense. Not "I've been faithful." Not "I deserve." Just — *I've got nothing and I need You.* That's the whole argument. It's the same argument as Psalm 40, Psalm 51, Psalm 69 — and it's the only one that works every time, because it's the only one that's always true.

*Hurry to me.* Second time. Bookends. The psalm opens with *hurry* and closes with *hurry*.

*Don't delay.* The last two words. Not a request — a *plea*. The kind of thing you say when the delay itself would be the disaster.

Five verses. Here's the whole thing: *God — help — NOW. Turn the mockers around. Let the seekers say You're great. I've got nothing. Hurry. Don't delay.*

Why is this in the book twice? Because Psalm 40 is for when you have time to tell the whole story. Psalm 70 is for when you don't. When the water's at your neck (Psalm 69) and you can't get seventeen verses out — you get five. And they're enough.

Memorize it. All five. So that when you can't think — you can still pray.

*God — hurry. Don't delay.*
psalms.notes: *Note on translation: v. 1 —* Elohim l'hatzileni *= "God, to deliver me" — verbless, urgent;* chushah *= hurry, hasten. v. 3 —* he'ach he'ach *= "Aha! Aha!" — an onomatopoeic taunt. v. 4 —* tamid *= continually. v. 5 —* ani v'evyon *= poor and needy;* al-t'achar *= do not delay/tarry. Cf. Psalm 40:13–17 for the source text; Ps 70 substitutes* Elohim *for* YHWH *in v. 1, 4 — Book Two editorial pattern. No* yirah*.*

psalms.title: PSALM 71 — Even When I'm Old and Gray
psalms.body:
This is the psalm for the second half of life. The writer's old. He says so. And he's not done.

**"In You, Lord, I take refuge. Don't let me be ashamed — ever. In Your right-standing — rescue me and free me. Turn Your ear to me and save me."**

Psalm 31's opening, almost word for word. He's *borrowing* — because when you're old, you've got a library of prayers that worked, and you reach for them.

**"Be my rock of refuge — where I can always go. You've given the command to save me — because You're my rock and my fortress."**

*Where I can always go.* The Hebrew is *lavo tamid* — to come continually. Not an emergency exit. A *home address*. The place he's been going for decades.

"Rescue me, my God, from the hand of the wicked — from the grip of the unjust and the cruel."

And then — the retrospective:

**"Because You are my hope, Master — Lord — my confidence from my youth."**

*From my youth.* He's tracing it back. Not "I found You late." *You've been there since I was a kid.*

**"On You I've leaned from birth. You brought me out of my mother's womb. My praise is continually of You."**

*From birth.* Before he could choose. Before he knew the name. The leaning started before the knowing.

**"I've become like a wonder to many — but You are my strong refuge."**

*A wonder.* The Hebrew is *mofet* — a sign, a portent, something people point at. He's saying: *people look at my life and don't know what to make of it.* Maybe because of how much he's survived. Maybe because of how strange his story is. Either way — he's a *sign*. And the sign points to the refuge.

**"My mouth is filled with Your praise — with Your glory all day long."**

Now — the old-age section. Read it slow:

**"Don't cast me off in the time of old age. Don't abandon me when my strength fails."**

There it is. The fear every aging person has and doesn't say. *When I can't produce anymore — will You still want me?* When the body slows, when the mind slips, when the useful years are behind — *don't throw me away.*

He asks it out loud. Because he's watched the world throw old people away and he wants to know God isn't like the world.

"Because my enemies talk against me. The ones watching for my life plot together. They say: 'God has abandoned him. Chase him. Grab him — there's no one to rescue him.'"

*God has abandoned him.* The enemies think old age is proof God left. That the weakness is a *verdict*. He's got no army, no strength, no defenders — so they read it as *forsaken*.

**"God — don't be far from me. My God — hurry to help me."**

Psalm 70's *hurry*. Still saying it at the end of life.

"Let my accusers be ashamed and consumed. Let the ones seeking my harm be covered with disgrace and shame."

And now — the pivot. This is where the psalm stops looking back and starts *refusing to quit*:

**"But I — I will hope continually. I will add to all Your praise."**

*I will add.* He's not done praising. He's got *more* to say. Every year of survival is new material.

**"My mouth will tell of Your right-standing — Your rescue — all day long — though I don't know how to count it all."**

*I don't know how to count it all.* Psalm 40 — *too many to count*. Now it's a lifetime's worth. He's lost track of the rescues. There've been too many.

**"I'll come with the mighty deeds of the Master — Lord. I'll make known Your right-standing — Yours alone."**

**"God — You've taught me from my youth. To this day I declare Your wonders."**

*To this day.* Still going.

And then — the verse the whole psalm is built around:

**"Even when I'm old and gray — God — don't abandon me — until I declare Your strength to the next generation — Your might to all who are to come."**

*Until.* Read that word. He's not asking to be kept alive to enjoy retirement. He's asking for time — *until I've told the next generation.* The old man's job isn't done. There are kids who haven't heard yet. He needs the years to *transfer* it.

That's what old age is *for*, in this psalm. Not rest. *Transmission.* Psalm 48 — *tell the next generation.* Here's the man doing it with his last strength.

**"Your right-standing, God, reaches to the heights. You've done great things — God — who is like You?"**

Now — the honest part:

**"You've shown me many bitter troubles — but You'll bring me back to life. From the depths of the earth You'll bring me up again."**

*Many bitter troubles.* He doesn't pretend the long life was easy. *You* showed them to me. And *You'll bring me up again.* From the depths. This is an old man talking about resurrection without having the word for it yet.

**"You'll increase my honor. You'll turn and comfort me."**

*Comfort.* The Hebrew is *nacham* — the Isaiah 40 word. *Comfort ye My people.* The old man gets comforted.

And then — the harp comes out:

**"So I'll praise You with the harp — for Your faithfulness, my God. I'll sing to You with the lyre — Holy One of Israel. My lips will shout for joy when I sing to You — because You've redeemed my soul."**

*My lips will shout.* Old lips. Still shouting.

**"My tongue will tell of Your right-standing all day long — because the ones seeking my harm are ashamed and disgraced."**

Twenty-four verses. Here's the shape: *You've been my refuge since the womb. I'm a sign people point at. Don't throw me away when my strength fails — the enemies say You've left. But I'll keep hoping. I've lost count of the rescues. Keep me alive until I've told the kids. You've shown me bitter things — You'll bring me up again. And I'll get the harp out one more time.*

If you're in the second half: this is yours. You're not done. You're the *transmission*. Don't put the harp away.
psalms.notes: *Note on translation: v. 3 —* lavo tamid *= to come/enter continually. v. 5 —* mibitchi mi-n'urai *= my confidence from my youth. v. 7 —* k'mofet *= like a sign/portent/wonder. v. 9 —* al-tashlicheni l'et ziknah *= "do not cast me off in the time of old age." v. 14 —* v'hosafti al-kol-t'hilatecha *= "and I will add to all Your praise." v. 18 —* ad-ziknah v'seivah *= until old age and gray hair;* ad-agid *= until I declare. v. 20 —* tashuv t'chayeni *= You will return [and] revive me. v. 21 —* t'nachameni *= You will comfort me (*nacham*). No* yirah*.*

psalms.title: PSALM 72 — The King Who Hears the Poor
psalms.body:
This is what a king is *supposed* to be. Read it as a job description. Then read it as a prophecy. Both are true.

**"God — give the king Your justice. The king's son — Your right-standing."**

*Your* justice. Not his own. The first thing asked for the king isn't power or wealth or victory. It's *God's sense of right*, installed in the man on the throne.

**"Let him judge Your people with right-standing — Your poor with justice."**

*Your poor.* God's poor. The first group named. Not the nobles, not the army — *the poor*. They're who the justice is *for*.

"Let the mountains bring peace to the people — and the hills, right-standing."

*The mountains bring peace.* When the king rules right, even the *landscape* gets better. The land itself produces peace like a crop.

**"Let him defend the afflicted among the people. Let him save the children of the needy. Let him crush the oppressor."**

Three verbs. *Defend. Save. Crush.* Defend the hurt. Save the poor kids. And *crush* — the one word of violence — aimed at exactly one target: *the one who oppresses them.* The king's sword has one job.

**"Let them stand in awe of You as long as the sun endures — as long as the moon — through all generations."**

*Awe.* *Yirah.* As long as the sun's up. That's the timeline.

**"Let him be like rain falling on mown grass — like showers watering the earth."**

*Rain on mown grass.* The field's been cut. It's stubble. It looks dead. And the rain comes — and it *greens*. That's what this king does to a people who've been cut down. He's *rain*.

**"In his days let the one who does right flourish — and abundance of peace — until the moon is no more."**

*Until the moon is no more.* Not a term limit. *Forever.* No human king gets that. The psalm already knows it's describing Someone else.

**"Let him rule from sea to sea — from the River to the ends of the earth."**

*Ends of the earth.* Book Two's obsession — the *nations*, the whole map. The king isn't for one country.

"Let the desert tribes bow before him. Let his enemies lick the dust. Let the kings of Tarshish and the islands bring tribute. Let the kings of Sheba and Seba present gifts. **Let all kings bow to him. Let all nations serve him."**

*All kings. All nations.* The Magi brought gold and frankincense to a child in Bethlehem — and the church has read *Sheba's gifts* here ever since.

Now — the *reason*. Why does every nation bow to this king? Not because he conquered them. Because of this:

**"Because he rescues the needy when they cry — and the afflicted who has no helper."**

*Who has no helper.* The person with *nobody*. No lawyer, no advocate, no family, no money. *That's* who this king rescues. That's what makes the nations bow — they've never seen a king who bends down for the one with no one.

**"He has compassion on the weak and the needy. He saves the lives of the needy."**

*Compassion.* The Hebrew is *chus* — to pity, to spare, to feel it in the gut. A king who *feels it*.

**"He redeems their life from oppression and violence. Their blood is precious in his eyes."**

*Precious in his eyes.* The poor man's blood — the blood nobody else counts — this king counts it *precious*. The word is *yakar* — Psalm 36, *how precious is Your loyal-love*. Same weight. The king weighs the blood of the nobody at the same value God weighs His own love.

"Long may he live! Let the gold of Sheba be given to him. Let prayer be made for him continually. Let them bless him all day long."

**"Let there be abundance of grain in the land — on the tops of the mountains let it wave. Let its fruit flourish like Lebanon. Let people blossom in the cities like grass of the field."**

*Grain on the mountaintops.* Where nothing grows — a *harvest*. *People blossoming like grass.* Under this king, *humans* flourish like a crop after rain.

**"Let his name endure forever. Let his name continue as long as the sun. Let all nations be blessed in him. Let them call him happy."**

*All nations blessed in him.* Genesis 12:3 — Abraham's promise. *In you all nations will be blessed.* The king is where the promise lands.

Then — the doxology. Book Two closing:

**"Blessed be the Lord God — the God of Israel — who alone does wonders. Blessed be His glorious name forever. Let the whole earth be filled with His glory. Amen and amen."**

*The whole earth filled with His glory.* Book Two started with a deer panting in exile (Psalm 42). It ends with the whole earth *full*.

And one more line — an editor's note, honest as anything in the Bible:

**"The prayers of David son of Jesse are ended."**

Not that David wrote no more — Books Three through Five have more. But *this collection* — the man who started with *why are You so far off* and ended praying for a King who hears the poor — this stretch is done.

Twenty verses. Here's the King: *God's justice, not his own. For the poor first. Defends, saves, crushes the oppressor. Rain on mown grass. Rules to the ends of the earth — because he rescues the one with no helper. Their blood is precious to him. Grain on mountaintops. All nations blessed in him.*

No throne has produced that. One manger did.
psalms.notes: *Note on translation: v. 1 —* mishpatecha *= Your justice/judgments. v. 4 —* yidke oshek *= crush the oppressor — the one violent verb, one target. v. 5 —* yira'ucha *=* yirah *= let them stand in awe of You. v. 6 —* k'matar al-gez *= like rain on the mown [grass]. v. 12 —* v'ein-ozer lo *= "and [who has] no helper for him." v. 13 —* yachos *= has compassion/pity. v. 14 —* yekar damam *= precious [is] their blood. v. 17 —* v'yitbar'chu vo kol-goyim *= "and all nations will be blessed in him" — Gen 12:3, 22:18. v. 18–19 — Book Two doxology. v. 20 — editorial colophon.*

psalms.title: PSALM 73 — I Almost Slipped
psalms.body:
This is the most honest psalm about doubt in the whole book. A worship leader almost walked away. He tells you exactly why — and exactly what stopped him.

**"Surely God is good to Israel — to the pure in heart."**

He starts with the conclusion. The thing he *now* believes. Then he tells you how close he came to not believing it.

**"But as for me — my feet almost stumbled. My steps nearly slipped."**

*Almost. Nearly.* He was on the edge. Not "I had a hard week." *I almost went over.*

**"Because I envied the arrogant — when I saw the prosperity of the wicked."**

There's the trigger. *Envy.* He looked at the people who didn't care about God — and they were *winning*. And he wanted what they had.

Now — what he saw. And he's specific:

**"They have no pain. Their bodies are healthy and strong. They're free from the burdens common to man. They're not plagued like other people."**

*No pain.* The wicked aren't just rich — they're *comfortable*. No back trouble. No sleepless nights. The people who ignore God look like they got a better deal on the *body*.

**"So pride is their necklace. Violence is the clothing they wear."**

They *wear* it. Pride like jewelry. Cruelty like a jacket. On display.

**"Their eyes bulge with fat. The imaginations of their heart run wild. They mock. They speak with malice. From on high they threaten oppression. Their mouth claims heaven. Their tongue takes possession of the earth."**

*Their mouth claims heaven.* They talk like gods. And nothing stops them.

**"So the people turn to them — and drink up their words like water."**

The *crowd* follows them. The wicked have *fans*. Everyone's lining up to hear what the arrogant have to say.

**"They say: 'How would God know? Does the Most High have knowledge?'"**

Psalm 10, Psalm 14 — the practical atheism. *He doesn't see.*

**"Look — this is what the wicked are like: always at ease. Increasing in wealth."**

Now — Asaph's conclusion at the low point:

**"Surely I've kept my heart pure for nothing. I've washed my hands in innocence — for nothing."**

*For nothing.* The Hebrew is *rik* — empty, vain, in vain. He's saying: *I did everything right and it got me NOTHING. They did everything wrong and got EVERYTHING.* That's the exact sentence people say right before they walk out of the church for good.

**"All day long I've been plagued. Every morning brings new punishment."**

*He's* the one in pain. Not them. The worship leader has the back trouble and the sleepless nights.

And here's the moment. Watch how close it gets:

**"If I'd said: 'I'll speak like this' — I would have betrayed the generation of Your children."**

*If I'd said it out loud.* He's got the whole argument ready. *God doesn't pay. Righteousness is a scam. Look at them — look at me.* And he *almost* says it. Almost preaches it. And the one thing that stops him is — *the kids*. *Your children.* The next generation, who'd hear a worship leader say *it's all for nothing* — and believe him.

He kept his mouth shut. Not because he'd resolved it. Because he knew what his words would do to the people listening.

**"When I tried to understand all this — it was oppressive to me —"**

*Oppressive.* He couldn't think his way out. The more he thought, the worse it got.

**"— until I entered the sanctuary of God. Then I understood their end."**

*Until.* One word. *Until I went in.* Not "until I figured it out." Until he *entered the sanctuary*. He stopped thinking and went to where God was. And *there* — not in the argument, in the *presence* — the picture changed.

*Their end.* He'd been looking at their *middle*. The comfortable years. The bulging eyes and the fans. In the sanctuary he saw where the road *goes*.

**"Surely You place them on slippery ground. You throw them down to ruin. How suddenly they're destroyed — completely swept away by terrors. Like a dream when one awakes — so when You arise, Master — You despise them as fantasies."**

*Like a dream when you wake up.* All that prosperity — a *dream*. You wake up and it's not there. Not because it wasn't vivid — because it was never *real*.

Now — Asaph turns on himself, and it's brutal and it's honest:

**"When my heart was bitter — and I was pierced inside — I was senseless and ignorant. I was a brute beast before You."**

*A brute beast.* He's calling himself an animal. Not to grovel — because he sees now that the envy had made him *stupid*. Psalm 49's animals — no understanding. He'd become one.

And then — the turn. The verse that saved his faith:

**"Yet I am always with You. You hold my right hand."**

*Yet.* Even as a brute beast. Even bitter. Even about to betray the children. *I am always with You.* Not because he held on. Because *You hold my right hand.* Psalm 63 — two hands. He'd let go. God hadn't.

**"You guide me with Your counsel. Afterward You'll receive me into glory."**

*Afterward.* The word Psalm 37 used — *acharit*. The end. *Their* end was the slippery ground. *His* end is *glory*. Same road, different destination.

**"Whom have I in heaven but You? And on earth — I desire nothing besides You."**

He started envying what they had. He ends *wanting nothing they have*. Not because he got their stuff. Because he got *God*, and it turned out that was the thing he actually wanted the whole time.

**"My flesh and my heart may fail — but God is the rock of my heart and my portion forever."**

*My flesh may fail.* He's still the one with the back trouble. The wicked are still healthy. He's not pretending it flipped. But — *rock. Portion. Forever.* Psalm 16 — *You are my portion.* He's got the land they can't buy.

"Those who are far from You will perish. You destroy all who are unfaithful to You."

**"But as for me — it is good to be near God. I've made the Master — Lord — my refuge. I will tell of all Your deeds."**

*It is good to be near God.* That's the whole psalm in seven words. Not "it pays." Not "it's fair." *It's good to be near.* The nearness *is* the reward — and once you know that, the wicked man's health and money look like what they are. A dream you're glad you woke up from.

Twenty-eight verses. Here's what saved Asaph: he kept his mouth shut for the kids' sake, he went into the sanctuary instead of thinking harder, he saw the end instead of the middle, he called himself a beast, and he found out God had never let go of his hand.

If you're almost slipping — go in. Not to figure it out. To be near. That's where the picture changes.
