**"Bless the Lord, O my soul — and forget not all His benefits —"**

*Forget not.* Psalm 78 — *they forgot*. Psalm 103 — *don't*. And then — the list. So you *can't* forget:

**"— who forgives all your sins — and heals all your diseases — who redeems your life from the pit — and crowns you with loyal-love and compassion — who satisfies your desires with good things — so that your youth is renewed like the eagle's."**

Five benefits. *Forgives. Heals. Redeems. Crowns. Satisfies.*

*All your sins.* Not some. *All your diseases.* Same word. *Redeems from the pit* — Psalm 88's pit. Psalm 40's mud. *Crowns you* — Psalm 8's crown on the speck. *Crowns* — not "gives" — *crowns* — with loyal-love and compassion. Two words, one crown.

*Youth renewed like the eagle.* The eagle molts — loses the old feathers, grows new ones — and looks like it did years ago. That's what God does to a worn-out person. New feathers. Isaiah 40 — *they will soar on wings like eagles*.

**"The Lord works right-standing and justice for all the oppressed."**

*For the oppressed.* Psalm 72, 82, 94 — always the crushed ones first.

**"He made known His ways to Moses — His deeds to the people of Israel."**

*Made known His ways to Moses.* Exodus 33 — Moses asked *show me Your ways* — and God did. And what He showed him is the next verse:

**"The Lord is compassionate and gracious — slow to anger — abounding in loyal-love."**

Exodus 34:6. God's own self-description. Psalm 86 quoted it. Psalm 103 *builds* on it. Four things: *compassionate. gracious. slow to anger. abounding.* This is the sentence God chose when Moses asked *who are You?*

**"He will not always accuse — nor will He harbor His anger forever."**

*Not forever.* Psalm 30 — *His anger is for a moment.* The correction has an *end date*. The love doesn't.

**"He does not treat us as our sins deserve — or repay us according to our wrongdoing."**

*Not as we deserve.* That's the whole gospel in one verse. The math *doesn't balance*. On purpose.

Now — the *distances*. Three of them:

**"As high as the heavens are above the earth — so great is His loyal-love for those who stand in awe of Him."**

*Heavens above earth.* Vertical. Immeasurable. That's the *height* of the love. And who gets it? The ones in *awe* — *yirah*. Not the ones in fear. The ones who *look up* and gasp.

**"As far as the east is from the west — so far has He removed our rebellions from us."**

*East from west.* Horizontal. And here's the thing — north and south have *ends*. You hit the pole. East and west *don't*. You can walk east forever. That's how far the sin's been taken. Not "to the edge." *There's no edge.*

**"As a father has compassion on his children — so the Lord has compassion on those who stand in awe of Him."**

*As a father.* Not "as a judge." Not "as a king." *Father.* Psalm 68 — *Father of the fatherless*. The Hebrew is *k'rachem av* — like the *womb-love* of a father. *Rachamim* — compassion — comes from *rechem* — womb. It's the love that's *gut-level*, that you don't choose, that's *in* you because they're yours. God has *that* — for the ones in *awe*. Second *yirah*.

**"Because He knows how we are formed. He remembers that we are dust."**

*He remembers we're dust.* Psalm 78:39 — *He remembered they were flesh.* Here's why the math doesn't balance: He *knows what He's working with*. He shaped the dust. He knows it cracks.

**"The life of mortals is like grass. They flourish like a flower of the field. The wind blows over it and it is gone — and its place remembers it no more."**

*Grass. Flower. Wind. Gone.* Psalm 90, 102 — but here it's not despair. It's *tenderness*. He's saying: *of course You're patient with us. Look how brief we are.*

**"But from everlasting to everlasting — the Lord's loyal-love is with those who stand in awe of Him — and His right-standing with their children's children — with those who keep His covenant and remember to obey His precepts."**

Third *yirah*. *Everlasting to everlasting.* Psalm 90 — *from everlasting to everlasting You are God.* The grass is gone in a day. The love is *forever*. And it reaches — *children's children*. Psalm 78's chain.

Now — the throne, and then the *whole choir*:

**"The Lord has established His throne in heaven — and His kingdom rules over all."**

Psalm 93. *Reigns.*

**"Bless the Lord, you His angels — you mighty ones who do His bidding — who obey His word. Bless the Lord, all His heavenly hosts — you His servants who do His will. Bless the Lord, all His works — everywhere in His dominion."**

*Angels. Hosts. All His works.* The whole created order — commanded to bless. Psalm 148 will do this in full. Psalm 103 starts it.

And the last line — back to where it started:

**"Bless the Lord, O my soul."**

*O my soul.* One more time. He started alone with his own guts. He ended with every angel in heaven. And then — *back to the soul*. Because the whole universe blessing God means nothing if *yours* doesn't.

Twenty-two verses. Not one request. Here's the shape: *Soul — bless Him. Don't forget — He forgives ALL, heals ALL, redeems, crowns, satisfies, renews like an eagle. He's compassionate, gracious, slow to anger, abounding. He won't accuse forever. He doesn't treat us as we deserve. Love high as heaven. Sin removed east-to-west — no edge. Father's womb-love. He remembers we're dust. Grass blows away — love is forever. Angels, hosts, all works — bless Him. Soul — bless Him.*

Command your soul. Then hand it the list.
psalms.notes: *Note on translation: v. 1, 22 —* barchi nafshi et-YHWH *= "bless, my soul, YHWH" — inclusio. v. 1 —* kol-k'ravai *= all my inward parts. v. 3 —* kol-avonechi / kol-tachalu'aychi *= all your iniquities / all your diseases. v. 5 —* ka-nesher *= like the eagle. v. 8 — Exodus 34:6 verbatim. v. 11, 13, 17 —* yere'av *=* yirah *= those who stand in awe of Him (x3). v. 12 —* kirchok mizrach mi-ma'arav *= "as far as east from west." v. 13 —* k'rachem av *= as a father has compassion —* rachamim *from* rechem *(womb). v. 14 —* zachur ki-afar anachnu *= "remembering that dust [are] we." v. 17 —* me-olam v'ad-olam *= from everlasting to everlasting.*

psalms.title: PSALM 104 — You Open Your Hand
psalms.body:
Psalm 103 blessed God for what He does for *people*. Psalm 104 blesses Him for *everything else*. Same opening line. Different subject.

**"Bless the Lord, O my soul. Lord my God — You are very great. You are clothed with splendor and majesty."**

*Clothed.* Psalm 93 — *robed in majesty*. And then — the wardrobe gets specific:

**"He wraps Himself in light as with a garment. He stretches out the heavens like a tent — and lays the beams of His upper chambers on their waters. He makes the clouds His chariot — and rides on the wings of the wind. He makes winds His messengers — flames of fire His servants."**

*Light as a garment.* Day one — *let there be light*. He *wore* it.

*The heavens like a tent.* Day two — the sky as a canvas He *pitched*. The upper chambers on the *waters* — the ancient picture of the sky as a roof over the deep.

*Clouds His chariot. Wind His wings.* Psalm 18 — *He rode on a cherub and flew*. The weather is His *transportation*.

**"He set the earth on its foundations. It can never be moved."**

Day three begins. *Never moved.* Psalm 93, 96 — the ground holds.

**"You covered it with the watery depths as with a garment. The waters stood above the mountains. But at Your rebuke the waters fled. At the sound of Your thunder they took to flight. They flowed over the mountains — they went down into the valleys — to the place You assigned for them. You set a boundary they cannot cross. Never again will they cover the earth."**

*The waters fled.* The chaos — running. *At Your rebuke.* One word and the sea *retreats* to where it's told. *A boundary they cannot cross.* Job 38 — *who shut up the sea behind doors?* This One.

Now — the springs, and this is where the psalm gets *tender*:

**"He makes springs pour water into the ravines. It flows between the mountains. They give water to all the beasts of the field. The wild donkeys quench their thirst."**

*Wild donkeys.* Not the useful animals. The *wild* ones. The ones nobody owns. God's making sure *they* get a drink.

**"The birds of the sky nest by the waters. They sing among the branches."**

Psalm 84's sparrow — but *everywhere*. Every stream's got a nest and a song.

**"He waters the mountains from His upper chambers. The land is satisfied by the fruit of His work. He makes grass grow for the cattle — and plants for people to cultivate — bringing forth food from the earth:**
**wine that gladdens human hearts — oil to make their faces shine — and bread that sustains their hearts."**

*Wine. Oil. Bread.* The three staples. And look at the *verbs*: wine *gladdens*. Oil makes faces *shine*. Bread *sustains*. God didn't just make food. He made food that makes you *happy*. Wine wasn't necessary. He added it. For *gladness*.

**"The trees of the Lord are well watered — the cedars of Lebanon that He planted. There the birds make their nests. The stork has its home in the junipers. The high mountains belong to the wild goats. The crags are a refuge for the rock badgers."**

*Rock badgers.* The hyrax. A small, furry, unimportant animal that lives in cracks. And God built the *crags* for them. *A refuge* — Psalm 46's word — for *badgers*. If He made a shelter for the hyrax, He made one for you.

**"He made the moon to mark the seasons — and the sun knows when to go down."**

Day four. *The sun knows.* Like it's got a schedule and keeps it.

**"You bring darkness — it becomes night — and all the beasts of the forest prowl. The lions roar for their prey — and seek their food from God."**

*The lions seek their food from God.* Read that. The apex predator — the thing at the top of every food chain — *praying for dinner*. Not consciously. But the psalm says that's what the roar *is*. A request. And God hears it.

**"The sun rises — and they steal away. They return and lie down in their dens. Then people go out to their work — to their labor until evening."**

Night shift. Day shift. Lions clock out; humans clock in. God runs the whole schedule.

**"How many are Your works, Lord! In wisdom You made them all. The earth is full of Your creatures."**

*Full.* Psalm 33 — *full of loyal-love*. Here — *full of creatures*. Teeming.

Now — the sea:

**"There is the sea — vast and spacious — teeming with creatures beyond number — living things both large and small. There the ships go to and fro — and Leviathan — which You formed to frolic there."**

*Leviathan.* Psalm 74 — *You crushed the heads of Leviathan*. Job 41 — the terror nobody can hook. And here — *You formed him to FROLIC.*

The Hebrew is *l'sachek* — to play. To *sport*. God made the sea monster — the symbol of chaos, the thing every ancient culture feared — *as a toy*. For *fun*. His own. Or Leviathan's. Either way — the monster's *playing*.

That's the most joyful verse in the psalm. The thing you were scared of is *God's pet*.

**"All creatures look to You — to give them their food at the proper time. When You give it to them — they gather it up. When You open Your hand — they are satisfied with good things."**

*You open Your hand.* Picture it. Every living thing on earth — donkeys, storks, badgers, lions, Leviathan — *looking up*. Waiting. And God *opens His hand*. And they eat.

That's the economy of the whole planet. One open hand.

**"When You hide Your face — they are terrified. When You take away their breath — they die and return to the dust. When You send Your Spirit — they are created — and You renew the face of the ground."**

*Your breath. Your Spirit.* Same word — *ruach*. Every breath every creature takes is *His* on loan. He gives it — they live. He takes it — dust. He sends it again — *new*. The whole cycle of life and death is God *breathing*.

**"May the glory of the Lord endure forever. May the Lord rejoice in His works."**

*May the Lord REJOICE in His works.* God — *happy* about what He made. Genesis 1 — *it was good*. Psalm 104 — *He's still glad about it*.

**"He who looks at the earth — and it trembles. Who touches the mountains — and they smoke."**

**"I will sing to the Lord all my life. I will sing praise to my God as long as I live. May my meditation be pleasing to Him — as I rejoice in the Lord."**

*As I rejoice.* God rejoices in His works. The psalmist rejoices in God. Mutual delight.

**"But may sinners vanish from the earth — and the wicked be no more."**

One line. The only shadow in thirty-five verses. Because the creation's *good* — and the thing that wrecks it doesn't belong.

**"Bless the Lord, O my soul. Praise the Lord!"**

*Praise the Lord.* *Hallelu-Yah.* The first *hallelujah* in the Psalms. Right here. After Leviathan frolicking and the lions praying for dinner and God opening His hand.

Thirty-five verses. Here's the shape: *He wears light. The sky's His tent. The sea ran when He spoke. Springs for the wild donkeys. Wine to make you glad. Crags for the badgers. Lions asking God for dinner. Leviathan — made to PLAY. You open Your hand — everyone eats. Your breath goes out — life. Comes back — dust. Goes out again — new. May He rejoice in what He made. Hallelujah.*

Go outside. Everything you see is looking up at an open hand. So are you.
psalms.notes: *Note on translation: v. 2 —* oteh-or ka-salmah *= "wrapping light like a garment." v. 4 — Hebrews 1:7 quotes this of angels. v. 11 —* p'ra'im *= wild donkeys/onagers. v. 15 —* yayin y'samach l'vav-enosh *= "wine gladdens the heart of man." v. 18 —* sh'fanim *= rock badgers/hyraxes. v. 21 —* l'vakesh me-El ochlam *= "to seek from God their food." v. 26 —* livyatan zeh-yatzarta l'sachek-bo *= "Leviathan whom You formed to play in it/with him." v. 28 —* tiftach yadcha *= You open Your hand. v. 29–30 —* ruach *= breath/spirit. v. 31 —* yismach YHWH b'ma'asav *= "may YHWH rejoice in His works." v. 35 —* hallelu-Yah *= first occurrence in the Psalter. No* yirah*.*

psalms.title: PSALM 105 — He Remembered His Covenant
psalms.body:
Psalm 78 told the history as a *warning* — here's how they failed. Psalm 105 tells it as a *celebration* — here's how God *didn't*. Same events. Different hero.

**"Give thanks to the Lord. Call on His name. Make known among the nations what He has done. Sing to Him. Sing praise to Him. Tell of all His wonderful acts."**

Five commands. *Thank. Call. Make known. Sing. Tell.* Then two more:

**"Glory in His holy name. Let the hearts of those who seek the Lord rejoice. Look to the Lord and His strength. Seek His face always."**

*Seek His face always.* David's obsession — Psalm 27. *Always.*

**"Remember the wonders He has done — His miracles — and the judgments He pronounced — you descendants of Abraham His servant — you children of Jacob, His chosen ones."**

*Remember.* You remember. And then — the whole psalm — *He* remembers:

**"He is the Lord our God. His judgments are in all the earth. He remembers His covenant forever — the promise He made — for a thousand generations."**

*He remembers His covenant.* *Zachar.* Psalm 98 — *He remembered His loyal-love*. Psalm 78 — *He remembered they were flesh*. Here's the whole thing: *forever. A thousand generations.* The people forget. God's memory is the only thing that holds.

**"— the covenant He made with Abraham — the oath He swore to Isaac. He confirmed it to Jacob as a decree — to Israel as an everlasting covenant: 'To you I will give the land of Canaan — as the portion you will inherit.'"**

Abraham. Isaac. Jacob. Three generations. One promise. *The land.*

**"When they were but few in number — few indeed — and strangers in it — they wandered from nation to nation — from one kingdom to another."**

*Few. Strangers. Wandering.* That's how it started. Not an army. A *family*. Homeless.

**"He allowed no one to oppress them. For their sake He rebuked kings: 'Do not touch My anointed ones. Do My prophets no harm.'"**

*Do not touch.* Pharaoh with Sarah. Abimelech. God stepping in front of the wandering family and saying *hands off.*

Now — Joseph:

**"He called down famine on the land — and destroyed all their supplies of food. And He sent a man before them — Joseph — sold as a slave."**

*He sent a man before them.* Read that carefully. Joseph was *sold*. Betrayed by his brothers. Thrown in a pit. Sold to traders. And the psalm says — *God SENT him.* The betrayal was the *delivery method*. Genesis 50:20 — *you meant it for evil; God meant it for good.*

**"They bruised his feet with shackles. His neck was put in irons — till what he foretold came to pass — till the word of the Lord proved him true."**

*Till.* Psalm 94's *till*. There's always a *till*. Joseph in chains — *till* the word proved true.

**"The king sent and released him. The ruler of peoples set him free. He made him master of his household — ruler over all he possessed — to instruct his princes as he pleased — and teach his elders wisdom."**

From the pit to the palace. The slave teaching the *elders*.

**"Then Israel entered Egypt. Jacob resided as a foreigner in the land of Ham. The Lord made His people very fruitful. He made them too numerous for their foes — whose hearts He turned to hate His people — to conspire against His servants."**

*Whose hearts He turned.* Even the *hatred* — inside the plan. The oppression that came next wasn't God losing control. It was the *setup*.

**"He sent Moses His servant — and Aaron, whom He had chosen. They performed His signs among them — His wonders in the land of Ham."**

Now — the plagues. Fast:

**"He sent darkness and made the land dark — for had they not rebelled against His words? He turned their waters into blood — causing their fish to die. Their land teemed with frogs — which went up into the bedrooms of their rulers. He spoke — and there came swarms of flies — and gnats throughout their country. He turned their rain into hail — with lightning throughout their land. He struck down their vines and fig trees — and shattered the trees of their country. He spoke — and the locusts came — grasshoppers without number. They ate up every green thing in their land — ate up the produce of their soil. Then He struck down all the firstborn in their land — the firstfruits of all their manhood."**

*He spoke — and.* Twice. Frogs in the *bedrooms* of the rulers. God's not subtle when He's making a point.

**"He brought out Israel — laden with silver and gold — and from among their tribes no one faltered."**

*No one faltered.* Not one person stumbled on the way out. The slaves walked out of the superpower *carrying its treasure*.

**"Egypt was glad when they left — because dread of Israel had fallen on them."**

*Glad when they left.* The oppressor *relieved* to see them go.

**"He spread out a cloud as a covering — and a fire to give light at night. They asked — and He brought them quail. He fed them well with the bread of heaven. He opened the rock — and water gushed out. It flowed like a river in the desert."**

Cloud. Fire. Quail. Manna. Water from rock. Psalm 78 told these as *complaints*. Psalm 105 tells them as *gifts*. Same events. This time — no grumbling in the text. Just *He gave*.

And the reason for all of it:

**"Because He remembered His holy promise — given to His servant Abraham."**

*He remembered.* Second time. The plagues, the exodus, the manna — all of it because God *didn't forget* a conversation He had with a childless old man in a tent five hundred years earlier.

**"He brought out His people with rejoicing — His chosen ones with shouts of joy. He gave them the lands of the nations — and they fell heir to what others had toiled for —"**

*What others had toiled for.* They walked into houses they didn't build. Deuteronomy 6.

**"— that they might keep His precepts — and observe His laws.**
**Praise the Lord!"**

*That they might keep.* The whole rescue had a *purpose*. Not just freedom *from*. Freedom *for*. And then — *hallelujah*. Second one in the Psalms.

Forty-five verses. Here's the shape: *Thank, call, tell, sing. He REMEMBERS His covenant — a thousand generations. Abraham, Isaac, Jacob — few and wandering. Hands off My anointed. Joseph — SENT by being sold. Chains till the word proved true. Egypt — frogs in the bedrooms. Out with the gold — nobody stumbled. Cloud, fire, quail, bread, water. Because He REMEMBERED Abraham. Into houses they didn't build. So they'd keep His word. Hallelujah.*

The hero of this psalm isn't Abraham or Joseph or Moses. It's God's *memory*. You'll forget. He won't. That's the covenant.
psalms.notes: *Note on translation: v. 4 —* bak'shu fanav tamid *= "seek His face always." v. 8 —* zachar l'olam b'rito *= "He remembers forever His covenant";* l'elef dor *= to a thousand generations. v. 12 —* m'tei mispar *= men of number (few). v. 15 —* al-tig'u vi-m'shichai *= "do not touch My anointed ones." v. 17 —* shalach lifneihem ish *= "He sent before them a man" — Joseph. v. 19 —* ad-et bo-d'varo *= until the time His word came. v. 25 —* hafach libam *= He turned their heart. v. 42 —* zachar et-d'var kodsho *= "He remembered His holy word." v. 45 —* hallelu-Yah*. No* yirah*.*

psalms.title: PSALM 106 — Many Times He Delivered Them
psalms.body:
Psalm 105 — *He remembered.* Psalm 106 — *we forgot.* Same events. Same God. Different subject in every sentence.

**"Praise the Lord! Give thanks to the Lord — because He is good. His loyal-love endures forever."**

*Hallelujah.* Then — the refrain that'll anchor Psalm 107, 118, and 136: *He is good — loyal-love forever.* The confession *opens* with praise. Because you can only confess safely to Someone whose love is *forever*.

**"Who can proclaim the mighty acts of the Lord — or fully declare His praise? Happy are those who act justly — who always do what is right."**

**"Remember me, Lord — when You show favor to Your people. Come to my aid when You save them — that I may enjoy the prosperity of Your chosen ones — share in the joy of Your nation — and join Your inheritance in giving praise."**

*Remember me.* One person. In the middle of a national confession. *Don't forget me when You fix this.*

And now — the confession. It starts with *we*:

**"We have sinned — even as our ancestors did. We have done wrong and acted wickedly."**

*We.* Not "they." The exiles owning the whole chain. Daniel 9 — *we have sinned*. Nehemiah 9. The generation in Babylon didn't say *our fathers did it.* They said *we*.

Then — the record. Eight failures. Watch them stack:

**One — the Red Sea.**

**"When our ancestors were in Egypt — they gave no thought to Your miracles. They did not remember Your many kindnesses — and they rebelled by the sea — the Red Sea."**

*Did not remember.* There it is. Psalm 105's hero — God's memory. Psalm 106's villain — *ours*. They were *at the sea*, watching it about to split — and complaining.

**"Yet He saved them for His name's sake — to make His mighty power known. He rebuked the Red Sea and it dried up. He led them through the depths as through a desert. He saved them from the hand of the foe. From the hand of the enemy He redeemed them. The waters covered their adversaries — not one of them survived. Then they believed His promises — and sang His praise."**

*Then they believed.* *After* the sea. For a minute.

**Two — the wilderness cravings.**

**"But they soon forgot what He had done — and did not wait for His plan. In the desert they gave in to their craving. In the wilderness they put God to the test. So He gave them what they asked for — but sent a wasting disease among them."**

*Soon forgot.* How soon? Three days. Exodus 15 to Exodus 16. *He gave them what they asked for.* Psalm 78's quail. Psalm 81's *I gave them over*. You can get what you want and lose what you need.

**Three — the mutiny.**

**"In the camp they grew envious of Moses — and of Aaron, who was consecrated to the Lord. The earth opened up and swallowed Dathan. It buried the company of Abiram. Fire blazed among their followers. A flame consumed the wicked."**

Numbers 16. The revolt against leadership. The ground *ate* them.

**Four — the calf.**

**"At Horeb they made a calf — and worshiped an idol cast from metal. They exchanged their glorious God — for an image of a bull — which eats grass."**

*Which eats grass.* The psalmist's contempt. *You traded the One who split the sea for a thing that eats LAWN.* Romans 1:23 — *they exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images.*

**"They forgot God who saved them — who had done great things in Egypt — miracles in the land of Ham — and awesome deeds by the Red Sea."**

*Forgot.* Second time.

**"So He said He would destroy them — had not Moses, His chosen one — stood in the breach before Him — to keep His wrath from destroying them."**

*Stood in the breach.* Exodus 32. Moses — *between* God and the people. Like a man stepping into a gap in the wall so the flood doesn't get through. One person standing where the wrath would've come. The psalm says that's what *saved* them. Hebrews 7 — *He always lives to intercede.* Moses was the sketch. Somebody else is the finished drawing.

**Five — the refusal.**

**"Then they despised the pleasant land. They did not believe His promise. They grumbled in their tents — and did not obey the Lord. So He swore to them with uplifted hand — that He would make them fall in the wilderness — make their descendants fall among the nations — and scatter them throughout the lands."**

*Despised the pleasant land.* They got to the border — the land God swore to Abraham — and *didn't want it*. Too scary. Giants. Psalm 95 — *they shall never enter My rest.*

**Six — Baal of Peor.**

**"They yoked themselves to the Baal of Peor — and ate sacrifices offered to lifeless gods. They aroused the Lord's anger by their wicked deeds — and a plague broke out among them. But Phinehas stood up and intervened — and the plague was checked. This was credited to him as right-standing — for endless generations to come."**

*Phinehas stood up.* Numbers 25. Another one standing in the breach.

**Seven — Meribah.**

**"By the waters of Meribah they angered the Lord — and trouble came to Moses because of them. Because they rebelled against the Spirit of God — rash words came from Moses' lips."**

*Trouble came to Moses.* Even *Moses* broke. Numbers 20 — struck the rock instead of speaking to it. And didn't enter the land. The people's rebellion cost the *intercessor*.

**Eight — the land.**

**"They did not destroy the peoples as the Lord had commanded them — but they mingled with the nations — and adopted their customs. They worshiped their idols — which became a snare to them. They sacrificed their sons and their daughters to false gods. They shed innocent blood — the blood of their sons and daughters — whom they sacrificed to the idols of Canaan — and the land was desecrated by their blood. They defiled themselves by what they did. By their deeds they prostituted themselves."**

*Sacrificed their sons and daughters.* The bottom. The people God carried out of Egypt on eagle's wings — burning their kids to Molech. The psalmist doesn't look away.

**"So the Lord was angry with His people — and abhorred His inheritance. He gave them into the hands of the nations — and their foes ruled over them. Their enemies oppressed them — and subjected them to their power."**

Exile. Judges. Assyria. Babylon.

And then — the verse. The whole psalm in one line:

**"Many times He delivered them — but they were bent on rebellion — and they wasted away in their sin."**

*Many times.* The Hebrew is *p'amim rabbot* — *many, many times*. Eight failures listed. Eight rescues implied. Every fall — a *catch*. And still — *bent on rebellion*.

**"Yet He took note of their distress — when He heard their cry."**

*Yet.* Psalm 78 — *yet He was merciful*. Psalm 106 — *yet He took note*. Eight rebellions. One *yet*. And it wins.

**"For their sake He remembered His covenant — and out of His great love He relented. He caused all who held them captive — to show them mercy."**

*He remembered.* Psalm 105's word — in Psalm 106. Even the confession psalm can't get to the end without it. *They* forgot — twice, named. *He* remembered.

*Out of His great love He relented.* The Hebrew is *va-yinachem* — Psalm 90's *relent*, Psalm 71's *comfort*. He *changed course* — because of love.

Now — the exiles' prayer:

**"Save us, Lord our God — and gather us from the nations — that we may give thanks to Your holy name — and glory in Your praise."**

*Gather us.* Psalm 147 — *He gathers the exiles*. They're asking.

And the Book Four doxology:

**"Praise be to the Lord — the God of Israel — from everlasting to everlasting. Let all the people say: 'Amen!'**
**Praise the Lord!"**

*Let all the people say Amen.* The whole congregation. Not just the psalmist. Everyone who just heard eight failures — *amen*. Because the *yet* held.

Forty-eight verses. Here's the shape: *Hallelujah — He's good — loyal-love forever. WE sinned — like our fathers. Red Sea — complained. Wilderness — craved. Camp — mutinied. Horeb — a bull that eats grass. Moses stood in the breach. Despised the land. Baal of Peor. Meribah — even Moses broke. Canaan — burned their kids. MANY TIMES He delivered them. Yet — He remembered. He relented. Gather us. Amen.*

Psalm 105 and 106 together are the whole Bible: *He remembered — we forgot — He remembered anyway.*

Book Four closes. Book Five opens with the four rescues — and the refrain that answers all eight failures.
psalms.notes: *Note on translation: v. 1 —* ki-tov ki l'olam chasdo *= "for [He is] good, for forever [is] His loyal-love" — refrain of 107, 118, 136. v. 6 —* chatanu im-avoteinu *= "we have sinned with our fathers." v. 7, 13, 21 —* lo zach'ru / shach'chu *= did not remember / forgot. v. 15 —* razon *= wasting/leanness. v. 20 —* shor ochel esev *= "a bull eating grass." v. 23 —* amad ba-peretz *= "stood in the breach." v. 31 — Phinehas (Num 25:10–13). v. 43 —* p'amim rabbot yatzilem *= "many times He delivered them." v. 45 —* va-yizkor lahem b'rito *= "and He remembered for them His covenant";* va-yinachem *= and He relented. v. 48 — Book Four doxology. No* yirah*.*

psalms.title: PSALM 107 — Let the Redeemed Say So
psalms.body:
Book Four closed with eight failures and one *yet*. Book Five opens with four ditches and one *then they cried*.

**"Give thanks to the Lord — because He is good. His loyal-love endures forever."**

Psalm 106's refrain — carried across the book break. Same words. New book. *Good. Forever.*

**"Let the redeemed of the Lord say so — those He redeemed from the hand of the foe — those He gathered from the lands — from east and west, from north and south."**

*Say so.* The Hebrew is *yom'ru* — *let them SAY*. Not think it. Not feel it. *Say it out loud.* If you've been redeemed — you've got a *job*: tell it. Psalm 66 — *come and hear what He did for me*. Psalm 107 makes it a command.

*From east and west, north and south.* The exiles — Psalm 106's *gather us* — *gathered*. From every direction.

Now — the four rescues. Each one has the same shape: *trouble → they cried → He delivered → thank Him.* Watch the pattern. It's *your* pattern.

**One — the lost.**

**"Some wandered in desert wastelands — finding no way to a city where they could settle. They were hungry and thirsty — and their lives ebbed away."**

*No way to a city.* Lost. Not in a dramatic way — just *nowhere*. Walking and walking and no destination appearing. Psalm 63's desert. If you've been *directionless* — this is you.

**"Then they cried out to the Lord in their trouble — and He delivered them from their distress. He led them by a straight way — to a city where they could settle."**

*Then they cried.* The first *then*. *A straight way.* Not a shortcut. *Straight.* And — *a city*. A place. An address.

**"Let them give thanks to the Lord for His loyal-love — and His wonderful deeds for mankind — because He satisfies the thirsty — and fills the hungry with good things."**

*Satisfies. Fills.* Psalm 63, 103, 104 — the *sated* words. The lost get *fed*.

**Two — the imprisoned.**

**"Some sat in darkness — in utter darkness — prisoners suffering in iron chains — because they rebelled against God's commands — and despised the plans of the Most High. So He subjected them to bitter labor. They stumbled — and there was no one to help."**

*Because they rebelled.* This group's in the ditch *because of what they did*. The psalm says so. No pretending. *Iron chains.* *Darkness.* *No one to help.* Psalm 88's pit. Addiction. The consequence you earned.

**"Then they cried out to the Lord in their trouble — and He saved them from their distress. He brought them out of darkness — utter darkness — and broke away their chains."**

*Then they cried.* Second *then*. Same words — even for the ones who *deserved* the chains. God doesn't check the cause before He breaks the iron.

**"Let them give thanks to the Lord for His loyal-love — and His wonderful deeds for mankind — because He breaks down gates of bronze — and cuts through bars of iron."**

*Gates of bronze. Bars of iron.* Isaiah 45. The prison's not locked to Him.

**Three — the sick.**

**"Some became fools through their rebellious ways — and suffered affliction because of their wrongdoing. They loathed all food — and drew near the gates of death."**

*Loathed all food.* Psalm 102 — *I forget to eat*. Sick from what they did to themselves. *Gates of death* — the door's right there.

**"Then they cried out to the Lord in their trouble — and He saved them from their distress. He sent out His word and healed them. He rescued them from the grave."**

*Then they cried.* Third *then*. *He sent out His word.* Psalm 33 — *He spoke and it was*. One word — *healed*. Matthew 8 — *just say the word and my servant will be healed.* The centurion knew this psalm.

**"Let them give thanks to the Lord for His loyal-love — and His wonderful deeds for mankind. Let them sacrifice thank offerings — and tell of His works with songs of joy."**

*Tell. Songs.* The healed *sing about it*.

**Four — the storm.**

**"Some went out on the sea in ships. They were merchants on the mighty waters. They saw the works of the Lord — His wonderful deeds in the deep."**

Sailors. Not lost, not chained, not sick — *working*. Doing their job. And the sea turned.

**"He spoke and stirred up a tempest — that lifted high the waves. They mounted up to the heavens — and went down to the depths. In their peril their courage melted away. They reeled and staggered like drunkards. They were at their wits' end."**

*At their wits' end.* The Hebrew is *kol-chochmatam titbala* — *all their wisdom was swallowed*. Every skill they had — useless. The experts — helpless. If you've been *competent* and hit something competence can't fix — this is you.

**"Then they cried out to the Lord in their trouble — and He brought them out of their distress. He stilled the storm to a whisper. The waves of the sea were hushed."**

*Then they cried.* Fourth *then*. *Stilled the storm to a whisper.* Mark 4 — *Peace, be still. And the wind died down and it was completely calm.* The disciples were sailors. They'd sung this psalm. And then they *watched it happen*.

**"They were glad when it grew calm — and He guided them to their desired haven."**

*Their desired haven.* The harbor they were *aiming for*. Not a random shore. The place they *wanted*.

**"Let them give thanks to the Lord for His loyal-love — and His wonderful deeds for mankind. Let them exalt Him in the assembly of the people — and praise Him in the council of the elders."**

*In the assembly. In the council.* Publicly. The sailors tell it in front of everyone.

Four ditches. Four *thens*. Four *let them thank*.

Now — the epilogue. God as the One who *reverses*:

**"He turned rivers into a desert — flowing springs into thirsty ground — and fruitful land into a salt waste — because of the wickedness of those who lived there. He turned the desert into pools of water — and the parched ground into flowing springs. There He brought the hungry to live — and they founded a city where they could settle."**

*Rivers to desert. Desert to pools.* Both directions. He can dry up the proud. He can *water* the empty. Psalm 65's overflow — for the *hungry*.

**"They sowed fields and planted vineyards — that yielded a fruitful harvest. He blessed them — and their numbers greatly increased — and He did not let their herds diminish."**

**"Then their numbers decreased — and they were humbled by oppression, calamity, and sorrow. He who pours contempt on nobles — made them wander in a trackless waste. But He lifted the needy out of their affliction — and increased their families like flocks."**

*Pours contempt on nobles. Lifts the needy.* Psalm 75 — *He brings one down, He lifts another.* Psalm 113. Mary's song.

**"The upright see and rejoice — but all the wicked shut their mouths."**

*Shut their mouths.* Nothing to say. The pattern's too obvious.

And the last verse — the instruction:

**"Let the one who is wise heed these things — and ponder the loyal-love of the Lord."**

*Ponder.* The Hebrew is *yitbon'nu* — *understand deeply*. Look at the four rescues. Look at the pattern. *Trouble — cry — delivered.* Every time. That's not luck. That's *chesed*. And the wise person *studies* it.

Forty-three verses. Here's the shape: *Give thanks — He's good. Redeemed? SAY SO. The lost cried — He led them to a city. The chained cried — He broke the iron. The sick cried — He sent a word. The sailors cried — He whispered the storm down. Four ditches — four cries — four rescues. He dries rivers and waters deserts. Wise? Study the pattern.*

You've been in one of the four. Maybe all of them. And you cried. And you're reading this — so you got out.

*Let the redeemed say so.* Say it.
psalms.notes: *Note on translation: v. 1 —* hodu la-YHWH ki-tov ki l'olam chasdo *= "give thanks to YHWH for [He is] good, for forever [is] His loyal-love." v. 2 —* yom'ru g'ulei YHWH *= "let the redeemed of YHWH say." v. 6, 13, 19, 28 —* va-yitz'aku el-YHWH ba-tzar lahem *= "then they cried to YHWH in their distress" — fourfold refrain. v. 8, 15, 21, 31 —* yodu la-YHWH chasdo *= "let them thank YHWH [for] His loyal-love" — fourfold. v. 16 —* daltot n'choshet *= gates of bronze (Isa 45:2). v. 20 —* yishlach d'varo v'yirpa'em *= "He sends His word and heals them." v. 27 —* kol-chochmatam titbala *= "all their wisdom is swallowed." v. 29 —* yakem s'arah li-d'mamah *= "He raises the storm to a whisper/stillness" — cf. Mark 4:39. v. 43 —* yitbon'nu *= let them consider/understand. No* yirah*.*

psalms.title: PSALM 108 — A Song Stitched from Two Others
psalms.body:
You've already read this psalm. Twice. In two different places. And the editors put it back together here for a reason.

Psalm 57 was David in the cave — *my heart is steadfast, I will awaken the dawn.* Psalm 60 was David losing a battle at home while winning one up north — *through God we will do valiantly.* Psalm 108 takes the *ending* of each and makes them one thing.

Here's the first half — the cave song's finish:

**"My heart, God, is steadfast. I will sing and make music with all my soul."**

*Steadfast.* The Hebrew is *nachon* — fixed, established. Psalm 57's word. David said it in a cave with Saul's army outside. Now it's said *from the throne*. Same steadfastness. Different room.

**"Awake, harp and lyre! I will awaken the dawn!"**

*I will awaken the dawn.* Sing first — sun follows. The most defiant line in Book Two, now the opening of a Book Five psalm.

**"I will praise You, Lord, among the nations. I will sing of You among the peoples. Because great is Your love — higher than the heavens. Your faithfulness reaches to the skies."**

*Among the nations.* Book Two's theme. Book Five keeps it.

**"Be exalted, God, above the heavens. Let Your glory be over all the earth."**

Psalm 57's refrain.

Now — the seam. And the second half — Psalm 60's ending:

**"Save us and help us with Your right hand — that those You love may be delivered."**

**"God has spoken from His sanctuary: 'In triumph I will parcel out Shechem — and measure off the Valley of Succoth. Gilead is Mine. Manasseh is Mine. Ephraim is My helmet. Judah is My scepter. Moab is My washbasin. On Edom I toss My sandal. Over Philistia I shout in triumph.'"**

God walking the property. *Mine, Mine, Mine.* Ephraim's His *hat*. Moab's His *foot-bath*. The whole map — inventoried and owned.

**"Who will bring me to the fortified city? Who will lead me to Edom? Is it not You, God — You who have rejected us — and no longer go out with our armies?"**

*You who have rejected us.* David keeps the hard line in. Even in the stitched-together victory song — the honesty stays. *You rejected us. And You're the only One who can fix it.*

**"Give us aid against the enemy — because human help is worthless."**

*Worthless.* *Shav.* Vapor. Psalm 33's horse.

**"With God we will gain the victory — and He will trample down our enemies."**

*With God.* The last line of Psalm 60 — *through God we will do valiantly.*

So — why stitch them?

Because the two halves are the two halves of *faith*. Psalm 57's half is *personal* — *my* heart is steadfast, *I* will wake the dawn. Psalm 60's half is *national* — *us*, *our* armies, *we* will do valiantly. The editors put them together to say: *the steadfast heart in the cave and the army marching on Edom are the same thing.* You don't get one without the other. Private worship — public courage. The dawn you woke alone — becomes the battle you fight together.

And notice what got *left out*. Psalm 57's first six verses — the lions, the net, the pit. Psalm 60's first four — *You've broken us, You've made us stagger.* Gone. Psalm 108 keeps only the *turn* from each. Not because the trouble wasn't real. Because *this* is the song for *after*. When you've been through both — and you want to sing just the part where it held.

That's allowed. Sometimes you sing the whole lament. Sometimes — later — you sing only the *yet*.

Thirteen verses. Here's the shape: *My heart is steadfast — I'll wake the dawn — among the nations. — God owns the map. You rejected us — You're our only help. Human help is vapor. With God — victory.*

Two old songs. One new one. Take the endings of your hardest seasons and *sew them together*. That's a song too.
psalms.notes: *Note on translation: v. 1–5 = Psalm 57:7–11 (with minor variants). v. 6–13 = Psalm 60:5–12. v. 1 —* nachon libi *= my heart is fixed/steadfast. v. 2 —* a'irah shachar *= "I will awaken the dawn." v. 7–9 — divine speech, the land-survey. v. 12 —* shav t'shu'at adam *= "vain [is] the salvation of man." v. 13 —* b'Elohim na'aseh-chayil *= "in/with God we will do valiantly." The compilation is deliberate — Book Five's editors reuse Book Two material to show continuity across the exile. No* yirah*.*

psalms.title: PSALM 109 — I Am Prayer
psalms.body:
This is the hardest psalm to read out loud. And it's in the Bible for exactly that reason.

**"My God, whom I praise — do not remain silent."**

*Whom I praise.* He starts with worship. Then he says everything else.

**"Because people who are wicked and deceitful have opened their mouths against me. They speak against me with lying tongues. With words of hatred they surround me. They attack me without cause."**

*Without cause.* Psalm 35, 69 — unprovoked. He didn't start this.

**"In return for my friendship they accuse me — but I am a man of prayer."**

The Hebrew is stark: *va-ani t'fillah* — *and I — prayer.* Not "I pray." *I AM prayer.* That's all he's got. They've got lawyers and lies and a mob. He's got — *prayer*. He's become it.

**"They repay me evil for good — and hatred for my friendship."**

Psalm 35 again — *I sat with them when they were sick.* Same wound.

Now — the curses. Twenty verses of them. And they're *brutal*. Some read these as David quoting what his *enemies* said about *him* — because verse 20 says *this is what my accusers say*. Some read them as David's own words. Either way — they're *in the book*. Here's the first stretch:

**"Appoint someone evil to oppose my enemy. Let an accuser stand at his right hand. When he is tried — let him be found guilty. May his prayers condemn him."**

*May his prayers condemn him.* The prayers themselves — evidence against him.

**"May his days be few. May another take his place of leadership."**

Acts 1:20 — Peter quoted *this line* about Judas. *Let another take his office.* And they chose Matthias.

**"May his children be fatherless — and his wife a widow. May his children be wandering beggars. May they be driven from their ruined homes. May a creditor seize all he has. May strangers plunder the fruits of his labor. May no one extend kindness to him — or take pity on his fatherless children. May his descendants be cut off. May their names be blotted out from the next generation."**

Stop. Sit with how bad that is. *His children fatherless. Wandering beggars. No pity for the orphans. Blotted out.* David's asking for the *family line* to end.

Why is this in Scripture?

Because *somebody's felt it*. If you've been destroyed by a liar — if someone you fed turned and took everything — there's a place in you where these words *live*. And you've got two choices: act on them, or *pray* them. David *prays* them. He doesn't send the assassin. He doesn't burn the house. He *writes it down and hands it to God*.

That's the whole function of imprecatory psalms. Psalm 58 — a *container*. Psalm 109 — the biggest one. You bring the ugliest thing in you *here* — *to God* — instead of to the person.

**"May the wrongdoing of his fathers be remembered before the Lord. May the sin of his mother never be blotted out. May their sins always remain before the Lord — that He may blot out their name from the earth."**

**"Because he never thought of doing a kindness — but hounded to death the poor and the needy and the brokenhearted. He loved to pronounce a curse — may it come back on him. He found no pleasure in blessing — may it be far from him. He wore cursing as his garment. It entered into his body like water — into his bones like oil. May it be like a cloak wrapped about him — like a belt tied forever around him."**

*He hounded the brokenhearted.* Psalm 34 — *the Lord is close to the brokenhearted*. This man *hunted* them. That's the crime under all the curses — he went after the ones God protects.

*Cursing as his garment.* He *wore* it. And David asks that it *stick*.

**"May this be the Lord's payment to my accusers — to those who speak evil of me."**

*This is what my accusers say* — some translations. Either way — David's done. Verse 20. The curses stop.

And now — the turn. And after twenty verses of that, it's *gentle*:

**"But You, Master — my Lord — deal well with me for Your name's sake. Out of the goodness of Your love — deliver me."**

*But You.* Psalm 102's move. God in the subject position.

**"Because I am poor and needy — and my heart is wounded within me."**

*Wounded.* The Hebrew is *chalal* — pierced. Same word as the slain on a battlefield. His *heart* has been *run through*. The curses weren't strength. They were a *pierced man screaming*.

**"I fade away like an evening shadow. I am shaken off like a locust. My knees give way from fasting. My body is thin and gaunt."**

*Shaken off like a locust.* Brushed off a sleeve. Nothing.

**"I am an object of scorn to my accusers. When they see me — they shake their heads."**

**"Help me, Lord my God. Save me according to Your loyal-love. Let them know that it is Your hand — that You, Lord, have done it."**

*Let them know it's Your hand.* Not mine. He wants the vindication to have *God's* fingerprints — not his.

**"May my accusers be clothed with disgrace — and wrapped in shame as in a cloak."**

One last echo of the curses. Then — done.

**"With my mouth I will greatly extol the Lord. In the great throng of worshipers I will praise Him."**

*In the throng.* Publicly. The pierced man — *singing* in a crowd.

And the last verse:

**"Because He stands at the right hand of the needy — to save their lives from those who would condemn them."**

*At the right hand of the needy.* Verse 6 asked for an *accuser* at the enemy's right hand. Verse 31 — *God* stands at the *needy man's* right hand. The place of the prosecutor — filled by the *Defender*. Romans 8:34 — *who is he that condemns? Christ is at the right hand of God, interceding.*

Thirty-one verses. Here's the shape: *I am prayer. They repaid friendship with hatred. — Twenty verses of the worst thing a human can wish on another. — But You. I'm poor. My heart is PIERCED. I'm a locust brushed off a sleeve. Save me — let them know it's Your hand. I'll praise You in the crowd. He stands at the right hand of the needy.*

Here's what to do with Psalm 109: when the rage is that big — bring it *here*. Say every word. To *God*. Then stop at verse 21. And let the One standing at your right hand handle the rest.

You don't have to be the accuser. That seat's taken — and not by you.
psalms.notes: *Note on translation: v. 4 —* va-ani t'fillah *= "and I — prayer" — verbless; "I am [a man of] prayer." v. 6–19 — the imprecations; some scholars (and the NIV footnote) read v. 6–19 as the enemies' words quoted, based on v. 20; the traditional reading is David's own. Both are defensible; the psalm's function as container for rage holds either way. v. 8 —* p'kudato yikach acher *= "his office let another take" — Acts 1:20. v. 16 —* nichei levav *= brokenhearted. v. 22 —* libi chalal b'kirbi *= "my heart is pierced within me" —* chalal *= slain, pierced through. v. 23 —* ka-arbeh *= like a locust. v. 31 —* ya'amod li-y'min evyon *= "He stands at the right hand of the needy" — inversion of v. 6. No* yirah*.*

psalms.title: PSALM 110 — Sit at My Right Hand
psalms.body:
Seven verses. And the whole New Testament kept reaching for them.

**"The Lord says to my Master: 'Sit at My right hand — until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.'"**

Read the pronouns. *The Lord* — YHWH — *says to my Master* — *adoni*, my lord. David — the *king* — is calling someone *his* lord. Who outranks David?

Jesus asked the Pharisees exactly that. Matthew 22. *If David calls him Lord — how is he David's son?* They couldn't answer. Because the answer is: *the Son of David who's also David's Lord.* Born after him. Ranked above him.

*Sit at My right hand.* The seat of honor. Not standing — *seated*. Work finished. Psalm 2 — *I have set My King on the hill.* Here — *sit.* Hebrews 1:3 — *He sat down at the right hand.* Hebrews 10:12 — the priests *stood* daily offering sacrifices that never finished. *This* one *sat*. Because it was done.

*Until I make your enemies a footstool.* God's the one doing the making. The King *sits*. The Father *works*. 1 Corinthians 15:25 — *He must reign until He has put all enemies under His feet.*

**"The Lord will extend your mighty scepter from Zion. You will rule in the midst of your enemies."**

*In the midst of.* Not after they're gone. *Among* them. Psalm 23's table *in the presence of my enemies*. The King rules while they're still in the room.

**"Your troops will be willing on your day of battle. Arrayed in holy splendor — your young men will come to you like dew from the morning's womb."**

*Willing.* The Hebrew is *n'davot* — freewill offerings. Psalm 54's word. The army isn't drafted. They *volunteer*. They come because they *want* to.

*Like dew from the morning's womb.* Dew appears at dawn — silently, everywhere, out of nowhere. That's the army. Not marching in formation. *Appearing*. Fresh. Countless. Born from the morning.

And then — the verse Hebrews spent chapters on:

**"The Lord has sworn — and will not change His mind: 'You are a priest forever — in the order of Melchizedek.'"**

*Sworn. Will not change His mind.* An *oath*. Psalm 89 — *I will not lie to David.* God doesn't swear casually.

*A priest forever.* Wait. Kings weren't priests. Priests weren't kings. Israel *separated* them — Saul lost his kingdom for offering a sacrifice. And here — God swears the King is *also* the Priest. *Forever.*

*In the order of Melchizedek.* Genesis 14. One scene. Abraham comes back from battle — and a man named Melchizedek — *king of Salem* and *priest of God Most High* — brings him bread and wine and blesses him. And Abraham *tithes* to him. Then he vanishes from the story.

King *and* priest. Of *Jerusalem* — *Salem*. Before Aaron. Before Levi. Before the Law. And *Abraham* — the father of everything — bows to *him*.

Hebrews 7 says: *that's the order Jesus belongs to.* Not Aaron's — which had to keep repeating. Melchizedek's — which had no beginning, no end, no successor. *A priest forever.* The One who brought bread and wine and blessed the father of the faith — and then showed up again with bread and wine in an upper room.

**"The Master is at your right hand. He will crush kings on the day of His wrath. He will judge the nations — heaping up the dead — and crushing the rulers of the whole earth."**

The warrior verses. The King who *sat* — also *fights*. Revelation 19 — the rider on the white horse. It's not one or the other. Seated *and* riding.

And the last verse — cryptic and worth the puzzle:

**"He will drink from a brook along the way — and so He will lift up His head."**

*Drink from a brook.* A soldier on the march — stopping at a stream. Human. Thirsty. Gideon's men drank from the brook before the battle. And the One who drinks — *lifts up His head*. Refreshed. Ready. The Priest-King who sits at the right hand — also *gets thirsty*. Also *stops for water*. John 4 — *give Me a drink*. John 19 — *I thirst*.

Seven verses. Here's the shape: *The Lord says to David's Lord — SIT. Rule among your enemies. Your army volunteers — like dew. You're a Priest forever — Melchizedek's order — sworn, unchangeable. The Master at your right hand crushes kings. And He drinks from a brook and lifts His head.*

Jesus quoted this to shut the Pharisees up. Peter quoted it to open three thousand hearts. Hebrews quoted it to explain why there's no more sacrifice.

Here's what it means for you: *the One who sits at God's right hand is your Priest.* Not a priest who has to keep going back in. *Forever.* The bread and wine He brought Abraham — He brings you. And He *sat down* — because the work's done.

Your enemies aren't a footstool yet. That's fine. He's *sitting*. The Father's working. *Until.*
psalms.notes: *Note on translation: v. 1 —* ne'um YHWH la-adoni *= "utterance of YHWH to my lord" — YHWH speaks to David's superior; Matt 22:41–46, Mark 12:35–37, Acts 2:34–35, Heb 1:13. v. 1 —* shev li-y'mini *= "sit at My right hand." v. 3 —* n'davot *= freewill offerings / willing ones;* me-rechem mishchar *= "from the womb of dawn." v. 4 —* nishba YHWH v'lo yinachem *= "YHWH has sworn and will not relent";* kohen l'olam al-divrati Malki-Tzedek *= "priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek" — Gen 14:18–20; Heb 5:6, 10; 6:20; 7:1–28. v. 7 —* mi-nachal ba-derech yishteh *= "from a brook on the way he drinks" — difficult; the humanity of the warrior-priest. Most-quoted psalm in the NT. No* yirah*.*

psalms.title: PSALM 111 — The Beginning of Wisdom
psalms.body:
Ten verses. Twenty-two lines. Alphabetical. This is a psalm built to be *memorized* — A to Z, what God is like.

**"Praise the Lord! I will extol the Lord with all my heart — in the council of the upright and in the assembly."**

*Hallelujah.* Then — *with all my heart*. Psalm 86 asked for an *undivided* heart. Here it's *all* of it, in public. *In the council. In the assembly.* Not private devotion. *Out loud, in the room.*

**"Great are the works of the Lord. They are pondered by all who delight in them."**

*Pondered.* The Hebrew is *d'rushim* — sought out, studied, investigated. God's works aren't just admired. They're *researched* — by people who *delight* in doing it. Faith with a magnifying glass.

**"Glorious and majestic are His deeds. His right-standing endures forever."**

**"He has caused His wonders to be remembered. The Lord is gracious and compassionate."**

*Caused to be remembered.* Psalm 105 — God's memory. Here — He makes *you* remember. Passover. Sabbath. The festivals. He *built* memory aids into the calendar so the wonders wouldn't slip.

*Gracious and compassionate.* Exodus 34 — the self-description. Psalm 103's words.

**"He provides food for those who stand in awe of Him. He remembers His covenant forever."**

*Provides food.* Psalm 104 — *You open Your hand.* For the ones in *awe* — *yirah*. Wonder gets fed.

*Remembers His covenant forever.* Psalm 105:8. Same words. The acrostic's building the same portrait.

**"He has shown His people the power of His works — giving them the lands of other nations."**

**"The works of His hands are faithful and just. All His precepts are trustworthy. They are established forever and ever — enacted in faithfulness and uprightness."**

*Trustworthy.* The Hebrew is *ne'emanim* — reliable, faithful. His *rules* are as reliable as His *works*. You can lean on both.

**"He provided redemption for His people. He ordained His covenant forever — holy and awesome is His name."**

*Awesome.* *Nora.* *Yirah* again — as a *name*. Psalm 99 — *great and awesome name*.

And now — the last verse. The one you've heard wrong your whole life:

**"The awe of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. All who follow His precepts have good understanding. To Him belongs eternal praise."**

*The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom.* That's how it's been printed for four hundred years. Proverbs 1:7, Proverbs 9:10, Job 28:28 — same sentence. And every kid who heard it in Sunday school learned that being *afraid of God* is where smart starts.

It's not. The Hebrew is *yirat YHWH* — *yirah*. The word this whole project has been correcting since Psalm 2. *Awe.* Wonder. The gasp at the Grand Canyon. The thing that makes you go quiet in front of something too big.

*The AWE of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.*

Think about what that changes. Wisdom doesn't start with *dread*. It starts with *wonder*. With looking up at the sky — Psalm 8 — and asking *what is man?* With watching the sea run when He speaks — Psalm 104 — and going *oh*. With standing in front of the ear He built — Psalm 94 — and realizing *He hears*. The person who's *amazed* by God is the one who starts getting *smart*. The person who's *scared* of God just gets *small*.

Every culture has a version of the scared-of-God person. Hiding. Bargaining. Performing. That's not wisdom. That's *anxiety with a religious label*. The wise one is the one who's *stopped* being afraid — because they've seen enough to be *astonished* instead.

*Beginning.* The Hebrew is *reshit* — the Genesis 1:1 word. *In the beginning.* Awe is where wisdom *starts*. The first thing. Everything else — the study, the precepts, the understanding — grows from the gasp.

*All who follow His precepts have good understanding.* The awe leads to the *doing*. Psalm 34 — *I will teach you awe: keep your tongue from evil, do good, seek peace.* Same sequence. Wonder → action → understanding.

*To Him belongs eternal praise.* The last line. The alphabet ends where it should — in praise.

Ten verses. Twenty-two lines. Here's the shape: *Hallelujah — all my heart, in public. His works are STUDIED by people who delight in them. He built memory into the calendar. He feeds the ones in awe. His rules are as reliable as His works. His name is awesome. — The AWE of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.*

Not fear. Never fear. *Awe.* Go stand in front of something too big to understand — and start getting wise.
psalms.notes: *Note on translation: Acrostic — 22 half-lines, alef to tav. v. 2 —* d'rushim l'chol-cheftzeihem *= "sought out by all who delight in them." v. 4 —* zecher asah l'nifl'otav *= "a memorial He made for His wonders." v. 5 —* li-re'av *=* yirah *= to those who stand in awe of Him. v. 9 —* nora sh'mo *=* yirah *= awesome [is] His name. v. 10 —* reshit chochmah yirat YHWH *= "the beginning of wisdom [is] the awe of YHWH" —* yirah*. THE key correction of this project. "Fear" is a mistranslation that has taught generations to dread God; the Hebrew is awe/reverence/wonder. Cf. Prov 1:7, 9:10; Job 28:28.* reshit *= beginning (Gen 1:1).*

psalms.title: PSALM 112 — He Will Not Be Afraid of Bad News
psalms.body:
Psalm 111 ended: *the awe of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.* Psalm 112 opens by describing the person who *has* it.

**"Praise the Lord! Happy is the one who stands in awe of the Lord — who finds great delight in His commands."**

*Hallelujah.* Then — *happy*. *Ashrei.* Psalm 1's word. And *who stands in awe* — *yirah*. The 111:10 person. What does their life look like?

*Great delight in His commands.* Psalm 1 — *delights in the instruction*. Psalm 19 — *sweeter than honey*. The awe-person doesn't *tolerate* the rules. They *enjoy* them. Because the rules came from the One they're amazed by.

**"Their children will be mighty in the land. The generation of the upright will be blessed."**

*Their children.* Psalm 78's chain. Psalm 103's *children's children*. The awe *transfers*.

**"Wealth and riches are in their houses — and their right-standing endures forever."**

*Wealth.* Yes, it says that. Not as a formula — Psalm 73 already destroyed the "righteous get rich" formula. As a *description*: the awe-person tends to have *enough*. Because they don't waste it on Psalm 62's vapor.

**"Even in darkness light dawns for the upright — for the one who is gracious and compassionate and right."**

*Even in darkness.* Psalm 97 — *light is sown for the righteous*. Here it *dawns*. Not "the upright never see darkness." *Even IN it* — light comes.

*Gracious and compassionate.* Stop. Those are *God's* words. Exodus 34. Psalm 103:8, 111:4 — *the Lord is gracious and compassionate*. And now — the *person in awe* is described with the *same two words*. That's the point of the twin psalms. Psalm 111: *God is gracious and compassionate.* Psalm 112: *the one in awe of Him becomes gracious and compassionate.* You turn into what you're amazed by.

**"Good will come to those who are generous and lend freely — who conduct their affairs with justice."**

*Generous. Lend freely.* Psalm 37 — *the righteous is generous and gives*. The awe-person's *hands are open* — because they've watched God's hand open (Psalm 104).

And then — the verse. The one that matters most for actual life:

**"Surely the righteous will never be shaken. They will be remembered forever. They will have no fear of bad news. Their heart is steadfast — trusting in the Lord."**

*Never be shaken.* The word — Psalm 15, 16, 21, 30, 46, 55, 62. Eight times now. *Not moved.*

*No fear of bad news.* Read that slow. Not "no bad news comes." *No FEAR of it.* The phone rings at 2 a.m. The test results come back. The email arrives. And the awe-person — *isn't afraid*. Not because they're numb. Because their heart is *steadfast* — Psalm 57, 108's *nachon*. Fixed. Already anchored to something the bad news can't move.

This is the practical payoff of *awe* over *fear*. The person who's *afraid of God* is afraid of *everything* — because they've been trained to expect the worst from the top. The person who's *in awe of God* has looked at the thing bigger than any bad news — and the bad news shrinks.

**"Their heart is secure. They will have no fear. In the end they will look in triumph on their foes."**

*Secure.* The Hebrew is *samuch* — supported, leaned-on. Like a wall you can put your back against.

**"They have freely scattered their gifts to the poor. Their right-standing endures forever. Their horn will be lifted high in honor."**

*Scattered.* Psalm 97's *sown*. They *throw* it — to the poor. Not carefully budgeted charity. *Scattered.* 2 Corinthians 9:9 — Paul quotes *this verse* about generous giving.

*Their horn lifted.* Psalm 75, 89, 92 — the horn of the humble, raised.

And the last verse — the contrast:

**"The wicked will see and be vexed. They will gnash their teeth and waste away. The longings of the wicked will come to nothing."**

*Gnash their teeth.* The wicked *watching* the awe-person — steady, generous, unafraid of the phone — and *grinding their molars*. Because they've got everything the awe-person doesn't chase, and none of the *steadiness*.

*Come to nothing.* Psalm 1 — *the way of the wicked will perish*. The twin psalms end where Psalm 1 did.

Ten verses. Here's the shape — and it's the *portrait* of 111:10's wisdom: *Happy is the one in awe — they DELIGHT in the commands. Their kids are strong. They have enough. Light dawns for them even in the dark. They're gracious and compassionate — GOD'S words. They give freely. They're never shaken. NO FEAR OF BAD NEWS — heart steadfast. They scatter to the poor. The wicked watch and grind their teeth.*

Here's the test. What happens in your chest when the phone rings late? If it's dread — you've been trained in fear. If it's steadiness — you've been trained in awe.

Psalm 112 says you can *switch*. Start with the gasp. The steadiness follows.
psalms.notes: *Note on translation: Acrostic — 22 half-lines, twin of Psalm 111. v. 1 —* ashrei-ish yare et-YHWH *= "happy [is] the man in awe of YHWH" —* yirah*. v. 4 —* chanun v'rachum v'tzadik *= "gracious and compassionate and righteous" — the divine attributes of Exod 34:6 / Ps 111:4 applied to the human. v. 6 —* l'olam lo-yimot *= "forever he will not be moved." v. 7 —* mi-sh'mu'ah ra'ah lo yira *= "of bad news he will not fear" — ordinary human dread (*yare*), correctly rendered as fear; the point is its ABSENCE in the one who has* yirah *of God. v. 8 —* samuch libo *= supported/secure [is] his heart. v. 9 —* pizar natan la-evyonim *= "he scattered, he gave to the needy" — 2 Cor 9:9.*

psalms.title: PSALM 113 — He Raises the Poor from the Dust
psalms.body:
Passover night. The lamb's eaten. The cups are poured. And the family sings — *these* psalms. 113 and 114 before the meal. 115 through 118 after. The last thing Jesus sang with His disciples was Psalm 118. The first was *this*.

**"Praise the Lord! Praise, you servants of the Lord — praise the name of the Lord."**

*Hallelujah.* Three *praises* in one verse. The Hallel — "praise" — earning its name.

**"Let the name of the Lord be praised — both now and forevermore. From the rising of the sun to the place where it sets — the name of the Lord is to be praised."**

*Now and forever. Sunrise to sunset.* Time and space — both covered. Every hour, every longitude. Psalm 19 — *nothing hides from its heat*. Here — *nothing's outside the praise*.

**"The Lord is exalted over all the nations. His glory is above the heavens."**

*Above the heavens.* Psalm 8 — *You've set Your glory above the heavens.* He's *higher* than the highest thing.

**"Who is like the Lord our God — the One who sits enthroned on high —"**

And then — the turn. The whole psalm is in the next line:

**"— who stoops down to look on the heavens and the earth?"**

*Stoops down.* The Hebrew is *ha-mashpili lir'ot* — *the One who lowers Himself to see*. He's *so high* that the *heavens themselves* are *below* Him — and He has to *bend* to look at them. Not at earth. At *heaven*. The sky is *down* from where He sits.

And He bends anyway.

That's the paradox the Hallel is built on. *Exalted over all the nations* — and *stoops*. Psalm 18 — *He bent the heavens and came down*. Psalm 40 — *He bent down to me and heard my cry*. The higher He is, the *further* the stoop. And He stoops *all the way*.

Now — what He does when He gets down there:

**"He raises the poor from the dust — and lifts the needy from the ash heap."**

*From the dust. From the ash heap.* The garbage pile outside the city. Where the lepers sat. Where Job sat. The lowest physical place a human could be. And God *reaches into it* and *lifts*.

*Raises. Lifts.* Two verbs. Same motion. *Up.*

**"— He seats them with princes — with the princes of His people."**

*With princes.* Not "gives them a meal and sends them off." *Seats them.* At the table. Next to royalty. The ash-heap person — *at the head table*. Psalm 23 — *You prepare a table before me.* Psalm 68 — *He sets the lonely in families.*

This is Hannah's song — 1 Samuel 2. *He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap. He seats them with princes.* Word for word. A barren woman who'd been mocked for years — praying it over a baby she thought she'd never have.

And it's *Mary's* song — Luke 1. *He has brought down rulers from their thrones — and lifted up the humble.* A teenage girl in a backwater town, pregnant with the One who'd sing this psalm at His last Passover.

**"He settles the childless woman in her home — as a happy mother of children."**

*The childless woman.* Hannah. Sarah. Rachel. Elizabeth. The ancient world's deepest shame — *barren*. And God *settles her* — gives her a *home* — makes her *a happy mother*. The Hebrew is *em ha-banim s'mechah* — *the mother of the children, rejoicing*. Psalm 68's *lonely in families* — with a *nursery*.

If you've been the one on the outside of the thing everyone else has — this verse. He *settles* you.

**"Praise the Lord!"**

*Hallelujah.* Bookend.

Nine verses. Here's the shape: *Praise — now, forever, sunrise to sunset. He's above the heavens. Who's like Him — so high He has to STOOP to see the sky — and stoops all the way down to the ash heap — and lifts the poor out of it — and seats them with PRINCES — and gives the barren woman a home full of kids. Hallelujah.*

Jesus sang this the night before the cross. *He stoops down.* And then He went and did it — all the way to the ash heap, all the way to the dust — so He could seat you with princes.

Passover starts here. So does everything.
psalms.notes: *Note on translation: Egyptian Hallel = Psalms 113–118, sung at Passover (Mishnah Pesachim 10). v. 1 —* hallelu *x3. v. 3 —* mi-mizrach-shemesh ad-m'vo'o *= "from the rising of the sun to its going." v. 5–6 —* ha-magbihi la-shavet ha-mashpili lir'ot *= "the One exalting to sit — the One lowering to see" — deliberate paradox;* ba-shamayim u-va-aretz *= "in the heavens and in the earth" — He stoops to see even heaven. v. 7 —* me-afar / me-ashpot *= from dust / from the ash heap (dung heap) — 1 Sam 2:8 verbatim. v. 8 —* im-n'divim *= with nobles/princes. v. 9 —* akeret ha-bayit *= barren one of the house;* em ha-banim s'mechah *= "mother of the children, joyful" — cf. Luke 1:52. No* yirah*.*

psalms.title: PSALM 114 — The Mountains Skipped Like Rams
psalms.body:
Second Hallel psalm. Sung before the Passover meal. The whole Exodus in eight verses — and the *landscape* is the main character.

**"When Israel came out of Egypt — the house of Jacob from a people of foreign tongue —"**

*A people of foreign tongue.* They couldn't understand their masters. Four hundred years in a place where the language wasn't theirs. That's exile — not just captivity. *Not being understood.*

**"— Judah became God's sanctuary. Israel His dominion."**

*Became His sanctuary.* Not "built a sanctuary." *Became* one. The *people* were the holy place — before there was a temple. Psalm 90 — *You have been our dwelling place.* Here — *we're His.* 1 Corinthians 3 — *you are the temple.*

Now — the earth reacts. And it's *physical comedy*:

**"The sea looked and fled. The Jordan turned back."**

*The sea LOOKED.* Saw something. Saw *Who* was coming. And *ran*. Psalm 77 — *the waters saw You and writhed*. Here — *fled*. The Red Sea didn't part. It *bolted*.

*The Jordan turned back.* Forty years later — Joshua 3 — the river stopped and *reversed*. Two bodies of water. Two retreats. Same cause.

**"The mountains leaped like rams. The hills like lambs."**

*Leaped like rams.* Sinai — Exodus 19 — *the whole mountain trembled violently*. Psalm 29 — *He makes Lebanon skip like a calf*. But here it's *rams and lambs*. A *flock* of mountains. *Bouncing.* Not in terror — in the way young animals bounce when the shepherd shows up. The hills are *excited*.

Psalm 68 — *why do you look with envy, you many-peaked mountains?* Psalm 114 — they've stopped being jealous. They're *playing*.

And now — the psalmist stops narrating and *talks to the geography*:

**"Why was it, sea, that you fled? Why, Jordan, did you turn back? Why, mountains, did you leap like rams? You hills — like lambs?"**

*Why, sea?* He's *interviewing the water*. *What did you see? What made you run?* Four questions to four features. Like a reporter at the scene.

And they don't answer. Because the answer's obvious. Verse 7:

**"Tremble, earth, at the presence of the Master — at the presence of the God of Jacob —"**

*At the presence.* That's why. Not a command. Not a threat. *Presence.* He *showed up* — and the sea *left*. The river *reversed*. The mountains *bounced*. Nothing was ordered. Everything *reacted*.

That's what presence does. You don't have to be told to move when the King walks in. Your legs do it.

**"— who turned the rock into a pool — the hard rock into springs of water."**

The last verse. After the sea running and the mountains leaping — *water from rock*. Exodus 17. Numbers 20. Psalm 78, 105. The thing that *shouldn't* give water — *gave it*. The hardest surface in the desert — a *spring*.

Look at the pattern. The sea — *should* be water — *fled*. The rock — *shouldn't* be water — *poured*. God reverses both. Where you expect the flow, He dries it. Where you expect the stone, He opens it.

If you're the rock — hard, dry, the one nobody expects anything from — this is the verse. *The hard rock into springs.*

Eight verses. Here's the shape: *Out of Egypt — from people who couldn't understand them. They BECAME the sanctuary. The sea saw and RAN. The Jordan reversed. The mountains bounced like rams. — Why, sea? Why, mountains? — Presence. He walked in. And the rock became a spring.*

Jesus sang this before the last meal. *The sea fled at His presence.* Then He went to the garden. Then the soldiers came. And for one moment — John 18:6 — *they drew back and fell to the ground* when He said *I am He.*

The sea's not the only thing that steps back when He shows up.
psalms.notes: *Note on translation: v. 1 —* me-am lo'ez *= "from a people of strange/stammering speech." v. 2 —* haytah Y'hudah l'kodsho *= "Judah became His holiness/sanctuary." v. 3 —* ha-yam ra'ah va-yanos *= "the sea saw and fled." v. 4 —* rak'du ch'elim *= skipped like rams;* ki-v'nei-tzon *= like sons of the flock (lambs). v. 5–6 — direct address to sea, Jordan, mountains, hills — apostrophe. v. 7 —* mi-lifnei Adon *= "from before the Master" — presence, not command. v. 8 —* ha-hofchi ha-tzur agam-mayim *= "the One turning the rock [into] a pool of water" — Exod 17:6, Num 20:11. No* yirah*.*

psalms.title: PSALM 115 — Those Who Make Them Will Be Like Them
psalms.body:
The meal's over. The cups are refilled. And the family sings about *idols*. Because Passover is the night you remember which God actually showed up.

**"Not to us, Lord — not to us — but to Your name be the glory — because of Your loyal-love and faithfulness."**

*Not to us.* Twice. The night they remember being *rescued* — and the first thing they say is *we didn't do it*. No credit taken. *Your name.*

**"Why do the nations say: 'Where is their God?'"**

Psalm 42, 79 — the taunt. *Where is He?* And the answer:

**"Our God is in heaven. He does whatever pleases Him."**

*Whatever pleases Him.* Not "whatever we ask." Not "whatever the nations expect." *Whatever He pleases.* That's the answer to *where is He* — He's *free*. Not on a leash. Not in a box. The nations want to see Him because they think gods live in boxes. Theirs do.

Now — the idol section. And it's *funny*. Deliberately:

**"But their idols are silver and gold — made by human hands."**

*Made by human hands.* That's the whole problem in five words. You *made* it. How's it going to save you?

**"They have mouths — but cannot speak. Eyes — but cannot see. They have ears — but cannot hear. Noses — but cannot smell. They have hands — but cannot feel. Feet — but cannot walk. Nor can they utter a sound with their throats."**

Seven body parts. Seven failures. *Mouth — silent. Eyes — blind. Ears — deaf. Nose — no smell. Hands — numb. Feet — stuck. Throat — nothing.* The idol's got *everything* a god should have — and *none* of it works. It's a mannequin. A very expensive mannequin.

Psalm 94 — *He who made the ear — does He not hear?* Psalm 115 — *they made an ear — and it can't.* God builds ears that work. Humans build ears that don't.

And then — the verse. The one that should scare you a little:

**"Those who make them will be like them — and so will all who trust in them."**

*Like them.*

You become what you worship. That's the law. Trust the silent thing — you go silent. Trust the blind thing — you stop seeing. Trust the thing with hands that can't feel — your hands go numb. The idol doesn't just *fail* you. It *shapes* you. Into itself.

Psalm 112 said the opposite: *the one in awe of God becomes gracious and compassionate — God's words.* Psalm 115: *the one who trusts the idol becomes deaf, blind, and mute — the idol's words.* Same principle. Different direction. You *always* turn into what you're looking at.

What's your idol? The thing you trust that has no ears? The phone. The number in the account. The approval. Look at it hard — *does it hear you?* Then look at what it's doing to your *hearing*.

Now — the turn. Three groups, one command:

**"All you Israelites — trust in the Lord. He is their help and shield. House of Aaron — trust in the Lord. He is their help and shield. You who stand in awe of Him — trust in the Lord. He is their help and shield."**

*Israel. Aaron. Those in awe.* The people, the priests, and — *the ones in awe*. That third group isn't ethnic. It's not a bloodline. It's *anyone amazed by Him*. Psalm 87 — *born in Zion*. The circle widens to *whoever's gasping*.

*Help and shield.* Three times. The idol has hands that can't feel. God is *help and shield* — hands that *work*.

**"The Lord remembers us and will bless us. He will bless His people Israel. He will bless the house of Aaron. He will bless those who stand in awe of Him — small and great alike."**

*Remembers.* Psalm 105, 106 — He *remembers*. *Small and great alike.* No tier system. The kid and the king — same blessing.

**"May the Lord cause you to flourish — both you and your children."**

*Your children.* Psalm 78, 103, 112. Always the kids.

**"Praise be to the Lord — the Maker of heaven and earth."**

*Maker.* Not made. The idols were *made by hands*. The Lord *made the hands*.

**"The highest heavens belong to the Lord — but the earth He has given to mankind."**

*Given to mankind.* Psalm 8 — *You made him ruler over the works of Your hands*. The earth's *yours*. Steward it. Don't build gods out of it.

And then — the reason to praise *now*:

**"It is not the dead who praise the Lord — those who go down to the place of silence. It is we who extol the Lord — both now and forevermore."**

*Not the dead.* Psalm 6, 30, 88 — *can dust praise You?* The Hallel's answer: *no — so praise while you're breathing.* The idol has a throat that can't make a sound. The dead have the same problem. *You* don't. Yet. Use it.

**"Praise the Lord!"**

Eighteen verses. Here's the shape: *Not to us — to Your name. Where's our God? In heaven, doing what He pleases. Their idols — mouth, eyes, ears, nose, hands, feet, throat — all broken. And you become what you trust. — Israel, Aaron, everyone in awe — trust the Lord. He's help and shield. He blesses small and great. He made heaven and earth. The dead can't praise — so praise NOW.*
