**"My son, if you receive my words and store up my commands inside you —"** that's the first if. Not just hear them. *Store* them. The Hebrew is *titzpon*, the word for hiding treasure. Put my words where you put the things you can't afford to lose.

**"— making your ear attentive to wisdom, bending your heart toward understanding —"** so it's active. You lean your ear in. You tilt your heart. Wisdom doesn't fall into a slouching man.

**"— if you call out for insight, raise your voice for understanding —"** that's prayer. That's asking. You heard Lady Wisdom yell in chapter one; now you're supposed to yell back.

And then verse four, the line that makes the chapter: **"if you seek it like silver and search for it like hidden treasure —"**

Think about what people do for silver. They dig. They go underground. They sweat for years. They get up before dawn and go back into the dark for one more vein. Nobody ever found a treasure by *hoping*. The father is saying: bring *that* energy. Bring the energy of a man who knows there's gold under the floor.

Now the *then*. Verse five: **"then you will understand the AWE of God, and find the knowledge of God."**

Read that again slowly, because the order matters. Chapter one said awe is the *beginning* of knowledge. Chapter two says awe is also what you *arrive at* when you dig. It's both. It's the doorway and the room. You start in awe, you dig, and you come up into deeper awe. And the word is *yirah* — awe, not fear. Nobody digs for years to arrive at terror. You dig to arrive at *wonder*. That's what's down there.

Why does the digging work? Verse six: **"Because God gives wisdom; from His mouth come knowledge and understanding."** It's not that you're smart enough to mine it. It's that He's already put it there and He *wants* you to find it. **"He stores up success for the upright; He is a shield to those who walk with integrity."** Same word — *stores up*. You store His words; He stores your success. It's a two-way vault.

Verses eight and nine: He guards the paths of justice and watches over the way of His loyal ones — then **you** will understand right-standing and justice and fairness, **"every good path."** He's guarding the road. You're learning to walk it. That's the partnership.

Verse ten: **"For wisdom will enter your heart, and knowledge will be pleasant to your soul."** Pleasant. *Yin'am*. Wisdom isn't supposed to taste like medicine. When it's real, when it's yours, it feels *good*. **"Discretion will watch over you; understanding will guard you."** Chapter one said your parents' wisdom is a necklace. Chapter two says it's a bodyguard.

Now — guard you from what? Two roads. And the father spends the back half of the chapter on them.

Road one, verses twelve through fifteen: **"to rescue you from the way of evil, from the man who speaks twisted things — those who abandon the straight paths to walk in dark ways, who are glad to do evil and celebrate the perversity of evil, whose paths are crooked and who are devious in their tracks."**

That's the crew from chapter one, grown up. These are the men who don't just do wrong — they *enjoy* it. Verse fourteen: they *rejoice* in it. That's the tell. Everybody slips. But watch for the ones who slip and then high-five about it. Those are the ones with the crooked tracks, and Wisdom's job is to make you notice the tracks before you're on them.

Road two, verses sixteen through nineteen: **"to rescue you from the strange woman, from the foreign woman with her smooth words, who abandons the companion of her youth and forgets the covenant of her God."**

Now, careful here. "Strange woman" — *ishah zarah* — doesn't mean a foreigner and it doesn't mean women are the problem. Proverbs is written father-to-son, so the temptation wears a female face; if it were mother-to-daughter, it'd wear a male one. The point is the *type*: someone who has already walked out on their own promises — left their partner, forgotten their covenant — and is now talking sweet to you. Someone who broke faith once and is inviting you to be the next break. That's the danger. Not gender. Faithlessness with a nice voice.

And the father is brutal about where that road goes. Verse eighteen: **"Her house sinks down to death, her tracks lead to the shades."** *Refa'im* — the dead, the ghosts. This isn't hell. It's the grave, the same Sheol-silence you learned in the Psalms. The road of the covenant-breaker doesn't end in fire. It ends in *nothing*. Verse nineteen: **"None who go to her come back, nor do they reach the paths of life."** That's the sound of a door that doesn't reopen. He's not threatening you. He's describing a one-way street so you don't take it.

Then he lifts his head. Verses twenty through twenty-two: **"So you will walk in the way of the good and keep to the paths of the right-standing. For the upright will dwell in the land, and the ones with integrity will remain in it — but the mark-missers will be cut off from the land, and the treacherous torn out of it."**

The land. That's the promise-language. Psalm 37 — the humble inherit the land. Proverbs is saying the same thing without the poetry: the people who dig for wisdom and walk straight get to *stay*. They get roots. The crooked get pulled up.

Here's the shape. It's one sentence. *If* you dig for wisdom like it's silver — *then* you come up into awe, and awe puts a guard on you, and the guard keeps you off two roads: the men who love doing wrong and the sweet-talker who already broke faith. And the ones who stay on the good path get to stay in the land.

Today: pick the thing you'd dig for if you knew it was buried under your house. Then ask yourself whether you've ever gone after wisdom with a tenth of that effort. Grab a shovel.
proverbs.notes: *Note on translation: 2:5* yirat YHWH *— "the fear of the LORD" in KJV — rendered "AWE of God." Here awe is the* result *of the search (v. 4→5), complementing 1:7 where it is the beginning; the chapter shows awe as both threshold and destination. 2:1* titzpon *("hide/store up") is treasure vocabulary, echoed in 2:7* yitzpon *(He stores up success) — a deliberate two-way echo. 2:4* matmonim *= buried treasure. 2:8* chasidav *= His loyal ones. 2:10* yin'am *= will be pleasant. 2:16* ishah zarah / nochriyah *— "strange/foreign woman" — is a type (the covenant-breaker with smooth speech), not an ethnic or gender statement; 2:17 makes this explicit: she has abandoned the* alluf ne'ureha *(companion of her youth) and forgotten the* berit *(covenant) of her God. 2:18* refa'im *= the shades / the dead — the grave, not hell; consistent with the Sheol treatment in the Psalms. 2:21–22* eretz *= the land, promise-language paralleling Ps 37:9, 11, 22, 29. Yirah in this chapter: 2:5.*

proverbs.title: PROVERB 3 — Trust With Your Whole Chest
proverbs.body:
You've probably had verse five and six on a coffee mug. Let's earn them this time.

**"My son, don't forget my teaching; keep my commands in your heart. They'll add length of days and years of life and peace to you."** *Shalom* — wholeness. Wisdom isn't just about living longer. It's about living *whole*.

Verse three: **"Don't let loyal-love and truth leave you; tie them around your neck, write them on the tablet of your heart."** *Chesed* and *emet* — you know those words from the Psalms. Loyal-love and faithfulness. God's own character words. The father says: wear them. Carve them into you. And then verse four: **"you'll find favor and good sense in the eyes of God and people."** Both. This isn't holy-but-useless. This is the kind of person everybody — heaven and the neighborhood — wants around.

Now the mug verses.

**"Trust in God with all your heart, and don't lean on your own understanding. In all your ways know Him, and He will make your paths straight."**

Hear what it actually says. "Trust with *all* your heart" — *b'chol libbecha* — the whole chest. Not the part of you that's got nothing better to do. All of it. "Don't *lean* on your own understanding" — *tishaen*, the word for propping your weight on a staff. You're allowed to *have* understanding. Chapter two just told you to dig for it. You're just not allowed to put all your weight on it, because it'll snap.

And verse six — most translations say "acknowledge Him." The Hebrew is *da'ehu* — *know* Him. In everything you do, know Him. Not tip your hat. *Know*. And then He straightens the path. Not "He'll give you a smooth path" — He'll make it *straight*, meaning you'll stop zigzagging. You'll stop walking in circles because you were leaning on the staff that kept breaking.

Verse seven: **"Don't be wise in your own eyes; stand in AWE of God and turn from evil."** There it is again. *Yirah*. Your Bible says "fear the LORD." But look at the pairing: the opposite of being wise in your own eyes isn't being scared — it's being *humbled by something bigger*. That's awe. The man in awe of the canyon doesn't think he's the biggest thing in the room. **"It will be healing to your body and refreshment to your bones."** Awe is medicine. Fear is a stomach ulcer. The Hebrew knows the difference.

Verses nine and ten: **"Honor God with your wealth, with the first of all your harvest — then your barns will be filled and your vats overflow with new wine."** Give the first, not the leftover. This isn't a money spell. It's an orientation — where the first fruit goes tells the truth about who you think it came from.

Now verses eleven and twelve, and pay attention because Hebrews 12 quotes this to the early church.

**"My son, don't despise the training of God, and don't resent His correction — because God corrects the one He loves, like a father the son he delights in."**

*Musar*. Training. Not punishment — the coach word from chapter one. When life sets you a hard rep, the father says: don't despise it, and don't *resent* it — *taqotz*, the word for being sick of something. Because the correction is proof of the relationship. You don't coach a kid you've given up on. You coach the one you *delight in*. Hebrews 12 picks this up and says the same thing — "whom the Lord loves, He trains" — and then adds: "no discipline seems pleasant at the time." The New Testament writer understood *musar*. It's the gym, not the woodshed.

Then verse thirteen turns and the whole thing goes lyrical. **"Happy is the one who finds wisdom, the one who gets understanding."** *Ashrei* — the Psalm 1 word. Flourishing. **"Her profit is better than silver, her yield better than fine gold. She's more precious than rubies; nothing you desire compares to her."** You dug for silver in chapter two. Here's the payoff: you come up with something worth more than what you were digging for.

Verses sixteen through eighteen: **"Length of days is in her right hand; in her left, riches and honor. Her ways are pleasant ways, and all her paths are peace. She is a tree of life to those who grab hold of her, and whoever holds her fast is happy."**

*A tree of life.* That's Genesis 3. That's the tree at the center of the garden that humanity got locked out of. Proverbs says: it's back. It grew again, and its name is Wisdom, and you can *grab* it — *machazikim*, both hands, white-knuckle. The thing we lost in the garden is standing in the street shouting for us to come take it.

And then verses nineteen and twenty — hold this, because chapter eight is going to blow it wide open: **"God by wisdom founded the earth; by understanding He established the heavens. By His knowledge the deeps broke open and the clouds drip dew."** Wisdom isn't just good advice. Wisdom is what God *used*. It's the blueprint. When you get wise, you're getting aligned with the same thing that laid the foundation of the planet. That's why it works.

Verses twenty-one through twenty-six come back down to you: keep sound judgment and discretion, they'll be life to your soul and grace to your neck. **"Then you'll walk your way securely and your foot won't stumble. When you lie down you won't be afraid; you'll lie down and your sleep will be sweet."** Psalm 3, Psalm 4 — I lay down and slept anyway. Same promise, now as a proverb. **"Don't be afraid of sudden dread, or of the storm that comes on the wicked — because God will be your confidence and will keep your foot from being caught."**

Notice — verse twenty-five says "don't be afraid," and that word is *tira* — real fear. And verse seven said stand in awe — *yirah*. The Hebrew separates them in one chapter: *don't* fear the sudden thing; *do* stand in awe of God. English hands you one word for both and calls it a day. The whole point of the chapter is that these pull in opposite directions. Awe of God is *what makes* the sudden terror lose its grip.

Now the last section, verses twenty-seven through thirty-five, and it's a run of don'ts that are really about being a good neighbor. **"Don't withhold good from the one it's owed to when it's in your power to do it. Don't say 'come back tomorrow, I'll give it to you then' when you've got it right now."** Don't plot against the neighbor who trusts you. Don't pick a fight for no reason. **"Don't envy the violent man or choose any of his ways —"** there's the crew again — **"because the crooked man is detestable to God, but with the upright He shares His secret."** *Sodo* — His confidence, His inner circle. The straight-dealer gets let in on things.

Verse thirty-three: His curse is on the house of the mark-misser; His blessing on the home of the right-standing. Verse thirty-four: **"He mocks the mockers, but gives grace to the humble."** James 4 and 1 Peter 5 both quote that — "God gives grace to the humble." And the last verse: **"The wise inherit honor, but fools lift up shame."** *Kesilim* — the dull ones. They walk around carrying their own disgrace like a trophy and don't know it.

Here's the shape. Trust with the whole chest, not the staff of your own thinking. Awe, not fear — the one that heals your bones. Don't resent the reps; they're proof you're loved. Wisdom is the tree of life, back in reach, and she's the same blueprint God built the universe with. And when you've got it, sleep sweet, and be good to your neighbor.

Today: find the one place you're leaning your whole weight on your own understanding — the thing you're white-knuckling because you're sure you've got it figured out. Loosen the grip. Know Him there instead.
proverbs.notes: *Note on translation: 3:7* yera et-YHWH *— "fear the LORD" in KJV — rendered "stand in AWE of God"; the antithesis to "wise in your own eyes" is humility before greatness, and 3:8 calls it healing (*rif'ut*), confirming the awe reading. 3:25* al-tira mi-pachad *— "be not afraid of sudden fear" — is genuine dread (*pachad*) and is rendered as fear; the chapter uses* yirah *and* pachad/tira *as opposites. 3:5* tishaen *= lean/prop weight on. 3:6* da'ehu *= "know Him," stronger than "acknowledge." 3:11* musar *= training;* taqotz *= be sick of/resent; quoted at Heb 12:5–6 (LXX). 3:12 some MSS/LXX read* yach'iv *("causes pain") vs. MT* uch'av *("and as a father") — MT retained. 3:13* ashrei *= happy/flourishing. 3:18* etz chayyim *= tree of life (Gen 2:9, 3:22);* machazikim *= grasp firmly. 3:19–20 wisdom as creation instrument — seed of Prov 8:22–31. 3:32* sodo *= His secret/inner counsel. 3:34 quoted at James 4:6 and 1 Pet 5:5 via LXX ("God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble"). 3:35* kesilim *= dull fools. Yirah in this chapter: 3:7.*

proverbs.title: PROVERB 4 — Guard the Heart, It's the Wellspring
proverbs.body:
Chapter four opens with something you don't see coming: the father quoting *his* father.

**"Hear, sons, a father's training; pay attention to gain understanding. I'm giving you good teaching — don't abandon my instruction."** And then, verse three: **"When I was a son with my father, tender and the only one in my mother's eyes, he taught me and said to me —"**

Stop there. This is Solomon saying: David sat *me* down. Whether or not it's literally David, the picture is three generations at the table. Wisdom isn't something one guy figures out. It's a *hand-off*. Your grandfather to your father to you. And if you didn't get it that way — if your chain was broken — then this book is offering to be the grandfather you didn't have.

Here's what his father said. Verse four: **"Let your heart hold my words; keep my commands and live. Get wisdom, get understanding; don't forget, don't turn from the words of my mouth."** Verse six: **"Don't abandon her and she'll guard you; love her and she'll keep you."**

And verse seven, which the old Bibles render as "wisdom is the principal thing": **"The beginning of wisdom is: get wisdom."** That's not a typo. The Hebrew is almost comic in its bluntness — *reshit chochmah, qeneh chochmah*. The first step in being wise is *deciding you want to be*. You don't drift into it. You go get it. **"And with everything you own, get understanding."** Sell what you have to. This is chapter two's silver-digging said even shorter.

Verses eight and nine: **"Prize her and she'll lift you up; embrace her and she'll honor you. She'll set a garland of grace on your head; a crown of beauty she'll hand you."** Chapter one — a garland. Chapter three — a necklace. Now a crown. The jewelry keeps upgrading. Wisdom makes you *look like royalty*, not like a scold.

Then verse ten, second lecture, and it's about roads. **"Hear, my son, receive my words and the years of your life will be many. I've guided you in the way of wisdom; I've led you on straight tracks. When you walk, your step won't be hemmed in; when you run, you won't stumble."**

You know Psalm 1. Two ways — the flourishing one and the one that blows away like chaff. Proverbs 4 paints the same picture in a different color. Verse thirteen: **"Hold on to training, don't let go; guard her, because she is your life."** *Musar* again — the coaching. Grip it. It's not a nice-to-have. It's *your life*.

Verses fourteen and fifteen, and hear how many times he says it: **"Don't enter the path of the mark-missers, don't walk the way of the evil. Avoid it. Don't pass on it. Turn from it. Go around."** Four commands for one road. He's not being repetitive by accident. He knows the pull. He knows you'll want to just *look*. He's saying: don't even walk past it.

Why? Verses sixteen and seventeen: **"They can't sleep unless they've done evil; their sleep is stolen unless they've made somebody fall. They eat the bread of wickedness and drink the wine of violence."** These people are *addicted*. That's the diagnosis. Wrongdoing is the thing they need to get to sleep. And you know that if you've been there — the itch that won't let you rest until you've scratched it on somebody.

Then verses eighteen and nineteen, and these are the two best lines in the chapter:

**"The path of the right-standing is like the light of dawn, shining brighter and brighter until full day. The way of the wicked is like deep darkness; they don't know what they're tripping over."**

Sit with that. The good road doesn't start bright. It starts like *dawn* — gray, barely there, you can hardly see. But it gets brighter. Every step, a little more light. The wrong road starts easy — you can see fine at dusk — and then the dark comes down and you're falling over things you can't even identify. That's the whole difference. Not where you are today. Which direction the light is going.

Now the third lecture, verse twenty, and it walks down the body.

**"My son, pay attention to my words; bend your ear to what I say. Don't let them leave your eyes; keep them in the middle of your heart. Because they are life to those who find them, and healing to all their flesh."** Healing again — *marpe*. Chapter three said awe heals your bones. Chapter four says wisdom heals your flesh. This book keeps insisting that living right is *good for your body*.

And then verse twenty-three. This is the one.

**"Above everything you guard, guard your heart — because out of it flow the springs of life."**

*Mikol mishmar* — more than any other watch-post. If you've only got one guard to station, put him here. The heart in Hebrew isn't the feelings — it's the *control room*. Mind, will, decision, desire — all of it. And it's a wellspring. *Totz'ot chayyim* — the outlets, the outflows of life. Everything you do comes up out of it. Poison the spring, poison the whole river. Keep the spring clean, and even the ordinary days downstream run clear.

Jesus said the same thing — "out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks." Out of the heart come the things that make a person unclean. He'd read this verse. He's telling you where the leak is.

Then the body parts, verses twenty-four through twenty-seven. **Mouth:** put away crooked speech, keep twisted talk far from your lips. **Eyes:** let them look straight ahead, fix your gaze directly in front. **Feet:** watch the path of your feet and all your ways will be sure. **"Don't swerve right or left; turn your foot from evil."**

That's the whole person. Heart at the center — that's the spring. Then mouth, eyes, feet — that's the three places the spring shows up. What you say, what you look at, where you go. Get the center right and the rest follows. Get the center wrong and you can white-knuckle the mouth and eyes and feet all you want; the leak is upstream.

Here's the shape. Wisdom is a hand-off — grandfather to father to son — and if your chain broke, this book is the grandfather. The first step of wisdom is *wanting* it. Two roads: one starts like dawn and gets brighter; the other starts easy and ends in a dark you can't see through. And the one guard you can't skip is the one on your heart, because that's where everything flows from.

Today: name what's been sitting in the control room. Whatever's in the middle of your heart right now — that's what's going to come out of your mouth, your eyes, your feet by evening. Guard it. Swap it if you have to.
proverbs.notes: *Note on translation: 4:1, 4:13* musar *= training/discipline (coaching sense), not punishment. 4:7* reshit chochmah qeneh chochmah *— KJV "Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom" — rendered literally: "the beginning of wisdom is: get wisdom."* Reshit *is the same word as 1:7 (*reshit da'at*), making this a deliberate echo: awe is the beginning;* choosing *to acquire wisdom is the beginning. The LXX omits v. 7 entirely; MT retained. 4:3* rach v'yachid *= tender and only-one — Solomon's self-description invokes David as the teaching father. 4:18–19* or nogah / afelah *— dawn-light vs. thick darkness; the same two-ways structure as Ps 1. 4:22* marpe *= healing (cf. 3:8* rif'ut*). 4:23* mikol mishmar n'tzor libbecha *— "above all guarding, guard your heart";* lev *= the whole inner control center (mind/will/desire), not emotions only;* totz'ot chayyim *= outflows/springs of life. Echoed by Jesus at Matt 12:34, 15:18–19; Luke 6:45. 4:14* resha'im *= mark-missers/wicked. No yirah in this chapter.*

proverbs.title: PROVERB 5 — Drink From Your Own Well
proverbs.body:
Chapter two mentioned her in passing. Chapter five gives her the whole floor — and then, halfway through, turns and gives *your own marriage* the floor, in language most churches are too embarrassed to read out loud. Let's read both.

**"My son, pay attention to my wisdom; bend your ear to my understanding, so you can keep discretion and your lips can guard knowledge."** Same opening as always. Lean in. This is going to matter.

Verse three: **"Because the lips of the strange woman drip honey, and her mouth is smoother than oil."**

Notice the father doesn't lie to you. He doesn't say she's ugly or obviously bad. He says she's *sweet*. Honey. Smooth. Because if he told you temptation was ugly, you'd never recognize it when it showed up beautiful. Wisdom is honest about what the trap looks like from the front.

Verse four: **"But in the end she's bitter as wormwood, sharp as a double-edged sword. Her feet go down to death; her steps take hold of Sheol."**

Honey at the start, wormwood at the end. *La'anah* — the bitterest herb they had. And her road goes to the grave. Not hell — the grave. The silence. Chapter two said the same: her house sinks down to the shades. The affair isn't punished by fire. It's punished by *death* — of the marriage, of the trust, of the self you used to be. Something dies that doesn't come back.

Verse six: **"She doesn't think about the path of life; her tracks wander and she doesn't even know it."** That's the key to the whole type. She's not a villain plotting. She's *lost*, and she's inviting you to be lost with her. She doesn't know where she's going. Why would you follow?

Verses seven through fourteen, the consequences. **"So now, sons, listen to me; don't turn from the words of my mouth. Keep your way far from her; don't go near the door of her house —"**

Chapter four said "go around" the wicked road. Same word. Don't walk past the door. Don't test yourself. **"— or you'll give your honor to others and your years to someone cruel."** Verse ten: **"strangers will feast on your strength, and your labor will end up in a foreigner's house."**

That's not a metaphor. That's the divorce settlement. That's child support to a house you don't live in. That's the years of work that end up furnishing someone else's life. The father is describing the economic wreckage of adultery three thousand years before the lawyers got involved.

And then verses eleven through fourteen — the groan at the end. **"You'll groan at your end, when your flesh and body are consumed, and you'll say: How I hated training! How my heart despised correction! I didn't listen to my teachers. I didn't bend my ear. And now I'm almost completely ruined, in front of the whole assembly."**

*Musar* and *tochachat*. Training and correction. The man at the end is not saying "I wish I'd been scared of God." He's saying "I wish I'd let myself be *coached*." That's the regret. Public ruin — *b'toch qahal v'edah* — in front of everyone — because he wouldn't take the reps when they were offered for free.

Then verse fifteen, and the whole chapter turns. Watch what the father does.

**"Drink water from your own cistern, running water from your own well."**

He's talking about your wife. And he's not whispering. Verses sixteen and seventeen: **"Should your springs be scattered outside, streams of water in the streets? Let them be yours alone, not for strangers with you."** Your intimacy is a *spring* — that's the word from 4:23, the wellspring. Don't pour it in the street. Keep it for the one it's meant for.

And then verse eighteen and nineteen, and I want you to hear this because Proverbs is not a prudish book: **"Let your fountain be blessed, and rejoice in the wife of your youth — a loving doe, a graceful deer. Let her breasts satisfy you at all times; be intoxicated with her love always."**

*Tishgeh* — that's the word. Be *drunk*. Stagger. Lose yourself. God's wisdom book says: be intoxicated with your own wife, always. The Bible is not against passion. It's against passion *poured in the street*. It wants your spring to be a fire hose *at home*. Song of Songs is eight chapters of this and it's in the same canon.

So the contrast isn't sex versus no sex. It's stolen honey that turns to wormwood versus your own well that stays sweet. The father is saying: you're not being asked to give something up. You're being asked to *drink deep* from the right well and stop being thirsty at the wrong one.

Verse twenty: **"Why would you be intoxicated with a stranger, and embrace the bosom of a foreign woman?"** Same word — *tishgeh*. He's saying, you can be drunk on one or the other. Choose the one that doesn't end in wormwood.

Verse twenty-one: **"Because the eyes of God are on a man's ways, and He weighs all his paths."** Not surveillance. *Mefales* — He levels, He measures. He sees the whole path, including the end you can't see from the door. That's why He tells you not to go in. Not because He's angry — because He can see the wormwood from here.

Verses twenty-two and twenty-three, the close: **"His own wrongs will trap the wicked man; he'll be held by the ropes of his own missing-the-mark. He'll die for lack of training; in the greatness of his folly he'll go astray."**

Ropes of his own making. Pit-digger. You know this move by now — Psalm 7, Psalm 9, Proverbs 1. And the cause of death, verse twenty-three: lack of *musar*. Not lack of fear. Not lack of rules. Lack of *coaching received*. He was offered the reps and said no.

Here's the shape. The stranger's lips drip honey, and the father admits it — but honey turns to wormwood and her feet go to the grave. Stay away from the door. Your strength and your years will end up in someone else's house. And then the turn: don't scatter your spring in the street — drink from your own well, be *intoxicated* with the wife of your youth, always. God isn't against the fire. He's against the arson.

Today: if you're married, go be drunk on the right well tonight — actually delight in the one you promised. If you're near a door you shouldn't be near, walk the other way *before* you can smell the honey.
proverbs.notes: *Note on translation: 5:3* ishah zarah *— "strange woman" — is a type (the covenant-breaker; cf. 2:16–17), not a gender indictment; the father-to-son frame produces a female tempter. 5:4* la'anah *= wormwood, bitterest herb. 5:5* Sheol *— "hell" in KJV — rendered "the grave"; consistent with the Psalms treatment; 2:18* refa'im *parallel. 5:6 the subject of* pen-tefales *is ambiguous (she doesn't consider / lest you consider); rendered as her not watching the path, following the majority reading. 5:12, 5:23* musar *= training; 5:12* tochachat *= correction — the regret is over refused coaching, not over insufficient fear. 5:14* b'toch qahal v'edah *= in the midst of assembly and congregation — public shame. 5:15–18* bor */* be'er */* maqor *= cistern / well / fountain — sexual metaphors for the wife, drawing on 4:23's* totz'ot *(springs). 5:19* dadeha *= her breasts (some translations soften to "love");* tishgeh *= stagger/be intoxicated — the same verb reused deliberately at 5:20 for the stranger, making the contrast one of* which *intoxication, not intoxication vs. sobriety. 5:21* mefales *= weighs/levels. 5:22* chavlei chattato *= ropes of his own missing-the-mark. No yirah in this chapter.*

proverbs.title: PROVERB 6 — Go Watch the Ant
proverbs.body:
Chapter six is four pieces of hard practical advice back to back. Money. Work. Character. Sex. The father is covering the four places grown men wreck their lives.

Piece one, verse one: **"My son, if you've put up security for your neighbor, if you've shaken hands on a stranger's debt — you've been snared by your own words, caught by the words of your mouth."**

Co-signing. That's what this is. You guaranteed someone else's loan. And the father doesn't say "that was wicked." He says "that was a trap, and you walked in." So verses three through five: **"Do this, my son, and free yourself, since you've fallen into your neighbor's hand: go, humble yourself, press your neighbor. Don't sleep. Don't let your eyelids close. Free yourself like a gazelle from the hand, like a bird from the fowler's hand."**

Urgency. Don't sleep on it. Go tonight. Get your name off the paper. This isn't about generosity — Proverbs is huge on generosity. It's about the difference between giving what you have and pledging what you don't. One is love. The other is a snare with your name in it.

Piece two, verse six, and it's the most famous animal in the book: "Go to the ant, you sluggard. Watch her ways and get wise."

Atzel. Sluggard. Proverbs has a whole running character with this name, and he's funny — until you recognize him. Verses seven and eight: **"She has no commander, no officer, no ruler — yet she prepares her food in summer and gathers her supplies at harvest."**

Nobody's yelling at the ant. Nobody's standing over her with a clipboard. She just knows what season it is and acts accordingly. That's the definition of wisdom in this book — knowing the time and doing the thing the time requires, without being told. Verses nine through eleven: **"How long will you lie there, sluggard? When will you get up from your sleep? A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest — and your poverty comes like a highwayman, your want like an armed man."**

"A little." Hear the word. That's the sluggard's entire vocabulary. Just a little more. Five more minutes. I'll start Monday. The father says: poverty doesn't announce itself. It doesn't knock. It comes like a mugger — fast, from behind, when you weren't looking, and it takes everything. You didn't lose your future in one big decision. You lost it in a thousand "a little"s.

Piece three, verse twelve: **"A worthless man, a man of wrong, walks with a crooked mouth — winking his eyes, shuffling his feet, pointing his fingers — with perversity in his heart, plotting evil, always sowing strife."**

That's a body-language profile. The wink, the shuffle, the point. He's the guy who talks out of the side of his mouth. Who's always signaling something to someone else in the room. Verse fifteen: **"So suddenly disaster comes on him; in a moment he's broken, past healing."** The man who lived on angles gets no angle when it counts.

Then verses sixteen through nineteen, a numbered saying, and Proverbs loves these: "Six things God hates — seven are detestable to Him: proud eyes, a lying tongue, hands that shed innocent blood, a heart that plots wicked schemes, feet quick to run to evil, a false witness who breathes lies, and one who sows strife among brothers."

Look at the list. It's another body walk — eyes, tongue, hands, heart, feet. Chapter four gave you the body guarded by wisdom. Here's the body run by the opposite. And notice what's at the top and the bottom: proud eyes first, and sowing strife among brothers last — the seventh, the emphasized one. God's most-hated thing on this list isn't murder. It's the guy who splits up the family. The one who walks into a room of brothers and leaves it a room of factions. Remember who does that professionally next time someone tries to turn you against your own people.

Piece four, verse twenty, and it's the third time the father has warned about this, so he clearly thinks it matters. "My son, keep your father's command and don't abandon your mother's teaching. Tie them on your heart always; bind them around your neck. When you walk they'll lead you; when you sleep they'll watch over you; when you wake they'll talk to you." Then verse twenty-three: **"For the command is a lamp and the teaching is a light, and the corrections of training are the way of life."** Psalm 119:105 — Your word is a lamp to my feet. And there's musar again — "the corrections of training" — tochachot musar — that's the coaching that keeps you alive. Not the beating. The feedback.

Verse twenty-four: what's the lamp for? "To keep you from the evil woman, from the smooth tongue of the stranger. Don't desire her beauty in your heart; don't let her capture you with her eyelids." He's honest again — she's beautiful. Her eyelids — the look. The father isn't pretending she's plain.

Verse twenty-six: **"For a prostitute costs a loaf of bread, but another man's wife hunts down a precious life."** He's drawing a line. He's not endorsing the first — but he's saying the second is categorically more dangerous. The stranger in this chapter is a married woman. She's not just wrong; she's someone else's, and someone is going to come looking.

Then the fire, verses twenty-seven and twenty-eight: **"Can a man scoop fire into his lap and his clothes not burn? Can he walk on hot coals and his feet not be scorched? So is the one who goes in to his neighbor's wife — no one who touches her goes unpunished."**

You can't hold fire and stay unburned. That's not a rule God invented to spoil the fun. That's just what fire is. Adultery burns the man who carries it. Not because heaven strikes — because he's holding fire.

Verses thirty through thirty-five, and this is where the father gets very specific about why. "People don't despise a thief who steals when he's starving — but if he's caught he pays back sevenfold, he gives everything in his house." Even the sympathetic thief pays. "But the one who commits adultery with a woman has no sense; he destroys his own life. Wounds and disgrace he'll get, and his shame will never be wiped away." Never — lo timacheh.

And then the reason it's different from theft, verses thirty-four and thirty-five: **"For jealousy enrages a husband, and he'll show no mercy on the day of vengeance. He won't accept any payment; he'll refuse it however large the bribe."** A thief can pay restitution. There is no restitution for this. You can't write a check that makes a betrayed husband whole. Some debts have no currency.

Here's the shape. Don't pledge what you don't have — and if you did, don't sleep till you're out. Watch the ant: no boss, no clipboard, she just knows what season it is. God's most-hated sin on the list is splitting up brothers. And adultery isn't just a sin — it's fire in your lap, and it's a debt no payment can clear. Today: pick your piece. Debt, sloth, strife, or fire. One of the four has your name on it right now. Go to the ant on it — no commander, no officer. Just do the thing the season requires.
proverbs.notes: *Note on translation: 6:1 aravta = stand surety / co-sign; the warning is against pledging what one does not own, not against generosity (cf. 11:15, 17:18, 22:26). 6:6 atzel = sluggard — a recurring Proverbs character (10:26, 13:4, 15:19, 19:24, 20:4, 24:30, 26:13–16). 6:11 k'mhallech — like a traveler/highwayman; ish magen = armed man. 6:12 adam beliyya'al = worthless man. 6:16–19 a "graded numerical saying" (x / x+1), the seventh item carrying the emphasis; shole'ach medanim bein achim = sows strife among brothers. 6:20 torat immecha = your mother's teaching. 6:23 tochachot musar — KJV "reproofs of instruction" — rendered "corrections of training." 6:24 MT eshet ra (evil woman); LXX reads eshet re'a (neighbor's wife), which matches 6:29 — both readings noted. 6:26 the Hebrew is compressed; "costs a loaf of bread" follows the majority reading. 6:29 lo yinnaqeh = will not go unpunished/clean. 6:33 lo timacheh = will not be wiped away. 6:35 kofer = ransom/payment. No yirah in this chapter.*

proverbs.title: PROVERB 7 — The Ox Didn't Know
proverbs.body:
The father has warned you three times. Now he stops lecturing and tells you a story. He watched it happen.

But first, the setup, verses one through five: **"My son, keep my words; store up my commands inside you. Keep my commands and live; guard my teaching like the pupil of your eye. Tie them on your fingers; write them on the tablet of your heart. Say to wisdom, 'You are my sister,' and call understanding your relative — to keep you from the strange woman, from the foreigner with her smooth words."**

Hear the move. Call wisdom your sister. Make her family. Because here's the truth the father knows: you're going to be in a relationship with some woman's voice in your head. Either Lady Wisdom's or the stranger's. He's saying — get the right one in the house first. Fill the seat before the wrong one takes it.

Then verse six, and the camera turns on. "At the window of my house, through my lattice, I looked down — and I saw among the naive, I noticed among the young men, a young man with no sense —" chasar lev — heart-lacking. Not evil. Empty. The control room from 4:23 has nobody in it.

**"— crossing the street near her corner, walking toward her house, at twilight, as the day faded, in the dark of night."**

Notice three time-markers in one verse. Twilight. Evening. Night. The father is telling you: this kid chose the hour. Nobody wanders past that corner at dusk by accident. The decision happened before he left home. By the time he's on her street, it's a formality.

Verse ten: **"And look — a woman comes to meet him, dressed like a prostitute, with a guarded heart."** N'tzurat lev. Her heart is guarded — the same word as 4:23, "guard your heart" — but inverted. She's guarded the wrong thing. She's protected her intentions, not her wellspring. The kid has no heart; she has a locked one. That's the pair.

Verses eleven and twelve: **"She's loud and rebellious; her feet don't stay home. Now in the street, now in the plazas, at every corner she lies in wait."** She's Lady Wisdom's shadow. Wisdom stood in the street and the plazas and shouted in chapter one — same words, same places. Now here's the counterfeit, in the same spot, using the same volume. That's the terrifying thing. They stand on the same corner. Only the message is different.

Verse thirteen: **"She grabs him and kisses him and, with a brazen face, says to him —"**

And now the father gives you her whole pitch. Every line. Memorize it, because it's still the pitch.

"I had to offer peace-offerings today; today I paid my vows." Line one: religion. She opens with church. She's just come from the temple. She's a good person. She's been giving. This is how it starts — with respectability. The affair always begins in a context where nobody would suspect.

"So I came out to meet you, to look for your face — and I found you." Line two: destiny. It was meant to be. I was looking for you specifically. Of all the men in the city. You're special. The kid who's chasar lev — heart-empty — has never been told he was special. This lands.

"I've spread my couch with coverings, colored linens from Egypt. I've perfumed my bed with myrrh, aloes, and cinnamon." Line three: sensory overload. Egypt linen — the imported stuff. Three spices. She's describing the room so he can smell it before he's in it. Whatever the modern version is — she's built the whole scene and now she's just narrating it.

"Come, let's drink our fill of love until morning; let's delight ourselves with lovemaking." Line four: no consequences. All night. Just pleasure. She uses the word dodim — the Song of Songs word for love. She's borrowing the marriage-bed vocabulary for the theft.

"Because my husband isn't home. He's gone on a long journey. He took a bag of money with him; he won't be back until the full moon." Line five, and it's the closer: the coast is clear. Nobody will know. He's far. He's got cash — he's on business, he's not coming back early. There's a calendar for this. She's done the math. And notice — she says "the man," ha-ish. Not "my husband." She won't even give him a title. She's already erased him in her mouth.

Verse twenty-one: **"With her persuasive words she turns him; with the smoothness of her lips she drives him."** Tadichennu — she pushes him. He doesn't walk in. He's herded in.

And then verse twenty-two, the line the whole chapter exists for: "Suddenly he follows her — like an ox goes to the slaughter, like a deer stepping into a noose — until an arrow splits his liver. Like a bird rushing into the snare, he doesn't know it will cost him his life."

The ox doesn't know. That's it. That's the whole tragedy. The ox walks calmly to the slaughterhouse because to the ox, it looks like a walk. The kid follows her because to him, it looks like the best night of his life. V'lo yada — and he doesn't know. Chapter one said the bird that sees the net escapes. This bird didn't see it. And the father, at the window, sees the whole thing — the corner, the hour, the speech, the noose — and the boy sees none of it.

That's why he told the story. Not to scare you. To give you the window. So next time you're the one on the street at twilight, some part of you is also upstairs, watching, and it can say: I know how this ends. I've seen this before.

Verses twenty-four through twenty-seven, the close: "So now, sons, listen to me; pay attention to the words of my mouth. Don't let your heart turn aside to her ways; don't stray onto her paths. Because many are the victims she's brought down; numerous are all her slain. Her house is the road to Sheol, going down to the chambers of death."

Not hell. The grave. Chadrei mavet — the rooms of death. Her bedroom, the one with the Egyptian linen and the three spices, has a back door, and the back door opens into the grave. Same as chapter two, same as chapter five. Not fire. Silence. Something in you that doesn't come back.

Here's the shape. Make wisdom your sister before the stranger makes herself your lover — the seat will be filled by somebody. The kid chose the hour before he chose the street. She stands on Wisdom's own corner, using Wisdom's own volume. Her pitch is religion, destiny, sensation, no-consequences, and the-coast-is-clear — and it's still the pitch. And the ox didn't know.

Today: put yourself at the window. Whatever your twilight street is — the one you tell yourself you're just walking past — look down at yourself from upstairs. You know how it ends. Turn around before the corner.
proverbs.notes: *Note on translation: 7:2 k'ishon einecha = like the pupil (lit. "little man") of your eye — the apple-of-the-eye idiom. 7:4 achoti at = "you are my sister" — kinship language; in Song of Songs "my sister, my bride" is the beloved, so wisdom is being offered the intimate seat. 7:7 chasar lev = lacking heart/sense — the empty control room (cf. 4:23). 7:10 n'tzurat lev — "subtle of heart" (KJV) — literally "guarded of heart," the same root as 4:23 n'tzor libbecha; the inversion is deliberate. 7:11–12 ba-chutz / ba-r'chovot = in the street / in the plazas — verbatim the locations of Lady Wisdom in 1:20–21. 7:14 zivchei sh'lamim = peace-offerings; her opening line is religious. 7:16 etun Mitzrayim = Egyptian linen. 7:18 dodim = lovemaking (Song of Songs vocabulary). 7:19 ha-ish — "the man," not ishi "my husband" — the erasure is in the Hebrew. 7:21 tadichennu = drives/pushes him. 7:22 the deer/noose clause is textually difficult (MT k'eches el-musar evil, "like an anklet to the correction of a fool"); the deer/stag reading follows LXX/Syriac and is the majority modern reconstruction — both noted. 7:22–23 v'lo yada = and he does not know. 7:27 Sheol / chadrei mavet — "hell" in KJV — rendered the grave / chambers of death. No yirah in this chapter.*

proverbs.title: PROVERB 8 — She Was There Before the Dirt
proverbs.body:
Chapter seven ended in the chambers of death. Chapter eight opens on the same street — and a different woman is standing there.

**"Doesn't Wisdom call out? Doesn't Understanding lift her voice? On the heights along the road, at the crossroads she takes her stand; beside the gates at the entrance to the city, at the doorways she cries out —"**

The heights. The crossroads. The gates. The doorways. That's every place the stranger stood — "now in the street, now in the plazas, at every corner." Wisdom has planted herself at the exact same spots. The father just showed you the counterfeit's pitch, word for word. Now here's the original's.

"To you, people, I call; my voice is to all humanity." Verse four. Not to "my son." To everyone. B'nei adam — the children of Adam. The stranger picked off one heart-empty kid at twilight. Wisdom addresses the species in broad daylight.

"Understand shrewdness, you naive ones; you dull ones, get a heart." Same three-fool vocabulary from chapter one. She hasn't given up on any of them.

Verses six through nine, her credentials: "Listen, because I speak noble things; the opening of my lips is what's right. My mouth speaks truth; wickedness is detestable to my lips. All the words of my mouth are right-standing; there's nothing twisted or crooked in them. They're all straight to the one who understands, and right to those who find knowledge."

The stranger's lips dripped honey and were smoother than oil. Wisdom's lips are straight. Not sweet — straight. That's the difference in the two pitches. One is designed to feel good on the way in. The other is designed to be true, and it'll feel good on the way out. Verses ten and eleven, and you've heard this: "Take my training instead of silver, knowledge rather than choice gold — because wisdom is better than rubies; nothing you could want compares to her." Chapter three said this. Chapter two told you to dig for her like silver. She's saying — skip the silver, take me directly.

Then verses twelve through twenty-one, and she describes what she actually does. "I, Wisdom, live with shrewdness; I find knowledge and discretion." Verse thirteen: **"The AWE of God is to hate evil. Pride and arrogance and the evil way and a perverse mouth — I hate them."**

There's the word again. Yirat YHWH. And notice what it's defined as. Not "being afraid of God." Hating evil. That's what awe does. If you stand at the canyon edge in real awe, you don't want to throw garbage in it. Awe of God makes ugliness offensive to you. And look what's first on the list: pride — ge'ah v'ga'on. Awe and pride can't share a room. That's why fear is the wrong translation — fear and pride coexist all the time; scared people are often proud. Awe and pride can't.

Verses fourteen through sixteen: **"Counsel and sound judgment are mine; I have understanding and strength. By me kings reign and rulers decree what's just; by me princes govern, and nobles, all the judges of the earth."** She's saying — every good government you've ever lived under ran on me. Every fair verdict. Every leader who didn't loot the place. That's Wisdom on the throne.

Verses seventeen through twenty-one: **"I love those who love me, and those who seek me find me. Riches and honor are with me — enduring wealth and right-standing. My fruit is better than fine gold; my yield beats choice silver. I walk in the way of right-standing, along the paths of justice, giving an inheritance to those who love me and filling their treasuries."**

She's generous. The stranger promised one night. Wisdom promises an inheritance. Full treasuries. The long game.

And then verse twenty-two. Sit down for this section. This is why this chapter is famous.

**"God possessed me at the beginning of His way, before His works of old."**

She's saying she was first. Before anything was made. The Hebrew word is *qanani* — possessed me, or begot me — the rabbis argued over it for a thousand years and the Christians argued over it for four hundred more. Both readings mean the same thing for us: before there was a universe, there was Wisdom, and she was with God. Verse twenty-three: **"From eternity I was appointed, from the first, before the earth ever was."** Me'olam — from forever.

Verses twenty-four through twenty-six, and listen to how she counts backward: "When there were no deeps, I was brought forth. Before the springs heavy with water. Before the mountains were set down, before the hills, I was brought forth — before He'd made the earth or the fields or the first dust of the world."

The first dust. Rosh afrot tevel. Before the first speck of dirt existed, Wisdom was already there. She's older than the ground you're standing on.

Verses twenty-seven through twenty-nine: **"When He established the heavens, I was there. When He drew a circle on the face of the deep, when He fixed the clouds above, when the fountains of the deep grew strong, when He gave the sea its boundary so the waters wouldn't cross His command, when He marked out the foundations of the earth —"**

She's walking you through Genesis 1 from the inside. The circle on the deep — that's the horizon. The sea's boundary — that's day three. Psalm 104 sang about this — "You set a boundary the waters may not pass." Wisdom says: I was in the room.

And then verse thirty, and this is the line:

**"— then I was beside Him, a master craftsman, and I was His delight day by day, playing before Him at every moment, playing in His inhabited world, and my delight was in the children of Adam."**

Amon — the craftsman, the architect's right hand. But then — m'sacheqet — playing. Laughing. Dancing. The word for *a* kid at recess. Wisdom wasn't standing at a drafting table with a frown. She was playing while the universe got built. And God delighted in her — sha'ashuim, the word for *what* you feel watching your child do something wonderful. And her delight was in us. B'nei adam. She played in the new world and the thing she loved most was the people.

So when the New Testament opens John's gospel — "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God… all things were made through Him" — and when Paul writes to the Colossians, "He is before all things, and in Him all things hold together… the firstborn of all creation" — they are quoting this chapter. They looked at Jesus and said: that's who was playing beside the Father before the first dust. Proverbs 8 is where the church got its language for who Jesus was before Bethlehem. When you read this, you're reading the blueprint they built on. Verses thirty-two through thirty-six, she comes back down to you: "So now, sons, listen to me — happy are those who keep my ways. Hear training and be wise; don't neglect it. Happy is the one who listens to me, watching daily at my doors, waiting at my doorposts."

Watching daily at my doors. The kid in chapter seven went to the stranger's door at twilight. Wisdom says: come to mine, and come every day. Not once — daily. Stand at the doorpost and wait. She'll open.

Verse thirty-five: **"For whoever finds me finds life and obtains favor from God."** Verse thirty-six: "But whoever misses me harms himself; all who hate me love death."

Chot'i — the one who misses me. Same root as missing the mark. Wisdom is the target. Miss her and you don't get punished — you just miss. And what you hit instead is death. Not because she's cruel. Because she's the only thing standing between you and the chambers at the end of the stranger's hall.

Here's the shape. Same corner, different woman. Her lips are straight, not sweet. Awe of God means hating evil — and awe can't share a room with pride. And then the reveal: she was there before the first dust, playing beside God while He drew the horizon, and the thing she loved most was you. John and Paul saw Jesus in this chapter. Come to her door daily. Miss her, and you miss life.

Today: go stand at the door. Give her ten minutes before the day starts. Not once — daily. She's been waiting since before the dirt.
proverbs.notes: *Note on translation: 8:13 yirat YHWH s'not ra — "the fear of the LORD is to hate evil" (KJV) — rendered "the AWE of God is to hate evil"; awe is here defined by its effect (moral revulsion), and its first listed enemy is pride (ge'ah v'ga'on) — a pairing that only coheres under the awe reading. 8:1–3 the four locations (m'romim / derech / netivot / sha'arim / p'tachim) deliberately reoccupy the stranger's stations from 7:8, 7:12 and Wisdom's own from 1:20–21. 8:4 b'nei adam = children of Adam / humanity — universal address. 8:10 musar = training. 8:22 qanani — "possessed me" (KJV, Aquila) vs. "created/begot me" (LXX ektisen, Targum); the Arian controversy (4th c.) hinged on this verb; both readings noted, both affirm Wisdom's priority to creation. 8:22–31 is the source text for John 1:1–3, Col 1:15–17, Heb 1:2–3, and the Wisdom-Christology of Sir 24 / Wis 7; the NT echo is named in the body. 8:26 rosh afrot tevel = the first dust of the world. 8:27 chug = circle/horizon on the deep (cf. Job 26:10). 8:29 sea-boundary = Ps 104:9. 8:30 amon — "as one brought up with him" (KJV) vs. "master craftsman" (majority modern, from Akkadian ummânu); m'sacheqet = playing/laughing (also 8:31); sha'ashuim = delight. 8:34 ashrei = happy. 8:36 chot'i = the one who misses me — the chata root, missing the mark. Yirah in this chapter: 8:13.*

proverbs.title: PROVERB 9 — Two Dinner Invitations
proverbs.body:
Nine chapters of the father at the kitchen table, and this is how he ends: two women, two houses, two dinner parties, same guest list. You're on both lists. You have to pick one.

**"Wisdom has built her house; she has hewn her seven pillars."**

Seven pillars. Complete. Solid. Chapter eight told you she was there when God laid the foundations of the earth — of course she can build a house. And it's not a shack. It's got columns.

Verse two: **"She has slaughtered her meat, mixed her wine, and set her table."** This is a real feast. Meat — that was rare. Mixed wine — spiced, prepared, not just poured. The table is set. Psalm 23 — "You set a table before me." Wisdom did the same.

Verse three: **"She has sent out her servant girls; she calls from the highest places of the city."** She's sending invitations. She's not waiting for you to find her. And she's using the high ground — the place where a voice carries.

And here's what she says, verse four: **"Whoever is naive, let him turn in here! To the one lacking heart, she says —"**

Stop. She's inviting the peti. The naive one. And the chasar lev — the heart-empty kid from chapter seven, the one who followed the stranger like an ox. Wisdom's guest list isn't the wise. It's the dumb ones who could still learn. She's specifically inviting the people who've already messed up. That's who the meat is for.

Verse five: **"Come, eat my bread and drink the wine I've mixed. Leave your naivety and live; walk in the way of understanding."**

Eat. Drink. Live. Isaiah 55 says it — "come, buy wine and milk without money." Jesus's parables are full of this — the king who sends servants to invite everyone to the wedding feast, and the ones who come are the ones from the streets. That's this. This is the first draft of the great banquet.

Then verses seven through twelve, a middle block that seems like a detour but isn't. It's about who can receive the invitation.

**"Whoever corrects a mocker gets shame for himself; whoever rebukes a wicked man gets a bruise. Don't correct a mocker or he'll hate you; correct a wise man and he'll love you."**

The letz. The mocker. The third grade of fool, the one who's made sneering a lifestyle. The father is honest: you can't reach him. You correct him, he hates you for it. Wisdom's servants are out there shouting, but the mocker isn't heart-empty — he's heart-armored. The invitation bounces off.

But: "Correct a wise man and he'll love you." That's the tell. The wise man isn't the one who never needs correcting. He's the one who thanks you for it. Verse nine: **"Give to a wise man and he'll get wiser; teach a right-standing man and he'll add to his learning."** Chapter one said this. The wise get wiser because they keep taking the reps.

And then verse ten. The thesis, one more time, as the section closes.

**"The beginning of wisdom is the AWE of God, and knowledge of the Holy One is understanding."**

Chapter one, verse seven opened the book with it. Chapter nine, verse ten closes the first section with it. It's bookends. Reshit chochmah yirat YHWH. And it's the same line as Psalm 111:10, word for word. Your Bible says "fear." It's awe. Nine chapters in, you've now seen what it does: it heals your bones, it makes you hate evil, it can't sit in a room with pride, it's a choice, and it's where you end up when you dig. Nothing in that list is fear. That's awe. That's the whole project of this book — making sure that one word is right, because everything else in Proverbs is built on it.

Verse eleven: **"For by me your days will be many, and years of life will be added to you."** Verse twelve: **"If you're wise, you're wise for yourself; if you mock, you alone will bear it."** Nobody can be wise for you. And nobody else pays for your mocking. This is the one decision that's completely yours.

Now verse thirteen, and the other house.

"The woman Folly is loud; she's naive and knows nothing." Eshet k'silut. Lady Folly. The stranger from chapters two, five, six, and seven — now given her formal name and set up as Wisdom's mirror. And note: she's naive too. P'tayyut. She's not a mastermind. She's as lost as the people she's inviting. The blind leading the blind to dinner.

Verse fourteen: **"She sits at the door of her house, on a seat at the high places of the city —"** The same high places Wisdom called from in verse three. Same elevation. Same acoustics. "— calling to those who pass by, who are going straight on their way —"

Ha-m'yashrim orchotam. The ones going straight. She's not going after people already headed her way. She's going after the ones walking the right road, trying to pull them off it. That's who she wants. Not the lost — the ones who are almost home.

And verse sixteen — listen to this. "Whoever is naive, let him turn in here! To the one lacking heart, she says —"

Word for word. Verse four and verse sixteen are identical in Hebrew. Wisdom's invitation and Folly's invitation are the same sentence. Same words, same target, same volume, same corner. The father has been telling you for nine chapters that the counterfeit uses the original's script. Here he just prints them next to each other so you can see it.

So what's the difference? The menu. Verse seventeen: **"Stolen water is sweet, and bread eaten in secret is pleasant."**

That's Folly's feast. Stolen water. Secret bread. Wisdom slaughtered meat and mixed wine and set the table in the open. Folly's got water — the cheapest thing there is — and it's only good because it's stolen. Bread that's only pleasant because it's hidden. The whole appeal is the sneaking. Take away the secrecy and it's tap water and a stale roll.

Verse eighteen, last line of the whole section: "But he doesn't know that the dead are there, that her guests are in the depths of Sheol."

V'lo yada. He doesn't know. The ox again — same words as 7:23. Her guests. She has guests too. They just aren't at the table. They're in the depths of the grave. Every man who ever took the stolen water is downstairs. That's the seating chart. Not hell — the grave. Silence. The place where the ones who chose the secret bread went quiet.

Here's the shape. Two houses, two women, two dinners, one guest list — and it's you. Wisdom built with seven pillars and served meat and wine in the open. Folly sat at her door and offered stolen water. They used the same invitation. The only difference is the menu and where the guests end up. And the hinge in the middle, one more time, bookending the whole first section: awe of God is where wisdom starts. Not fear. Awe.

Today: you're going to get both invitations before sundown. Same words. Check the menu. If it's only good because it's secret — that's the wrong house.
proverbs.notes: *Note on translation: 9:10 t'chillat chochmah yirat YHWH — "the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom" (KJV) — rendered "the beginning of wisdom is the AWE of God." This bookends 1:7 (reshit da'at) and is verbatim Ps 111:10; the first nine chapters open and close on the yirah thesis. T'chillah (9:10) and reshit (1:7) are near-synonyms for "beginning." Da'at q'doshim = knowledge of the Holy One (plural of majesty). 9:1 chatzvah amudeha shiv'ah = hewn her seven pillars — completeness. 9:2 mas'chah yeinah = mixed/spiced her wine. 9:4 and 9:16 are identical in the MT — mi-peti yasur hennah, chasar-lev am'rah lo — the parallel is intentional and is the chapter's central device. 9:5 the banquet-invitation is echoed at Isa 55:1–2, Matt 22:1–10, Luke 14:16–24. 9:7–8 letz = mocker (third fool-grade, incorrigible). 9:8 hochach = correct/rebuke. 9:13 eshet k'silut = Lady Folly (from kesil); p'tayyut = naivety — Folly is herself naive. 9:15 ha-m'yashrim orchotam = those making their paths straight — she targets the ones on the right road. 9:17 mayim g'nuvim = stolen water; lechem s'tarim = bread of secrets. 9:18 r'fa'im = the dead/shades; imqei Sheol — "the depths of hell" (KJV) — rendered depths of the grave; v'lo yada repeats 7:23. LXX adds several verses after 9:12 and 9:18 (not in MT); MT followed. Yirah in this chapter: 9:10.*

proverbs.title: PROVERB 10 — The Mouth Is the Tell
proverbs.body:
Nine chapters of lecture. Now the father stops explaining and starts firing. From here to chapter twenty-two, Proverbs is one-liners — two beats each, and each one designed to stick in your head and go off later. You don't read these like a story. You read them like a bag of stones and pick up the one you need today.

Verse one, the title: "The proverbs of Solomon." Then the first stone: "A wise son makes a father glad; a dull son is his mother's grief." That's the frame for the whole collection. Every saying that follows is a father hoping for the first half.

Let's pick up the stones by what they're for.

First handful — work and wealth. Verse two: **"Treasures gained by wickedness don't profit, but right-standing rescues from death."** Verse three: **"God doesn't let the right-standing go hungry, but He thwarts the craving of the wicked."** Verse four: **"A slack hand makes poor, but a diligent hand makes rich."** Verse five: **"The one who gathers in summer is a wise son; the one who sleeps at harvest is a shameful son."**

The ant from chapter six, said in one line. Know what season it is. Verse fifteen: **"A rich man's wealth is his strong city; the ruin of the poor is their poverty."** That's just observation — the father isn't pretending money doesn't matter. Verse sixteen sharpens it: "The wage of the right-standing leads to life; the income of the wicked leads to missing the mark." Same paycheck, different destination. Verse twenty-two: **"The blessing of God makes rich, and hard toil adds nothing to it."** Hear the balance — verse four says work hard, verse twenty-two says work can't replace blessing. Both true. Both stones in the bag.

Verse twenty-six, and it's the funniest line in the chapter: "Like vinegar to the teeth and smoke to the eyes, so is the sluggard to the one who sends him." You've had that employee. You've been that employee. Sending the sluggard on an errand is like getting smoke in your eyes — it's not that he's evil, it's that he stings.

Second handful — the mouth. This is where chapter ten spends most of its stones, and it's not an accident. Chapter four told you to guard the heart because everything flows from it; this chapter watches what flows.

Verse eight: **"The wise of heart receives commands, but the babbling fool comes to ruin."** Verse ten repeats the second half: "the babbling fool comes to ruin" — twice in three verses, because the father means it. Evil s'fatayim — the fool of lips. The one who never stops talking.

Verse eleven: **"The mouth of the right-standing is a fountain of life, but the mouth of the wicked conceals violence."** Fountain — m'qor. That's chapter five's word for your own well. A good man's mouth waters people. Verse thirteen: **"On the lips of the discerning wisdom is found, but a rod for the back of the one lacking heart."** Verse fourteen: **"The wise store up knowledge, but the mouth of a fool is near ruin."** Store up — the treasure word from chapter two. The wise bank what they learn. The fool spends it as fast as it comes in, out loud.

Verse eighteen: **"Whoever hides hatred has lying lips, and whoever spreads slander is a dull fool."** Both sides of the coin — the smiler with hate underneath, and the loudmouth who says the hate out loud. Both wrong. Verse nineteen, and this one should be framed: "When words are many, missing the mark isn't lacking — but the one who restrains his lips is wise." The more you talk, the more you miss. Statistically. Just by volume. The wise man wins by saying less.

Verse twenty: **"The tongue of the right-standing is choice silver; the heart of the wicked is worth little."** Notice: tongue matched to heart. What comes out the mouth is a direct read on what's in the control room. Verse twenty-one: **"The lips of the right-standing feed many, but fools die for lack of heart."** Feed. A good man's words are food. People leave a conversation with him fuller than they came.

Verses thirty-one and thirty-two close the chapter on it: "The mouth of the right-standing produces wisdom, but the twisted tongue will be cut off. The lips of the right-standing know what's fitting, but the mouth of the wicked knows only what's twisted." Ratzon — what's fitting, what's acceptable, what lands well. The wise man knows what the moment needs. The fool knows only one setting.

So the mouth is the tell. You want to know what's in a man's heart? Don't ask him. Listen for ten minutes. Third handful — the two ways. Psalm 1 said it. Chapter four said it. Now it's in stones.

Verse six: **"Blessings crown the head of the right-standing, but the mouth of the wicked conceals violence."** Verse seven: **"The memory of the right-standing is a blessing, but the name of the wicked will rot."** That's the long game — what people say at your funeral versus your name turning into a bad smell.

Verse nine: **"The one who walks with integrity walks securely, but the one who twists his ways will be found out."** Yivadea — will be known. Not necessarily caught by a cop. Known. Twisted paths always eventually show.

Verse twelve — and Peter and James both quote this one: "Hatred stirs up strife, but love covers all wrongs." Ahavah t'chasseh. Love covers. Not ignores — covers, the way you cover a wound. 1 Peter 4:8 — "love covers a multitude of sins." James 5:20 — "covers a multitude of sins." They got it here.

Verse seventeen: **"Whoever heeds training is on the path of life, but whoever ignores correction leads others astray."** Musar and tochachat. Coaching and feedback. Ignore them, and it's not just you who wanders — you take people with you.

Verses twenty-three through twenty-five: **"Doing wrong is like a game to a dull fool, but wisdom to a man of understanding. What the wicked dreads will come on him; what the right-standing desire will be granted. When the storm passes, the wicked are gone — but the right-standing are a foundation forever."** Psalm 1's chaff in the wind, said in three lines. And look at verse twenty-four — m'gorat rasha — the wicked man's dread. That's real fear. The father uses the fear word here, for the wicked, correctly. The wicked dread, and the thing they dread comes.

Verses twenty-eight through thirty: **"The hope of the right-standing is joy, but the expectation of the wicked comes to nothing. The way of God is a stronghold to the one with integrity, but ruin to those who do wrong. The right-standing will never be uprooted, but the wicked will not remain in the land."** Lo-yimot — will not be shaken. There's your Psalms thread — 15, 16, 21, 30, 46, 55, 62, 112, 125 — now in Proverbs. And "the land" — chapter two's promise, Psalm 37's inheritance.

And the one yirah stone. Verse twenty-seven:

"The AWE of God adds days, but the years of the wicked are cut short." Your Bible says "the fear of the LORD prolongeth days." Think about that for one second as fear. Chronic fear shortens your life. Cortisol, blood pressure, sleepless nights. Fear does not add days. Awe does. Awe slows your breathing. Awe makes you stand still and look up. Chapter three said awe is healing to your body. This verse says it's longevity. The physiology of the Hebrew is *right*; the physiology of the King James is backwards.

And verse twenty-four gave us the contrast in the same chapter — m'gorah, the wicked man's dread. Two different words. One adds years; the other eats them. English gave both of them the same name.

Here's the shape. From here on the book fires stones, not lectures — pick up the one you need. Work like the ant, but know work can't replace blessing. The mouth is the tell: a fountain or a fool, and the fewer words the fewer misses. Two ways — one is a foundation forever and one rots. And awe — not fear — adds days.

Today: count your words. Just today. Every time you're about to say the second sentence, ask if the first one was enough. Verse nineteen is a math problem, and you can win it by subtraction.
proverbs.notes: *Note on translation: 10:27 yirat YHWH tosif yamim — "the fear of the LORD prolongeth days" (KJV) — rendered "the AWE of God adds days"; the health/longevity claim (cf. 3:7–8) is physiologically coherent only under awe, not dread. 10:24 m'gorat rasha = the dread of the wicked — genuine fear (magor root), correctly rendered as dread; the chapter contrasts yirah (v. 27) and m'gorah (v. 24). 10:1 m'shalim = proverbs; the superscription marks the start of the Solomonic sayings collection (10:1–22:16, 375 sayings = the numerical value of Sh'lomoh). 10:8, 10:10 evil s'fatayim = fool of lips / babbling fool; 10:10b duplicates 10:8b in MT (LXX has a different second line: "he who reproves boldly makes peace") — MT followed. 10:11 m'qor chayyim = fountain of life (cf. 5:18). 10:12 ahavah t'chasseh kol-p'sha'im = love covers all transgressions — quoted at 1 Pet 4:8, James 5:20. 10:13 shevet = rod — here for the back of the chasar-lev; see 13:24 note for the shevet discussion. 10:14 yitz'p'nu = store up (treasure vocabulary, 2:1, 2:7). 10:17 musar / tochachat = training / correction. 10:19 lo-yechdal pasha = missing the mark does not cease. 10:22 etzev = toil/pain — "hard toil adds nothing" (alt.: "He adds no sorrow with it") — both readings viable; the first followed. 10:26 atzel = sluggard. 10:30 lo-yimot = will not be shaken/uprooted — the Psalms mot thread; eretz = the land. 10:32 ratzon = what is fitting/acceptable. Yirah in this chapter: 10:27.*

proverbs.title: PROVERB 11 — Honest Scales
proverbs.body:
Chapter eleven opens with a shopkeeper's tool. "False scales are detestable to God, but an honest weight is His delight."

Even sh'lemah — a whole stone, a full weight. In the market you weighed grain against a stone. A crooked seller filed the stone down. God says: that's to'evah — detestable, the word reserved for idols and abominations. Rigging the scale gets filed in the same drawer as worshipping Molech. That's how seriously heaven takes fair dealing.

Let's pick up the stones.

First handful — how you deal. Verse three: **"The integrity of the upright guides them, but the crookedness of the treacherous destroys them."** Verse five: **"The right-standing of the blameless makes his path straight, but the wicked falls by his own wickedness."** Verse six: **"The right-standing of the upright rescues them, but the treacherous are trapped by their own craving."** Three in a row saying the same thing: your character is your GPS. Crooked people don't get caught so much as they fall over — their own crookedness is the tripwire. The pit-digger, again.

Verse eighteen: **"The wicked earns a deceptive wage, but the one who sows right-standing gets a real reward."** Sheker — the wage is a lie. It looks like money. It doesn't spend. Verse twenty: **"God detests the twisted of heart, but the blameless in their way are His delight."** Same word pair as verse one — to'evah and ratzon. Twisted heart, twisted scale: same offense.

Verse twenty-seven: **"Whoever seeks good finds favor, but whoever hunts for evil — it comes to him."** You get what you go looking for. Verse thirty-one: **"If the right-standing are repaid on earth, how much more the wicked and the mark-misser."** Peter quotes the Greek of this — "if the righteous is scarcely saved, what will become of the ungodly?" Both directions pay out. Here, not just later. That's Psalm 58:11 — there is a God who judges in the earth. Second handful — pride and humility. Verse two: **"Pride comes, then shame comes; but with the humble is wisdom."** Zadon — arrogance walks in the door and shame walks in right behind it. They travel together. Verse twelve: **"Whoever despises his neighbor lacks heart, but a man of understanding keeps quiet."** Verse twenty-two, and the father is being funny: "Like a gold ring in a pig's snout is a beautiful woman without discretion." The jewelry's real. The pig's real. The two don't go together. Beauty without judgment isn't ugly — it's wasted.

Third handful — the city. Proverbs cares about the neighborhood, not just the individual soul. Verse ten: **"When the right-standing prosper the city rejoices; when the wicked perish there's shouting."** Verse eleven: **"By the blessing of the upright a city is lifted up, but by the mouth of the wicked it's torn down."** Good people are infrastructure. A town with honest men in it is a better town — everybody feels it, even the ones who don't know why.

Verse fourteen: **"Without guidance a people falls, but in many counselors there's safety."** Get advisors. Plural. Verse twenty-six: **"The people curse the one who hoards grain, but a blessing is on the head of the one who sells it."** That's the man who sits on food in a famine waiting for the price to go up. The whole town curses him. Contrast with the one who opens the storehouse. Proverbs has an economics, and it's not "whatever the market will bear."

Verses eight and nine: **"The right-standing is rescued from trouble, and the wicked walks into it instead. With his mouth the godless destroys his neighbor, but by knowledge the right-standing are rescued."** Verse twenty-nine: **"Whoever brings trouble on his own house inherits the wind, and the fool becomes servant to the wise of heart."** Yinchal ruach — inherits wind. That's the estate the troublemaker leaves. Hosea used the same phrase: "they sow the wind and reap the whirlwind."

Fourth handful — generosity. This is the chapter's heart, and it runs against every instinct.

Verse twenty-four: **"One gives freely and gains more; another withholds what's owed and comes to poverty."** Verse twenty-five: **"The generous soul is made fat, and whoever waters will himself be watered."** Nefesh b'rachah — a soul of blessing. The one who pours out gets poured into. It's not a formula for getting rich. It's a description of how the water table works. Watering makes wells. Hoarding makes deserts. Verse twenty-eight: **"Whoever trusts in his riches will fall, but the right-standing will flourish like a green leaf."** Psalm 1's tree by the water, Psalm 52's olive. Ka-aleh — like foliage. Green because it's connected, not because it's stockpiled.

Verse four: **"Wealth is worthless on the day of wrath, but right-standing rescues from death."** Verse seven: **"When a wicked man dies his hope perishes, and the expectation of the strong comes to nothing."** Verse twenty-three: **"The desire of the right-standing is only good; the hope of the wicked is wrath."** Tiqvah — hope, expectation. Not fear. The wicked man's forward-looking — the thing he's counting on — turns out to be wrath. He was banking on the wrong future.

Verse fifteen, a repeat from chapter six: "Whoever puts up security for a stranger will suffer, but whoever hates shaking hands on it is safe." Don't co-sign. Verse sixteen: **"A gracious woman gets honor, but the ruthless get riches."** Aritzim — the violent. They do get rich. The father doesn't deny it. He just notes what they don't get. Verse seventeen: **"A kind man does good to his own soul, but the cruel man harms his own flesh."** Kindness is self-care. Cruelty is self-harm that happens to have a target.

Fifth handful — the mouth. Verse thirteen: **"A gossip reveals a secret, but the faithful of spirit keeps a matter covered."** M'chasseh — covers. Chapter ten's word: love covers. The trustworthy person is the one your secret is safe with. Verse twenty-one: **"Be sure of it — the wicked won't go unpunished, but the offspring of the right-standing escape."** Verse nineteen: **"Steadfast right-standing leads to life, but the one who chases evil chases his own death."**

And verse thirty, the one to walk away with.

**"The fruit of the right-standing is a tree of life, and the wise one takes hold of souls."**

Chapter three said Wisdom is a tree of life. Now the fruit of a good man's life is a tree of life — meaning other people get to eat off him.
