And the second half — loqeach n'fashot — the old Bibles said "winneth souls," and the phrase got turned into a slogan. But hear the Hebrew plain: the wise person takes hold of people. Gathers them. Draws them in. Not by argument — by being edible. You've met that person. You leave them fed. That's a tree of life walking around.

Here's the shape. Honest scales — God files a rigged weight next to idolatry. Your character is your GPS; the crooked trip over themselves. Good people are infrastructure — the whole city is better with them in it. Pour out and you'll be poured into; hoard and inherit wind. And the good man's life is a tree other people eat from.

Today: check your scale. Somewhere you're weighing something — time, money, credit, blame — with a stone you filed down. Put the whole stone back. Then find one person and be edible.
proverbs.notes: *Note on translation: No yirah in this chapter. 11:23 tiqvat r'sha'im evrah — "the expectation of the wicked is wrath" — tiqvah = hope/expectation, not fear; some translations import "fear" here, wrongly. 11:1 moz'nei mirmah / even sh'lemah = deceitful scales / whole stone; to'evah (detestable) is the idolatry word (Deut 7:25, 18:12), here applied to commercial fraud; the to'evah / ratzon pair recurs at 11:20. 11:2 zadon = arrogance. 11:16 aritzim = the violent/ruthless — "strong men" (KJV) understates; LXX has a longer text here, MT followed. 11:18 sheker = deceptive/lying wage. 11:22 nezem zahav b'af chazir — gold ring in a pig's snout. 11:24 mi-yosher = "more than is right / what is owed" — the withholder keeps what he should have released. 11:25 nefesh b'rachah = soul of blessing; marveh = one who waters. 11:26 bar = grain — anti-hoarding in famine. 11:28 ka-aleh = like foliage/a green leaf (cf. Ps 1:3, 52:8). 11:29 yinchal ruach = inherits wind (cf. Hos 8:7). 11:30 etz chayyim = tree of life (3:18); loqeach n'fashot — "winneth souls" (KJV) — literally "takes/gathers souls"; LXX reads "the souls of transgressors are cut off," a different text — MT followed; the evangelistic slogan reading is not wrong but is narrower than the Hebrew, which describes the drawing power of a wise life. 11:31 quoted (via LXX) at 1 Pet 4:18.*

proverbs.title: PROVERB 12 — A Good Man Is Kind to His Donkey
proverbs.body:
Chapter twelve starts with a diagnostic question: how do you take criticism?

**"Whoever loves training loves knowledge, but whoever hates correction is stupid."**

Ba'ar — that's the word. Not kesil, not evil — ba'ar, brutish, an ox. The father is saying: the one thing that separates a person from livestock is the ability to hear "you got that wrong" and be grateful. Love musar — the coaching. Chapter nine said the wise man loves you for correcting him. Here it's the entry test. Fail it and you're grazing.

Verse fifteen makes the same cut: "The way of a fool is right in his own eyes, but the wise one listens to advice." The fool isn't the one who's wrong. Everyone's wrong sometimes. The fool is the one who can't imagine he's wrong.

First handful — the household. Verse four: **"A woman of strength is her husband's crown, but a shameful one is like rot in his bones."** Eshet chayil — hold that phrase. It's the title of the woman in chapter thirty-one, the acrostic at the end of the whole book. Strength. Valor. The military word. Not "virtuous" the way the old Bibles soften it — chayil is what you call a soldier. She's a crown; he wears her in public and stands taller. The opposite — rakav — is bone-rot. Internal, invisible, structural.

Verse seven: **"The wicked are overthrown and gone, but the house of the right-standing stands."** Verse three: **"No one is established by wickedness, but the root of the right-standing can't be moved."** Bal-yimot — won't be shaken. Psalms thread. Verse twelve: **"The wicked covets the catch of evil men, but the root of the right-standing yields fruit."** Root, root, root. The good house isn't upright because it's tall. It's upright because it's deep. Second handful — animals and land. Verse ten, and this is the one the chapter is named for: "The right-standing man knows the soul of his animal, but the compassion of the wicked is cruel."

Yodea nefesh b'hemto. He knows the soul of his beast. Proverbs measures a man by how he treats the creature that can't talk back. The donkey. The dog. The people under him who can't complain. And then the twist in the second line: the wicked man's compassion — rachamei — is cruel. Even when he's being nice, it lands like a blow. Because kindness from a heart that doesn't know you is just a different shape of using you.

Verse eleven: **"Whoever works his land will have plenty of bread, but whoever chases empty things lacks heart."** M'radef reiqim — chases empties. Vapor projects. Get-rich schemes. Work the ground in front of you. Verse nine: **"Better to be lightly regarded and have a servant than to play the big man and have no bread."** Better to be modest and solvent than look rich and be hungry.

Verses twenty-four and twenty-seven: **"The hand of the diligent will rule, but the slack hand ends up in forced labor. The slack one doesn't even roast his game, but the diligent man's wealth is precious."** The sluggard caught the deer and then didn't cook it. He got the hard part done and quit at the easy part. You know that pattern.

Third handful — the mouth. This chapter has more mouth-sayings than any yet. Chapter ten said the mouth is the tell. Chapter twelve zooms in.

Verse six: **"The words of the wicked lie in wait for blood, but the mouth of the upright rescues."** Words as an ambush. Verse thirteen: **"The evil man is trapped by the wrongdoing of his lips, but the right-standing escapes trouble."** Your mouth can be the trap you fall into. Verse fourteen: **"From the fruit of his mouth a man is filled with good, and the work of a man's hands comes back to him."** What you say feeds you — good or bad, you eat your own words.

Verses seventeen through nineteen: **"Whoever breathes truth tells what's right, but a false witness, deceit. Some speak rashly like a sword thrust, but the tongue of the wise brings healing. Truthful lips endure forever, but a lying tongue lasts only a moment."**

Yafiach emunah — breathes faithfulness. Truth as exhale. It's just what comes out when he opens his mouth, no effort. And the sword — madqarot charev — stab wounds. Some people talk and you bleed. The wise tongue is marpe — healing, the medicine word from chapters three and four. Same organ, opposite instrument. Scalpel or shiv. And the durability line — truth lasts la'ad, forever; a lie lasts ad-argiah, the blink of an eye. Lies are fast. They work immediately. That's their whole appeal. But they have the shelf life of milk.

Verse twenty-two: **"Lying lips are detestable to God, but those who act faithfully are His delight."** To'evah again — the idolatry word from 11:1. Rigged scales, twisted hearts, lying lips. Same drawer.

Verse twenty-three: **"A prudent man conceals knowledge, but the heart of fools proclaims folly."** The wise man knows things he doesn't say. Not hiding — restraint. Chapter ten, verse nineteen: fewer words, fewer misses. Verse sixteen: **"A fool's irritation is known at once, but the prudent man covers an insult."** Koseh qalon — covers the shame. Somebody insults him and it doesn't show. Not because he didn't feel it. Because he doesn't let his face run his mouth. Verse eighteen's sword-talker is the one whose every irritation is immediately public.

Verses twenty-five and twenty-six: **"Anxiety in a man's heart weighs him down, but a good word lifts him up. The right-standing man guides his neighbor, but the way of the wicked leads them astray."** D'agah — anxiety, dread, the weight. And the remedy isn't a program. It's davar tov — one good word. You've been that heavy. Someone said one sentence and you could stand up. Be the one who says it.

Fourth handful — the two ways, briefly. Verse two: **"A good man obtains favor from God, but the schemer He condemns."** Verse five: **"The plans of the right-standing are just; the counsels of the wicked are deceit."** Verse eight: **"A man is praised according to his good sense, but the twisted of heart is despised."** Verses twenty and twenty-one: **"Deceit is in the heart of those who plot evil, but counselors of peace have joy. No harm befalls the right-standing, but the wicked are filled with trouble."**

And the last verse, twenty-eight, and it's a whisper: "In the path of right-standing is life, and the way of its path is no-death."

Al-mavet. No-death. The Hebrew is *strange* there — most translations fix it to "there is no death" or "immortality." Leave it strange. It's the same al-mut that appeared in Psalm 48:14 — "He will guide us to the edge and beyond." The right-standing path doesn't just add days. Somewhere down it, death isn't there.

Here's the shape. Loving correction is the line between a man and an ox. A woman of strength — the soldier word — is a crown. The good man knows the soul of his donkey, and the wicked man's kindness is cruel. The mouth is a scalpel or a shiv; truth lasts forever and lies last a blink; one good word lifts a heavy man. And the path ends in no-death.

Today: find your donkey — the person or creature under you who can't talk back — and know their soul for a minute. Then say one good word to someone who's carrying weight.
proverbs.notes: *Note on translation: No yirah in this chapter. 12:1 musar / tochachat = training / correction; ba'ar = brutish, ox-like — a fourth fool-word, harsher than kesil. 12:3, 12:7 bal-yimot = will not be shaken — Psalms mot thread. 12:4 eshet chayil — "virtuous woman" (KJV) — chayil = strength/valor/military might (Ruth 3:11, Prov 31:10); rendered "woman of strength"; rakav = rot (bone-rot). 12:9 niqleh v'eved lo = lightly regarded but with a servant — the Hebrew is compressed; some read "and works for himself"; majority followed. 12:10 yodea nefesh b'hemto = knows the soul of his animal; rachamei r'sha'im achzari = the compassions of the wicked are cruel. 12:11 m'radef reiqim = pursues empty things. 12:16 koseh qalon = covers insult/shame (cf. 10:12, 11:13 kasah). 12:17 yafiach emunah = breathes out faithfulness/truth. 12:18 madqarot charev = sword-stabs; marpe = healing (3:8, 4:22). 12:19 la'ad / ad-argiah = forever / for a blink. 12:22 to'evah = detestable (idolatry register; 11:1, 11:20). 12:25 d'agah = anxiety/dread — a worry word, not yirah; davar tov = a good word. 12:27 lo-yacharoch = does not roast/catch — the verb is uncertain; "roast" follows most. 12:28 MT al-mavet — "no death"; many emend to el-mavet ("to death," making the second line negative); MT retained as an early immortality whisper, cf. Ps 48:14 al-mut and Ps 16:10.*

proverbs.title: PROVERB 13 — The Rod Is a Shepherd's Tool
proverbs.body:
Let's get the hard one out of the way first, because it's been sitting in the room since chapter one.

Verse twenty-four: **"Whoever spares his rod hates his son, but whoever loves him is diligent to train him."**

You know how this verse has been used. "Spare the rod, spoil the child" — which isn't even in the Bible; it's a 17th-century English poem — has been the permission slip for three centuries of hitting kids and calling it God's will. People have been beaten with this verse. Some of you were. So let's read what it actually says.

Shevet — the rod. What is it? It's the same word as Psalm 23:4. "Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me." The shepherd's rod. Nobody reads Psalm 23 and pictures God beating the sheep. The rod was for counting them, guiding them, hooking one back from the cliff edge, knocking a wolf off. It's the tool of the one responsible for the flock. It means authority exercised for the animal's good. When Proverbs says "rod," a Hebrew ear heard "the shepherd's job," not "the whip."

And the second line gives the meaning away. Whoever loves him shicharo musar — is early with his training. Shachar — dawn. Gets up early. Is diligent about it. There's the musar word again — coaching, discipline in the athletic sense — and the verb isn't "strikes." It's "is up at dawn about it." The loving father is the one who shows up early and consistently to shape the kid. The unloving one is the one who can't be bothered. That's the contrast: engaged versus absent. Not violent versus gentle.

Now — was corporal punishment part of ancient Israelite child-rearing? Yes. Every ancient culture did it. I'm not going to pretend the text was written in a modern living room. But here's what the text doesn't say: it never says "beat." It never gives a method. It gives a principle — take responsibility for shaping the child, early and steadily, because leaving him alone is what actually hates him. If your grandfather used this verse to justify what he did to your father, the verse didn't tell him to do that. He brought the belt; the verse only brought the shepherd.

And there's a control text. Chapter three, verses eleven and twelve: God corrects the one He loves, as a father the son he delights in. That's how God does musar. Ask yourself how God has disciplined you. Did He beat you? Or did He let you walk into the consequence, then meet you there and refuse to leave? That's the rod. That's the shepherd hooking you back from the edge. That's what you owe your kids.

Okay. Now the rest of the bag.

First handful — the mouth. Verse one: **"A wise son takes his father's training, but the mocker won't listen to a rebuke."** Letz — the third-grade fool, the one chapter nine said you can't reach. Verse two: **"From the fruit of his mouth a man eats good, but the soul of the treacherous, violence."** Verse three: **"Whoever guards his mouth keeps his life, but the one who opens his lips wide comes to ruin."** Poseq s'fatav — spreads his lips wide. The mouth-breather of talk. Chapter ten, chapter twelve — the fewer words, the fewer misses.

Verse five: **"The right-standing hates falsehood, but the wicked man acts shamefully and disgracefully."** Verse thirteen: **"Whoever despises the word will be ruined by it, but whoever reveres the command is rewarded."** Careful — the old Bibles say "feareth the commandment." The word is *yare*, and here the object is a command, not God — it means taking the instruction seriously, respecting it. Not dread, not the yirah-of-the-God phrase. Just: don't blow off the word.

Verse fourteen: **"The teaching of the wise is a fountain of life, turning one away from the snares of death."** M'qor chayyim — fountain, chapter five's word, chapter ten's word. Wise teaching waters. Verse seventeen: **"A wicked messenger falls into trouble, but a faithful envoy is healing."** Marpe, again. A trustworthy person carrying a message is medicine to the whole system.

Second handful — wealth and want. Verse seven: **"One pretends to be rich and has nothing; another pretends to be poor and has great wealth."** You can't tell from the outside. Verse eight: **"A man's wealth may ransom his life, but the poor man never hears a threat."** Nobody kidnaps the man with nothing. There are freedoms in poverty the rich don't get.

Verse eleven: **"Wealth from nothing dwindles, but whoever gathers by hand grows it."** Me-hevel — from vapor, from a puff. Fast money evaporates at the same speed it arrived. Slow money — al-yad, by the hand, bit by bit — stays. Verse twenty-two: **"A good man leaves an inheritance to his grandchildren, but the wealth of the mark-misser is stored up for the right-standing."** Three generations forward. Plan for people you'll never meet. Verse twenty-three: **"Abundant food comes from the tillage of the poor, but there's what's swept away by injustice."** The Hebrew is *rough* there, but the point cuts: the poor man's field does produce — it's the system, not the soil, that takes it from him. Proverbs sees that. Verse twenty-five: **"The right-standing eats to satisfaction, but the belly of the wicked goes wanting."**

Verse four: **"The soul of the sluggard craves and gets nothing, but the soul of the diligent is made fat."** The sluggard wants. He's not without desire. He's without motion. Verse eighteen: **"Poverty and shame come to the one who ignores training, but whoever heeds correction is honored."** Musar, tochachat. Again, the coaching words.

Third handful — hope and desire. Verse twelve, and it's one of the great lines: "Hope deferred makes the heart sick, but a longing fulfilled is a tree of life."

Tochelet m'mushachah — hope stretched out, dragged. You know that sickness. The thing that keeps being almost. And the other side — ta'avah va'ah — the desire that arrives — is etz chayyim. Tree of life. Third time in the book. Wisdom is one; a good man's fruit is one; and a longing finally met is one. God knows what deferred hope does to a chest. He put it in the wisdom book.

Verse nineteen: **"A desire fulfilled is sweet to the soul, but fools detest turning from evil."** Verse nine: **"The light of the right-standing rejoices, but the lamp of the wicked goes out."** The good man's light is glad — it's alive, it dances. The other one just goes dark. Verse twenty-one: **"Trouble pursues mark-missers, but good repays the right-standing."** T'radef — the Psalm 23 hunting-verb. Trouble hunts the wicked; goodness hunts the good.

Fourth handful — company and pride. Verse ten: **"Only by pride comes strife, but wisdom is with those who take advice."** Raq b'zadon — only by arrogance. Every fight, at the root, is someone who couldn't be wrong. Verse sixteen: **"Every prudent man acts with knowledge, but a fool spreads out his folly."** Yifros — lays it out like a merchant's blanket. Look at all my stupid.

Verse six: **"Right-standing guards the blameless in his way, but wickedness overturns the mark-misser."** Verse fifteen: **"Good sense wins favor, but the way of the treacherous is hard."** Eitan — permanent, unyielding, stony. Verse twenty: **"Walk with the wise and become wise; a companion of fools suffers harm."** The Hebrew has a pun — ro'eh (companion) sounds like yeroa (be broken). Hang with fools, get broken. You become the average of the room. Choose the room.

Here's the shape. The rod is the shepherd's tool — Psalm 23's rod, the one that comforts. The verse says show up early and steadily; it never says hit. Guard the mouth. Slow money stays; vapor money evaporates. Deferred hope makes the heart sick, and a longing met is a tree of life. Every fight is only pride. Pick the room you become.

Today: if you're a parent, be early about it — engaged today, not reactive tonight. If you were the kid, hear it: the verse was never about the belt. The shepherd was hooking you back from the edge, and somebody misread the tool.
proverbs.notes: *Note on translation: No yirah in this chapter. 13:13 yare mitzvah — "feareth the commandment" (KJV) — the object is the command, not God; rendered "reveres/takes seriously the command." Not the yirat YHWH formula. 13:24 shevet — the rod — is the shepherd's rod of Ps 23:4 (shivt'cha), Mic 7:14, Lev 27:32 (counting sheep); rendered "rod" with the shepherd meaning made explicit. Chosech shivto = withholds his rod = abdicates the shepherd's role. Shicharo musar — "chasteneth him betimes" (KJV) — shachar = dawn/early, musar = training; the verb is "is early with," not "strikes." The maxim "spare the rod and spoil the child" is Samuel Butler, Hudibras (1662), not Scripture. Related rod verses 22:15, 23:13–14, 29:15 handled in their chapters; 10:13 and 26:3 use shevet for the back of fools/animals. Control text: 3:11–12 (divine musar as love). 13:1 letz = mocker. 13:3 poseq s'fatav = opens his lips wide. 13:11 me-hevel — MT "from vapor"; LXX/Vulg read m'vohal "hastily gotten" — same sense; al-yad = by hand, gradually. 13:12 tochelet m'mushachah = hope drawn out; etz chayyim = tree of life (3:18, 11:30). 13:14 m'qor chayyim = fountain of life (10:11). 13:15 eitan = enduring/hard — some emend to eidam "their ruin"; MT kept. 13:17, 13:9 note: marpe = healing; yismach = rejoices (the light itself is glad). 13:20 ro'eh / yeroa pun. 13:21 t'radef = pursues (Ps 23:6 verb). 13:23 textually difficult; rendered to preserve the injustice reading (b'lo mishpat = without justice). 13:24 remains the single most-abused verse in the book; the note is as important as the script here.*

proverbs.title: PROVERB 14 — Awe Is a Fortress
proverbs.body:
Chapter fourteen opens with the two women from chapter nine, one more time, in a single line: "Wisdom builds her house, but Folly tears it down with her own hands."

B'yadeha — with her own hands. Nobody demolishes the fool's house. She does it herself, board by board, and calls it living. Hold that, because the chapter comes back to the house at the end.

First handful — the road that feels right. Verse twelve, and it's one of the most quoted lines in the book — so quoted that it shows up again word-for-word at 16:25: "There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the ways of death."

Yashar lifnei ish — straight, in front of a man. It doesn't say the road looks wrong and he takes it anyway. It says it looks straight. It feels right. That's the horror. Sincerity isn't a compass. You can be completely convinced and completely lost. Chapter twelve said the fool's way is right in his own eyes — here's what happens at the end of that road.

Verse eight: **"The wisdom of the prudent is to understand his way, but the folly of fools is deceit."** Mirmah — the fool isn't just wrong, he's self-deceiving. Verse fifteen: **"The naive believes everything, but the prudent considers his steps."** Peti — the first-grade fool, the one who can still learn. His problem is credulity. He believes the road because it told him it was straight. Verse eighteen: **"The naive inherit folly, but the prudent are crowned with knowledge."**

Verse six: **"A mocker seeks wisdom and doesn't find it, but knowledge comes easy to the discerning."** Letz — he seeks, and can't find, because the sneer is in the way. Verse seven: **"Leave the presence of a fool — you won't find knowledge on his lips."** Lech mi-neged — walk away. Sometimes the wise move is to physically leave the room. Verse nine: **"Fools mock at guilt, but among the upright is favor."** They joke about the thing that should stop them. Verse twenty-four: **"The crown of the wise is their wealth; the folly of fools is folly."** That second line's almost a shrug — folly just produces more folly. It doesn't turn into anything. Second handful — the heart nobody sees. Verse ten: **"The heart knows its own bitterness, and no stranger shares its joy."**

Sit with that. There's a room in you no one else can enter. Your bitterness is yours; your joy is yours. This isn't loneliness as a complaint — it's just true, and Proverbs says it plain. Which is why verse thirteen follows: "Even in laughter the heart may ache, and the end of joy is grief." The father knows people laugh at parties and drive home crying. He's not shaming it. He's naming it.

Verse thirty: **"A tranquil heart is life to the body, but envy is rot in the bones."** Marpe — the healing word — a healing heart. And qin'ah, jealousy, is rakav, bone-rot, chapter twelve's word for the shameful wife. Envy rots you from the frame out.

Verse twenty-nine: **"Whoever is slow to anger has great understanding, but the quick-tempered exalts folly."** Erech apayim — long of nostrils. Slow to flare. It's the phrase God uses about Himself in Exodus 34. Verse seventeen: **"A quick-tempered man does foolish things, and a man of schemes is hated."** Q'tzar apayim — short of nostrils. Two nose-lengths. Pick yours.

Verse thirty-three: **"Wisdom rests in the heart of the discerning, but among fools it's made known."** Wisdom rests — tanuach — in the wise. It sits quiet. Fools broadcast whatever they've got.

Third handful — the poor and the neighbor. This chapter has a conscience. Verse twenty: **"The poor is hated even by his own neighbor, but the rich has many friends."** That's not approval. That's observation — and it's damning. Verse twenty-one follows immediately: "Whoever despises his neighbor misses the mark, but happy is the one who is kind to the poor." Ashrei — the Psalm 1 word.

Verse thirty-one, and this is the one: "Whoever oppresses the poor insults his Maker, but whoever is kind to the needy honors Him."

Cheref osehu — reproaches the One who made him. The poor man is God's handiwork. Grind him and you've spit on the Craftsman. Feed him and you've honored the Craftsman. Jesus said it in Matthew 25 — "whatever you did to the least of these, you did to Me." He had this verse. Verse thirty-two: **"The wicked is thrust down by his own evil, but the right-standing has refuge even in death."** B'moto — in his death. Even there. Another whisper past the grave, like 12:28.

Verse twenty-two: **"Do those who plot evil not go astray? But loyal-love and truth are for those who plan good."** Chesed v'emet — God's pair. Verse twenty-five: **"A truthful witness saves lives, but a deceitful one breathes lies."** Verse five, same: "A faithful witness does not lie, but a false witness breathes out lies." Yafiach k'zavim — exhales lies, chapter twelve's breath-word inverted. Some people lie the way they breathe.

Fourth handful — work and money. Verse four: **"Where there are no oxen the stall is clean, but abundant harvest comes by the strength of the ox."** You want a clean barn? Don't have oxen. You want food? Get used to the mess. Every real thing is messy. Verse twenty-three: **"In all toil there is profit, but mere talk leads only to poverty."** D'var s'fatayim — lip-words. Talking about it isn't doing it. Verse eleven: **"The house of the wicked is destroyed, but the tent of the upright flourishes."** Yafriach — blossoms. The good man's tent — the temporary thing — outlasts the wicked man's house. Verse nineteen: **"Evil men bow before the good, and the wicked at the gates of the right-standing."** Verse fourteen: **"The backslider in heart gets what his ways deserve, and the good man his."** Verse three: **"In the mouth of a fool is a rod for his pride, but the lips of the wise protect them."** Choter — a shoot, a rod — his own mouth is the stick he gets hit with.

Fifth handful — the nation. Verse twenty-eight: **"In a multitude of people is a king's glory, but without people a prince is ruined."** Verse thirty-five: **"A king favors a wise servant, but his wrath is on the one who acts shamefully."** And verse thirty-four, the one carved on courthouses: "Right-standing exalts a nation, but missing-the-mark is a disgrace to any people." Chesed l'umim chattat — the Hebrew literally says sin is the chesed — the "loyal-love," the shame-ironic sense — of nations. It's dark wordplay. What a nation loves faithfully, if it's sin, is its disgrace.

And the awe verses. Four of them. Verse two: **"Whoever walks uprightly stands in AWE of God, but the crooked in his ways despises Him."** Y're YHWH — the one in awe walks straight. The opposite isn't "the fearless" — it's bozehu, the one who despises Him. Awe versus contempt. Not fear versus courage.

Verse sixteen: **"The wise one is in awe and turns from evil, but the fool is reckless and confident."** Chacham yare — the wise one reveres. Here it's absolute — no object stated — and the contrast is the fool who's mit'abber u-boteach, storming through and sure of himself. Awe is the thing that makes a wise person check. Not panic. Pause. The fool has no pause.

And then verses twenty-six and twenty-seven, back to back:

**"In the AWE of God there is strong confidence, and His children will have a refuge."**

"The AWE of God is a fountain of life, turning one away from the snares of death." Read verse twenty-six as the King James has it — "in the fear of the LORD is strong confidence." Fear is confidence? That's a contradiction. But awe is confidence — the person who has stood at the canyon and been made small by it walks away steadier, not shakier. Mivtach-oz — a stronghold of trust. Psalm 46's fortress. And it's inheritable — l'vanav, for his children. Your awe becomes your kids' refuge. The house that Wisdom built in verse one — this is what it's made of.

Verse twenty-seven takes chapter thirteen's line about wise teaching — a fountain of life turning from the snares of death — and swaps in yirat YHWH as the subject. So awe of God and the teaching of the wise are the same fountain. And ask yourself: is fear a fountain of life? Fear is a drain. Awe is the spring. The Hebrew is *consistent* every single time; only the English breaks it.

Here's the shape. Folly tears down her own house with her own hands. There's a road that feels straight and ends in death — sincerity is not a compass. Your heart has a room nobody enters; guard it from envy, which rots the bones. Grinding the poor insults the Maker. And awe — four times — is upright walking, the wise man's pause, a fortress your children inherit, and a fountain of life.

Today: find the road that feels straight — the one you're most sure about — and ask one wise person to check the map. Then do one kind thing for someone poor. You'll be honoring the Craftsman.
proverbs.notes: *Note on translation: 14:2 y're YHWH — "feareth the LORD" (KJV) — rendered "stands in AWE"; antithesis is bozehu (despises Him), so the contrast is awe vs. contempt. 14:16 chacham yare — absolute use, no object — "the wise man is in awe/reverent"; contrast mit'abber u-boteach = rages/storms through and is confident. 14:26 b'yirat YHWH mivtach-oz — "in the fear of the LORD is strong confidence" (KJV) — the awe reading resolves the apparent contradiction (fear ≠ confidence; awe → steadiness); l'vanav = for his children — inherited refuge. 14:27 yirat YHWH m'qor chayyim — identical structure to 13:14 with torat chacham swapped for yirat YHWH; the substitution equates awe and wise teaching; "fountain of life" cf. 5:18, 10:11. 14:1 b'yadeha = with her own hands. 14:12 verbatim at 16:25. 14:10 marrat nafsho = bitterness of his soul. 14:17 / 14:29 q'tzar apayim / erech apayim = short/long of nostrils — the Exod 34:6 divine self-description. 14:30 lev marpe = healing heart; qin'ah = envy; rakav = rot (12:4). 14:31 cheref osehu = reproaches his Maker; echoed Matt 25:40, 45. 14:32 b'moto — MT "in his death"; LXX reads b'tummo "in his integrity" — MT retained (cf. 12:28). 14:34 chesed l'umim chattat — chesed here in its rare negative sense (shame/reproach, cf. Lev 20:17); wordplay noted. 14:24 second line is tautological in MT (ivvelet k'silim ivvelet); some emend to liv'yat "garland" — MT kept. Yirah in this chapter: 14:2, 14:16, 14:26, 14:27.*

proverbs.title: PROVERB 15 — A Soft Answer
proverbs.body:
Chapter fifteen opens with the single most useful sentence in the book for anyone who has ever been in an argument.

**"A soft answer turns away wrath, but a painful word stirs up anger."**

Ma'aneh rach — a tender answer. Not a weak one. Not a doormat. Soft — the way you'd handle something that might break. And yashiv chemah — it turns back the heat. You've watched it. Someone comes in hot, you go quiet and gentle, and they don't know what to do with it. The fire needs fuel and you didn't hand it any. And the other side — d'var etzev — a word that hurts — ya'aleh-af, makes the nostril flare. Chapter fourteen's nose-length, again.

First handful — the mouth. This chapter is thick with it. Verse two: **"The tongue of the wise dispenses knowledge, but the mouth of fools pours out folly."** Yabbia — gushes. The fool's mouth is a broken hydrant. Verse four: **"A healing tongue is a tree of life, but a twisted one breaks the spirit."** Marpe lashon — a tongue of healing. Fourth tree of life in the book. Chapter twelve said the wise tongue heals; now it is the tree. And the twisted tongue — shever b'ruach — breaks the spirit. That's what a cruel word does. It doesn't wound the body. It cracks the thing underneath.

Verse seven: **"The lips of the wise spread knowledge, but the heart of fools isn't right."** Verse fourteen: **"The heart of the discerning seeks knowledge, but the mouth of fools feeds on folly."** Yir'eh — grazes. Fools graze on stupidity. It's their pasture. Verse twenty-three: **"A man finds joy in giving an apt reply — and a word at the right time, how good it is!"** Davar b'itto — a word in its season. Timing is half of wisdom. Verse twenty-six: **"God detests the thoughts of the wicked, but pleasant words are pure."** Imrei-noam — words of pleasantness. They're tahor, clean, the temple word. Verse twenty-eight: **"The heart of the right-standing weighs how to answer, but the mouth of the wicked pours out evil."** Yehgeh la'anot — meditates on the answer. He thinks first. The wicked mouth is the hydrant again — yabbia, same word as verse two. Two chapters running on the same theme: the wise one pauses; the fool has no pause.

Second handful — the eyes of God. Verse three: **"The eyes of God are in every place, watching the evil and the good."** Not surveillance. Tzofot — the word for *a* watchman on a wall. He's keeping watch. Psalm 139 — where can I go from Your presence? Same fact, turned to comfort there and to accountability here. It's the same eyes.

Verse eleven: **"Sheol and Abaddon lie open before God — how much more the hearts of men!"** Sheol va'avaddon — the grave and the place of ruin. Not hell. The deepest, darkest, most hidden places that exist — and God sees to the bottom of them. So your heart isn't hiding anything. Verse eight: **"The sacrifice of the wicked is detestable to God, but the prayer of the upright is His delight."** To'evah / ratzon — the pair from chapter eleven. You can't buy Him off with a ritual. He wants the prayer of the straight man, not the offering of the crooked one. Verse nine: **"God detests the way of the wicked, but He loves the one who pursues right-standing."** Ye'ehav — loves. Not tolerates. Verse twenty-nine: **"God is far from the wicked, but He hears the prayer of the right-standing."** Verse twenty-five: **"God tears down the house of the proud, but He maintains the widow's boundary."** G'vul almanah — the widow's property line. God personally defends the fence of the woman nobody else defends.

Third handful — the cheerful heart. Verse thirteen: **"A glad heart makes a cheerful face, but by heartache the spirit is crushed."** Ruach n'khe'ah — a beaten-down spirit. It shows. You can see the heart on the face; the mask never quite works.

Verse fifteen: **"All the days of the afflicted are bad, but a good heart is a continual feast."** Mishteh tamid — a constant banquet. Chapter nine's feast, made portable. You can carry Wisdom's table around in your chest and eat at it all day. Verse thirty: **"Bright eyes gladden the heart; good news puts fat on the bones."** M'or einayim — the light of the eyes. Psalm 13, Psalm 19 — light up my eyes. Someone else's lit eyes do it to you. And good news — sh'muah tovah — fattens the bones. Chapter fourteen said envy rots them. Good news is the antidote — it feeds the skeleton.

Verse sixteen, first yirah verse:

"Better a little with the AWE of God than great treasure with turmoil in it." Verse seventeen right behind it: "Better a meal of vegetables where love is than a fattened ox with hatred." Two "better than"s. A small house with awe in it beats a mansion with m'humah — chaos, panic. A salad with people who love you beats steak with people who don't. Notice what the awe verse is paired with: love at the table. Awe and love are the same kind of thing — the thing that makes a small room enough. Fear doesn't do that. Fear makes every room feel too small.

Fourth handful — correction. Verse five: **"A fool despises his father's training, but whoever heeds correction is prudent."** Musar / tochachat. Verse ten: **"Harsh training is for the one who leaves the path; whoever hates correction will die."** Musar ra — severe training. When you leave the path, the coaching gets harder — not because God's angry, because the ditch is steeper. Verse twelve: **"A mocker doesn't love being corrected; he won't go to the wise."** Letz, again. He won't go. It's a refusal, not an inability.

Verse thirty-one: **"The ear that listens to life-giving correction will lodge among the wise."** Tochachat chayyim — correction that gives life. And talin — lodges overnight, the guest-word from Psalm 30. Take correction and you get to stay in Wisdom's house. Verse thirty-two: **"Whoever ignores training despises his own soul, but whoever heeds correction gains heart."** Ignoring coaching isn't self-love. It's self-contempt. You're saying your own soul isn't worth the trouble of getting better.

Verse twenty: **"A wise son gladdens his father, but a dull man despises his mother."** Verse twenty-one: **"Folly is joy to the one lacking heart, but a man of understanding walks straight."** Verse twenty-two: **"Plans fail without counsel, but with many advisors they succeed."** Chapter eleven, verse fourteen — get advisors, plural. Verse nineteen: **"The way of the sluggard is a hedge of thorns, but the path of the upright is a highway."** The sluggard's road isn't just slow — it's overgrown, because he never cleared it. Verse six: **"In the house of the right-standing is much treasure, but the income of the wicked brings trouble."** Verse eighteen: **"A hot-tempered man stirs up strife, but the slow to anger calms a quarrel."** Erech apayim — long-nostriled, the God-word from Exodus 34. Verse twenty-seven: **"Whoever is greedy for gain troubles his own house, but whoever hates bribes will live."** Verse twenty-four: **"The path of life leads upward for the wise, so he turns away from Sheol below."** L'ma'lah — upward. Away from the grave. Not from hell — from the grave, the same place verse eleven said God can see into.

And verse thirty-three, the last line of the chapter, and it's a bookend to the whole first half of the book:

"The AWE of God is the training of wisdom, and before honor comes humility." Yirat YHWH musar chochmah. Awe of God is the musar — the training, the coaching — of wisdom. Chapter one: awe is the beginning. Chapter nine: awe is the beginning. Chapter fifteen: awe is the training. It's not just the first step. It's the whole gym. Every rep of wisdom is a rep of awe. And the second line tells you what the training produces: lifnei kavod anavah — before honor, humility. The one who stands at the canyon and lets himself be made small gets lifted. Chapter three, verse thirty-four — grace to the humble. Chapter eighteen and twenty-two will say it again. Awe → humility → honor. That's the sequence. Fear → hiding → shame is the other sequence, and it's the one the mistranslation accidentally teaches.

Here's the shape. A soft answer turns away wrath — the fire needs fuel you didn't hand it. The healing tongue is a tree of life; the twisted one breaks the spirit. God's eyes see to the floor of the grave, so your heart isn't hidden. A glad heart is a continual feast; good news fattens the bones. Better a little with awe than a lot with chaos. Take correction and you get to lodge with the wise. And awe is the training — before honor comes humility.

Today: the next time someone comes in hot, go soft. Not weak — soft. Watch what happens when the fire gets no fuel. That's awe doing a rep.
proverbs.notes: *Note on translation: 15:16 b'yirat YHWH — "with the fear of the LORD" (KJV) — rendered "with the AWE of God"; the pair with 15:17 (love at a poor table) makes awe and love parallel goods; contrast m'humah = turmoil/panic. 15:33 yirat YHWH musar chochmah — "the fear of the LORD is the instruction of wisdom" (KJV) — rendered "the AWE of God is the training of wisdom"; with 1:7 and 9:10 it completes the thesis set for the first half; lifnei kavod anavah recurs at 18:12 and cf. 22:4, 3:34. 15:1 ma'aneh rach = soft/tender answer; yashiv chemah = turns back heat; d'var etzev = a word of pain. 15:2, 15:28 yabbia = gushes/pours out. 15:3 tzofot = keep watch (watchman verb). 15:4 marpe lashon = healing tongue; etz chayyim = tree of life (3:18, 11:30, 13:12); shever b'ruach = a breaking in the spirit. 15:8–9, 15:26 to'evah / ratzon = detestable / delight (11:1 pair). 15:11 Sheol va'avaddon — "hell and destruction" (KJV) — the grave and ruin; neged YHWH = in front of God; cf. Ps 139:8. 15:13 ruach n'khe'ah = stricken spirit. 15:14 yir'eh = grazes (shepherd verb, of fools feeding). 15:15 mishteh tamid = perpetual feast. 15:18 erech apayim = long of nostrils (Exod 34:6). 15:19 m'sukat chadeq = hedge of thorns; s'lulah = built-up highway. 15:23 davar b'itto = a word in its time. 15:24 l'ma'lah … mi-Sheol mattah — "hell beneath" (KJV) — the grave below. 15:25 g'vul almanah = the widow's boundary. 15:30 m'or einayim = light of the eyes (Ps 13:3, 19:8); t'dashen etzem = fattens bone (antidote to 14:30 rakav). 15:31 tochachat chayyim = correction of life; talin = lodges (Ps 30:5). 15:32 poreia musar = one who lets training go — despises his own soul. Yirah in this chapter: 15:16, 15:33.*

proverbs.title: PROVERB 16 — The Lot Is in His Lap
proverbs.body:
Chapter sixteen is the hinge of Proverbs. It's near the exact middle of the book, and it starts with God nine times in a row — the most concentrated block of God's name in the whole collection. Then it hands off to kings. Then it comes down to you. Read it as three floors.

Top floor — God and your plans. Verse one: **"To man belong the plans of the heart, but from God comes the answer of the tongue."** You plan. You lay it out. And when you open your mouth to say it, what comes out is His. Verse nine says it back: "A man's heart plans his way, but God establishes his steps." Yachin tza'ado — He sets the footstep. You draw the map; He decides where your foot actually lands. Psalm 37:23 — "the steps of a good man are established by God." Same verb.

Verse two: **"All a man's ways are pure in his own eyes, but God weighs the spirits."** Chapter fourteen's road that seems right, now with the correction: tochen ruchot — He puts the spirits on the scale. Chapter eleven's honest weight, applied to you. Verse three: **"Roll your works onto God, and your plans will be established."** Gol — roll, Psalm 37:5's verb. You don't hand it over carefully. You roll it off you like a boulder.

Verse four: **"God has made everything for its purpose — even the wicked for the day of trouble."** Nothing's outside the plan. Not even the man ruining your week. Verse five: **"Everyone proud of heart is detestable to God; be sure of it — he won't go unpunished."** To'evah — the idolatry word. Pride gets filed with the idols because pride is one.

Verse six, the yirah verse, and it's the strangest one so far:

"By loyal-love and truth wrongdoing is atoned for, and by the AWE of God a man turns from evil." Two halves. First: b'chesed ve'emet y'chuppar avon — by loyal-love and faithfulness iniquity is covered. That's kaphar — the Day of Atonement verb. Proverbs is saying that God's own character words — chesed and emet, the Exodus 34 pair — are what do the covering. Not your effort. His loyalty. Second half: b'yirat YHWH sur me-ra — by awe of God, turning from evil. So here's the sequence: His loyal-love covers the wrong; your awe turns you away from doing it again. Forgiveness first, awe second. That's Psalm 130:4 exactly — "there is forgiveness with You, so that You may be held in awe." The KJV inverts it to "that Thou mayest be feared," as if the forgiveness were a threat. It's not. Being forgiven produces awe. Awe produces turning. That's the engine. You've heard it in 3:7, 8:13, 14:16 — awe turns you from evil every time it's mentioned. Fear makes you hide the evil. Awe makes you leave it.

Verse seven: **"When a man's ways please God, He makes even his enemies be at peace with him."** Verse eight: **"Better a little with right-standing than great income without justice."** Chapter fifteen's "better a little" again — with awe there, with right-standing here. Same little. Same enough.

Middle floor — the king. Verse ten: **"An inspired verdict is on the lips of a king; his mouth doesn't betray justice."** Qesem — literally a divination, an oracle. The ideal king's judgment carries something beyond himself. Verse eleven interrupts: "Honest scales and balances are God's; all the weights in the bag are His work." The market stones — chapter eleven — belong to God. Every weight in a merchant's bag is His property. Fraud is theft from Him.

Verses twelve through fifteen: **"Doing evil is detestable to kings, because a throne is established by right-standing. Right lips are a king's delight; he loves the one who speaks straight. A king's wrath is a messenger of death, but a wise man will appease it. In the light of a king's face is life; his favor is like a cloud of spring rain."** Malqosh — the late rain that makes the harvest. The good ruler's approval is weather — it makes things grow. And his wrath is a messenger — mal'achei mavet. That's not a flattering picture of kings. It's a realistic one: power is dangerous, so be wise around it.

Ground floor — you. Verse sixteen: **"How much better to get wisdom than gold — to get understanding is to be chosen over silver."** Chapter two, three, eight — the silver keeps losing. Verse seventeen: **"The highway of the upright turns away from evil; whoever guards his way guards his soul."** M'sillat — the built-up road, chapter fifteen's word. Verse twenty: **"Whoever attends to a matter finds good; whoever trusts in God — happy is he."** Ashrei. Verses eighteen and nineteen, the pride pair: "Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall. Better to be lowly in spirit with the humble than to divide plunder with the proud." Lifnei shever ga'on — before the break, pride. You've heard it as "pride goeth before a fall" — it's this verse, and it's destruction, shever, the shattering word from chapter fifteen. Pride is the precursor. If you feel it rising, the break is already on the calendar.

Verse thirty-two, and this is the one to keep:

**"Better the slow to anger than a warrior, and the one who rules his spirit than the one who takes a city."**

Erech apayim — long-nostriled — again, the God-word. And the comparison: the man who can hold his own temper has done something harder than sacking a city. Israel had war heroes. Proverbs says the guy who didn't blow up at dinner outranks them.

Verse thirty-one: **"Gray hair is a crown of splendor; it's found in the way of right-standing."** Ateret tif'eret — a crown of beauty. The gray head isn't a decline. It's the medal. Chapter three, four — the jewelry keeps upgrading. This one you grow. Verse twenty-two: **"Understanding is a fountain of life to its owner, but the training of fools is folly."** Verse twenty-six: **"The worker's appetite works for him; his hunger drives him on."** Hunger is a tool. Verse twenty-one: **"The wise of heart is called discerning, and sweet lips increase persuasion."** Meteq s'fatayim — sweetness of lips. Verse twenty-three: **"The heart of the wise instructs his mouth and adds persuasion to his lips."** The heart teaches the mouth. Chapter four — heart first, mouth downstream. Verse twenty-four: **"Pleasant words are a honeycomb — sweet to the soul and healing to the bones."** Marpe la'atzem — healing to the bone. Chapter fifteen fattened them; here they're healed. The book is sure that good words are physical medicine.

Now the dark cluster, twenty-seven through thirty: "A worthless man digs up evil, and on his lips is like a scorching fire. A twisted man spreads strife, and a whisperer separates close friends. A violent man entices his neighbor and leads him on a path that isn't good. Whoever winks his eye plots perversity; whoever purses his lips has finished evil." Chapter six's body-language profile — the wink, the pursed lip. And nirgan — the whisperer — mafrid alluf, separates the alluf, the intimate, the close friend. Chapter six's seventh sin. God's most-hated thing: the one who splits people who were close.

Verse twenty-five, and you've heard this one word for word: "There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the ways of death." It's 14:12, exactly. The editors put it in twice. When a book that prizes economy repeats itself verbatim, it's because it wants the line to land twice. Sincerity is not a compass. Twice.

And verse thirty-three, the last line:

**"The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from God."**

Goral — the lot, the dice, the thing you throw when you don't know. They threw lots for land, for temple duty, for who'd go first. The whole point of a lot is that nobody controls it. And Proverbs says: kol-mishpato — the entire verdict of it — is His. The roll you can't control, He controls. That's the chapter's bookend. Verse one: you plan, He answers. Verse thirty-three: you throw, He decides. Everything in between is how to live in a world where the dice aren't yours.

Here's the shape. Three floors. Top: you plan, you weigh yourself pure, you roll your works onto Him — and His loyal-love covers the wrong so your awe can turn you from it. Middle: kings are weather and messengers of death; be wise near power. Ground: pride is the precursor to the break, ruling your temper beats taking a city, the gray head is a medal, and the same road that feels right ends in death — twice. And the lot is in His lap.

Today: name the dice you've been trying to control — the roll that isn't yours. Roll it onto Him instead. Then go rule your spirit in one conversation. That's the city worth taking.
proverbs.notes: *Note on translation: 16:6 u-v'yirat YHWH sur me-ra — "by the fear of the LORD men depart from evil" (KJV) — rendered "by the AWE of God a man turns from evil"; the first half b'chesed ve'emet y'chuppar avon uses kaphar (atone/cover), making the verse's logic forgiveness → awe → turning, exactly parallel to Ps 130:4 and the reverse of the KJV's implicit threat. Every prior awe verse (3:7, 8:13, 14:16) also pairs awe with sur me-ra. 16:1 ma'aneh lashon = answer of the tongue. 16:2 tochen ruchot = weighs spirits. 16:3 gol = roll (Ps 37:5). 16:5, 16:12 to'evah = detestable (idolatry register). 16:9 yachin tza'ado = establishes his step (Ps 37:23). 16:10 qesem = divination/oracle — used positively of the ideal king's verdict. 16:11 avnei-kis = the stones of the bag — all weights are God's ma'aseh. 16:14 mal'achei mavet = messengers of death. 16:15 malqosh = spring/late rain. 16:18 lifnei shever ga'on — source of "pride goeth before a fall"; shever = shattering. 16:19 sh'fal-ruach = lowly of spirit. 16:20 ashrei = happy. 16:21, 16:23 meteq s'fatayim / leqach = sweetness of lips / persuasion. 16:22 musar evilim ivvelet = the training of fools is folly. 16:24 tzuf-d'vash = honeycomb; marpe la'atzem = healing to the bone (15:30). 16:25 = 14:12 verbatim. 16:28 nirgan = whisperer; mafrid alluf = separates the intimate friend (cf. 6:19, 17:9). 16:30 otzeh einav / qotzetz s'fatav = shuts his eyes / compresses his lips — body-language of plotting (6:13). 16:32 erech apayim = long of nostrils (Exod 34:6); moshel b'rucho = rules his spirit. 16:33 goral = lot; kol-mishpato = its whole judgment/decision. Yirah in this chapter: 16:6.*

proverbs.title: PROVERB 17 — A Friend at All Times
proverbs.body:
Chapter seventeen opens at the dinner table, the same table as chapter fifteen: "Better a dry crust with quiet than a house full of feasting with strife."

Pat charevah — a dry piece. Shalvah — tranquility. Stale bread and peace beats a banquet with a fight going. Three "better a little"s now — with awe (15:16), with love (15:17), with quiet (17:1). The book keeps telling you what makes a small room enough.

First handful — the household and friendship. Verse two: **"A wise servant will rule over a shameful son and share the inheritance with the brothers."** Blood doesn't guarantee the estate. Wisdom does. Verse six: **"Grandchildren are the crown of the aged, and the glory of children is their fathers."** Ateret — crown, again, chapter sixteen's gray-head word. The old get crowned with grandkids. Verse twenty-one: **"He who fathers a fool gets grief; the father of a dull one has no joy."** Verse twenty-five: **"A foolish son is a grief to his father and bitterness to her who bore him."** The father says it twice because he's watched it. Nothing in the book hurts like this line, and he doesn't dress it up.

Verse nine: **"Whoever covers an offense seeks love, but whoever repeats a matter separates close friends."** M'chasseh pesha — covers the wrong, chapter ten's love-that-covers. And the other side: mafrid alluf — separates the intimate — chapter sixteen's whisperer. The person who keeps bringing it up isn't seeking truth. He's seeking distance.

Verse thirteen: **"Whoever returns evil for good — evil won't leave his house."** Verse fourteen: **"Starting a quarrel is like opening a floodgate; drop the matter before the fight breaks out."** Poter mayim — releasing water. Once the dam's open you don't get to decide how much comes out. So lifnei hitgalla ha-riv n'tosh — before the quarrel bares itself, drop it. The fight you didn't start is the one you win.

Verse seventeen, and this is the one the chapter is named for: "A friend loves at all times, and a brother is born for adversity."

B'chol-et — at every time. Not when it's convenient. Not when you're fun. Every. That's the definition. And ach l'tzarah yivvaled — a brother is born for the tight place. The whole point of having one is the day everything closes in. If they're not there for the tight place, they were a contact, not a brother. Chapter eighteen will say it sharper — there's a friend who sticks closer than a brother.

Verse eighteen, the co-signing warning, third time: "A man lacking heart shakes hands and puts up security in front of his neighbor." Verse nineteen: **"Whoever loves transgression loves strife; whoever makes his gate high invites a break."** Magbiah pitcho — the tall door. The man who builds his entrance too big to make a statement is asking for shever — the shattering.

Second handful — the crucible. Verse three: **"The crucible is for silver and the furnace for gold, but God tests hearts."**

Matzref / kur — the refiner's pot, the furnace. Psalm 66 — "You tested us like silver." Psalm 11 — bachan, the assayer's word. The heat isn't punishment. It's assay. The refiner heats the metal to find out what it's worth and to get the junk to float. When your life goes into the furnace, the question isn't "what did I do wrong?" It's "what is He finding in here?" Verse twenty-two: **"A glad heart is good medicine, but a crushed spirit dries up the bones."** Gehah — a cure, healing. Chapter fifteen's continual feast is pharmacy. And the crushed spirit — ruach n'khe'ah — chapter fifteen's word — dries the bone. The book keeps a running medical chart: envy rots the bones, good news fattens them, kind words heal them, a crushed spirit dries them. Your skeleton is keeping score of your inner life.

Third handful — fools. Verse ten: **"A rebuke goes deeper into a discerning man than a hundred blows into a fool."** Techat g'arah — a rebuke sinks in. One word to a wise man does more than a hundred lashes to a fool. There's your rod commentary from chapter thirteen, for free — the book itself says beating a fool doesn't work. Verse twelve: **"Better to meet a bear robbed of her cubs than a fool in his folly."** The father would rather run into a grieving mother bear than a fool who's committed to an idea. Think about who that's describing. Verse sixteen: **"What use is money in a fool's hand to buy wisdom, when he has no heart?"** He'd pay for the course and not attend. Verse twenty-four: **"Wisdom is in front of the face of the discerning, but the eyes of a fool are on the ends of the earth."** B'qtzeh-eretz — the far horizon. The fool's always looking over there. The wise man is looking at what's in front of him. Verse twenty-six: **"Fining the right-standing is not good, nor striking nobles for their integrity."** Verse seven: **"Fine speech doesn't fit a fool; how much less lying lips a ruler."** Verse eleven: **"An evil man seeks only rebellion; a cruel messenger will be sent against him."** Verse twenty: **"The twisted of heart finds no good, and the one with a perverse tongue falls into trouble."** Verse four: **"An evildoer listens to wicked lips; a liar gives ear to a destructive tongue."** You hear what you are. The liar has an ear for lies. Verse five: **"Whoever mocks the poor insults his Maker; whoever rejoices at calamity won't go unpunished."** Chapter fourteen, verse thirty-one — again. Cheref osehu. Mock the poor, mock the Craftsman. Twice now.

Fourth handful — bribes and justice. Verse eight: **"A bribe is a charm in the eyes of its owner; wherever he turns, he prospers."** That's not endorsement — it's diagnosis. The briber thinks it's a magic stone. Verse twenty-three: **"The wicked takes a bribe from the fold of the garment to bend the paths of justice."** Me-cheq — from the bosom, the inside pocket. The under-the-table exchange, described three thousand years before there were tables. Verse fifteen: **"Acquitting the guilty and condemning the innocent — God detests both."** To'evah — the idolatry word, chapter eleven's drawer. A rigged verdict either direction gets filed with the idols.

And the two on silence. Verse twenty-seven: **"Whoever restrains his words has knowledge, and the cool of spirit is a man of understanding."** Q'ar-ruach — cool of spirit. Not cold — cool. The person who doesn't heat up. Chapter fourteen's long nostril, chapter fifteen's soft answer, now as a temperature.

And verse twenty-eight, the last line, and it's funny on purpose:

**"Even a fool who keeps silent is counted wise; when he shuts his lips, he's discerning."**

Read it straight: the fool can pass for wise just by not talking. That's how powerful silence is. It works even for people who don't deserve it. The proverb's making a joke — but the joke is a mercy: if you know you're not sharp today, you have a move. Shut it. Chapter ten said fewer words, fewer misses. Chapter seventeen says the floor is zero, and zero works.

Here's the shape. Dry crust with quiet beats a feast with fighting. Grandkids are the crown. Cover the offense or split the friendship. A friend loves at every time and a brother is born for the tight place. The furnace is assay, not punishment. One rebuke to a wise man beats a hundred blows to a fool — the book knows beating doesn't work. Bribes come from the inside pocket, and God detests a rigged verdict either way. And a fool who shuts up passes for wise.

Today: find the one who was born for your tight place and tell them so. Then, in one conversation where you'd normally be the smartest voice, try being the quiet one. See if you pass.
proverbs.notes: *Note on translation: No yirah in this chapter. 17:1 pat charevah v'shalvah = a dry crust and quiet. 17:3 matzref / kur = crucible / furnace; bochen libbot = tests hearts (Ps 11:5, 66:10 bachan). 17:5 cheref osehu = reproaches his Maker (= 14:31). 17:6 ateret = crown (16:31). 17:8 even-chen = stone of favor/charm — the bribe as talisman, descriptive not approving. 17:9 m'chasseh pesha = covers transgression (10:12); mafrid alluf = separates the intimate friend (16:28). 17:10 techat g'arah = a rebuke descends/sinks in; me-hakkot k'sil me'ah = than a hundred blows to a fool — the book's own testimony that striking fools is ineffective (cf. 13:24 note). 17:12 dov shakkul = a bear bereaved of cubs. 17:14 poter mayim = one releasing water. 17:15 to'evah = detestable (idolatry register, 11:1). 17:17 b'chol-et = at every time; ach l'tzarah yivvaled = a brother is born for distress. 17:18 co-signing (6:1, 11:15, 22:26). 17:19 magbiah pitcho = raises his doorway high; shever = breaking. 17:22 gehah = healing/cure (hapax); ruach n'khe'ah = crushed spirit (15:13); t'yabbesh-garem = dries the bone — the bone-chart: 12:4, 14:30, 15:30, 16:24. 17:23 me-cheq = from the bosom-fold. 17:24 b'qtzeh-eretz = at the ends of the earth. 17:27 q'ar-ruach — Ketiv "precious of spirit," Qere q'ar "cool of spirit" — Qere followed. 17:28 the fool-passes-for-wise saying is deliberate irony; cf. 10:19.*

proverbs.title: PROVERB 18 — The Name Is a Tower
proverbs.body:
Chapter eighteen opens with a man who's walked away from everybody.

**"Whoever isolates himself seeks his own desire; he breaks out against all sound judgment."**

Nifrad — the one who has separated himself. Chapter sixteen and seventeen used the same root for the whisperer who separates friends. Here the man's done it to himself. And notice the diagnosis: he's not seeking solitude — he's seeking ta'avah, his own craving. The man who pulls away from everyone isn't usually pursuing peace. He's pursuing himself, with no one around to say no. And yitgalla — he breaks out, picks a fight — against anything sensible. Loneliness makes you combative. You've seen it.

First handful — fools and pride. Verse two: **"A fool takes no pleasure in understanding, but only in airing his own heart."** B'hitgallot libbo — in uncovering his heart. He doesn't want to learn. He wants to be heard. Verse three: **"When wickedness comes, contempt comes too, and with dishonor, reproach."** They arrive as a set. Verse twelve: **"Before destruction a man's heart is proud, but before honor is humility."** Lifnei shever — before the break. Chapter sixteen, verse eighteen, and chapter fifteen, verse thirty-three, fused into one line. Pride is the precursor to the break; humility is the precursor to the honor. Two roads, two front-runners. Whichever one's out front, you know what's coming behind it.

Verse nine: **"Whoever is slack in his work is brother to the destroyer."** Ach hu l'va'al mashchit — he's kin to the wrecker. The sluggard and the vandal end up with the same result; one just took longer.

Second handful — the mouth. Verse four: **"The words of a man's mouth are deep waters; the fountain of wisdom is a flowing brook."** Mayim amuqqim — deep waters. A person's speech goes all the way down; you're never hearing the bottom. Verse six: **"A fool's lips bring strife, and his mouth invites a beating."** Verse seven: **"A fool's mouth is his ruin, and his lips are a snare to his soul."** Moqesh nafsho — the trap for his own life. He set it himself, with his teeth. Verse eight: **"The words of a whisperer are like delicacies; they go down to the inner chambers of the belly."** K'mit'lahamim — like treats. Gossip is tasty. That's why it works. It goes down easy and sits in your gut. This exact line repeats at 26:22.

Verse thirteen: **"Whoever answers before he hears — it's folly to him and shame."** Meshiv davar b'terem yishma — returns a word before hearing. You know that person. You've been that person. The answer was loaded before the question finished. Verse seventeen: **"The first to plead his case seems right — until the other comes and examines him."** Rishon b'rivo tzaddiq — the first one sounds righteous. Always. Every story sounds airtight until the other side walks in. Never rule on one side.

Verse twenty: **"From the fruit of his mouth a man's stomach is filled; the produce of his lips satisfies him."** You eat your own words — chapter twelve, again. And then verse twenty-one, the line the whole cluster stands on:

**"Death and life are in the hand of the tongue, and those who love it eat its fruit."**

Mavet v'chayyim b'yad-lashon. Death and life — death first. Not "the tongue can be positive or negative." Death and life — the two ultimate things — are in the hand of the tongue, like it's a person with a grip. Chapter fifteen said the twisted tongue breaks the spirit; chapter twelve said it stabs like a sword. Here it's the whole range: your tongue can kill and it can resurrect, and you eat the fruit either way. James read this — "the tongue is a fire… it can bless and curse from the same mouth." He got it here.

Third handful — the tower. Verse ten:

**"The name of God is a strong tower; the right-standing runs into it and is set high."**

Migdal-oz — a tower of strength. Psalm 61 — "You have been a strong tower against the enemy." Psalm 18 — my rock, my fortress. In a walled city, the tower was the last place — when the wall fell, you ran there. And the good man runs — yarutz — he doesn't stroll. This is the emergency exit. And nisgav — he's lifted, set high, out of reach. The name — shem — is the personal name YHWH, the one the old Bibles hid behind "LORD" and this series renders simply as God. The name itself is the tower. Not a place. A who.

Verse eleven, immediately after, the counterfeit: "A rich man's wealth is his strong city, and like a high wall in his own imagination." B'maskito — in his imagination. Same words — strong, high — but the tower in verse ten is real and the wall in verse eleven is a picture in his head. The rich man thinks his money is a wall. Verse ten's man knows his God is a tower. One of them's going to find out.

Fourth handful — poor and rich, and the gift. Verse twenty-three: **"The poor man speaks in pleas, but the rich answers roughly."** Tachanunim — supplications, begging. The poor ask; the rich bark. Observation, not approval. Verse sixteen: **"A man's gift opens the way for him and brings him before the great."** That's just how doors work — a gift gets you in the room. Verse five: **"It's not good to show partiality to the wicked, to push aside the right-standing in judgment."** S'et p'nei rasha — lifting the face of the wicked. Giving him the nod because of who he is. Verse eighteen: **"Casting the lot ends disputes and separates the powerful."** Chapter sixteen's lot, again — when two strong men can't settle it, throw the dice and let God decide. It ends it, yashbit — Sabbath verb. The argument gets to rest.

Verse fourteen: **"A man's spirit sustains him in sickness, but a crushed spirit — who can bear it?"** Ruach n'khe'ah — chapter fifteen, seventeen. The spirit can carry a sick body. Nothing carries a crushed spirit. That's why the book spends so much time protecting it. Verse fifteen: **"The heart of the discerning acquires knowledge, and the ear of the wise seeks it."** Yiqneh — buys it, chapter four's "get wisdom." Verse nineteen: **"A brother offended is harder than a strong city, and quarrels are like the bars of a fortress."** Ach nifsha — a brother who's been wronged. The same tower-and-wall language, but now the wall is between you. Family rifts are the hardest fortresses to take. The book knows.

And the closing pair. Verse twenty-two: **"Whoever finds a wife finds good, and obtains favor from God."** Matza ishah matza tov — finds a wife, finds good. The Hebrew just says tov — the Genesis word, "and it was good." A wife is tov. Not "a good wife" — the old Bibles add "good" to the wife and the Hebrew doesn't; it puts the good in what you found. She's the good. Chapter five's own well, chapter twelve's crown, chapter thirty-one's woman of strength — and ratzon, favor, God's delight word. Finding her is God smiling.

And verse twenty-four, the last line, the one that answers chapter seventeen:

**"A man of many companions comes to ruin, but there is a friend who sticks closer than a brother."**

Ish re'im l'hitro'ea — a man of friends, to be broken. The Hebrew puns — re'im (friends) and hitro'ea (shattered) sound alike. Many acquaintances, no anchor. And then: ohev daveq me'ach — a lover who clings closer than a brother. Daveq — the Genesis 2 word, a man cleaves to his wife. There is a friend who cleaves. Chapter seventeen said a brother is born for adversity. Chapter eighteen says there's one who beats even the brother. Many companions is a crowd. One who cleaves is a tower.

Here's the shape. The isolated man is chasing himself with no one to say no. A fool wants to be heard, not to learn. Death and life are in the hand of the tongue — and you eat the fruit. The name is a strong tower you run into; the rich man's wall is a picture in his head. Hear both sides before you rule. A wife is good — the Genesis word. And there's a friend who cleaves closer than a brother.

Today: check whether you've been the nifrad — the one who pulled away and picked fights. If so, run into the tower first, then call the one who cleaves. And before you answer anyone today, let them finish.
proverbs.notes: *Note on translation: No yirah in this chapter. 18:1 nifrad = one who separates himself (root of mafrid, 16:28, 17:9); ta'avah = craving; yitgalla = breaks out/quarrels. 18:2 b'hitgallot libbo = in uncovering his heart. 18:4 mayim amuqqim = deep waters. 18:7 moqesh nafsho = snare of his soul. 18:8 k'mit'lahamim = like dainties — hapax, sense uncertain but "delicacies" is the majority; = 26:22 verbatim. 18:9 ach l'va'al mashchit = brother to a master of destruction. 18:10 migdal-oz shem YHWH = the name of God is a strong tower (Ps 61:3, 18:2); yarutz = runs; nisgav = is set high/inaccessible. 18:11 b'maskito = in his imagination/imagery — the wall is mental; contrast with v. 10's real tower. 18:12 fuses 16:18 and 15:33. 18:13 meshiv davar b'terem yishma = returns a word before he hears. 18:14 ruach n'khe'ah = crushed spirit (15:13, 17:22). 18:17 rishon b'rivo tzaddiq = the first in his case is righteous [seeming]. 18:18 yashbit = causes to cease (Sabbath root). 18:19 ach nifsha — text uncertain; MT "a brother transgressed against"; LXX differs — MT followed. 18:21 mavet v'chayyim b'yad-lashon = death and life in the hand of the tongue; cf. James 3:5–10. 18:22 matza ishah matza tov — KJV/LXX add "good" to "wife"; MT has no adjective: the wife is the tov; ratzon = favor/delight. 18:23 tachanunim = supplications. 18:24 ish re'im l'hitro'ea — Ketiv/Qere and root disputed (ra'ah friend vs. ra'a' shatter); the pun is likely intentional; ohev daveq = a loving one who cleaves (Gen 2:24 davaq).*

proverbs.title: PROVERB 19 — Lend to God
proverbs.body:
Chapter nineteen is about the poor man — how the world treats him, how God treats him, and what the gap between those two tells you.

First handful — the poor and their friends. Verse one: **"Better a poor man who walks in integrity than one with twisted lips who is a fool."** Fourth "better a little." Verse four: **"Wealth adds many friends, but the poor is separated from his friend."** Me-re'ehu yippared — separated — chapter eighteen's word, the isolation word. Poverty does the separating. His one friend drifts. Verse seven: **"All the brothers of a poor man hate him — how much more do his friends go far from him! He pursues them with words, but they're gone."** M'radef amarim lo-hemmah — he chases them with speech, and they're not. The Hebrew of that last clause is broken — it just trails off. Like the poor man's sentence does.

Verse six: **"Many seek the favor of a generous man, and everyone is a friend to the one who gives gifts."** The rich man has a crowd; verse four's poor man has an empty room. Chapter fourteen said this. Chapter nineteen says it three times, because it's the most observable injustice there is.

And then verse seventeen, and this is the pivot of the chapter:

**"Whoever is kind to the poor lends to God, and He will repay him for his deed."**

Malveh YHWH — lends to God. Read that literally. When you give to a poor man, the receipt has God's signature on it. He's the borrower. You've just extended credit to heaven. And g'mulo y'shallem-lo — He'll pay back his deed. Not with interest, the book doesn't say that. Just: paid in full, by a debtor who's never defaulted. Chapter fourteen said oppressing the poor insults the Maker. Chapter nineteen says helping them makes the Maker your debtor. Jesus: "whatever you did to the least of these, you did to Me." Same ledger. Verse twenty-two: **"What a man desires is loyal-love, and better a poor man than a liar."** Ta'avat adam chasdo — a person's craving is chesed. What every human being actually wants, under everything, is loyal-love. Not wealth. To be kept.

Second handful — anger and the king. Verse three: **"A man's folly ruins his way, and his heart rages against God."** Yiz'af libbo — his heart storms at God. He wrecked his own road, then blamed the sky. Verse eleven: **"Good sense makes a man slow to anger, and it's his glory to overlook an offense."** He'erich apo — lengthens his nostril. Chapter fourteen, fifteen, sixteen — same idiom — but now with a payoff: tif'arto — his glory, his beauty, is passing over the offense. Not confronting every slight isn't weakness. It's ornament. Verse nineteen: **"A hot-tempered man pays the penalty; rescue him, and you'll have to do it again."** G'dol-chemah — great of heat. Bail him out, he'll be back. Anger is a repeat customer.

Verse twelve: **"A king's rage is like a lion's roar, but his favor is like dew on the grass."** Chapter sixteen's king as weather — dew this time, gentle, morning, life-giving. Verse ten: **"Luxury doesn't fit a fool; how much less for a slave to rule princes."** Verse six, again — the crowd around power. Verse twenty-five: **"Strike a mocker and the naive learn prudence; correct a discerning man and he gains knowledge."** Notice — the letz gets hit and someone else learns. The mocker himself doesn't. Chapter seventeen said one rebuke to a wise man beats a hundred blows to a fool. Here the blows to the fool are at best a demonstration for the people watching. And hochiach l'navon — correct the discerning — a word does it. The book is consistent: violence doesn't teach the target. Words teach the teachable.

Verse twenty-nine: **"Judgments are prepared for mockers, and beatings for the backs of fools."** Mahalumot — blows. Yes, the text says it. And read the previous verse's logic with it: this is what happens to the fool — consequence — not what the wise man is told to do. The fool's back will meet the stick because the fool walked into it. Chapter thirteen's shepherd's rod is a different thing.

Third handful — the mouth and the witness. Verse five: **"A false witness won't go unpunished, and whoever breathes lies won't escape."** Verse nine says it again almost word for word: "A false witness won't go unpunished, and whoever breathes lies will perish." Yafiach k'zavim — exhales lies, chapter twelve, fourteen. When the book repeats itself four verses apart, it's underlining. Verse twenty-eight: **"A worthless witness mocks at justice, and the mouth of the wicked swallows iniquity."** Y'valla-aven — gulps it. He doesn't just speak wrong — he drinks it. Verse twenty-seven: **"Stop listening to training, my son, and you'll stray from the words of knowledge."** The Hebrew's ironic — "go ahead, stop listening" — a father's sarcasm. Fourth handful — the sluggard. Verse fifteen: **"Laziness casts into a deep sleep, and the idle soul goes hungry."** Tardemah — the Genesis 2 sleep, the deep one Adam was in when his rib came out. Laziness puts you under. Verse twenty-four, and it's the book's funniest sluggard line: "The sluggard buries his hand in the dish and won't even bring it back to his mouth." He got the hand into the food. That's most of the work. And then — nope. Chapter twelve's man who caught the deer and didn't cook it. Same guy.

Fifth handful — the household. Verse thirteen: **"A foolish son is a disaster to his father, and a wife's quarreling is a constant dripping."** Delef tored — a dripping that doesn't stop. The leak you can't find. Verse fourteen, right behind it: "House and wealth are inherited from fathers, but a prudent wife is from God." Ishah maskalet — a wife with insight. You can inherit a house. You can't inherit her. She comes from God directly. Chapter eighteen: finds a wife, finds good. The book pairs the bad-marriage verse with the good-marriage verse on purpose — so you'd hear the difference is her wisdom, not her existence.

Verse eighteen: **"Train your son while there's hope, and don't set your heart on killing him."** Wait — read that. Yasser — train, musar's verb — while there is hope. And the second half: el-hamito al-tissa nafshecha — literally, "don't lift your soul to put him to death." Some translations soften it to "don't be a willing party to his death." Either way, the father has to say this — which means he's seen fathers whose discipline crossed the line into harm. This is the book's own guardrail on the rod verses. Train while there's hope — early, chapter thirteen — and never let the correction become the thing that destroys him. Proverbs knew what abusive fathers do, and it told them to stop.

Verse twenty-six: **"Whoever robs his father and drives out his mother is a shameful and disgraceful son."** Verse twenty: **"Listen to advice and accept training, so you may be wise in your later days."** B'acharitecha — in your afterward, Psalm 37's word. Verse two: **"Desire without knowledge isn't good, and whoever hurries with his feet misses the mark."** Chote — misses. Rushing is missing. Verse eight: **"Whoever gets heart loves his own soul; whoever keeps understanding finds good."** Chapter fifteen — ignoring training is self-contempt. Getting heart is self-love. The only kind the book endorses. Verse sixteen: **"Whoever keeps the command keeps his soul; whoever despises his ways will die."** Verse twenty-one: **"Many plans are in a man's heart, but the purpose of God will stand."** Atzat YHWH hi taqum — His counsel is what stands up. Chapter sixteen, verse nine.

And verse twenty-three, the yirah verse: "The AWE of God leads to life, and one rests satisfied, not visited by harm."

Yirat YHWH l'chayyim — awe toward life. Chapter ten: awe adds days. Chapter fourteen: awe is a fountain of life. Chapter nineteen: awe is the direction of life. And then — v'savea yalin — satisfied, he lodges overnight. Psalm 30's word — yalin, spends the night. The one with awe sleeps full. Bal-yippaqed ra — harm doesn't come visit. Now — put "fear" back in there. "The fear of the LORD leads to life, and one sleeps satisfied." Nobody sleeps on fear. Fear is what keeps you up. Awe is a pillow. Chapter three, verse twenty-four — "you'll lie down and your sleep will be sweet." That sweetness is this verse's awe. The English has you terrified into slumber. The Hebrew has you awed into rest.

Here's the shape. The world separates the poor man from his last friend; God signs the receipt when you give to him — you've lent to God. Overlooking an offense is your glory. A false witness, twice. The sluggard got his hand in the dish and quit. A prudent wife comes from God, not from your father's estate — and never let training become destruction. And awe is a pillow: you sleep satisfied and harm doesn't visit.

Today: find one poor person and lend to God. Then tonight, when you lie down, try the Hebrew instead of the English — not afraid, awed — and see which one you actually fall asleep on.
proverbs.notes: *Note on translation: 19:23 yirat YHWH l'chayyim v'savea yalin — "the fear of the LORD tendeth to life: and he that hath it shall abide satisfied" (KJV) — rendered "the AWE of God leads to life, and one rests satisfied"; yalin = lodges overnight (Ps 30:5); the sleep imagery makes the fear-reading self-refuting; cf. 3:24. 19:1 = 28:6 (near-verbatim). 19:4, 19:7 yippared / m'radef amarim lo-hemmah — 7c is textually broken in MT; LXX has a longer text; rendered to preserve the trailing-off. 19:11 he'erich apo = lengthens his nostril; tif'arto = his glory/beauty. 19:12 dew (tal) vs. 16:15 rain. 19:13 delef tored = a continual dripping (= 27:15). 19:14 ishah maskalet = insightful wife — me-YHWH, from God. 19:15 tardemah = deep sleep (Gen 2:21). 19:17 malveh YHWH chonen dal = one who is gracious to the poor lends to God; g'mulo y'shallem-lo = He will repay his deed; cf.
