Ps 41:1, Matt 25:40. 19:18 yasser = train (musar verb); b'yesh tiqvah = while there is hope; el-hamito al-tissa nafshecha — "let not thy soul spare for his crying" (KJV) is a mistranslation; the Hebrew warns against killing/destroying him — the book's own guardrail on 13:24. 19:19 g'dol-chemah = great of heat. 19:22 ta'avat adam chasdo = a man's desire is his loyal-love. 19:24 = 26:15 (near-verbatim); b'tzallachat = in the dish. 19:25 letz takkeh u-peti ya'rim = strike a mocker and the naive learns — the blow instructs the bystander, not the target; hochiach l'navon = correct the discerning [by word]. 19:27 ironic imperative. 19:28 y'valla-aven = swallows iniquity. 19:29 mahalumot = blows — descriptive of consequence, not prescriptive. 19:21 atzat YHWH hi taqum = God's counsel, it stands (16:9). Yirah in this chapter: 19:23.*

proverbs.title: PROVERB 20 — Who Can Find a Faithful Man?
proverbs.body:
Chapter twenty opens with a drink.

**"Wine is a mocker, strong drink a brawler, and whoever staggers under it isn't wise."**

Letz hayyayin — wine is a letz, the third-grade fool, the one who sneers and can't be corrected. Proverbs personifies the bottle as that guy. And shogeh — staggers, the same verb chapter five used for being drunk on your own wife. You can stagger on love or stagger on liquor. One of them mocks you. Chapter twenty-three will spend a whole passage on this; here it's one stone, thrown early.

First handful — the heart nobody sees. This is the chapter's spine. Verse five: **"Counsel in a man's heart is deep water, but a man of understanding draws it out."** Mayim amuqqim — chapter eighteen's deep waters. What's inside a person is a well. Most people never get to the bottom of themselves. And the wise person is yidlennah — the one who draws — lowers the bucket, patiently, into someone else, and brings up what they couldn't reach alone. That's what a real conversation is.

Verse six: **"Many a man proclaims his own loyal-love, but a faithful man — who can find?"**

Ish emunim mi yimtza. Everyone says they're chesed. Everyone advertises loyalty. And the actual faithful person — find one. The father's not cynical. He's counting. And the count is low. Chapter thirty-one will ask the same question about a woman of strength — "who can find?" — with the same word. The rarest thing in the book is someone who is what they say.

Verse nine: **"Who can say, 'I have made my heart clean; I am pure from my missing-the-mark'?"** Nobody. The book leaves the question hanging. Psalm 51 — "in sin my mother conceived me" — Psalm 130 — "if You kept a record of wrongs, who could stand?" Proverbs gives the same answer by not answering. That's not despair. It's honesty as the entry fee. You can't start the work if you think you're done.

Verse twenty-seven: **"The breath of a man is the lamp of God, searching all the inner chambers of the belly."** Nishmat adam — the breath, the Genesis 2 breath God blew into the dust. That breath in you is God's lamp. He's not searching you from outside with a flashlight. He gave you the light on the inside, and it's already in every room. Chapter fifteen — Sheol lies open before Him. Chapter twenty — so do you, and the lamp is your own breath.

Verse twenty-four: **"A man's steps are from God — how then can a man understand his own way?"** Chapter sixteen, verse nine. You don't even know where your feet are going. Verse twelve: **"The hearing ear and the seeing eye — God made them both."** Your senses are gifts. What you notice, you were given the equipment to notice. Use it.

Second handful — the mouth and the market. Verse ten: **"Differing weights and differing measures — God detests them both."** Verse twenty-three says it again: "Differing weights are detestable to God, and false scales are not good." Even va'even — a stone and a stone. Two stones in the bag: one for buying, one for selling. Chapter eleven, chapter sixteen, chapter twenty — twice in one chapter. To'evah, the idolatry drawer. The book won't let go of this. Rigged commerce gets more repetitions than adultery.

Verse fourteen: **"'Bad, bad,' says the buyer — then goes off and boasts."** That's haggling. He tells the seller it's junk, gets the price down, then brags about the deal. Observation, not command — but you're meant to laugh and then recognize yourself. Verse seventeen: **"Bread gained by deceit is sweet to a man, but afterward his mouth is full of gravel."** Chatzatz — grit. Chapter nine's stolen water, chapter five's honey to wormwood. The stolen thing tastes great going in.

Verse fifteen: **"There is gold and abundant rubies, but lips of knowledge are a precious vessel."** Verse nineteen: **"A gossip reveals secrets, so don't associate with one who opens his lips wide."** Poteh s'fatav — the wide-lipped one, chapter thirteen. Verse twenty: **"Whoever curses his father or mother — his lamp will go out in deep darkness."** B'ishon choshech — in the pupil of darkness, the black center. Chapter twenty-seven's lamp, extinguished. Verse eleven: **"Even a child is known by his actions, whether his conduct is pure and right."** You can tell early. The deeds are the tell, not the words. Verse three: **"It's honor for a man to keep away from strife, but every fool breaks out."** Yitgalla — chapter eighteen's isolated man. The fool picks fights; the honored man walks past them.

Verse twenty-five: **"It's a snare for a man to say rashly, 'It's holy!' and only afterward to consider his vows."** Yala qodesh — blurts out "consecrated!" — pledges something to God in the heat of the moment and then thinks about it. Don't promise heaven anything on a rush. Ecclesiastes 5 — better not vow than vow and not pay. Verse twenty-two: **"Don't say, 'I'll repay evil'; wait for God and He'll rescue you."** Qavveh la-YHWH — Psalm 27's wait, Psalm 40's waiting-I-waited. Revenge is a debt you don't have to collect. It's His.

Third handful — the sluggard and the field. Verse four: **"The sluggard doesn't plow in autumn; at harvest he looks and there's nothing."** Me-choref — from the cold season. It's cold, he doesn't want to go out, so he doesn't plow. Then he asks at harvest — v'sha'al, he goes and inquires — and there's nothing to find. Chapter six's ant, inverted. He didn't know what season it was. Verse thirteen: **"Don't love sleep or you'll become poor; open your eyes and you'll be satisfied with bread."** P'qach einecha — open your eyes. Chapter twelve gave you seeing eyes. Use them before noon.

Verses sixteen and twenty-one: **"Take the garment of one who puts up security for a stranger; hold it as collateral for the foreigner."** — the co-signer's cloak gets seized; fourth time on this. "An inheritance gained hastily at the beginning won't be blessed at the end." M'vohelet — grabbed in a rush. Chapter thirteen's vapor money.

Fourth handful — the king. Verse two: **"The dread of a king is like a lion's roar; whoever provokes him forfeits his life."** Eimat melech — the terror a king inspires. That's a genuine fear-word, and it's about a human, not God. Note it: the book uses eimah for the dread of power and yirah for awe of God. Different words. Different things. English merged them.

Verse eight: **"A king who sits on the throne of judgment winnows all evil with his eyes."** M'zareh — sifts, like chaff from grain, Psalm 1. Verse twenty-six: **"A wise king winnows the wicked and drives the wheel over them."** Same verb — the threshing wheel, the cart that separates grain from straw. Justice as agriculture. Verse eighteen: **"Plans are established by counsel; make war with guidance."** Chapter eleven, fifteen — get advisors. Verse twenty-eight: **"Loyal-love and truth guard the king, and by loyal-love his throne is upheld."** Chesed ve'emet — the Exodus 34 pair, chapter sixteen's atoning pair. The throne stands on the same two words God's character stands on. Not on the roar.

And the last two, young and old. Verse twenty-nine: **"The glory of young men is their strength, and the splendor of old men is gray hair."** Tif'eret bachurim kocham — the young man's beauty is his power; hadar z'qenim seivah — the old man's majesty is the gray. Chapter sixteen, verse thirty-one — the crown of splendor. Two different ornaments for two different seasons. Neither is better. Don't try to wear the wrong one. And verse thirty, the hard last line: "Blows that wound cleanse away evil, and strokes the inner chambers of the belly."

The text is rough there. What it seems to say: sometimes the thing that hurts is the thing that cleans. Chadrei-vaten — the inner rooms of the belly — chapter eighteen's phrase for where gossip lands, chapter twenty-seven's rooms the lamp searches. The wound goes to the same depth as the light. That's not a rod verse — it's not about a parent. It's about life. The thing that hit you hardest went to the room that needed cleaning. You know that's true. You wish it weren't.

Here's the shape. Wine is a mocker; don't stagger on it. Everyone advertises loyalty — find one who is it. Nobody can say "my heart is clean," and that honesty is the entry fee. Your own breath is God's lamp inside you. Two stones in the bag, twice — God files it with the idols. Don't blurt "holy!" and think later. Dread of a king is eimah; awe of God is yirah; English lost the difference. And the wound that went deepest cleaned the room that needed it.

Today: lower the bucket into one person — draw out the deep water instead of skimming. Then check your bag for a second stone. You know which deal it's for.
proverbs.notes: *Note on translation: No yirah in this chapter. 20:2 eimat melech — "the fear of a king" (KJV) — eimah = terror/dread, a genuine fear-word applied to human power; correctly rendered as dread and explicitly distinguished from yirat YHWH. 20:1 letz hayyayin = wine is a mocker; shogeh = staggers (5:19–20 verb). 20:5 mayim amuqqim = deep waters (18:4); yidlennah = draws it up (well-bucket verb). 20:6 ish emunim mi yimtza = a man of faithfulnesses, who can find — cf. 31:10 eshet chayil mi yimtza. 20:9 unanswered rhetorical question; cf. Ps 51:5, 130:3, 1 Kgs 8:46. 20:10, 20:23 even va'even, eifah v'eifah = a stone and a stone, a measure and a measure — to'evah (11:1, 16:11). 20:14 haggling saying — descriptive. 20:16 = 27:13 (near-verbatim); Ketiv nochrim, Qere nochriyah. 20:17 chatzatz = gravel. 20:20 b'ishon choshech — Ketiv b'ishon, Qere be'eshun; "pupil/blackest part of darkness." 20:22 qavveh la-YHWH = wait for God (Ps 27:14, 40:1). 20:24 = 16:9 theme. 20:25 yala qodesh = rashly utters "holy" — hasty consecration vow (Eccl 5:4–5). 20:26 ofan = threshing wheel. 20:27 nishmat adam ner YHWH = the breath of man is the lamp of God (Gen 2:7 n'shamah); chadrei-vaten = inner chambers of the belly (18:8, 20:30). 20:28 chesed ve'emet = loyal-love and truth (Exod 34:6; 16:6). 20:29 tif'eret / hadar = glory / majesty; seivah = gray hair (16:31). 20:30 chabburot petza tamruq b'ra — MT is difficult ("bruising wounds are a scouring of evil"); Ketiv/Qere variants; LXX differs; rendered to preserve the wound-cleanses sense, and noted as not a parental-discipline verse.*

proverbs.title: PROVERB 21 — The Horse Is Ready, the Victory Is His
proverbs.body:
Chapter twenty-one opens and closes with the same claim: the thing you think you control, He controls. First line: the king's heart. Last line: the war horse. Everything in between is how to live in the middle.

**"The king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of God; He turns it wherever He wants."**

Palgei-mayim — irrigation channels. A farmer cuts a ditch and the water goes where he sends it. The most powerful man in the country — his heart, the control room — is a channel in God's hand. Whatever the king thinks he decided, the water went where it was routed.

First handful — God over your plans. Verse two: **"Every man's way is right in his own eyes, but God weighs hearts."** Chapter sixteen, verse two, again — tochen libbot. You think it's straight; He puts it on the scale. Verse thirty: **"There is no wisdom, no understanding, no counsel that can stand against God."** L'neged YHWH — facing off against Him. You can be brilliant, and if you're facing the wrong way, brilliance doesn't help.

And verse thirty-one, the last line: "The horse is prepared for the day of battle, but the victory belongs to God."

Sus muchan — the horse is ready. Notice: it doesn't say don't prepare the horse. Prepare it. Feed it, train it, saddle it. And then know that la-YHWH ha-t'shuah — the rescue, the win, is His. Psalm 20 — some trust in chariots and horses. Psalm 33 — the horse is a lie you tell yourself. Proverbs threads the needle: get the horse ready and don't believe in it. Do the work; hold the outcome loosely. That's the posture for everything. Second handful — the wicked and their offerings. Verse three: **"To do right-standing and justice is more acceptable to God than sacrifice."** Verse twenty-seven: **"The sacrifice of the wicked is detestable — how much more when he brings it with evil intent!"** B'zimmah — with a scheme. He's not just an unworthy worshipper; he's using worship as the scheme. Chapter fifteen, verse eight. Psalm 51 — You don't want sacrifice; You want a broken spirit. Psalm 50 — do you think I'm hungry? Same argument, all the way down the Bible: God is not a vending machine, and the coin He won't take is a rigged life.

Verse four: **"Proud eyes and an arrogant heart — the lamp of the wicked is missing-the-mark."** Nir r'sha'im — the wicked man's lamp, or possibly his tillage — the very thing he lives by is off-target. Verse ten: **"The soul of the wicked craves evil; his neighbor finds no mercy in his eyes."** Ivvetah ra — he appetites for it. Verse seven: **"The violence of the wicked drags them away, because they refuse to do justice."** Verse twelve: **"The Right-Standing One observes the house of the wicked; He throws the wicked down to ruin."** That capital — tzaddiq here is most likely God Himself, the Righteous One. Verse eighteen: **"The wicked is a ransom for the right-standing, and the treacherous for the upright."** Verse twenty-nine: **"A wicked man hardens his face, but the upright considers his way."** He'ez ish rasha b'fanav — he makes his face strong. You've seen it — the jaw sets, the eyes go flat, nothing's getting in. The upright man yavin darko — thinks about where he's going. One of them can still turn.

Verse eight: **"The way of the guilty is crooked, but the conduct of the pure is straight."** Verse fifteen: **"When justice is done, it's joy to the right-standing, but terror to evildoers."** M'chittah — dread. A real fear-word, and look who it's for: the ones who did wrong. Justice isn't scary to the good. That's the whole point. Verse sixteen: **"The man who strays from the way of understanding will rest in the assembly of the dead."** Q'hal r'fa'im — the congregation of the shades. Chapter two, chapter nine. Not hell — the grave. He rests there, yanuach — same verb as Sabbath rest, twisted. Verse eleven: **"When a mocker is punished, the naive becomes wise; when the wise is instructed, he gains knowledge."** Chapter nineteen, verse twenty-five — the letz gets the consequence, the peti learns from watching, the chacham learns from a word. Three grades, three delivery methods.

Third handful — the mouth and the house. Verse nine: **"Better to live on a corner of the roof than share a house with a quarrelsome woman."** Eshet midyanim — a woman of contentions. And verse nineteen, the same thought, harder: "Better to live in a desert land than with a quarrelsome and angry woman." Midbar — the wilderness. Now hear this right: the book already said a wife is tov, a prudent wife is from God, a woman of strength is a crown. This isn't about women. It's about strife in the house — and because it's father-to-son, the strife wears a wife's face. Flip the genders and it's just as true: the roof corner beats a full house where someone's always angry. The father keeps saying it — chapter seventeen, chapter nineteen's dripping — because peace at home is the thing he'd trade everything else for. Verse twenty-five is the desert outside; verse nine is the desert inside.

Verse twenty-three: **"Whoever guards his mouth and tongue guards his soul from trouble."** Shomer — the watchman word, Psalm 121. Verse six: **"Getting treasure by a lying tongue is a fleeting vapor and a snare of death."** Hevel niddaf — a driven vapor, Psalm 1's chaff, Ecclesiastes' word. Lie money blows away. Verse twenty-eight: **"A false witness will perish, but the man who listens will speak forever."** Ish shomea la-netzach y'daber — the listener is the one whose words last. Because he heard first. Chapter eighteen, verse thirteen. Verse twenty-four: **"Proud, arrogant — 'Mocker' is his name; he acts with insolent pride."** Letz sh'mo — that's literally his name tag. Verse twenty-two: **"A wise man scales the city of the mighty and brings down the stronghold they trusted."** One wise man beats a fortified city. Chapter sixteen, verse thirty-two — ruling your spirit beats taking a city; here wisdom actually takes one.

Fourth handful — the sluggard and the spender. Verse five: **"The plans of the diligent lead only to profit, but everyone who hurries comes only to want."** Kol-atz — everyone who rushes. Chapter nineteen: hurrying feet miss. Verse twenty-five: **"The craving of the sluggard kills him, because his hands refuse to work."** T'mitennu — it kills him. Chapter thirteen said the sluggard wants and gets nothing; here the wanting itself is fatal. He dies of unacted desire. Verse twenty-six: **"All day long he craves and craves, but the right-standing gives and doesn't hold back."** One man wants all day. The other man gives all day. That's the difference between them — not wealth. Direction. Verse seventeen: **"Whoever loves pleasure will be poor; whoever loves wine and oil won't be rich."** Verse twenty: **"Precious treasure is in the house of the wise, but a fool swallows it."** Y'val'ennu — gulps it, chapter nineteen's verb for swallowing iniquity. The fool eats his inheritance.

Fifth handful — the poor and the merciful. Verse thirteen: **"Whoever shuts his ear to the cry of the poor will himself cry out and not be answered."**

Read that with chapter nineteen, verse seventeen — lending to God. Here's the other side of the ledger. Shut your ear to the poor man's za'aqah — his scream — and one day you'll scream, and the line will be closed. Not as revenge. As echo. The ear you closed is the ear that gets closed. Jesus's rich man and Lazarus is this verse with names. Verse fourteen: **"A gift in secret calms anger, and a bribe in the bosom, strong wrath."** Observation — that's how bribes work, and that they work is the problem. Verse twenty-one: **"Whoever pursues right-standing and loyal-love finds life, right-standing, and honor."** Rodef — the Psalm 23 hunting-verb. Hunt chesed and it turns around and gives you life. Chapter twenty-one, verse three said God prefers justice to sacrifice; verse twenty-one says the man who hunts it gets the whole set.

Here's the shape. The king's heart is a ditch in God's hand. Your way looks straight; He weighs it. God won't take a rigged life as an offering — the coin is a broken spirit. Better a roof corner than a house full of fighting. The listener is the one whose words last. The sluggard dies of wanting; the right-standing man gives all day. Shut your ear to the poor and yours gets shut. And the horse is ready — prepare it — but the victory is His.

Today: prepare your horse. Do every rep. Then, before the battle, say out loud who the win belongs to — and see how much lighter the saddle gets.
proverbs.notes: *Note on translation: No yirah in this chapter. 21:15 m'chittah = terror/ruin — genuine dread, for evildoers only; correctly a fear-word. 21:1 palgei-mayim = irrigation channels. 21:2 tochen libbot = weighs hearts (16:2). 21:3 justice > sacrifice; cf. 15:8, 21:27, Ps 40:6, 51:16–17, Hos 6:6, 1 Sam 15:22. 21:4 nir r'sha'im — "the plowing of the wicked" (KJV) vs. "lamp" (ner) — both readings viable; lamp favored (13:9, 20:20, 24:20). 21:9 = 25:24 (verbatim); eshet midyanim = woman of contentions — the strife, not the gender, is the subject (cf. 18:22, 19:14 for the positive wife-sayings). 21:12 tzaddiq here = God as the Righteous One (majority reading). 21:13 za'aqat-dal = the poor man's cry; the reciprocal principle echoed Luke 16:19–31, Matt 25:41–45. 21:16 q'hal r'fa'im — "congregation of the dead" — the grave, not hell; yanuach = rests (ironic Sabbath verb). 21:18 kofer = ransom. 21:20 y'val'ennu = swallows it (19:28). 21:21 rodef = pursues (Ps 23:6). 21:25 ta'avat atzel t'mitennu = the craving of the sluggard kills him. 21:27 b'zimmah = with a scheme/evil intent. 21:28 ish shomea la-netzach y'daber — text uncertain; "the man who listens will speak forever/successfully" — majority followed. 21:29 he'ez … b'fanav = makes strong with his face. 21:30 l'neged YHWH = over against God. 21:31 sus muchan … la-YHWH ha-t'shuah = the horse is prepared … to God belongs the victory (Ps 20:7, 33:17).*

proverbs.title: PROVERB 22 — A Good Name Over Great Riches
proverbs.body:
Chapter twenty-two is a seam. Halfway through, the voice changes — Solomon's two-liners end, and a new teacher starts numbering his sayings. Read the first half as the last of the stones, and the second half as the opening of a new bag.

**"A good name is to be chosen over great riches; favor is better than silver and gold."**

Nivchar shem — a name is to be chosen. The Hebrew just says shem, "name" — the "good" is implied. Your name is the one asset that follows you into the room before you get there and stays after you leave. Chapter ten said the name of the wicked rots. Chapter eighteen said the Name is a tower. Choose yours over the money. You'll need it longer.

First handful — rich and poor. Verse two: **"The rich and the poor meet together; God is the Maker of them all."** Nifgashu — they run into each other. Same street, same Maker. Whatever the difference in their bank accounts, the difference in their origin is zero. Chapter fourteen and seventeen said grinding the poor insults the Maker — here's why: same Craftsman.

Verse seven: **"The rich rules over the poor, and the borrower is servant to the lender."** Eved — slave. That's not approval; that's the mechanism. Debt is a leash. Verse sixteen: **"Whoever oppresses the poor to increase his own wealth, or gives to the rich — both come to poverty."** Verse twenty-two, in the new section: "Don't rob the poor because he's poor, and don't crush the afflicted at the gate." Ki dal hu — because he's poor. Don't take from him precisely because he can't fight back. That's the definition of predation, and the book names it. Verse twenty-three: **"For God will plead their case and rob the life of those who robbed them."** Yariv rivam — He takes their lawsuit. The poor man has counsel. It's God. Verse nine: **"The one with a generous eye will be blessed, for he gives his bread to the poor."** Tov-ayin — good of eye. The opposite of chapter twenty-three's evil eye. Generosity is a way of seeing. Verse twenty-six and twenty-seven, the co-signing warning one last time: "Don't be one of those who shake hands and put up security for debts. If you have nothing to pay, why should your bed be taken from under you?" Fifth time. They'll take the bed.

Second handful — the mouth and the heart. Verse eleven: **"He who loves purity of heart and has gracious lips — the king is his friend."** T'hor-lev — clean of heart, Psalm 24's word. Verse ten: **"Drive out the mocker and strife goes out; quarrels and insults cease."** Garesh letz — expel him. Sometimes the fix for a room is one person leaving it. Verse twelve: **"The eyes of God guard knowledge, but He overthrows the words of the treacherous."** Verse fourteen: **"The mouth of the strange woman is a deep pit; the one God is angry with falls in."** Shuchah amuqqah — chapter seven's stranger, now as a pit. The pit-digger, from the other side. Verse eight: **"Whoever sows injustice reaps trouble, and the rod of his fury will fail."** You reap what you sow — Paul in Galatians got it here — and shevet evrato, the rod of his rage, yichleh, is finished. The man who rules by anger runs out of rod. Verse thirteen: **"The sluggard says, 'There's a lion outside! I'll be killed in the streets!'"** He invents a lion. Chapter twenty-six will have him say it again. Every excuse is a lion he made up.

Third handful — the child. Two verses, and they're the most quoted parenting lines in Scripture.

Verse six: **"Train up a child according to his way, and even when he's old he won't turn from it."**

Chanoch la-na'ar al-pi darko. Everyone knows "train up a child in the way he should go." But al-pi darko is "according to his way" — the child's own way, his bent, his grain. The Hebrew doesn't say "the right way." It says his way. Which means the verse is either a promise — learn how this kid is wired and shape him along that grain, and it holds — or a warning — let a kid do whatever he wants and that holds too. Both readings are honest to the Hebrew. And both say the same thing to a parent: pay attention to the actual child. Not the child you planned. The one in front of you. And chanoch — that's the word for *dedicating* a house or a temple. You're not programming him. You're dedicating him. Consecrating a life.

Verse fifteen: **"Folly is bound up in the heart of a child, but the rod of training drives it far from him."**

Here's the second rod verse. Chapter thirteen gave you the shepherd's rod — Psalm 23's, the one that comforts. Here it's shevet musar — the rod of training, coaching's rod, the shepherd's job. And notice what it says folly is: q'shurah — tied, knotted into the kid's heart. Not evil — folly, the naive-and-thick-headed kind, chapter one's ivvelet. Every child comes with it knotted in. And the shepherd's job is yarchiqennah — to move it far away. Untie the knot; put distance between the kid and his own foolishness. That's a long verb. It doesn't happen in one blow. It happens over years of showing up early, chapter thirteen. Read verse six and fifteen together: know the child's grain; steadily separate him from his folly. Neither one says hit. And chapter nineteen already told you where the line is — never let training become destruction.

The yirah verse. Verse four:

**"The reward for humility is the AWE of God — riches, honor, and life."**

Or, the more common reading: eqev anavah yirat YHWH — "the result of humility and awe of God is riches, honor, and life." Either way the Hebrew glues anavah and yirah together — humility and awe are one thing, or one produces the other. Chapter fifteen: awe is the training; before honor, humility. Chapter eighteen: before honor, humility. Now: humility plus awe yields honor. And put "fear" in there — "the reward for humility is the fear of the LORD." Being humble gets you terror? No. Being small before something great is what awe is. Humility is awe from the inside; awe is humility looking up. Same thing. Three payoffs: riches, honor, chayyim. Life. Again.

Now the seam. Verse seventeen: **"Incline your ear and hear the words of the wise; apply your heart to my knowledge. For it's pleasant if you keep them within you, if all of them are ready on your lips."**

New teacher. New collection — the old Bibles miss it, but the Hebrew of verse twenty says shalishim — "thirty" — "have I not written you thirty sayings?" Most translations render it "excellent things," but the letters spell thirty, and if you count the units from here to 24:22, you get thirty. This is a numbered course. And it looks a lot like an Egyptian one — the Instruction of Amenemope, written centuries before Solomon, has the same sequence: honest boundaries, don't rob the poor, don't eat with the stingy, don't befriend the hot-tempered. Israel's wise men read the neighbors' wisdom and baptized it — kept what was true, put God's name on it. That's not embarrassing. That's what wisdom does. Truth is truth wherever you dig it up.

Verse nineteen: **"So your trust may be in God — I've made them known to you today, even to you."** Af-attah — even you. He's looking at one person. Verse twenty-one: **"To make you know truth, reliable words, so you can bring back a true report to those who sent you."** Whoever sent you — your family, your boss, your God — you're supposed to come back with the truth. Saying two, verse twenty-four and twenty-five: **"Don't befriend a hot-tempered man; don't go with a wrathful man, or you'll learn his ways and get your soul snared."** Ba'al af — master of nostril. You catch anger from people. Chapter thirteen — choose the room. Saying three, twenty-six and twenty-seven — the bed. Saying four, twenty-eight: "Don't move the ancient boundary stone your fathers set up." Amenemope has this one almost word for word. Property lines. Chapter fifteen — God defends the widow's boundary. Don't be the one who nudges the fence overnight.

And saying five, verse twenty-nine, the last line: "Do you see a man skilled in his work? He'll stand before kings; he won't stand before obscure men."

Ish mahir bi-mlachto — a man quick, skilled at his craft. Not a rich man. Not a well-connected one. A man who's good at the thing. That man ends up in rooms he couldn't have bought his way into. Skill is its own introduction. Bezalel built the tabernacle because he could work metal. Get so good they can't not call you.

Here's the shape. Choose a name over riches. Rich and poor have the same Maker — don't rob a man because he can't fight back; God takes his case. Know your child's actual grain and steadily move his folly far off — no verse says hit. Humility and awe are one thing, and it pays life. Then a new teacher with thirty numbered sayings, some borrowed from Egypt and baptized. Don't catch anger from the angry. Don't move the fence. And get so skilled they call you into the king's room.

Today: pick the one skill you'd stand before kings with, and put an hour into it. Then look at the child — yours or someone's — and ask what their actual grain is, not the one you drew up.
proverbs.notes: *Note on translation: 22:4 eqev anavah yirat YHWH — "by humility and the fear of the LORD are riches" (KJV) — rendered with yirah = awe; the syntax either equates humility with awe or makes awe the reward of humility — both readings unify the two; cf. 15:33, 18:12. 22:1 shem alone — "good" is supplied. 22:2 nifgashu = meet/encounter; oseh chullam = Maker of them all (14:31, 17:5). 22:6 chanoch la-na'ar al-pi darko — chanoch = dedicate (Deut 20:5, 1 Kgs 8:63); al-pi darko = according to HIS way — the "way he should go" of KJV is interpretive; both the promise-reading and the warning-reading are noted; the verse is absent from the LXX. 22:8 shevet evrato yichleh = the rod of his wrath fails — a rod that runs out; zorea avlah yiqtzor-aven → Gal 6:7. 22:9 tov-ayin = good of eye (contrast 23:6, 28:22 ra-ayin). 22:13 sluggard's lion = 26:13. 22:14 shuchah amuqqah = deep pit. 22:15 ivvelet q'shurah v'lev-na'ar = folly is bound/knotted in the child's heart; shevet musar = rod of training — the shepherd's rod (13:24 note); yarchiqennah = drives it FAR from him — durative; control texts 17:10, 19:18. 22:17 begins the Thirty Sayings; 22:20 Ketiv shilshom ("formerly"), Qere shalishim ("officers/excellent things") — emended by most modern scholars to sh'loshim = "thirty," matching the count of units to 24:22 and the thirty-chapter Instruction of Amenemope (c. 1300–1075 BCE), whose parallels include 22:22 (ch. 2), 22:24–25 (ch. 9), 22:28 (ch. 6), 22:29 (ch. 30), 23:1–3, 23:4–5, 23:6–8, 23:10–11. 22:22 ki dal hu = because he is poor. 22:23 yariv rivam = pleads their plea. 22:24 ba'al af = master of nostril/anger. 22:26 co-signing (6:1, 11:15, 17:18, 20:16). 22:29 ish mahir bi-mlachto = a man skilled/swift in his work. Yirah in this chapter: 22:4.*

proverbs.title: PROVERB 23 — Wings Like an Eagle
proverbs.body:
Chapter twenty-three is the Thirty Sayings at full length — the two-liners give way to little paragraphs, and the teacher sits down across from you. It's the most intimate chapter since the father's lectures in one through nine, and it ends with the most vivid drunk in the Bible.

Saying six — the ruler's table. Verses one through three: **"When you sit down to eat with a ruler, consider carefully what's in front of you. Put a knife to your throat if you're a man of big appetite. Don't crave his delicacies — it's deceptive food."**

Lechem k'zavim — bread of lies. The powerful man's table has a price on it, and the price isn't on the menu. Amenemope told Egyptian civil servants the exact same thing: don't eat greedily in front of the boss — it's a test. The knife-to-the-throat is comic. Restrain yourself that hard. Every free meal from a man who wants something is a hook with food on it.

Saying seven — riches with wings. Verses four and five: **"Don't wear yourself out to get rich; have the sense to stop. Will you set your eyes on it? It's gone — because it makes itself wings and flies to the heavens like an eagle."**

Ta'uf ha-shamayim k'nesher — it flies off like an eagle. Amenemope: "riches make themselves wings like geese and fly to the sky." Israel swapped the goose for an eagle and kept the picture. You look at the money and it isn't there. Chapter thirteen's vapor. Chapter eleven's inherited wind. And the phrase in the middle — mi-binatcha chadal — literally "from your understanding, cease." Be smart enough to stop. Ambition without a brake is not wisdom. Knowing when enough is enough is.

Saying eight — the stingy host. Verses six through eight: **"Don't eat the bread of a man with an evil eye; don't crave his delicacies. He's the kind who's always calculating — 'eat and drink,' he says to you, but his heart isn't with you. You'll vomit up the morsel you ate and waste your pleasant words."** Ra-ayin — evil of eye. Chapter twenty-two's good eye, flipped. The stingy man feeds you and resents it, and you can taste the resentment. The Hebrew for *his* calculating is ki-k'mo-sha'ar b'nafsho — "like a gate-keeper in his soul," counting every bite through the gate. You'll throw the meal up. And your thank you was wasted on him. Don't eat where you're not wanted, no matter how good the food.

Sayings nine through eleven — fools, fences, and the child. Verse nine: **"Don't speak in a fool's ears — he'll despise the sense in your words."** Chapter nine — you can't reach the letz. Save your breath. Verses ten and eleven: **"Don't move the ancient boundary stone or encroach on the fields of orphans, for their Redeemer is strong; He'll plead their case against you."** Go'alam chazaq — their Redeemer, the kinsman-redeemer word, Psalm 19's goel, Ruth's Boaz. The orphan has no family to fight for his fence. So God is the family. Chapter twenty-two, verse twenty-three. Move a fatherless kid's fence and you've picked a fight with his big brother, and his big brother is God.

Verse twelve: **"Apply your heart to training and your ears to words of knowledge."** Musar — coaching. It leads straight into the hardest lines.

Verses thirteen and fourteen: **"Don't withhold training from a child; if you strike him with the rod, he won't die. Strike him with the rod and you'll rescue his soul from Sheol."**

Third rod verse, and this one does say strike — takkennu. I won't pretend it doesn't. So let's read it honestly, all of it.

First, the frame: al-timna mi-na'ar musar — don't withhold coaching from the kid. That's the command. The rest is the ancient teacher's assumption of how coaching happens in his world. Second, lo yamut — "he won't die." Why would the teacher have to say that? Because he's heard fathers use it as an excuse to do nothing — "I don't want to hurt him" — and he's answering: correcting your child won't kill him. It's permission to parent. Third, the goal: mi-sh'ol tatzil — rescue him from the grave. Not hell — the grave. The premature death that comes from unrestrained folly; chapter seven's ox. The rod is between the kid and the cliff. That's Psalm 23's rod, hooking the sheep back.

And now the guardrails the book itself put around this verse. Chapter nineteen, verse eighteen: train while there's hope, and never let it become the thing that destroys him — the Hebrew explicitly forbids that. Chapter seventeen, verse ten: one rebuke does more in a wise heart than a hundred blows in a fool's. Chapter nineteen, verse twenty-five: the blow teaches the bystander, not the one hit. Chapter twenty-two, verse eight: the man who rules by the rod of his fury runs out of rod. The book gave you the shepherd's rod in thirteen and then spent six chapters telling you what it isn't for. Read all of it, or don't quote any of it. The teacher's culture had corporal discipline; the teacher's principle is: don't abandon the kid to his own folly, because that road ends in the grave. You are allowed — you are required — to find the version of that principle that works without the belt. God found one for you. Chapter three, verse twelve. Go be that father.

Sayings twelve through sixteen — the father's plea. This is where the teacher's voice cracks. Verses fifteen and sixteen: **"My son, if your heart is wise, my heart will be glad too — yes, mine. My innermost being will rejoice when your lips speak what's right."** Gam ani — even I, me too. He's not teaching. He's hoping. Verse nineteen: **"Hear, my son, and be wise, and direct your heart in the way."** Verse twenty-two: **"Listen to your father who gave you life, and don't despise your mother when she's old."** Both parents again. Verses twenty-four and twenty-five: **"The father of a right-standing child will greatly rejoice; whoever fathers a wise son delights in him. Let your father and mother be glad; let her who bore you rejoice."** Verse twenty-six: **"My son, give me your heart, and let your eyes delight in my ways."** T'nah-libbecha li — give me your heart. Not your obedience. Your heart. That's the whole ask, and it's the same one God makes.

And in the middle of the plea, verses seventeen and eighteen, the awe verse:

**"Don't let your heart envy mark-missers, but be in the AWE of God all day long — because surely there is a future, and your hope won't be cut off."**

Al-y'qanne libbecha ba-chatta'im — don't let your heart burn with envy at the ones who get away with it. That's Psalm 73 — "I envied the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked." Every honest person has stood there. And the answer isn't "be afraid of God." The Hebrew is *ki* im-b'yirat YHWH kol-ha-yom — literally, "but [be] in awe of God all the day." Stay in the awe. All day. The antidote to envying the cheater is standing in the canyon long enough that his sports car looks small. And then the reason: ki im-yesh acharit — surely there's an afterward, Psalm 37's word. Tiqvat'cha lo tikkaret — your hope won't be cut off. Fear doesn't give you a future. Awe does — because it puts you next to the One who owns the afterward.

Sayings seventeen and eighteen — wine and women, briefly. Verses twenty and twenty-one: **"Don't be among winebibbers or gluttonous eaters of meat — the drunkard and the glutton come to poverty, and drowsiness clothes a man in rags."** Verses twenty-seven and twenty-eight: **"A prostitute is a deep pit; a strange woman is a narrow well. She lies in wait like a robber and increases the treacherous among men."** Chapter twenty-two's pit, chapter seven's ambush. Nothing new — the teacher's repeating the father because the son still hasn't heard it.

Saying nineteen — the drunk. Verses twenty-nine through thirty-five. This is the one.

"Who has woe? Who has sorrow? Who has quarrels? Who has complaining? Who has wounds for no reason? Who has bloodshot eyes?" Six questions, one answer: "Those who linger long over wine, who go looking for mixed drinks."

Then the warning, and it's beautiful, which is the point: "Don't look at wine when it's red, when it sparkles in the cup, when it goes down smoothly." Yit'hallech b'meisharim — it walks in straight — it goes down easy. The teacher doesn't say wine is ugly. He says it's gorgeous. Chapter five's honey. Chapter seven's Egyptian linen. The trap is always pretty from the front.

"In the end it bites like a snake and stings like a viper." The morning-after. "Your eyes will see strange things, and your heart will speak twisted things." Zarot — strange things — the stranger word. Hallucinations, and the mouth saying things you don't mean. "You'll be like one lying down in the middle of the sea, like one lying on top of a mast." The spins. The room moving. The teacher has been there or watched someone there — nobody writes "lying on top of a mast" from a textbook.

And then verse thirty-five, the last line, in the drunk's own voice: "'They hit me — I didn't feel it. They beat me — I didn't know it. When will I wake up? I'll go find another drink.'"

Osif avaqshennu od. I'll seek it again. That's the disease in one sentence. He got beaten and didn't feel it. He knows he's been beaten. And the very next thought is more. Anybody who's been in a room with recovery knows that voice exactly. Proverbs wrote it down three thousand years ago and didn't blink. The teacher doesn't moralize. He just lets the drunk finish his sentence, and the sentence is the whole argument.

Here's the shape. The powerful man's table is a hook. Riches grow wings — be smart enough to stop. Don't eat where the host resents you. God is the orphan's big brother. Don't abandon the kid to his own folly — and read the book's own guardrails on how. Envy the cheater? Stand in awe all day instead; awe has a future and fear doesn't. Give your father your heart. And the drunk's last line is "I'll go find another." Don't let it be yours.

Today: if you're chasing money, find your brake — from your understanding, cease. If you're envying someone who got away with it, spend the day in the canyon instead. And if verse thirty-five is your voice, or someone's you love — the teacher heard it too. Wake up is still on the table.
proverbs.notes: *Note on translation: 23:17 ki im-b'yirat YHWH kol-ha-yom — "but be thou in the fear of the LORD all the day long" (KJV) — rendered "be in the AWE of God all day long"; the context is envy of the wicked (Ps 73) and the promise of acharit (a future, 37:37) — awe, not dread, is the posture that has a future. 23:1–3 ≈ Amenemope ch. 23; lechem k'zavim = bread of lies. 23:4–5 ≈ Amenemope ch. 7 (geese → eagle); mi-binatcha chadal = from your understanding, cease; Ketiv/Qere on ta'uf/ya'uf. 23:6 ra-ayin = evil of eye (contrast 22:9). 23:7 ki-k'mo-sha'ar b'nafsho — very difficult; "like a gatekeeper in his soul / as he reckons within himself"; KJV "as he thinketh in his heart, so is he" is a famous misreading — the verse is about the host's calculating, not a general maxim about self-image. 23:10–11 ≈ Amenemope ch. 6; go'alam chazaq = their Redeemer is strong (kinsman-redeemer, Ps 19:14). 23:13–14 takkennu va-shevet = strike him with the rod — the only rod verse with an explicit striking verb; lo yamut = he will not die (permission-to-parent against neglect); mi-sh'ol tatzil — "deliver his soul from hell" (KJV) — from the GRAVE, premature death by folly (cf. 7:27); shevet = shepherd's rod (13:24 note); guardrails 17:10, 19:18, 19:25, 22:8, 3:12. 23:15–16 gam ani = even I. 23:26 t'nah-libbecha li = give me your heart. 23:27 shuchah amuqqah / be'er tzarah = deep pit / narrow well. 23:29–35 the drunkard portrait; yit'hallech b'meisharim = goes down smoothly/straight; zarot = strange things (the zar root of the strange woman); b'rosh chibbel = on top of a mast; 23:35 osif avaqshennu od = I will seek it yet again. Yirah in this chapter: 23:17.*

proverbs.title: PROVERB 24 — Seven Times Down, Seven Times Up
proverbs.body:
Chapter twenty-four finishes the Thirty Sayings and then adds a coda. The teacher's last big theme is how to hold steady while the wicked seem to be winning — the Psalm 37 problem, the Psalm 73 problem — and he answers it with the most encouraging line in the book.

Saying twenty — don't envy them. Verses one and two: **"Don't envy evil men or desire to be with them, for their hearts plot violence and their lips talk trouble."** Chapter twenty-three, verse seventeen — same command. The teacher says it twice in eight verses because the envy is that sticky. You look at what the cheater has and something in you goes I want that. He's saying: look at what's in him. You don't want that.

Verses nineteen and twenty say it a third time: "Don't get heated over evildoers, and don't envy the wicked — for the evil man has no future, and the lamp of the wicked will be snuffed out." Al-titchar — don't burn — Psalm 37's word, three times in that psalm, now here. Ein acharit la-ra — no afterward for the wicked. Chapter twenty-three said your hope has a future. Here: his doesn't. And his lamp — chapter thirteen, twenty, twenty-one — goes out. Every time you burn about the wicked man's success, you're standing in the light of a lamp that's about to be yid'ach — snuffed.

Saying twenty-one — the house. Verses three and four: **"By wisdom a house is built, by understanding it's established, and by knowledge its rooms are filled with all precious and pleasant riches."** Chapter nine — Wisdom built her house. Chapter fourteen — Folly tears hers down with her own hands. Here: your house. Three words — chochmah, t'vunah, da'at — the same three God used to build the universe in chapter three, verses nineteen and twenty. Build your household with the tools He built the cosmos with. It'll hold. Verses five and six: **"A wise man is strong; a man of knowledge grows in power. For by wise guidance you wage war, and victory comes through many counselors."** Chapter eleven, fifteen, twenty — plural advisors. Chapter twenty-one — the win is God's. Bring counsel; expect Him to deliver it.

Saying twenty-two — the fool at the gate. Verse seven: **"Wisdom is too high for a fool; at the gate he doesn't open his mouth."** Evil — the thick-headed one. When the real decisions get made — the city gate, the council — he's got nothing. Verses eight and nine: **"Whoever plots evil will be called a schemer. The scheme of folly is missing-the-mark, and the mocker is detestable to men."** To'evah l'adam — the letz is detestable to people. Not just God. Everyone hates the sneerer.

Saying twenty-three — rescue. Verse ten: **"If you falter in the day of trouble, your strength is small."** Tzar kochecha — your strength is narrow. Then verses eleven and twelve, and these are the ones that get people out of their chairs:

**"Rescue those being led away to death; hold back those staggering toward the slaughter. If you say, 'Look, we didn't know about this' — doesn't He who weighs hearts perceive it? Doesn't He who guards your soul know it? And He'll repay each man according to his deeds."**

Hatzel l'quchim la-mavet. Rescue the ones being taken to death. Not the ones who've asked. The ones being dragged. Chapter seven's ox going to slaughter — here, the book tells you to grab the ox. And then it strikes the excuse dead before you can use it: lo-yadanu zeh — "we didn't know." He who weighs hearts — chapter sixteen, twenty-one — He knows whether you knew. This verse has been read at every abolition meeting, every rescue, every time someone had to decide whether to look. It's the Bible's answer to I didn't want to get involved.

Saying twenty-four — honey and the future. Verses thirteen and fourteen: **"My son, eat honey, for it's good; the honeycomb is sweet to your taste. Know that wisdom is like that to your soul; if you find it, there's a future, and your hope won't be cut off."** Yesh acharit — there's an afterward. The exact phrase from 23:18. Wisdom tastes like honey and has a future. The stranger's honey turns to wormwood — chapter five. This honey stays sweet.

Saying twenty-five — the one to walk away with. Verses fifteen and sixteen: **"Don't lie in wait like a wicked man against the dwelling of the right-standing; don't destroy his resting place. For the right-standing falls seven times and rises again, but the wicked stumble in calamity."**

Sheva yippol tzaddiq va-qam. Seven times the right-standing man falls. Not "might fall." Falls. Seven — the complete number. He falls all the way, as many times as it takes to count as thoroughly fallen. And va-qam — and he gets up. That's the difference. Not that the good man doesn't fall. That he rises. The wicked man yikkash'lu b'ra'ah — stumbles in the trouble and stays there. The falling isn't the tell. The getting up is. Micah 7:8 — "though I fall, I will rise." Psalm 37:24 — "though he fall, he won't be thrown down." Every single person in recovery, every person who's blown it more than once and still shown up the next day — this is your verse. Seven times down. Seven times up. That's not failure. That's what the book calls right-standing.

Saying twenty-six — don't gloat. Verses seventeen and eighteen: **"Don't rejoice when your enemy falls; don't let your heart be glad when he stumbles — or God will see it and be displeased, and turn His anger away from him."** That last clause is sharp: gloat over your enemy and God might stop judging him. Because now you're the problem. Chapter twenty-five will say feed him. Here: at minimum, don't dance.

Saying twenty-seven — the awe verse. Verses twenty-one and twenty-two:

**"My son, be in AWE of God and the king; don't associate with rebels — for their calamity rises suddenly, and who knows the ruin both can bring?"**

Y'ra et-YHWH b'ni va-melech. Revere God, and the king. Now, here's where the awe reading actually does work the fear reading can't: you can't stand in canyon-awe of a human king the way you do of God — but you can respect him. The single verb yare is stretching across two objects, and its core meaning — take seriously, hold in regard — covers both, while "be terrified of" fits neither God (the whole book has said so) nor a legitimate ruler. Peter says it: "honor the emperor; revere God." Two levels of one posture. And the shonim — the rebels, the ones who change, who overthrow — their end comes fast. Don't get in bed with the coup.

The appendix — "these also are from the wise." Verse twenty-three. Verses twenty-three through twenty-five: **"Partiality in judging is not good. Whoever says to the guilty, 'You're innocent' — peoples will curse him, nations denounce him. But those who convict the guilty will have delight, and a good blessing will come on them."** Chapter seventeen, verse fifteen — rigged verdicts in the idolatry drawer. Verse twenty-six: **"He who gives an honest answer kisses the lips."** S'fatayim yishaq — an honest answer is a kiss. Truth is affection. Verses twenty-eight and twenty-nine: **"Don't testify against your neighbor without cause — would you deceive with your lips? Don't say, 'I'll do to him as he did to me; I'll pay him back.'"** Chapter twenty, verse twenty-two. The revenge ledger isn't yours. Verse twenty-seven: **"Prepare your work outside and get your fields ready; afterward, build your house."** Income first, then the house. Order of operations.

And then the last saying, verses thirty through thirty-four, and it's a story: "I passed by the field of a sluggard, by the vineyard of a man lacking heart — and look, it was all overgrown with thorns, the ground covered with nettles, its stone wall broken down. I looked, I took it to heart; I saw, and received training from it."

Laqachti musar — I took coaching from it. From a field. The wise man walks past a wreck and learns from it. He doesn't sneer, he doesn't pity — he gets educated. And here's what he learned — the same four lines as chapter six, verses ten and eleven, word for word: "A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest — and your poverty comes like a highwayman, your want like an armed man."

The teacher walked past a vineyard and heard the ant proverb come true. That's how these sayings work. You hear them, and then one day you walk past the field and see one.

Here's the shape. Don't envy the wicked — three times — his lamp's about to go out and he has no afterward. Build your house with the three tools God built the cosmos with. Rescue the ones being dragged to death, and don't say you didn't know. Wisdom is honey that stays sweet and has a future. The right-standing falls seven times and gets up — the rising is the tell. Don't gloat. Hold God and the king in the regard each deserves. Truth is a kiss. And take coaching from the overgrown field.

Today: if you're down — third time, fifth time, seventh time — the verse already counted you and already wrote your next move. Va-qam. Get up. Then go find someone being dragged, and grab the rope.
proverbs.notes: *Note on translation: 24:21 y'ra et-YHWH b'ni va-melech — "fear thou the LORD and the king" (KJV) — rendered "be in AWE of / revere"; one verb, two objects — the shared sense is regard/reverence, graded (cf. 1 Pet 2:17 phobeisthe ton theon, ton basilea timate); shonim = those who change/rebel (some read "those who differ"). 24:1 ≈ 23:17, 24:19 — triple prohibition on envying the wicked; 24:19 al-titchar = do not get heated (Ps 37:1, 7, 8); ein acharit la-ra = no future for the evil; yid'ach = is snuffed (13:9, 20:20). 24:3 chochmah / t'vunah / da'at — the creation triad of 3:19–20. 24:7 ramot = too high (Ketiv/Qere ra'mot). 24:9 to'evah l'adam = detestable to men. 24:11 hatzel l'quchim la-mavet = rescue those being taken to death; matim la-heregh = staggering to the slaughter (cf. 7:22). 24:12 tochen libbot = weigher of hearts (16:2, 21:2); notzer nafsh'cha = guardian of your soul. 24:14 yesh acharit = there is a future (= 23:18). 24:16 sheva yippol tzaddiq va-qam = seven times the righteous falls and rises — the falling is real and complete (seven), the rising is the distinguishing mark; cf. Ps 37:24, Mic 7:8. 24:18 turning wrath from the enemy when you gloat — the gloater becomes the offender. 24:23 gam-elleh la-chachamim = these also are for/of the wise — appendix marker. 24:26 s'fatayim yishaq = kisses lips — honest answer as affection. 24:29 = 20:22 principle. 24:32 laqachti musar = I took training [from it]. 24:33–34 = 6:10–11 verbatim. Yirah in this chapter: 24:21.*

proverbs.title: PROVERB 25 — Coals on His Head
proverbs.body:
New collection. Verse one tells you who saved it: "These also are proverbs of Solomon, which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied."

Hezekiah — the king who tore down the idols, reopened the temple, and watched God turn back the Assyrian army overnight; Psalm 46, Psalm 76, Isaiah 37. In the middle of that revival, his scribes went into the archives and copied out the old wisdom. Reform always includes recovering the text. What you're about to hear survived because a king thought it was worth the ink.

First handful — God and king. Verse two: **"It is the glory of God to conceal a matter, and the glory of kings to search a matter out."** K'vod Elohim haster davar. God's honor is in the hiding. He keeps things in the dark — not from meanness, from majesty; you don't get to see everything. And the king's honor is in digging. That's the human job: search out what He left buried. Chapter two's silver-mining, from the throne. Verse three: **"As the heavens are high and the earth is deep, so the heart of kings is unsearchable."** Even the king's heart, chapter twenty-one's irrigation ditch, has a floor you can't see.

Verses four and five: **"Remove the dross from silver, and out comes a vessel for the smith. Remove the wicked from the king's presence, and his throne is established in right-standing."** The furnace again — chapter seventeen. You don't fix bad silver by adding. You remove. Same with a court. Verses six and seven: **"Don't exalt yourself in the king's presence or stand in the place of the great; it's better to be told 'come up here' than to be humbled before a noble."** Jesus told this exact parable — take the low seat at the wedding, so the host says "friend, come up higher." Luke 14. He was quoting Hezekiah's scribes. Second handful — the neighbor and the lawsuit. Verse seven's tail and verses eight through ten: **"What your eyes have seen, don't rush to bring to court — for what will you do in the end when your neighbor puts you to shame? Argue your case with your neighbor himself, and don't reveal another's secret — or whoever hears it will shame you, and your bad reputation will never leave."** Riv'cha riv et-re'echa — take the fight to the neighbor, not to the judge. Matthew 18 — go to your brother alone first. And don't win the case by leaking someone's secret; that stain doesn't come out.

Verse seventeen: **"Let your foot be seldom in your neighbor's house, or he'll get his fill of you and hate you."** Hoqar ragl'cha — make your foot rare, precious. Don't wear out your welcome. Verse eighteen: **"Like a club, a sword, and a sharp arrow is a man who testifies falsely against his neighbor."** Three weapons. Verse nineteen: **"Like a bad tooth and a foot out of joint is trusting a treacherous man in the day of trouble."** You lean on him and he gives. You bite down and it hurts. Verse twenty: **"Like one who takes off a garment on a cold day, like vinegar on soda, is one who sings songs to a heavy heart."** Shar ba-shirim al lev-ra. Cheerful songs to a grieving heart — that's taking their coat off in the cold. Don't do it. Sit with them. Chapter fourteen — the heart knows its own bitterness. Don't sing at it.

Third handful — the mouth as fruit and weather. Verse eleven: **"A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in settings of silver."** Davar davur al-ofnav — a word spoken on its wheels, rolling exactly right. Chapter fifteen's word in season. Verse twelve: **"Like a gold ring or an ornament of fine gold is a wise reprover to a listening ear."** Mochiach — the one who corrects you — is jewelry, if you've got the ear. Verse fifteen: **"With patience a ruler can be persuaded, and a soft tongue breaks a bone."** Lashon rakkah tishbor-garem. A soft tongue — chapter fifteen's soft answer — breaks bone. Not a hard tongue. The soft one. Water cuts stone.

Verse thirteen: **"Like the cold of snow at harvest time is a faithful messenger to those who send him; he refreshes his master's soul."** Verse fourteen: **"Like clouds and wind without rain is a man who boasts of a gift he doesn't give."** The whole sky promises and nothing falls. Verse twenty-three: **"The north wind brings rain, and a backbiting tongue, angry looks."** L'shon sater — a tongue of secrets, gossip. It changes the weather in the room. Verse twenty-five: **"Like cold water to a weary soul is good news from a far country."** Chapter fifteen — good news fattens the bones. Here it's water to someone parched. Be the far-country letter to somebody. Verse twenty-six: **"Like a muddied spring and a polluted well is a right-standing man who gives way before the wicked."** Mat — who totters, the mot word. When the good man is shaken, the town's water goes bad. Everybody drinks from him. Fourth handful — honey and self-rule. Verse sixteen: **"Have you found honey? Eat only what you need, or you'll have too much and vomit it."** Verse twenty-seven: **"It's not good to eat too much honey, nor to seek honor upon honor."** Chapter twenty-four said eat honey, it's good. Chapter twenty-five says: only enough. Even the good thing has a dose. And the second half — cheqer k'vodam kavod — hunting glory after glory is too much honey. Praise-seeking is a sugar problem.

Verse twenty-eight, the last line: "Like a city broken into, without walls, is a man who has no rule over his spirit."

Ein ma'tzar l'rucho — no restraint on his spirit. Chapter sixteen, verse thirty-two — ruling your spirit beats taking a city. Here's the negative: the man without self-rule is the taken city. Walls down. Anyone walks in. Every impulse is an invader with the gate open.

And the center — verses twenty-one and twenty-two.

**"If your enemy is hungry, give him bread to eat; if he's thirsty, give him water to drink — for you'll heap burning coals on his head, and God will reward you."**

Paul quotes this word for word in Romans 12 and then adds his own gloss — "don't be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good." Jesus said love your enemies, pray for your persecutors. Both of them are standing on Hezekiah's scribes. Now — the coals. People have read it as revenge in disguise: be nice so he feels terrible. But there's an old Egyptian ritual where a penitent carried a pan of live coals on his head as a sign of repentance — and either way, the point is that your kindness does something to him. It burns. Not his skin — his certainty. He came at you expecting a fight and got a sandwich, and now he has to rethink everything. That's the coals. The bread is disarming. Chapter twenty-four said don't gloat when he falls. Chapter twenty-five says feed him. And the reward isn't his gratitude — va-YHWH y'shallem-lach — God pays it.

Here's the shape. Hezekiah's men copied this out mid-revival. God's glory is in hiding; the king's is in digging. Take the low seat. Take the fight to the neighbor, not the court. Don't sing at a grieving heart. A soft tongue breaks bone. Good news from far away is cold water. Even honey has a dose. The man with no self-rule is a city with the wall down. And feed your enemy — the coals are the rethinking you just forced on him.

Today: find your hungry enemy — the person who's been coming at you — and hand him bread. Actual or otherwise. Then walk away and let the coals do their work. You don't have to watch.
proverbs.notes: *Note on translation: No yirah in this chapter. 25:1 he'tiqu = copied/transcribed — the Hezekian scribal collection (c. 715–686 BCE); cf. 2 Kgs 18–20, 2 Chr 29–32. 25:2 k'vod Elohim haster davar = the glory of God is to hide a matter; chaqor davar = to search out. 25:6–7 → Luke 14:7–11. 25:9 riv'cha riv et-re'echa = plead your case with your neighbor (→ Matt 18:15). 25:11 davar davur al-ofnav — "fitly spoken"; ofnav is obscure — "on its wheels / in its circumstances" — sense: exactly right. 25:12 mochiach = reprover/corrector. 25:15 lashon rakkah tishbor-garem = a soft tongue breaks bone (cf. 15:1). 25:17 hoqar ragl'cha = make your foot rare/precious. 25:20 shar ba-shirim al lev-ra = one singing songs to a bad/heavy heart; first line (garment on a cold day) has textual issues; LXX shorter; MT followed. 25:21–22 quoted verbatim Rom 12:20 (LXX); gechalim atah choteh al-rosho = you heap coals on his head — the Egyptian penitence-ritual reading (coals carried on the head as contrition) is one option; the majority sense is shame/remorse induced by kindness, not covert vengeance; va-YHWH y'shallem-lach = and God will repay you. 25:23 l'shon sater = tongue of secrecy. 25:24 = 21:9 verbatim (quarrelsome woman/roof corner — see 21:9 note on strife, not gender). 25:26 mat = tottering (the mot root). 25:27 cheqer k'vodam kavod — MT difficult; "searching out their glory is glory" — rendered per the honey parallel as excess honor-seeking; alt. emendations exist. 25:28 ein ma'tzar l'rucho = no restraint to his spirit (cf. 16:32).*

proverbs.title: PROVERB 26 — Answer a Fool, Don't Answer a Fool
proverbs.body:
Chapter twenty-six is a rogues' gallery. Four portraits, each one a type you've met. The scribes lined them up so you'd recognize the face before the name.

Portrait one — the fool. Twelve verses, and the word kesil — the dull one — is in almost every one.

Verse one: **"Like snow in summer and rain at harvest, so honor isn't fitting for a fool."** It's not wrong, it's out of season. Snow in July isn't evil; it's ruinous. Honor a fool and you've rained on the harvest. Verse three: **"A whip for the horse, a bridle for the donkey, and a rod for the back of fools."** Shevet — the rod, again. Here it's animal control — whip, bridle, rod — listed with the horse and the donkey. That's not a parenting verse; that's the scribes saying the kesil responds to nothing subtler. It's descriptive of his level, not a command about children. Chapter thirteen's shepherd rod is a different tool in a different hand.

Verses four and five, side by side, on purpose:

**"Don't answer a fool according to his folly, or you'll be like him yourself."**

**"Answer a fool according to his folly, or he'll be wise in his own eyes."**

That's not a scribal error. Hezekiah's men put them next to each other. Proverbs are tools, not laws — and here's the book teaching you that in the plainest way it can: two true sayings that contradict, and you have to know which room you're in. Sometimes engaging the fool drags you to his level — walk away. Sometimes silence lets him think he won — answer. The wisdom isn't in either verse. It's in knowing which one it's time for. That's the whole book in two lines. Anybody who quotes one without the other has missed the point the editors were making. Verse two: **"Like a fluttering sparrow, a darting swallow, a curse without cause doesn't land."** Somebody cursed you for nothing? It won't land. It's a bird with no branch. Verse six: **"Whoever sends a message by a fool cuts off his own feet and drinks violence."** Verse seven: **"Like the legs hanging limp on a lame man is a proverb in the mouth of a fool."** He's got the saying — he just can't walk on it. Verse nine says it again: "Like a thorn branch in the hand of a drunk is a proverb in the mouth of a fool." He's waving the wisdom around and stabbing people with it. You've heard a fool quote Scripture. That's this.

Verse eight: **"Like tying a stone in a sling is giving honor to a fool."** You tied the stone in. It's not going anywhere. Chapter one's honor, wasted. Verse ten: **"Like an archer who wounds everyone is one who hires a fool or hires passersby."** The Hebrew's rough, but the picture holds: hire a fool and everybody gets hit.

Verse eleven: **"Like a dog returning to its vomit is a fool who repeats his folly."** Shoneh b'ivvalto — repeats his folly. Peter quotes this for the apostates in 2 Peter 2. It's the drunk's last line from chapter twenty-three — "I'll go find another" — as a dog. The fool doesn't fail once. He goes back.

And verse twelve, which turns the whole gallery on you: "Do you see a man wise in his own eyes? There's more hope for a fool than for him." After eleven verses on the kesil, the scribes say — there's someone worse. The one who thinks he's not in this chapter. Chapter three, verse seven; chapter twelve, verse fifteen. If you read the first eleven verses nodding at other people, verse twelve is for you.

Portrait two — the sluggard. Verses thirteen through sixteen, and the scribes are laughing.

"The sluggard says, 'There's a lion in the road! A lion in the streets!'" Chapter twenty-two's invented lion, now two lions. The excuse has grown. "As a door turns on its hinge, so the sluggard on his bed." He moves — just not forward. Back and forth, back and forth, same spot. "The sluggard buries his hand in the dish; he's too tired to bring it back to his mouth." Chapter nineteen's line, repeated — he got the hand in. "The sluggard is wiser in his own eyes than seven men who answer sensibly." Seven men. He's outvoted seven to one and he's still right. The sluggard isn't lazy about everything — he's industrious about excuses.

Portrait three — the meddler and the gossip. Verse seventeen: **"Like one who grabs a dog by the ears is a passerby who gets into a quarrel not his own."** You grabbed the dog. Now you can't let go, and you can't hold on. Every fight you inserted yourself into. Verses eighteen and nineteen: **"Like a madman shooting firebrands and arrows is a man who deceives his neighbor and says, 'I was only joking!'"** Ha-lo m'sacheq ani — "wasn't I just playing?" That's the word — sacheq — chapter eight's Wisdom playing before God at creation. Here it's the liar's cover story. "Just kidding" after the arrow's already in somebody.

Verses twenty and twenty-one: **"Without wood a fire goes out, and without a gossip a quarrel dies down. As charcoal to embers and wood to fire, so is a quarrelsome man for kindling strife."** Nirgan — the whisperer, chapter sixteen, eighteen. Every fight has a fuel source. Find the person adding wood. Often the fight doesn't need resolving — it needs starving. Verse twenty-two, chapter eighteen's line again word for word: "The words of a whisperer are like delicacies; they go down to the inner chambers of the belly." Gossip is tasty. That's why the fire never runs out of wood.

Portrait four — the hater with smooth lips. Verse twenty-three: **"Like silver glaze over earthenware are fervent lips with an evil heart."** Kesef sigim — silver dross, the skim off the furnace — painted on a clay pot. Looks like silver. Is a pot. Chapter five's honey lips, chapter seven's smooth talk. Verses twenty-four through twenty-six: **"The one who hates disguises it with his lips, but inside he stores up deceit. When he speaks graciously, don't believe him — for there are seven abominations in his heart. His hatred may be covered with deceit, but his wickedness will be exposed in the assembly."** Sheva to'evot — seven detestable things. Chapter six's seven. Same drawer. And tiggaleh ra'ato b'qahal — it comes out in public. Chapter ten — the twisted way will be known.

Verse twenty-seven: **"Whoever digs a pit falls into it; whoever rolls a stone, it rolls back on him."** The pit-digger. Psalm 7, Psalm 9, Psalm 35, Psalm 57, Proverbs 1, 5, 22. The scribes couldn't finish a chapter on the hater without it.

And verse twenty-eight, the last line: "A lying tongue hates those it crushes, and a flattering mouth works ruin."

L'shon-sheqer yisna dakkav. A lying tongue hates its victims. Read that — the liar doesn't just deceive you; he despises you for being deceived. And peh chalaq — a smooth mouth — ya'aseh midcheh — makes a stumbling, a downfall. Flattery isn't harmless. It's engineering. Someone laying a floor for you to fall through.

Here's the shape. Four portraits. The fool: honor him and it's snow in July; answer him and don't — know which room you're in; he goes back to his vomit — and the one who thinks he's not the fool is worse. The sluggard: two lions now, a door on a hinge, right against seven men. The meddler: grabbed the dog by the ears, "just kidding" after the arrow. The hater: silver dross on a clay pot, seven abominations, and he hates the people he fools.

Today: find the fire in your life that's still going, and stop looking for who started it. Look for who's adding wood. If it's you — put the log down and watch it go out.
proverbs.notes: *Note on translation: No yirah in this chapter. 26:3 shevet l'gev k'silim = a rod for the back of fools — listed with whip and bridle for animals; descriptive of the kesil's level, not a child-discipline text (cf. 10:13, 19:29; contrast 13:24 shepherd's rod). 26:4–5 deliberate juxtaposed contradiction — the editors' lesson that proverbs are situational tools, not universal laws. 26:2 Ketiv lo ("to him"), Qere lo ("not") — "does not land/come" (Qere followed). 26:7 dalyu shoqayim mi-pisseach = legs dangle from the lame. 26:8 k'tzror even b'margemah — "as he that bindeth a stone in a sling" — sense: pointless/self-defeating; alt. "like a bag of gems on a heap of stones." 26:10 MT very difficult (rav m'cholel-kol); rendered per majority "archer/master wounds all." 26:11 shoneh b'ivvalto = repeats his folly → 2 Pet 2:22. 26:12 the self-wise worse than the fool (3:7, 12:15, 28:11). 26:13 = 22:13 (lion doubled: shachal / ari). 26:15 ≈ 19:24. 26:16 mi-shiv'ah m'shivei ta'am = than seven who answer with sense. 26:17 machaziq b'oznei-kelev = grabs a dog by the ears. 26:19 ha-lo m'sacheq ani = "am I not playing?" — the sacheq root of 8:30–31, inverted. 26:20 nirgan = whisperer (16:28, 18:8). 26:22 = 18:8 verbatim. 26:23 kesef sigim = silver of dross; s'fatayim dol'qim — "burning lips" (KJV) — dolqim = fervent/ardent; some emend to chalaqim "smooth" (cf. v. 28). 26:25 sheva to'evot = seven abominations (6:16). 26:27 pit-digger (Ps 7:15, 9:15, 57:6; Prov 1:18, 5:22, 22:14). 26:28 l'shon-sheqer yisna dakkav = a lying tongue hates its crushed ones; peh chalaq ya'aseh midcheh = a smooth mouth makes a downfall.*

proverbs.title: PROVERB 27 — Iron Sharpens Iron
proverbs.body:
Chapter twenty-seven is about friends — the real kind, the kind that hurt you on purpose because they love you — and it ends, strangely, in a sheep pasture. Stay for the pasture. It's the point.

First handful — tomorrow and praise. Verse one: **"Don't boast about tomorrow, for you don't know what a day will bring forth."** Mah-yeled yom — what a day will give birth to. Tomorrow is pregnant and you don't know with what. James 4 — "you don't know what tomorrow will bring; you're a mist." He got it here. Verse two: **"Let another praise you, and not your own mouth; a stranger, and not your own lips."** If it's true, someone else will say it. If only you're saying it, check. Verse twenty-one: **"The crucible for silver and the furnace for gold, and a man is tested by his praise."** Chapter seventeen's furnace — but here the heat is praise. L'fi mahalalo — according to the praise he gets, or according to what he praises. Both readings work. What you praise reveals you; how you handle being praised refines you. Fame is a furnace. Watch what floats.

Verses three and four: **"A stone is heavy and sand is weighty, but a fool's provocation is heavier than both. Wrath is cruel and anger is a flood, but who can stand before jealousy?"** Qin'ah — jealousy, chapter fourteen's bone-rot. Rage is a flood you can see coming. Jealousy just stands there and nobody can face it down.

Second handful — friends and wounds. Verse five: **"Better open correction than hidden love."** Tochachat m'gullah me-ahavah m'suttaret. A rebuke out loud beats love that never says anything. If you love someone and never tell them the hard thing, the love is hidden — from them, and from use.

Verse six: **"Faithful are the wounds of a friend, but the kisses of an enemy are profuse."**

Ne'emanim pitz'ei ohev. The wounds of one who loves you are faithful — the emunah word, God's own reliability word. The friend who hurts you can be trusted. And the enemy's kisses are na'tarot — many, lavish, overflowing. Judas kissed. Chapter twenty-six's silver dross on a clay pot. The one who only ever makes you feel good is not necessarily your friend. The one who told you the thing you didn't want to hear — Psalm 141, "let the righteous strike me, it's a kindness" — that's the faithful wound.

Verse nine: **"Oil and perfume make the heart glad, and the sweetness of a friend comes from his earnest counsel."** Meteq re'a me-atzat-nafesh — the sweetness of a friend is from soul-counsel. Not from agreement. From advice that costs him something to give. Verse ten: **"Don't forsake your friend or your father's friend, and don't go to your brother's house in the day of your disaster — better a neighbor nearby than a brother far away."** Tov shachen qarov me-ach rachoq. Chapter seventeen: a brother is born for adversity. Chapter eighteen: a friend who cleaves closer than a brother. Chapter twenty-seven: the one who's actually there. Proximity is a virtue. Blood far away is theory. The neighbor next door is practice. Keep your father's friends — they knew you before you knew yourself.

Verse fourteen: **"Whoever blesses his neighbor with a loud voice early in the morning — it'll be counted as a curse to him."** Ba-boqer hashkem — at dawn. The scribes are being funny again. The loud early blesser. Even a blessing has a volume and a time.

Third handful — iron and faces. Verse seventeen:

**"Iron sharpens iron, and one man sharpens the face of his friend."**

Barzel b'varzel yachad, v'ish yachad p'nei-re'ehu. You've heard it on a poster. Hear what it means. Iron on iron — that's friction. Sparks. Noise. You don't sharpen a blade by petting it. And the second half isn't "sharpens his friend" — it's the face of his friend. P'nei. The countenance. The expression. A real friend changes how you look — sharpens the edge of your face, wakes you up. That's verse six's wound and verse nine's costly counsel, as metallurgy. Find the iron in your life. Stop only spending time with the people who leave you dull.

Verse nineteen: **"As water reflects the face, so a man's heart reflects the man."** Ha-adam la-adam — the heart of a man to a man. You see your face in still water; you see yourself in another person's heart. That's why friends are mirrors and why the wrong friend shows you a distorted face. Chapter thirteen — walk with the wise and become wise. You're being reflected all day. Pick the water.

Fourth handful — the heart's hunger. Verse seven: **"A full soul tramples honeycomb, but to a hungry soul every bitter thing is sweet."** Satiety makes you kick the honey. Hunger makes you eat the bitter. Both are distortions. Know which one you're in before you judge the meal. Verse twenty: **"Sheol and Abaddon are never satisfied, and the eyes of man are never satisfied."** Lo tisba'nah. The grave never says "enough." Neither do your eyes. That's the diagnosis of every ad you've ever seen. Not hell — the grave, chapter fifteen's word — the appetite that only stops at death. Verse twelve: **"The prudent sees danger and hides; the naive keep going and pay for it."** Chapter twenty-two's line repeated — the peti just walks on. Verse thirteen: **"Take the garment of one who puts up security for a stranger; hold it as collateral for the foreign woman."** The co-signer's cloak — chapter twenty. Sixth time on this. The scribes really didn't want you to co-sign.

Verse eight: **"Like a bird that strays from its nest is a man who strays from his home."** Noded mi-m'qomo — wanders from his place. Chapter eighteen's isolated man. You have a place. Wandering from it isn't freedom; it's a bird with no nest at dusk. Verse eleven: **"Be wise, my son, and make my heart glad, so I can answer whoever reproaches me."** The teacher's own reputation is riding on the student. Verses fifteen and sixteen: **"A continual dripping on a rainy day and a quarrelsome woman are alike; restraining her is like restraining the wind or grasping oil with the right hand."** Chapter nineteen's delef tored — the drip you can't find. And here's the twist — you can't restrain it. Strife in the house isn't managed by clamping. Chapter twenty-six — you starve a fire; you don't grab it. Verse eighteen: **"Whoever tends a fig tree eats its fruit, and whoever guards his master is honored."** Shomer — the keeper, Psalm 121. Tend the tree; guard the man. Same faithfulness, two objects. Verse twenty-two: **"Though you grind a fool in a mortar with a pestle among the grain, his folly won't leave him."** You can pulverize him and the folly stays. Chapter seventeen — a hundred blows. Same lesson: force doesn't reach a fool.

And the pasture — verses twenty-three through twenty-seven.

**"Know well the condition of your flocks; give attention to your herds. For riches don't last forever, and does a crown endure to every generation? When the hay is removed and new growth appears and the grass of the hills is gathered — the lambs will provide your clothing, and the goats the price of a field. There'll be goats' milk enough for your food, food for your household, and life for your servant girls."**

Eight verses of farming at the end of a chapter about friendship. Why? Yadoa teda p'nei tzonecha — know — know knowingly — the faces of your sheep. Same word as verse seventeen.
