You sharpen your friend's face; you know your sheep's faces. Chapter twelve — the good man knows the soul of his animal. This is the scribes saying: real wealth isn't the gold that grows wings — chapter twenty-three — it's the living things you've tended. The flock feeds you every year. The crown doesn't pass to every generation. And look at the end of the list — chayyim l'na'arotecha — life for your servant girls. The household economy goes all the way down. When you tend the flock, the lowest person in the house eats. That's what the scribes wanted the last word of the friendship chapter to be: tend what's alive and everyone gets fed.

Here's the shape. Tomorrow is pregnant and you don't know with what. Let someone else praise you; praise is a furnace. The wounds of a friend are faithful; the enemy's kisses are many. The neighbor who's there beats the brother who isn't. Iron sharpens iron — and it sharpens the face. The grave and your eyes never say "enough." Force never reaches a fool. And know the faces of your sheep — tend what's alive, and the servant girl eats.

Today: thank the friend whose wound was faithful — the one who told you the thing. Then go check the faces of your flock — whatever's alive and depending on you — and make sure the last person in the house is fed.
proverbs.notes: *Note on translation: No yirah in this chapter. 27:1 mah-yeled yom = what a day gives birth to → James 4:13–14. 27:4 qin'ah = jealousy (14:30). 27:5 tochachat m'gullah me-ahavah m'suttaret = open rebuke [is better] than hidden love. 27:6 ne'emanim pitz'ei ohev = faithful are the wounds of a lover/friend; na'tarot = profuse/abundant (hapax; some read "perverse"); cf. Ps 141:5. 27:9 meteq re'a me-atzat-nafesh — MT compressed; "the sweetness of a friend [comes] from counsel of the soul"; LXX differs. 27:10 tov shachen qarov me-ach rachoq = better a near neighbor than a far brother. 27:13 ≈ 20:16. 27:14 ba-boqer hashkem = early in the morning. 27:15 ≈ 19:13 (delef tored); 27:16 tzofneha tzafan-ruach = restraining her is restraining wind; shemen y'mino yiqra — "oil [that] his right hand encounters/grasps" — difficult; sense: ungraspable. 27:17 barzel b'varzel yachad v'ish yachad p'nei-re'ehu = iron with iron sharpens, and a man sharpens the FACE of his friend — p'nei is in the Hebrew and usually dropped in English. 27:19 ka-mayim ha-panim la-panim ken lev-ha-adam la-adam = as water face to face, so the heart of man to man — mirror principle. 27:20 Sheol va'avaddon — "hell and destruction" (KJV) — the grave and ruin (15:11); lo tisba'nah = not satisfied. 27:21 l'fi mahalalo = according to his praise — either received or given; both noted. 27:22 mortar-and-pestle: force cannot extract folly (cf. 17:10). 27:23 yadoa teda p'nei tzonecha = know surely the FACES of your flock — echoes v. 17 p'nei; cf. 12:10. 27:24 nezer = crown/diadem. 27:27 chayyim l'na'arotecha = life for your maidservants — the household economy reaches its lowest member.*

proverbs.title: PROVERB 28 — Bold as a Lion
proverbs.body:
Chapter twenty-eight opens with a man running from nobody.

**"The wicked flee when no one pursues, but the right-standing are bold as a lion."**

Nasu v'ein-rodef rasha. He ran, and there's no pursuer. That's the guilty man's whole life — the footsteps behind him are his own. And the right-standing man — kikfir yivtach — is confident like a young lion. Not aggressive. Unhurried. He's not looking over his shoulder because there's nothing back there. Chapter fourteen — awe is a fortress. Chapter nineteen — awe is a pillow. Here's what it looks like from outside: the lion doesn't check the exits.

First handful — rulers and the poor. This chapter thinks about government more than any since sixteen. Verse two: **"When a land rebels it has many rulers, but with a man of understanding and knowledge it endures."** Coups breed coups. Stability comes from one wise head. Verse three: **"A poor man who oppresses the poor is a driving rain that leaves no food."** Gever rash v'osheq dallim — a poor man crushing the poor. That's the worst version — the one who got a little power and used it on people below him. Rain that destroys the crop instead of feeding it. Verse fifteen: **"Like a roaring lion or a charging bear is a wicked ruler over a helpless people."** Chapter seventeen's bereaved bear, now on the throne. Verse sixteen: **"A ruler who lacks understanding is a great oppressor, but the one who hates unjust gain will prolong his days."**

Verse twelve: **"When the right-standing triumph there's great glory, but when the wicked rise, people hide."** Y'chuppas adam — a person gets searched for — everyone's gone to ground. Verse twenty-eight, the last line, says it again: "When the wicked rise, people hide; when they perish, the right-standing increase." The scribes bookend the chapter with it. You can read a regime by whether the street is full or empty. Chapter eleven — when the right-standing prosper, the city rejoices.

Verse eight: **"Whoever increases his wealth by interest and profit gathers it for one who is kind to the poor."** B'neshech v'tarbit — by biting and increase — the loan-shark words. The usurer is saving up for the generous man; it'll end up in his hands. Chapter thirteen, verse twenty-two. Verse eleven: **"A rich man is wise in his own eyes, but a poor man with understanding sees through him."** Yachq'rennu — searches him out. The poor man with sense can read the rich fool like a book. Verse six: **"Better a poor man who walks in integrity than a rich man whose ways are crooked."** Chapter nineteen, verse one — repeated. Verse twenty-seven: **"Whoever gives to the poor will not lack, but whoever hides his eyes will get many curses."** Ma'lim einav — hides his eyes. The verse doesn't say refuses. It says doesn't look. That's how most people fail the poor — not with a "no," with an averted gaze. Chapter twenty-one — shut your ear and yours gets shut. Here it's the eyes.

Second handful — torah-keepers. The word torah — teaching, instruction, not "law" — shows up four times. Verse four: **"Those who forsake the teaching praise the wicked, but those who keep it fight them."** Yitgaru vam — they contend with them. Keeping the teaching isn't passive. Verse seven: **"A discerning son keeps the teaching, but a companion of gluttons shames his father."** Verse nine: **"Whoever turns his ear from hearing the teaching — even his prayer is detestable."** To'evah — the idolatry drawer, chapter eleven — applied to prayer. Stop your ears to the instruction, and even your praying gets filed with the idols. Chapter fifteen — the sacrifice of the wicked is detestable. Verse five: **"Evil men don't understand justice, but those who seek God understand it all."** Verse eighteen: **"Whoever walks in integrity will be saved, but the one who is crooked in his ways will fall at once."** Verse ten: **"Whoever leads the upright astray on an evil path will fall into his own pit, but the blameless inherit good."** Pit-digger. The scribes never tire of it.

Third handful — the confession. Verse thirteen:

**"Whoever conceals his wrongs won't prosper, but whoever confesses and forsakes them finds compassion."**

M'chasseh f'sha'av — the one who covers his transgressions. Chapter ten said love covers — same verb — but that's covering someone else's wrong. Covering your own is the opposite move. Psalm 32 — "when I kept silent my bones wasted away… then I confessed, and You forgave." David knew exactly this verse's shape. Modeh v'ozev — confesses and abandons. Both. You can confess without abandoning — that's a hobby. You can abandon without confessing — that's pretending it didn't happen. The one who does both — y'rucham — is shown compassion. Racham, the womb-word, God's Exodus 34 word. First John — "if we confess, He is faithful to forgive." Every step-five in every church basement is this verse.

And verse fourteen, right behind it, and read it carefully because the English has damaged it:

**"Happy is the man who is always in dread, but whoever hardens his heart falls into calamity."**

Your Bible says "happy is the man that feareth alway," and you've heard it preached as "fear God constantly." But the word here is not yirah. It's m'fached — pachad — the genuine fear word, the panic word, chapter one's "dread of harm," chapter three's "sudden fear." So what's the verse saying? Look at what it's paired with — verse thirteen's confession, and the hardened heart in the second line. This is the awareness of your own capacity to fall. The man who's "always in dread" is the man who knows he could go back to the vomit, chapter twenty-six, and stays alert. Ashrei — happy — is the person who never stops watching himself. The contrast is maqsheh libbo — the one who hardens his heart, Pharaoh's word, and drops his guard. So: this is not awe of God — that's yirah, and it's not here. It's healthy dread of your own weakness. Anyone in recovery knows the difference. Complacency kills. The scribes said: happy is the one who stays scared of the slip. And the next verse's roaring lion is what happens when nobody's watching the king's heart either.

Fourth handful — the greedy and the hasty. Verse nineteen: **"Whoever works his land will have plenty of bread, but whoever chases fantasies will have plenty of poverty."** Sova-rish — he'll be full of poverty. Chapter twelve, verse eleven. Verse twenty: **"A faithful man abounds with blessings, but whoever hurries to get rich won't go unpunished."** Verse twenty-two: **"A man with an evil eye hurries after wealth and doesn't know that want will come on him."** Ra-ayin — the stingy eye, chapter twenty-three. Verse twenty-five: **"A greedy man stirs up strife, but whoever trusts in God will prosper."** R'chav-nefesh — wide of soul, a soul with a big mouth. Verse twenty-one: **"Showing partiality isn't good — a man will do wrong for a piece of bread."** Verse twenty-four: **"Whoever robs his father or mother and says, 'It's not wrong' — he's a companion of a destroyer."** Ein-pasha — "no transgression." He's told himself it's fine. Chapter twenty-six's "just kidding." Verse seventeen: **"A man burdened with the guilt of blood will flee to the pit; let no one support him."** Ad-bor yanus — he flees to the pit — the grave, not hell. The runner from verse one, arrived.

Verse twenty-three: **"Whoever rebukes a man will afterward find more favor than one who flatters with the tongue."** Acharai — afterward. Not right away. The rebuke stings, and then — later — they thank you. Chapter twenty-seven's faithful wound. Flattery gets the smile now and the contempt later.

And verse twenty-six, the one to leave with:

**"Whoever trusts in his own heart is a fool, but whoever walks in wisdom will be delivered."**

Boteach b'libbo hu k'sil. Trusting your own heart makes you a kesil. The culture says the opposite — "follow your heart." Proverbs, which has spent twenty-eight chapters telling you to guard your heart, chapter four, says: guard it, yes — trust it, no. The heart is the wellspring; it's also deceitful above all things, Jeremiah 17. Verse thirteen said confess; verse fourteen said stay alert; verse twenty-six says don't hand the wheel to the thing you're supposed to be watching. Walk in wisdom — the outside thing, God's thing — and yimmalet, you get out.

Here's the shape. The wicked run from nobody; the right-standing don't check the exits. A poor man crushing the poor is rain that kills the crop. When the wicked rise, the street empties. Stop your ears to the teaching and even your prayer is filed with the idols. Confess and abandon — both — and find the womb-word. Stay in healthy dread of your own slip; the hardened heart falls. And don't trust your own heart — guard it, and walk in something wiser.

Today: find the thing you've been covering — yours, not someone else's. Confess it to one person and leave it. Then stop running. There's nobody behind you but you.
proverbs.notes: *Note on translation: No yirah in this chapter. 28:14 ashrei adam m'fached tamid — "happy is the man that feareth alway" (KJV) — the verb is pachad (dread), NOT yirah; there is no divine object; the antithesis is maqsheh libbo (hardens his heart, Pharaoh's verb, Exod 7:3) — the verse commends vigilant dread of one's own capacity to fall, not fear of God; a false "awe" correction here would be wrong, and the traditional "fear God" reading imports an object that isn't there. Paired deliberately with 28:13. 28:1 nasu v'ein-rodef = they flee with no pursuer; kikfir yivtach = confident as a young lion. 28:3 gever rash — MT "poor man"; some emend to rosh "ruler/head" — MT retained (the poor oppressing the poor). 28:4, 7, 9 torah = teaching/instruction, not "law." 28:8 b'neshech v'tarbit = by bite (interest) and increase — usury vocabulary (Lev 25:36–37). 28:9 to'evah — prayer filed as detestable (15:8, 21:27). 28:11 yachq'rennu = searches him out. 28:12, 28:28 y'chuppas adam = a man is searched for — people go into hiding; bookends. 28:13 m'chasseh f'sha'av = covers his transgressions (contrast 10:12, 17:9 — covering another's); modeh v'ozev = confesses and forsakes; y'rucham = is shown compassion (racham, Exod 34:6) → Ps 32:3–5, 1 John 1:9. 28:17 ad-bor yanus = flees to the pit — the grave, not hell. 28:19 sova-rish = full of poverty. 28:22 ra-ayin = evil of eye (23:6). 28:23 acharai = afterward. 28:24 ein-pasha = "no transgression" — self-justification. 28:25 r'chav-nefesh = wide of soul/appetite. 28:26 boteach b'libbo hu k'sil = one trusting in his own heart is a fool (cf. 4:23 guard vs. trust; Jer 17:9); yimmalet = escapes.*

proverbs.title: PROVERB 29 — Where There Is No Vision
proverbs.body:
Chapter twenty-nine is the last of Solomon's sayings — after this, two outsiders and a mother finish the book. So the scribes close with a summary of everything the collection cared about: rulers, the poor, the fool, the child, the mouth, and the one thing you should be afraid of and the one thing you shouldn't.

**"A man often corrected who stiffens his neck will be broken suddenly, beyond healing."**

Ish tochachot maqsheh-oref. A man of many corrections — he's been told, and told — who hardens his neck. Chapter twenty-eight's hardened heart; here it's the neck. The ox that won't take the yoke. And ein marpe — no healing. The medicine word, chapter three, four, twelve, fifteen, sixteen — withdrawn. The correction was the medicine. He refused every dose. Now there isn't one.

First handful — rulers and the poor. Verse two: **"When the right-standing increase, the people rejoice; when the wicked rule, the people groan."** Chapter twenty-eight — full street, empty street. Here — cheering, groaning. Verse four: **"By justice a king gives a land stability, but one who takes bribes tears it down."** Ish t'rumot — a man of offerings, the temple word, twisted — he treats bribes like sacrifices owed to him. Verse twelve: **"If a ruler listens to lies, all his officials become wicked."** The staff becomes what the boss rewards. Verse fourteen: **"A king who judges the poor faithfully — his throne will be established forever."** L'ad — forever. The permanence of a government is indexed to how it treats the dal, the weak.

Verse seven: **"The right-standing knows the rights of the poor; the wicked doesn't understand such knowledge."** Yodea tzaddiq din dallim. He knows their case — he's read their file. Chapter twelve — knows the soul of his animal. Chapter twenty-seven — knows the faces of his sheep. The right-standing man knows the poor. Not pities. Knows. Verse thirteen: **"The poor man and the oppressor meet together; God gives light to the eyes of both."** Chapter twenty-two, verse two — rich and poor have one Maker. Here: the oppressor and his victim both see by the same sun. God lit both their eyes. Verse twenty-six: **"Many seek a ruler's favor, but justice for a man comes from God."** Don't lobby the governor. Mishpat-ish me-YHWH. The verdict that matters is filed upstairs.

Verse sixteen: **"When the wicked increase, transgression increases, but the right-standing will see their downfall."** Verse twenty-seven: **"An unjust man is detestable to the right-standing, and one whose way is straight is detestable to the wicked."** To'evah both ways. The last line of the whole Solomonic collection is mutual revulsion — the good man and the crooked man each find the other's way unbearable. That's not hatred; it's incompatibility. Chapter twenty-nine wants you to know which side of that you're on before the outsiders start talking.

Second handful — the fool and the angry man. Verse nine: **"If a wise man goes to court with a fool, the fool rages and laughs, and there's no quiet."** V'ragaz v'sachaq — he storms and laughs. There's no nachat — no rest. You can't get a settlement from someone who alternates between fury and mockery. Verse eleven: **"A fool gives full vent to his anger, but a wise man holds it back."** Kol-rucho yotzi — brings out his whole spirit. All of it, every time. The wise man y'shabb'chennah — quiets it — the word for *stilling* a storm. Verse twenty: **"Do you see a man hasty in his words? There's more hope for a fool than for him."** Chapter twenty-six, verse twelve, with speech swapped for self-regard. The fast-talker is beneath the fool. Verse twenty-two: **"An angry man stirs up strife, and a wrathful man is full of transgression."** Ba'al chemah — master of heat. Chapter twenty-two — don't befriend him; you'll catch it.

Verse eight: **"Mockers set a city aflame, but the wise turn away wrath."** Yafichu qiryah — they blow on the city, fan it. The letz is an arsonist with his breath. Chapter twenty-six's man adding wood. And the wise yashivu af — turn back the nostril, chapter fifteen's soft answer at city scale. Verse ten: **"Bloodthirsty men hate the blameless and seek the life of the upright."** Verse twenty-four: **"The partner of a thief hates his own life; he hears the oath and says nothing."** He hears the court's summons and stays silent — Leviticus 5 — and the silence is his confession. Verse six: **"An evil man is snared by his own wrong, but the right-standing sings and rejoices."** Yarun v'sameach — he shouts and is glad. The pit-digger, one more time — and the good man, singing past the pit.

Third handful — children and servants. Verse three: **"A man who loves wisdom makes his father glad, but a companion of prostitutes wastes his wealth."** Verse seventeen: **"Train your son and he'll give you rest; he'll bring delight to your soul."** Yasser bincha vi-nichecha — coach your son and he'll give you rest — nuach, the Sabbath verb. The payoff of musar is the parent gets to rest. Verse twenty-one: **"Whoever pampers his servant from childhood will find him a son in the end."** The Hebrew's disputed — "a son" or "ungrateful" — but the shape is: how you raise the one under you determines what he becomes. Verse nineteen: **"A servant isn't corrected by words alone; he understands but doesn't respond."** Some people understand and don't move. Words aren't reaching them — not because they're stupid; because they've decided not to answer.

And verse fifteen, the last rod verse in the book:

**"The rod and correction give wisdom, but a child left to himself brings shame to his mother."**

Shevet v'tochachat — the rod and correction — yitten chochmah, give wisdom. Hear the pairing. The rod isn't alone. It's with tochachat — the reasoning, the explanation, the feedback. Chapter thirteen's shepherd's rod plus chapter one's correction — the whole musar toolkit. And what's the alternative the verse warns about? Not "the un-hit child." Na'ar m'shullach — a child sent off, let loose, abandoned to himself. The opposite of the rod isn't gentleness. It's neglect. Every rod verse in this book — thirteen, twenty-two, twenty-three, twenty-nine — is aimed at the absent father, not the gentle one. The shepherd who doesn't show up is the villain. And the shame lands on immo — his mother. She's the one who's left holding what the absent shepherd wouldn't. Read all four rod verses together and the book's message is: be there, early, steadily, with the guiding rod and the explaining word — and never let it become the thing that destroys him. Chapter nineteen wrote the guardrail. Chapter three showed you how God does it. That's the whole doctrine. Anyone who pulls one verse out of it to justify a belt has read a quarter of the book.

Fourth handful — the mouth, the poor, the flatterer. Verse five: **"A man who flatters his neighbor spreads a net for his feet."** Machaliq — smooths. Chapter twenty-six's smooth mouth engineering a fall. Verse twenty-three: **"A man's pride brings him low, but the lowly in spirit gains honor."** Sh'fal-ruach yitmoch kavod — the low of spirit grasps honor. Chapter fifteen, sixteen, eighteen, twenty-two — before honor, humility. Fifth time. The scribes are hammering.

And the two famous ones — eighteen and twenty-five.

Verse eighteen: **"Where there is no vision, the people are unrestrained; but happy is the one who keeps the teaching."**

You've seen "where there is no vision, the people perish" on a thousand leadership posters. That's not what it says. Chazon — vision — is a prophetic word: the revelation, the word from God, the thing Samuel received in 1 Samuel 3 when "the word of God was rare." It's not a mission statement. And yippara am — the people don't perish; they go loose, run wild, get unrestrained — same root as chapter one's "you ignored all my advice." No word from God, and everybody does whatever they want. The corrective is the second line, which the poster always cuts: shomer torah ashrehu — happy is the one who keeps the teaching. The verse isn't about corporate strategy. It's about revelation and obedience — when God's word isn't heard, a society throws off its bridle. Fix the poster.

Verse twenty-five: **"The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in God will be set high."**

Cherdat adam. The trembling before people — charad, the quake word, Isaac trembling, the earth shaking. This is a fear word, and I'm rendering it as fear — because this is what the book wants you afraid of being afraid of. Not God. People. What they'll think. What they'll say. Whether they'll approve. That trembling is yitten moqesh — a trap-setter. And the way out isn't more courage — it's boteach ba-YHWH, trusting God, and you get y'suggav — set high, the tower-word from chapter eighteen. Psalm 118:6 — "God is with me; I won't fear — what can man do to me?" Twenty-nine chapters after "the awe of God is the beginning," the book finally names the wrong fear by its real name. Awe of God, up. Dread of people, out. The English gave both the same word and made it impossible to hear the difference. The Hebrew never confused them for a second.

Here's the shape. Stiffen the neck against every correction and the medicine gets withdrawn. A throne lasts as long as it judges the poor faithfully. The fool storms and laughs; the wise man stills the storm. Coach your son and rest. The rod is with correction, and its enemy is the absent father, not the gentle one. "No vision" is no word from God, and the people don't perish — they run wild. And the fear the book wants gone is the trembling before people; the trust it wants is in God, who sets you high.

Today: name the person you've been trembling before — the one whose opinion is running your decisions. Then say Psalm 118:6 out loud. That's the last thing Solomon's collection wanted you to know before the outsiders speak.
proverbs.notes: *Note on translation: No yirah in this chapter. 29:25 cherdat adam yitten moqesh — "the fear of man bringeth a snare" (KJV) — charad/cheradah = trembling/quaking — a genuine dread word, correctly rendered as fear; its object is adam (people), and the antithesis is boteach ba-YHWH (trust in God); this is the book's explicit contrast between the wrong fear (of people) and the right posture toward God (trust/awe) — the distinction the English "fear of the LORD" erases; cf. Ps 118:6, 56:4, 27:1. 29:18 b'ein chazon yippara am — "where there is no vision, the people perish" (KJV) — chazon = prophetic revelation (1 Sam 3:1, Isa 1:1), not strategic vision; yippara = are let loose/unrestrained (para, cf. 1:25, 8:33, 13:18, 15:32), not "perish"; second line shomer torah ashrehu = happy is the keeper of the teaching. 29:1 ish tochachot maqsheh-oref = a man of rebukes stiffening his neck; ein marpe = no healing. 29:4 ish t'rumot = man of offerings (bribes as tribute). 29:6 yarun v'sameach = sings and rejoices. 29:7 yodea tzaddiq din dallim = the righteous knows the case of the poor. 29:8 yafichu qiryah = blow upon/inflame a city. 29:9 v'ragaz v'sachaq = rages and laughs; ein nachat = no rest. 29:11 kol-rucho yotzi = brings out all his spirit; y'shabb'chennah = stills it. 29:13 me'ir einei sh'neihem = gives light to the eyes of both (22:2). 29:15 shevet v'tochachat yitten chochmah = rod AND correction give wisdom — the pairing is in the Hebrew; na'ar m'shullach = a child sent away/let loose — the antithesis of the rod is neglect, not gentleness; mevish immo = shames his mother; see 13:24, 22:15, 23:13–14 and guardrails 17:10, 19:18, 19:25, 22:8, 27:22. 29:17 yasser bincha vi-nichecha = train your son and he will give you rest (nuach). 29:21 manon — hapax; "son/heir" or "ungrateful/grief" — disputed; both noted. 29:23 sh'fal-ruach yitmoch kavod = the low of spirit grasps honor (15:33, 16:19, 18:12, 22:4). 29:24 the heard oath (Lev 5:1). 29:26 mishpat-ish me-YHWH = a man's judgment is from God. 29:27 to'evah both directions — mutual revulsion closes the Solomonic collection.*

proverbs.title: PROVERB 30 — I Am Too Stupid to Be a Man
proverbs.body:
Solomon's done. The king's sayings are over. And the scribes hand the mic to a man nobody's heard of, who opens by saying he's an idiot.

**"The words of Agur son of Jakeh, from Massa. The man's oracle: 'I am weary, O God; I am weary, O God, and worn out.'"**

The Hebrew of that first line is so rough that the old Bibles turned the words into names — "unto Ithiel, even unto Ithiel and Ucal." But l'iti'el can be read as la'iti El — "I am weary, God" — and ukhal as va-ekhel, "and I am spent." So the outsider doesn't open with a proverb. He opens with exhaustion. And then:

**"Surely I am too stupid to be a man; I don't have human understanding. I haven't learned wisdom, and I have no knowledge of the Holy One."**

Ba'ar anochi me-ish. I am more brutish than a man — chapter twelve's ba'ar, the ox-word. Twenty-nine chapters of the wisest man in Israel, and then a foreigner says: I'm dumber than the average person. And the scribes kept it. Because this is what the awe the whole book has been about sounds like from inside a human chest. Psalm 131 — "I don't concern myself with things too great for me." Job, after the whirlwind — "I spoke of things I didn't understand." Agur is the book's Job. The beginning of wisdom is awe, chapter one said; awe feels like this.

Verse four, and he's looking up: "Who has gone up to heaven and come down? Who has gathered the wind in his fists? Who has wrapped the waters in a cloak? Who has established all the ends of the earth? What is his name, and what is his son's name — surely you know!"

Job 38 — "where were you when I laid the foundations?" Chapter eight — Wisdom was there before the first dust. Agur asks the same questions and doesn't claim to have been in the room. Mah-sh'mo u-mah-shem-b'no — what's his name, and his son's name. Christians have heard the Son in that line for two thousand years; the plain sense is Agur demanding the credentials of anyone who claims to know how the world was built. "Tell me his name — you seem so sure." That's the sarcasm of a humble man at a confident one.

Verses five and six: **"Every word of God is refined; He is a shield to those who take refuge in Him. Don't add to His words, or He'll rebuke you and prove you a liar."** Tz'rufah — refined, the furnace-word, chapter seventeen, twenty-seven — God's words have been through the fire. Yours haven't. So al-tosef — don't add. Deuteronomy 4. The man who says he knows nothing is the one qualified to say: stop adding to what God said. Psalm 18:30 — "the word of God is refined; He is a shield." Agur is quoting David back at Solomon's heirs.

The prayer — verses seven through nine. The only prayer in Proverbs.

**"Two things I ask of You; don't refuse me before I die: Remove falsehood and lying far from me. Give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me the bread that is my portion — or I'll be full and deny You and say, 'Who is God?' Or I'll be poor and steal, and profane the name of my God."**

Lechem chuqqi — the bread of my allotment. My ration. That's give us this day our daily bread — Jesus prayed Agur's prayer. And look at the logic: too much, and I'll forget You exist. Too little, and I'll steal and drag Your name through it. He's not asking for comfort. He's asking for the amount that keeps him honest. Chapter fifteen — better a little with awe. Chapter thirty — exactly enough, please, for the sake of my honesty. That's a prayer almost nobody prays and everybody should.

Verse ten and the generation. Verse ten: **"Don't slander a servant to his master, or he'll curse you and you'll pay for it."** Even the slave has a defender. Then verses eleven through fourteen, four lines each beginning dor — "a generation": "A generation that curses its father and doesn't bless its mother. A generation pure in its own eyes, yet not washed of its filth. A generation — how lofty its eyes, how lifted its eyelids! A generation whose teeth are swords and whose jaws are knives, to devour the poor from the earth and the needy from among men." Four generations, or one seen four ways: contempt for parents, self-righteousness, arrogance, and teeth that eat the poor. Agur doesn't finish the sentence — there's no verb, no "will be punished." He just describes the generation and stops. You're supposed to recognize it.

The numerical sayings. This is Agur's signature — chapter six's "six things, seven," now as a style. Verses fifteen and sixteen: **"The leech has two daughters: 'Give! Give!' Three things are never satisfied — four never say 'Enough!': Sheol, the barren womb, the land never satisfied with water, and fire that never says 'Enough!'"** Hav hav — give, give. The leech's daughters. Then the four that never say hon. The grave — chapter twenty-seven, never satisfied. The empty womb — Rachel, Hannah, give me children or I die. Dry ground. Fire. Agur's putting the barren woman's ache next to the grave's, and he's not judging it. He's saying: some hungers are structural. They don't stop. Know which of yours is one.

Verse seventeen: **"The eye that mocks a father and scorns obedience to a mother — the ravens of the valley will pluck it out; the young eagles will eat it."** The eye that looked down on the parents, eaten by birds. Brutal, and it's about the eye — the contempt, the look.

Verses eighteen and nineteen, the best one: "Three things are too wonderful for me — four I don't understand: the way of an eagle in the sky, the way of a serpent on a rock, the way of a ship in the heart of the sea, and the way of a man with a young woman."

Nifl'u mimenni — too wonderful for me — Psalm 139's word, Psalm 131's. Four ways, derech, four paths that leave no trace and can't be explained: the eagle's route through air, the snake's over stone, the ship's through water — and derech gever b'almah, the way of a man with a woman. Agur puts falling in love on the list of things that are past understanding, right next to how an eagle finds its way. Not "how a man conquers." The way. The mystery of it. Song of Songs in one line, from the man who says he's too stupid to be human. He understands exactly one thing: that some things are nifla'ot, and you stand in awe of them instead of explaining them.

Verse twenty, right after, the anti-portrait: "This is the way of the adulteress: she eats and wipes her mouth and says, 'I've done nothing wrong.'" Lo-fa'alti aven. Chapter twenty-eight's "it's not wrong." Same derech word, ruined. The wonder of verse nineteen, reduced to a meal and a napkin.

Verses twenty-one through twenty-three: **"Under three things the earth trembles — under four it can't bear up: a slave who becomes king, a fool who is full of bread, an unloved woman who gets a husband, and a maidservant who displaces her mistress."** Four things out of place — power to the unready, food to the kesil, and two household upheavals. Agur isn't defending the class system. He's saying sudden reversals shake the ground, whoever they happen to.

Verses twenty-four through twenty-eight, the four small and wise: "Four things on earth are small, yet they are exceedingly wise: the ants — a people without strength, yet they store their food in summer; the rock badgers — a people without power, yet they make their homes in the cliffs; the locusts — they have no king, yet all of them march in rank; the lizard — you can catch it in your hands, yet it's in kings' palaces." Am lo-az — a people not strong. Chapter six's ant, now in a set of four. Every one of them is weak and wise, and the wisdom is knowing what you are — the ant stores, the badger hides in rock, the locust moves together, the lizard is in the palace because nobody bothers to stop something that small. Agur, the man who called himself brutish, loves the small wise things. He's one of them.

Verses twenty-nine through thirty-one: **"Three things are stately in their stride — four stately in their walk: the lion, mightiest among beasts, who turns back from nothing; the strutting rooster; the he-goat; and a king with his army around him."** Chapter twenty-eight — bold as a lion. And a rooster. Agur puts the chicken on the list of majestic walkers, on purpose, so you'd laugh and then look at the king differently.

And verses thirty-two and thirty-three, the last: "If you've been foolish in exalting yourself, or if you've been scheming — hand over mouth! For pressing milk produces curd, pressing the nose produces blood, and pressing anger produces strife."

Yad l'feh — hand to mouth. Shut it. The whole chapter's advice, from the man who opened by saying he knew nothing: if you've been lifting yourself up — nasa, the carrying-word — put your hand over your mouth. Chapter seventeen — even a fool who's silent passes for wise. And then the last picture, three pressings with the same word mitz: churn milk, get curd; squeeze a nose, get blood; squeeze af — nostril, anger — get a fight. Stop squeezing. That's how Agur ends. Not with a proverb about God. With: take your hand off the nose.

Here's the shape. The outsider opens exhausted and says he's dumber than a man — and that is the awe the book's been teaching. Who gathered the wind in his fist? Tell me his name — you seem sure. God's words are refined; don't add to them. Give me exactly enough bread to stay honest. Four things never say "enough," and the barren womb is one of them. Four ways too wonderful to understand, and a man with a woman is one of them. Small, weak, and wise. And when you've been puffing yourself up — hand over mouth; stop squeezing the nose.

Today: pray Agur's prayer, out loud — not too much, not too little; the ration that keeps me honest. Then find your one nifla'ot — the thing you can't explain and shouldn't try to — and stand there a minute.
proverbs.notes: *Note on translation: No yirah in this chapter. 30:1 ha-massa — "the prophecy" (KJV) — better read as the toponym Massa (Gen 25:14, an Ishmaelite tribe), making Agur a non-Israelite; l'iti'el l'iti'el v'ukhal — KJV "unto Ithiel, even unto Ithiel and Ucal" (as names) — widely repointed as la'iti El, la'iti El va-ekhel = "I am weary, God, I am weary, God, and spent" — both readings noted; the weariness reading followed. 30:2 ba'ar anochi me-ish = I am more brutish than a man (12:1 ba'ar). 30:3 da'at q'doshim = knowledge of the Holy One (9:10). 30:4 cf. Job 38:4–11, Ps 8, Prov 8:22–31; mah-shem-b'no — the Christological reading is noted as reception history; plain sense = a challenge to anyone claiming cosmic knowledge. 30:5 tz'rufah = refined (Ps 18:30, 12:6); 30:6 al-tosef (Deut 4:2, 12:32). 30:8 lechem chuqqi = bread of my portion/allotment → Matt 6:11 epiousios; mi YHWH = "Who is God?" — the denial of the sated. 30:11–14 dor ×4 — a description without a main verb; rendered as a catalog. 30:15 aluqah = leech; hav hav = give, give. 30:16 Sheol — "the grave" (KJV here, correctly); otzer racham = a closed/barren womb — placed among structural hungers without judgment. 30:17 liqhat-em — "obedience to a mother"; some emend to "the old age of a mother." 30:18–19 nifl'u mimenni = too wonderful for me (Ps 139:6, 131:1); derech gever b'almah = the way of a man with a young woman — almah = young woman of marriageable age (Isa 7:14); the mystery, not conquest, is the subject. 30:20 lo-fa'alti aven = I have done no wrong (cf. 28:24). 30:26 sh'fannim = rock badgers/hyrax (KJV "conies"). 30:28 s'mamit = lizard (KJV "spider") — lizard is the majority modern reading. 30:31 zarzir motnayim — "greyhound" (KJV) — literally "girt of loins"; rooster is the majority reading (LXX alektor); melech alqum immo — "a king against whom there is no rising up" (KJV) or "a king with his army/people with him" — disputed; the latter followed. 30:32 yad l'feh = hand to mouth; nasa = lift up (self-exaltation). 30:33 mitz ×3 = pressing/squeezing; appayim = nostrils/anger — the pun is in the Hebrew.*

proverbs.title: PROVERB 31 — A Woman Who Stands in Awe
proverbs.body:
Thirty chapters. The father spoke, then Solomon's stones, then a new teacher with thirty sayings, then Hezekiah's scribes, then an exhausted outsider who said he was too dumb to be a man. And now — the last two voices in Proverbs are both women. A mother teaching her son. And a portrait of a woman that the book saves for its final word, and gives the whole alphabet to.

Part one — Lemuel's mother. Verse one: **"The words of King Lemuel of Massa, which his mother taught him."**

Asher-yiss'rattu immo. The musar verb — his mother coached him. Same word as every "training" in the book. Chapter one said don't abandon your mother's teaching; chapter six said the same; chapter twenty-three said don't despise her when she's old. Here's what she said.

Verse two: **"What, my son? What, son of my womb? What, son of my vows?"** Mah b'ri — the Aramaic bar, "son" — three times, like a mother who can't quite believe he's grown enough to need this talk. Bar-n'darai — son of my vows. Hannah's language — she promised this boy to God before he was born. That's the voice: a mother who prayed for him and now has to warn him.

Verse three: **"Don't give your strength to women, or your ways to those who destroy kings."** Chapter five, seven — the stranger, now from the mother's mouth. She's not against women; she is one. She's against the kind of entanglement that has ended dynasties, and she's seen it.

Verses four through seven: **"It's not for kings, Lemuel — not for kings to drink wine, nor for rulers to crave strong drink — or they'll drink and forget what's been decreed, and pervert the rights of all the afflicted. Give strong drink to the one who's perishing, and wine to the bitter of soul; let him drink and forget his poverty and remember his misery no more."** Chapter twenty, twenty-three — wine is a mocker. But the mother's angle is different: a king can't drink because a king has to remember the law and judge the poor. And then — a mercy: the dying man, the bitter — let him drink. She's not a prohibitionist. She's saying: the one who holds power over others doesn't get to be numb.

Verses eight and nine, her last words, and they're the reason her son was a king worth remembering:

**"Open your mouth for the mute, for the rights of all who are left desolate. Open your mouth, judge rightly, and defend the rights of the poor and needy."**

P'tach-picha l'illem. Open your mouth for the one who can't speak. Twice — p'tach-picha — open your mouth. Chapter twenty-four — rescue the ones being dragged. Chapter twenty-nine — the throne lasts as long as it judges the poor faithfully. The mother distills the entire political teaching of the book into one instruction: you have a voice; use it for the ones who don't. That's what a mother who made vows over a baby tells him when he's a king.

Part two — the Woman of Strength. Verse ten, and the book starts counting the alphabet.

**"A woman of strength — who can find? Her worth is far beyond rubies."**

Eshet chayil mi yimtza. Three things.

First, the word. Your Bible says "virtuous woman." Chayil is not "virtuous." Chayil is valor. Might. It's what you call a soldier — gibbor chayil, a mighty warrior. It's the word Boaz used for Ruth — "all my people know you are an eshet chayil." A woman of strength. A woman of force. Chapter twelve said she's her husband's crown. The English softened her into a lady with good manners. The Hebrew put her in armor.

Second, the question. Mi yimtza — who can find? Chapter twenty, verse six: **"a faithful man — who can find?"** Same words. The book asked it about a man and left it hanging. Now it asks about a woman — and answers it, for twenty-two verses. The faithful man was rare and undescribed. The woman of strength gets the whole alphabet.

Third, the alphabet. Verse ten starts with aleph. Verse eleven, bet. Verse twelve, gimel. All the way to verse thirty-one, tav. Twenty-two letters, twenty-two verses. Psalm 119 did this — Psalm 111 and 112 did this. It means completeness. A to Z. The scribes are saying: here is a whole life, nothing left out, every letter used. And they gave that structure — the most careful, most complete form they had — to her.

Now — who is she? Two answers, and both are right. One: she's a real woman, and Jewish husbands have sung this passage to their wives every Friday night at the Sabbath table for centuries. Eshet Chayil. It's a love song. Two: she's Lady Wisdom — the woman who built her house in chapter nine, set her table, called from the corners in chapter one and eight — come home. Wisdom stopped being a voice on the street and became a woman at a real table, with real servants and real wool. The book that opened with Wisdom as an idea closes with Wisdom as a person you could marry. Hold both. The scribes meant both.

Let's walk the alphabet.

Bet, verse eleven: **"Her husband's heart trusts in her, and he lacks no gain."** Batach bah lev ba'lah — he trusts her. The book said don't trust your own heart, chapter twenty-eight; trust God, sixteen. Here's the one human it says a heart can rest on. Gimel, verse twelve: **"She does him good and not harm all the days of her life."** Dalet, verse thirteen: **"She seeks out wool and flax and works with willing hands."** B'chefetz kappeha — her palms delight in the work. She's not grinding. She likes it. He, verse fourteen: **"She is like the merchant ships, bringing her food from afar."** Ships. She's commerce. She's logistics.

Vav, verse fifteen: **"She rises while it is still night and gives food to her household, and a portion to her servant girls."** B'od laylah — while it's still night. Psalm 57 — I'll wake the dawn. Psalm 30 — weeping stays the night; joy in the morning. She's up before the sun and she's feeding people. And choq l'na'aroteha — the ration, Agur's word from 30:8, for the servant girls. Chapter twenty-seven — life for the maidservants. She's the shepherd of the flock, and the lowest in the house eats first.

Zayin, verse sixteen: **"She considers a field and buys it; from her earnings she plants a vineyard."** Zam'mah sadeh — she sizes up a field. She's in real estate. She evaluates and buys. This is a woman with capital and judgment about how to use it, three thousand years ago. Chet, verse seventeen: **"She girds her loins with strength and makes her arms strong."** Chag'rah v'oz motneha — she belts herself with power. The warrior word again. T'ammetz z'ro'oteha — she strengthens her arms. This is physical. She lifts.

Tet, verse eighteen: **"She perceives that her merchandise is good; her lamp doesn't go out at night."** Chapter thirteen, twenty, twenty-four — the lamp of the wicked goes out. Hers doesn't. She's the lit lamp, all night. Yod, verse nineteen: **"She puts her hands to the distaff, and her palms grasp the spindle."** Craft. Actual skill in the hands, chapter twenty-two's man who stands before kings.

Kaf, verse twenty: **"She opens her palm to the poor and stretches out her hands to the needy."** Kappah par'sah le-ani. Her palm — same word as verse thirteen's delighting palms and verse nineteen's spinning palms — opened to the poor. The hand that works is the hand that gives. Chapter fourteen, seventeen — grinding the poor insults the Maker. Chapter nineteen — giving to the poor lends to God. Chapter twenty-eight — hiding your eyes brings curses. She doesn't hide her eyes. She opens her palm. The mother said "open your mouth for the mute"; the woman opens her hand for the poor. Two openings. That's the whole ethic of the book, in a mother and a wife.

Lamed, verse twenty-one: **"She isn't afraid of snow for her household, for all of them are clothed in scarlet."** Lo-tira — she does not fear. Real fear, yare in its plain human sense — and she doesn't have it, about winter, because she prepared. The ant, chapter six. Awe of God, yes — verse thirty — but dread of the snow? No. She stocked the closet. Mem, verse twenty-two: **"She makes coverings for herself; her clothing is fine linen and purple."** Shesh v'argaman — linen and purple. Royal cloth. She's not dowdy. She dresses like the queen she is. Nun, verse twenty-three: **"Her husband is known in the gates, when he sits among the elders of the land."** He's respected — because of her. Chapter twelve — a woman of strength is her husband's crown. Here's the crown at the city gate, and everybody knows who made it. Samech, verse twenty-four: **"She makes linen garments and sells them, and supplies sashes to the merchants."** Export. She's got a supply chain.

Ayin, verse twenty-five:

**"Strength and majesty are her clothing, and she laughs at the days to come."**

Oz-v'hadar l'vushah. Strength and majesty — hadar. Those aren't just nice words. Psalm 93 — "God reigns, He is clothed in majesty." Psalm 104 — "You are clothed with splendor and majesty." Oz v'hadar is what God wears. The scribes put God's own wardrobe on a human woman. And then — va-tischaq l'yom acharon — she laughs at the last day. Chapter eight — Wisdom playing before God at creation, m'sacheqet, same root. Chapter twenty-seven — don't boast about tomorrow, you don't know what it'll birth. She's not boasting. She's laughing — because she's prepared for the snow, and because acharit, the future, chapter twenty-three and twenty-four — she has one. That's what awe looks like on a face. Not terror. Laughter at tomorrow.

Pe, verse twenty-six: **"She opens her mouth with wisdom, and the teaching of loyal-love is on her tongue."**

Torat-chesed al-l'shonah. The torah — the instruction — of chesed — loyal-love — is on her tongue. Chapter three — bind loyal-love and truth around your neck. Chapter sixteen — by chesed wrong is covered. She's got it in her mouth. When she talks, what comes out is the teaching of covenant faithfulness. Chapter ten said the mouth is the tell; here's what hers tells. And — pat'chah piha — she opens her mouth. The mother said "open your mouth for the mute." The woman opens hers with wisdom — the same verb, the third opening.

Tzade, verse twenty-seven: **"She watches over the ways of her household and doesn't eat the bread of idleness."** Tzofiyah — she keeps watch — the watchman word, chapter fifteen: "the eyes of God are in every place, keeping watch." She has God's eyes on the house. And lechem atzlut — the bread of sluggardness — she doesn't touch it. The sluggard's whole chapter twenty-six, negated in one line.

Qof, verse twenty-eight: **"Her children rise up and call her happy; her husband also, and he praises her."** Va-y'ash'ruha — they call her ashrei. The Psalm 1 word. The first word of the Psalter. Happy, flourishing, on the right track. Her kids stand up and say it. Resh, verse twenty-nine, and it's his line: "'Many women have done valiantly, but you surpass them all.'" Asu chayil — done chayil, done valor. The husband, at the Sabbath table, to his wife: a lot of women have been strong. You're the strongest.

Shin, verse thirty. This is the one. This is the last yirah in the book, and the whole book has been walking toward it.

**"Charm is deceptive and beauty is a breath — but a woman who stands in AWE of God, she is to be praised."**

Read your Bible's version: "a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised." Now put thirty-one chapters behind it. Chapter one: awe is the beginning of knowledge. Chapter two: awe is what you dig your way to. Chapter three: awe heals your bones. Chapter eight: awe is hating evil and can't sit in a room with pride. Chapter nine: awe is the beginning of wisdom. Chapter ten: awe adds days. Chapter fourteen: awe is a fortress your children inherit, and a fountain. Chapter fifteen: awe is the training, and before honor comes humility. Chapter sixteen: God's loyal-love covers the wrong, and then awe turns you. Chapter nineteen: awe is a pillow — you sleep satisfied. Chapter twenty-two: humility and awe are one thing and they pay life. Chapter twenty-three: stay in awe all day and you'll have a future. And every time the book meant real fear — dread of harm, dread of a king, dread of people, dread of your own slip — it used a different word, and we kept it as fear, so you could hear the difference.

Yir'at-YHWH. Awe. And here she is: the woman who has it. Hi tit'hallal — she — emphatic — she is the one to be praised. Not the charming one. Sheqer ha-chen — charm is a lie. Not the beautiful one. Hevel ha-yofi — beauty is hevel, Ecclesiastes' vapor, Psalm 39's four-fingers-wide breath. Those are real and they're gone by morning. What lasts — what's praiseworthy — is a human being who stands in awe of God. Who's been made small by something great and got bigger for it. Who laughs at tomorrow because she knows Who holds it. Psalm 111 said awe is the beginning of wisdom, and then Psalm 112 painted the man who had it. Proverbs 1:7 said awe is the beginning of knowledge, and then Proverbs 31 painted the woman who has it. Both times — the awe-person turns out to be gracious, generous, unshaken, open-handed to the poor, laughing at the future. That's the portrait. Not a cowering servant. A queen in linen and purple with God's own majesty on her shoulders and a spindle in her hand, up before dawn feeding the maidservants.

If the word had been "fear" all along — if the book were really about being scared of God — this woman would make no sense. She isn't afraid of the snow. She laughs at the last day. Fear doesn't produce her. Awe does. She is the proof, at the end of the book, that the translation was wrong and the Hebrew was right.

Tav, verse thirty-one, the last letter, the last line: "Give her the fruit of her hands, and let her works praise her in the gates."

T'nu-lah mi-p'ri yadeha. Give her — imperative — the fruit of her hands. Chapter twelve, thirteen, eighteen — you eat the fruit of your own mouth, your own deeds. The book's whole justice system — you get what you sowed — ends with a command to make sure she gets hers. And y'hal'luha va-sh'arim ma'aseha — her works praise her in the gates. Not her husband, this time. Not her kids. Her works. The things she did stand up in the public square and testify. Chapter twenty-two, verse twenty-nine — the skilled worker stands before kings. She doesn't even have to show up. Her work stands there for her.

Here's the shape of the last chapter. A mother who made vows over a baby tells the king: don't get numb, and open your mouth for the mute. Then twenty-two letters for a woman of strength — the soldier word — who sizes up fields, belts herself with power, rises in the dark to feed the lowest in the house, opens her palm to the poor, wears God's own strength and majesty, laughs at tomorrow, and speaks the teaching of loyal-love. And at the second-to-last letter, the book's final yirah: charm lies and beauty evaporates, but the one who stands in awe of God — she is to be praised. Give her the fruit of her hands.

And here's the shape of the whole book. It opened with a father at a kitchen table saying awe is where it starts. It closes with a woman at a Sabbath table who is what awe looks like when it grows up. Wisdom shouted on the corner in chapter one; in chapter thirty-one she's home, and the lamp's still lit. Today — and this is the last "today" of the series: find your eshet chayil, or the person in your life who's closest to her — man or woman, wife or mother or friend — the one who's up before dawn feeding people and laughing at the future. Give them the fruit of their hands. Say it out loud. And then go be someone who stands in awe — not afraid, awed — because thirty-one chapters just told you that's the only thing about a human being worth praising when the beauty's gone.

Ashrei. Happy is the one. That's where the Psalms started. That's where Proverbs ends.
proverbs.notes: *Note on translation: 31:30 ishah yir'at-YHWH hi tit'hallal — "a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised" (KJV) — rendered "a woman who stands in AWE of God — SHE is to be praised." This is the final yirah in the book and the closing bookend to 1:7 (reshit da'at) and 9:10 (t'chillat chochmah); the portrait it crowns (vv. 10–31) is incompatible with dread — she lo-tira (does not fear, v. 21, plain human yare) and tischaq l'yom acharon (laughs at the last day, v. 25). Hi is emphatic — "she, and not the charming or beautiful one." Sheqer ha-chen = charm is a lie; hevel ha-yofi = beauty is vapor (Eccl 1:2, Ps 39:5). 31:1 Lemuel melech massa — Massa as toponym (30:1); yiss'rattu immo = his mother trained him (musar verb). 31:2 bar (Aramaic) ×3; bar-n'darai = son of my vows (1 Sam 1:11). 31:8 p'tach-picha l'illem = open your mouth for the mute; b'nei chalof = children of passing/desolation — disputed; "those left desolate" follows the majority. 31:10–31 alphabetic acrostic, aleph→tav (cf. Ps 111, 112, 119; Lam 1–4). 31:10 eshet chayil — "virtuous woman" (KJV) — chayil = strength/valor/military might (Ruth 3:11; gibbor chayil 1 Sam 16:18); mi yimtza = who can find (= 20:6 ish emunim mi yimtza). 31:11 batach bah lev ba'lah = her husband's heart trusts in her (contrast 28:26). 31:13 b'chefetz kappeha = with the delight of her palms. 31:15 b'od laylah = while still night; choq l'na'aroteha = a ration for her maidservants (30:8 chuqqi; 27:27). 31:16 zam'mah sadeh = she considers/plans a field. 31:17 chag'rah v'oz motneha = girds her loins with strength. 31:18 lamp not extinguished (contrast 13:9, 20:20, 24:20). 31:20 kappah par'sah le-ani = spreads her palm to the poor (14:31, 19:17, 28:27). 31:21 lo-tira = does not fear — genuine human fear, absent. 31:22 shesh v'argaman = fine linen and purple — royal. 31:25 oz-v'hadar l'vushah = strength and majesty are her clothing — YHWH's own vesture (Ps 93:1, 104:1, 96:6); tischaq = laughs (8:30–31 m'sacheqet). 31:26 torat-chesed = teaching of loyal-love. 31:27 tzofiyah = keeps watch (15:3 tzofot); lechem atzlut = bread of sluggardness; the resemblance to Greek sophia is coincidental and not claimed. 31:28 va-y'ash'ruha = call her happy (ashrei, Ps 1:1, Prov 3:13). 31:29 asu chayil = have done valiantly. 31:31 t'nu-lah mi-p'ri yadeha = give her from the fruit of her hands; y'hal'luha va-sh'arim ma'aseha = let her works praise her in the gates. Liturgical use: sung at the Friday-night Sabbath table (Eshet Chayil). The Lady-Wisdom-embodied reading (1:20–33, 8, 9:1–6 → 31:10–31) is noted alongside the literal-wife reading. Yirah in this chapter: 31:30 — the last in the book.*
